paragraphs.text: I. SEVEN BOOKS OF QUESTIONS ON THE HEPTATEUCH
BOOK ONE. QUESTIONS ON GENESIS

As I went through the holy Scriptures called canonical, reading them and comparing them with other manuscripts of the Septuagint translation, I decided to put into writing the questions that came to mind, so that they would not slip from memory. Some I would only raise, either noting them briefly or even discussing them at some length; others I would answer as best I could, as someone in a hurry. My aim was not to explain them fully, but to be able to look them over when needed. Then I could be reminded of what still had to be investigated, or else, from what already seemed to have been found, I could be equipped, as far as I was able, both for thinking and for answering. So if anyone does not disdain to read these notes because of their unpolished style, the result of my haste, he should not think he has gained nothing from the questions he finds raised but not solved, for knowing what to ask is no small part of finding. And where he is pleased with a solution, let him not despise the plain wording but rather be glad to have shared in some teaching; for truth is not sought for the sake of argument, but argument for the sake of truth. Leaving aside, then, the matters that can be treated in many ways from the beginning, where God is said to have made heaven and earth, up to the sending of the first two human beings out of paradise, which I have discussed elsewhere as best I could, these are the things that occurred to me as I read and that I wished to commit to writing.

QUESTION 1. How could Cain found a city, since a city is surely established for some multitude of people, while there are said to have been only the two parents and two sons, one of whom was killed by the other, and another son is said to have been born in place of the one killed? Or does the question arise only because readers think that the only people living then were those whom divine Scripture mentions, and do not notice that the two who were created first, and also those they begot, lived so long that they could beget many? For Adam himself did not beget only those whose names we read, since Scripture, speaking of him, concludes by saying that he begot sons and daughters. Therefore, since they lived many more years than the Israelites were in Egypt, who does not see how many people could have been born to fill that city, if the Hebrews were able to multiply as they did in a much shorter time?

It is often asked how, according to the reckoning of his years, Methuselah could have lived after the flood, when everyone except those who entered the ark is said to have perished. But this question was produced by errors in many manuscripts. For not only is the reading different in the Hebrew, but even in the Septuagint translation, in fewer but more accurate manuscripts, Methuselah is found to have died six years before the flood.

It is likewise asked how angels could have lain with the daughters of men, from whom the giants are said to have been born, although a number of manuscripts, both Latin and Greek, have not "angels" but "sons of God." To solve this question, some have held that these were righteous men, who could also be called by the name of angels. For of John, a man, it is written: "Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way." But what is puzzling is either how giants could have been born from human intercourse, or how they could have mingled with women if they were not men but angels. As for the giants, that is, people exceedingly large and strong, I do not think it should surprise us that they could be born from human beings, since some such people are found to have existed even after the flood, and some human bodies of incredible size have appeared in our own times as well, not only of men but also of women. So it is more believable that righteous men, called either angels or sons of God, fell through lust and sinned with women, than that angels, who do not have flesh, could have descended to that sin. And yet so many stories are told by so many people about certain demons who are lewd toward women that it is not easy to reach a definite judgment on this matter.

About Noah's ark it is often asked whether, with the capacity described, it could have held all the animals said to have entered it, together with their food. Origen solves this question by means of the geometric cubit, asserting that Scripture did not say for nothing that Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who loved geometry. He says that a geometric cubit is equal to six of our cubits. If, then, we understand cubits of that size, there is no question that the ark was large enough to hold all those things.

It is likewise asked whether so great an ark could have been built in a hundred years by four men, that is, Noah and his three sons. But if they could not, it would have been no great matter to employ other builders. They, once paid for their work, would not have cared whether Noah was building it wisely or foolishly, and so did not enter it, because they did not believe what he believed.

What does he mean when, speaking of the building of the ark, he says: "You shall make it with a lower part, two-storied and three-storied"? For the lower parts were not going to be two-storied and three-storied. Rather, by this distinction he wanted the whole structure to be understood: it was to have a lower part; it was to have an upper level above the lower, which he called two-storied; and it was to have a level above that, which he called three-storied. For in the first space, that is, in the lower part, the ark had a single deck; in the second space, above the lower one, it was now two-decked; and so in the third, above the second, it was without doubt three-decked.

God said that the animals were not only to live in the ark but also to be fed there, and he commanded Noah to take from every kind of food for himself and for those that were to come in to him. So it is asked how lions or eagles, which usually live on meat, could have been fed there. Were extra animals beyond that number brought in to be food for the others? Or—as is more to be believed—were some foods other than meat provided by that wise man, or shown to him by God, that would also suit the diet of such creatures?

It is written: "Of clean birds and of unclean birds, and of clean cattle and of unclean cattle, and of all creeping things on the earth"—where "clean and unclean" is not added but is understood—and then it continues: "two by two they went in to Noah into the ark, male and female." It is asked why earlier he set the unclean apart as going in two by two, but now says that clean and unclean alike went in two by two. But this refers not to the number of clean or unclean animals but to male and female, because in all of them, whether clean or unclean, there are two, male and female.

Note that what is written, "in which is the spirit of life," is said not only of human beings but also of cattle. This matters because some want to understand the Holy Spirit in the passage where it is written: "And God breathed into his face the spirit of life," which some manuscripts render better as "the breath of life."

On the height of the mountains, all of which the water is written to have exceeded by fifteen cubits: this is raised because of the account of Mount Olympus. For if earth could intrude into the space of that calm upper air, where it is said that no clouds are seen and no winds are felt, why could water not do so as well by rising?

It is written: "And the water was raised up over the earth for a hundred and fifty days." It is asked whether it went on rising until that day, or whether for all those days it stayed at the height to which it had risen, since other translators seem to say this more plainly. For Aquila said "held," and Symmachus "they prevailed," meaning the waters.

It is written that after a hundred and fifty days a wind was brought over the earth, and the water ceased, and the fountains of the deep and the floodgates of heaven were shut, and the rain from heaven was held back. It is asked whether these things happened after the hundred and fifty days, or whether all of them are mentioned by way of recapitulation, having begun to happen after the forty days of rain. On this view, only one thing would belong to the hundred and fifty days: that the water was raised up until then, either from the fountains of the deep once the rain had stopped, or because it stayed at its height while no wind dried it. The other things that are mentioned did not all happen after the hundred and fifty days; rather, all the things are mentioned that began to happen from the end of the forty days.

It is written that the raven was sent out and did not return, and that after it the dove was sent out and did return, because it had not found rest for its feet. The question commonly arises whether the raven died or could somehow have survived. For surely, if there was land where it could rest, the dove too could have found rest for its feet. Hence many conjecture that the raven could have settled on a corpse, something the dove by nature shuns.

It is likewise a question how the dove did not find a place to settle if, as the order of the narrative runs, the mountain peaks had already been laid bare. This question seems to be solvable either by recapitulation, so that things narrated later are understood to have happened earlier, or rather because the peaks had not yet dried out.

What does the Lord mean when he says: "I will not again curse the earth because of the works of men, for the mind of man is bent on evil from youth. I will not again strike all living flesh as I have done"? And then he adds the gifts that, in the abundance of his goodness, he bestows on unworthy human beings. Is the mercy of the New Testament prefigured here, while the earlier punishment belongs to the Old Testament—the one to the severity of the law, the other to the goodness of grace?

What does this mean: "And from the hand of a man's brother I will require the life of man"? Did he want every human being to be understood as the brother of every other, by kinship derived from one origin?

It is asked why, when Ham sinned by offending his father, the curse fell not on him but on his son Canaan. Perhaps it was because it was in some way prophesied that the children of Israel, who would come from the seed of Shem, were to receive the land of Canaan after the Canaanites had been driven out and conquered.

It is asked how it can be said of Nimrod, "He began to be a giant on the earth," when Scripture mentions that giants had been born before. Is it perhaps because, after the flood, the new beginning of the human race being restored is being recounted afresh, and in that new beginning he began to be a giant on the earth? [?]

It is asked what this means: "And to Eber were born two sons; the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided." Perhaps in his days that diversity of languages arose, through which it came about that the nations were divided.

"And all the earth was one speech." How can this be understood, when it was said above that the sons of Noah, or of his sons, were distributed over the earth according to their tribes, nations, and languages—unless by recapitulation he afterward recounts what came before? But the obscurity arises because he has framed these things in such a way of speaking that it seems a narrative of later events is following.

"Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top will reach to heaven." If they believed they could do this, their boldness is seen to be exceedingly foolish, and impious too. And since God's punishment followed for this, so that their languages were divided, it is not absurd to believe that this was what they had in mind.

"Come, let us go down and confuse their language there, so that no one may understand his neighbor's speech." Is the Lord to be understood as having said this to the angels? Or is it to be taken in the same way as what is read at the beginning of the book: "Let us make man in our image and likeness"? For afterward it is said in the singular: "because there the Lord confused the speech of the earth"; just so, there too, after it had been said, "Let us make man in our image," what follows is not "they made" but "God made."

It is written: "And Arphaxad was a hundred and thirty-five years old when he begot Cainan. And Arphaxad lived after he begot Cainan four hundred years," or, as we find in the Greek, three hundred years. It is asked how God could have said to Noah: "And the years of their life shall be a hundred and twenty." For Arphaxad had not yet been born when God said this, nor was he in the ark with his parents. How, then, are the years of human life from that time on understood to have been foretold as a hundred and twenty, when a man is found to have lived more than four hundred years? Perhaps it is understood that God said this to Noah twenty years before the ark began to be built, which is found to have taken a hundred years, when he was already announcing that he would bring the flood. On this view he was not foretelling the span of human life for those who would be born after the flood, but the life of the people he was going to destroy by the flood.

It is asked why it is written, "Shem was the father of all the sons of Eber," when Eber is found to be fifth from Shem son of Noah. Is it because the Hebrews are said to have been named after him? For the line of descent passes through him to Abraham. So it is rightly asked which is more probable: that the Hebrews were named after Eber, as though "Eberites," or after Abraham, as though "Abrahamites."

How are we to understand this: when Terah, Abram's father, was seventy years old, he begot Abram; afterward he settled with all his family in Haran, lived two hundred and five years in Haran, and died; and the Lord said to Abram that he should leave Haran, and he left when Abram was seventy-five years old? The answer is that recapitulation shows that the Lord spoke while Terah was still alive, and that Abram, following the Lord's command, left Haran while his father was alive, at seventy-five years of age, in the hundred and forty-fifth year of his father's life—if the days of his father's life were two hundred and five years. That is why it is written, "The years of Terah's life in Haran were two hundred and five": because it was there that he completed all the years of his whole life. So the question is solved by recapitulation, though otherwise it would remain insoluble. For if we took it that the Lord spoke to Abram, telling him to leave Haran, after Terah's death, Abram could not then still have been seventy-five years old once his father had died. His father had begotten him in the seventieth year of his age, so after his father's death Abram would have been a hundred and thirty-five, if all his father's years were two hundred and five. This recapitulation, then, if it is noticed in the Scriptures, solves many questions that might seem insoluble, as the explanation of earlier questions by means of the same recapitulation has also shown.

Some, however, solve this question in another way. They say that the years of Abram's age are counted from the time he was delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans. He had been thrown into it to be burned because he refused to worship that fire according to the superstition of the Chaldeans. Although his deliverance from it is not read in the Scriptures, it is handed down in Jewish tradition. The question can also be solved like this. When Scripture said, "When Terah was seventy years old, he begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran," it surely did not mean that he begot all three in that same seventieth year of his age; rather, Scripture mentioned the year in which he began to beget. It may be, then, that Abram was born later but was named first because of his preeminence, for which he is highly praised in the Scriptures. In the same way the prophet named the younger first: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated"; and in Chronicles, although Judah was fourth in order of birth, he is mentioned first, the one from whom the Jewish people takes its name, because of the royal tribe. It is all the more convenient when several ways out are found by which difficult questions may be solved.

We should certainly consider Stephen's account of this matter, to see which of these explanations it is less at odds with. It does force us to conclude that God spoke to Abram, telling him to leave his kindred and his father's house, not after Terah's death, as Genesis seems to narrate it. Rather, God spoke to him when he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran but after he had already left the land of the Chaldeans, so that God is understood to have spoken to him on that journey. But what Stephen then goes on to say—"Then Abram left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. And from there, after his father died, he settled him in this land"—causes no small difficulty for this explanation by recapitulation. For it seems that Abram had received the Lord's command, spoken to him on his journey through Mesopotamia after he had left the land of the Chaldeans and while he was going to Haran, and that he obediently carried out this command after his father's death, since it says: "And he settled in Haran. And from there, after his father died, he settled him in this land." So the question remains how this can be true, if he was seventy-five years old when he left Haran, as the text of Genesis plainly says. Perhaps, however, Stephen's words, "Then Abram left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran," are not to be taken as "he left then, after the Lord had spoken to him"—for, as was said above, he was already in Mesopotamia when he heard this from the Lord. Rather, by the very rule of recapitulation, Stephen meant to join the two together and say at once where he left from and where he settled, when he said: "Then Abram left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran." In between, that is, between his departure from the land of the Chaldeans and his settling in Haran, God spoke to him. And as for what Stephen adds next—"And from there, after his father died, he settled him in this land"—we must note that he did not say, "and after his father died, he left Haran," but "from there God settled him in this land." So after living in Haran he was settled in the land of Canaan: he did not leave after his father's death, but was settled in the land of Canaan after his father's death. The order of the words would then be: "He settled in Haran; and from there he settled him in this land after his father died." We would thus understand that Abram was settled or established in the land of Canaan at the time when he received there his grandson, whose entire offspring was to reign there, having been given the inheritance by God's promise. For from Abram himself Ishmael was born of Hagar, and others were born of Keturah, and the inheritance of that land did not belong to them. And from Isaac was born Esau, who was likewise excluded from that inheritance. But all the sons born to Jacob, Isaac's son—that is, his whole offspring—had a share in that inheritance. So Abram was settled and established in that land in this sense, since he lived until Jacob's birth. If this is rightly understood, the question is solved by recapitulation, although the other solutions are not to be despised either.

"So when the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife.'" And it came to pass that as soon as Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. How are we to understand the fact that Abram, on coming into Egypt, wanted to hide that Sarah was his wife, given everything that is written about this matter? Was this fitting for so holy a man, or should it be seen as a lapse in his faith, as some have thought? I have already discussed this matter in my work against Faustus, and the presbyter Jerome has explained it more carefully. Sarah spent some days with the king of Egypt, but it does not follow that she should be believed to have been defiled by lying with him. It was the royal custom to admit his women to himself in turn, and no woman went in to the king until her body had first been carefully prepared for a long time with cleansing lotions and ointments. While this was going on, Pharaoh was struck by the hand of God and returned her untouched to her husband. Her husband had entrusted her to God himself. He kept silent about her being his wife, but he did not lie in saying that she was his sister. In this way he guarded against what he could, as far as a man could, and commended to God what he could not guard against. For if he had left to God even what he himself could guard against, he would have been found not to believe in God but rather to put God to the test.

Before it was destroyed, the land of Sodom and Gomorrah is compared to the paradise of God because it was well watered, and also to the land of Egypt, which the Nile waters. This shows clearly enough, I think, how we ought to understand the paradise that God planted, where he placed Adam. For I do not see what else could be understood by the paradise of God. Some suppose that the fruit-bearing trees in paradise are to be taken as virtues of the soul, and that no bodily paradise was planted on earth with real kinds of trees. If that were so, it certainly would not have been said of this land: "like the paradise of God."

"Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, to the north and the south and the east and the sea, for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring for ever." The question here is how we are to understand that only as much land was promised to Abraham and his offspring as he could survey with his eyes toward the four quarters of the world. After all, how much land can the sight of the bodily eye reach? But there is no question at all if we notice that this was not the only thing promised. It is not said, "I will give you only as much land as you see," but, "I will give you the land that you see." Since land farther away on every side was also being given, this land that he could see was certainly given above all. Then we must pay attention to what follows. So that Abram himself would not think that only the land he could look at or look around at was being promised, God says, "Arise and walk through the land, in its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you." By walking through it, he would come to land that he could not see with his eyes while standing in one place. What is meant here, however, is the land that the first people received, Israel, the offspring of Abraham according to the flesh, and not that wider offspring according to faith. So that this other offspring would not go unmentioned, he was told that it would be like the sand of the sea. That is a hyperbole, to be sure, but it still means a number so great that no one could count it.

"He brought word to Abram, the man from beyond the river." The Greek copies also make it quite clear that Abram was called "the man from beyond the river." The reason he was called this seems to be that he came from Mesopotamia, crossed the river Euphrates and settled in the land of Canaan, and so he was named after the region from which he had come. That is why Joshua son of Nun says to the Israelites: "What? Do you want to serve the gods of your fathers, who are beyond the river?"

On what is written: "Now about sunset a dread fell upon Abram, and behold, a great fear came over him." This question must be dealt with because of those who maintain that such disturbances do not befall the mind of the wise man. Is this something like what Aulus Gellius relates in his books of the Attic Nights? He tells of a certain philosopher who was on board a ship during a great storm at sea. The philosopher was badly shaken, and a dissolute young man noticed it. Once the danger had passed, the young man mocked him for having been so quickly shaken, since he himself had neither feared nor turned pale. The philosopher replied that the young man had not been shaken because he had no reason to fear anything for his own utterly worthless soul, since it was not worth fearing for. The other passengers on the ship who were serious students waited to hear more, and the philosopher brought out a book by Epictetus the Stoic. In it one could read that the Stoics did not hold that no such disturbance befalls the mind of the wise man, as though nothing of the kind ever appeared among their feelings. Rather, they defined it as a disturbance when reason gives way to such movements; when reason does not give way, it is not to be called a disturbance. But I must look into exactly how Aulus Gellius says this and insert it carefully.

"And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land in which you dwell, all the cultivated land, as an eternal possession." The question is how he could call it "eternal," when it was given to the Israelites only for a time. Perhaps it was called eternal with reference to this age. The Greek word aiōnion comes from aiōn, which also means "age," as if one could say "age-long" in Latin. Or are we compelled to understand something here according to the spiritual promise, so that it was called eternal because something eternal is signified by it? Or is this rather an idiom of the Scriptures? They may call something eternal when no end is set to it, or when it is not done in such a way that it will afterward have to be done again, so far as this depends on the care or power of the one who does it. As Horace says: "He will be a slave for ever who does not know how to make do with little." A person cannot be a slave for ever when the very life in which he serves cannot be eternal. I would not cite this testimony if it were not a matter of idiom, for such writers are authorities for us on words, not on things or on doctrines. And if the Scriptures are defended by appeal to their own peculiar expressions, which are called idioms, how much more by appeal to expressions they share with other languages!

The question is how we should take what was said to Abraham about his son: "And kings of nations shall come from him." Since this did not come about in terms of earthly kingdoms, should it be understood as referring to the Church? Or did it also happen literally, through Esau?

"And when he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them, and bowed down to the ground and said: 'Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant.'" The question is this: since there were three men who had appeared to him, why does he address them as one, calling them "Lord" and saying, "Lord, if I have found favor before you"? Did he understand that one of them was the Lord and the others angels? Or did he perceive the Lord in the angels and choose to speak to the Lord rather than to the angels? After all, one of the three stayed behind with Abraham, and the two who were sent to Sodom are addressed by Lot as though he were speaking to the Lord.

"Let water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest under the tree. And I will bring bread, and you shall eat." The question is this: if he understood them to be angels, how could he invite them to such hospitality? It is needed to refresh mortal flesh, not by angels, who are immortal.

"Now Abraham and Sarah were elderly, advanced in days, and the ways of women had ceased for Sarah." The age of the elderly comes before that of the old, although the old are also called elderly. Some physicians claim that an elderly man cannot beget children with an elderly woman, even if she still has her periods. If that is true, we can understand on this basis why Abraham marveled at the promise of a son, and why the apostle presented Abraham's "body as good as dead" as a miracle. "Body as good as dead" is not to be understood as though he could have had no power at all to beget, even if the woman had been young. It means "as good as dead" in the sense that he could no longer beget with a woman of advanced age. That is why he was able to beget children by Keturah, for he found her young in years. For the physicians teach that when a man's body has declined so far that he cannot beget with a woman of advanced [?] age, even though she still has her periods, he can beget with a young girl. Again, a woman of advanced age who still has her periods, but cannot bear children to an elderly man, can bear them to a young one. So this was a miracle because, as we have said, the man's body was as good as dead and the woman too was so far advanced in age that the ways of women had ceased for her. Someone might press the apostle's word "dead" in "body as good as dead." Because he said "dead," one would then have to understand that Abraham no longer even had a soul but was a corpse, which is utterly absurd and false. This, then, is how the question is solved. Otherwise it would rightly trouble us. Abraham was about middle-aged by the standard of how long people lived then, and later he begot children by Keturah. How, then, could the apostle say that his body was as good as dead, and proclaim it a miracle that he begot a son?

"And the Lord said to Abraham: 'Why did Sarah laugh within herself, saying, "Shall I really bear a child? But I have grown old"?'" The question is why the Lord rebukes her, when Abraham also laughed. The answer must be that his laughter came from wonder and joy, but Sarah's from doubt. This could be discerned by him who knows the hearts of men.

"Sarah denied it, saying, 'I did not laugh,' for she was afraid." How did they understand that it was God who was speaking, when Sarah even dared to deny that she had laughed, as though he could be unaware of it? Perhaps Sarah thought they were men, while Abraham understood that it was God. But Abraham himself offered them the acts of hospitality I spoke of above, which could only be necessary for weak flesh. So it would be surprising if he did not at first think that they were men. But perhaps, you will say, he understood that God was speaking because there were certain signs present and visible of divine majesty, just as Scripture testifies that such signs often appeared in men of God. But then the question arises again: if that is so, how did they later know that these had been angels? Perhaps it was because they went up to heaven while Abraham and Sarah watched.

"For I knew that he will command his children and his household after him, and they will keep the ways of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that he has spoken to him." Notice that here the Lord promises Abraham not only rewards but also the obedient righteousness of his children, so that the promised rewards may also be fulfilled in them.

"I will go down, then, and see whether they are doing altogether according to the outcry against them that has come to me; and if not, that I may know." There is no question here if we take these words as those of someone angry and threatening, not of someone uncertain which of two outcomes is more likely. In the Scriptures God speaks to people in a human way, and those who know how to understand his anger know that it involves no disturbance in him. We ourselves often speak in a threatening way like this: "Let's see if I don't do it to you," or "Let's see if I don't do it to him," and "If I can't do it to you, at least I'll know," meaning, "I'll find out for myself whether I can or not." When this is said as a threat rather than out of ignorance, it is clearly the feeling of an angry person. But disturbance does not befall God. This way of speaking is customary among people and suited to human weakness, and God adapts his speech to that weakness.

People often ask about God's saying that he would not destroy Sodom if even ten righteous people were found there. Was this a particular judgment about that city, or should it be understood generally of all places, so that God spares any place where there are even ten righteous people? In this question we are not compelled to apply it to every place. In the case of Sodom it could be said in this way because God knew that there were not even ten there. So Abraham was answered in this way to indicate that even that many could not be found there, and so to emphasize how great their wickedness was. God did not have to spare such wicked people in order not to destroy the righteous along with them, since he could free the righteous from there and then inflict on the ungodly the punishment they deserved. But, as I said, he said, "If I find ten there, I will spare the whole city," to show how wicked that multitude was. It is as if he were saying: "I can certainly avoid destroying the godly with the ungodly without sparing the ungodly on that account, because once the godly have been freed and separated from them I can repay the ungodly as they deserve. Even so, if ten are found there, I will spare it." The point is that not even that many could be found there. There is something similar in Jeremiah, where he says: "Go round the ways of Jerusalem, and look, and search in its streets, and find out whether you will find a man who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to their sins." That is: "Find even one, and I will spare the rest." This is said to emphasize and show that not even one could be found there.

Lot went out to meet the angels and bowed down with his face to the ground, so he seems to have understood that they were angels. But then he invites them to refresh their bodies, which is something mortals need, so he seems to have thought they were men. So the question is solved in the same way as it was solved in the case of the three who came to Abraham: by certain signs it was evident that they were sent by God, yet they were believed to be men. The Letter to the Hebrews says this too when it speaks of the good of hospitality: "For by this some have entertained angels without knowing it."

Lot says to the men of Sodom: "I have two daughters who have not known a man. I will bring them out to you; use them as you please. Only do no wrong to these men." He was willing to prostitute his daughters as a trade-off, so that the men who were his guests would suffer nothing of the kind from the Sodomites. It is right to ask, then, whether such a trade-off in shameful acts or any sins is permissible, so that we may do some evil to keep another person from doing a greater evil. Or should Lot's saying this be put down to his agitation rather than to deliberate judgment? Without doubt, allowing such a trade-off is extremely dangerous. And if it is put down to human agitation, to a mind thrown into turmoil by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated.

"And they struck the men who were at the door of the house with blindness." The Greek has aorasia, which would be better rendered, if one could say it, as "unseeing." This would make people fail to see, not everything, but what they need to see. It is reasonable to wonder how they could grow weary searching for the door if they had been struck with such blindness that they could see nothing at all. In that case they would have been so upset by their misfortune that they would not have kept looking for the door. Those who were looking for Elisha were also struck with this aorasia. Those who walked with the Lord on the road after his resurrection and did not recognize him also had it, although that word is not used there; the thing itself is understood.

"And Lot said to them: 'I pray, Lord, since your servant has found mercy before you, and you have magnified your righteousness which you show to me, that my soul may live: but I cannot be saved in the mountain, lest perhaps evils overtake me and I die.'" Out of agitation and fear he did not trust the Lord himself, whom he recognized in the angels. It was the same agitation that made him speak about prostituting his daughters. This lets us see that what he said about the shameful treatment of his daughters is not to be taken as authoritative, just as his failure to trust God is not to be taken as authoritative either.

"And God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow." Scripture points out that Lot was set free more because of Abraham's merits. From this we understand that Lot was called righteous in a certain sense: chiefly because he worshiped the one true God, and also by comparison with the crimes of the Sodomites, since he lived among them and yet could not be drawn into a life like theirs.

"And Lot went up out of Zoar and dwelt in the mountain." It would be surprising if this were not the same mountain that he climbed of his own accord after refusing to climb it when the Lord urged him to. Either there is no other mountain, or none is apparent.

"For he was afraid to dwell in Zoar." Out of regard for his weakness and fear, the Lord had granted him the city that Lot himself had chosen, and had promised him safety in it, saying that he would spare the city for his sake. Yet even there Lot was afraid. So his faith was not very strong.

"And Abraham said of Sarah his wife: 'She is my sister'; for he was afraid to say, 'She is my wife,' lest the men of the city should kill him because of her." People often ask how, at her age, Abraham could still fear being in danger because of Sarah's beauty. But we should marvel rather at the power of her beauty, which could still inspire love, than regard this as a difficult question.

God said to Abimelech about Sarah: "And I spared you, so that you would not sin against me." He said this when he warned him that the woman he thought was Abraham's sister was Abraham's wife. We should notice and take note that people sin against God when they commit sins that they think should be taken lightly, as mere sins of the flesh. We should also note that when God said to him, "Behold, you shall die," he spoke as though predicting what would certainly happen, when in fact he was saying it as a warning, so that Abimelech would be careful to keep from sin.

It is reasonable to ask why Abraham held a feast neither on the day his son was born nor on the day he was circumcised, but on the day he was weaned. Unless this is referred to some spiritual meaning, the question has no solution. The meaning is that there should be great joy over spiritual maturity when someone has become a new, spiritual person. Such a person is not like those to whom the apostle says: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Even now you are not able, for you are still fleshly."

Sarah said, "Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." The question is why Abraham was saddened, since this was a prophecy, and he surely ought to have understood it better than Sarah. One possible explanation is that Sarah said this by revelation, since it had been revealed to her first, while Abraham, whom the Lord afterward instructed about it, was moved by a father's love for his son. Another is that neither of them knew at first what this meant, and that it was spoken prophetically through Sarah without her knowing it, while she herself was moved by a woman's feelings because of the slave woman's arrogance.

We should note that Ishmael too was called Abraham's offspring by God. This is because of the saying "In Isaac shall your offspring be called," which the apostle teaches us to understand as follows: "It is not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise who are counted as offspring." So this saying properly applies to Isaac, who was not a child of the flesh but a child of the promise, the promise in which all nations are included.

"And Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave them to Hagar; and he put them on her shoulders, and the boy; and he sent her away." People often ask how he could have put on her shoulders a boy who was so big. Ishmael had been circumcised at thirteen, before Isaac was born, when Abraham was ninety-nine, and Isaac was born when his father was a hundred. Ishmael was playing with Isaac when Sarah was provoked, and Isaac was then already a fairly big boy, since he had already been weaned. So Ishmael must have been more than sixteen years old when he was driven out of his father's house with his mother. Even if we take the statement that he played with the little boy as a recapitulation of something that happened before Isaac was weaned, it is still quite absurd to believe that a boy of more than thirteen was put on his mother's shoulders along with a skin and loaves of bread. But the question is easily solved if we do not supply "put" but "gave." For, as it is written, Abraham gave the bread and the skin to the boy's mother, and she put them on her shoulders. And when "and the boy" is added, we supply "gave," referring to the one who had given the bread and the skin, not "put on her shoulders."

"And the water in the skin ran out, and she cast the boy under a fir tree. And she went away and sat down opposite him, about a bowshot away, for she said, 'I will not see the death of my son.' And she sat down opposite him. And the boy cried out and wept. And God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was. And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her: 'What is it, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of your son from the place where he is. Rise, take the boy and hold him by your hand, for I will make him a great nation.'" People often ask how, when the boy was more than fifteen years old, his mother could have cast him under a tree and gone a bowshot away so as not to see him die. The words seem to suggest that she cast down someone she had been carrying, especially since it then says, "The boy wept." But we must understand that he was cast off, not by someone carrying him, but, as happens, in her mind, as one who was about to die. Likewise, the one who wrote, "I am cast out from before your eyes," was not being carried. In everyday speech too, a person is said to be cast off by someone he was with when that person does not want to see him or stay with him. We must also understand something Scripture does not mention: the mother left her son in such a way that the boy did not know where she had gone, and she hid among the woodland bushes so as not to see her son dying of thirst. Is it any wonder that the boy, even at that age, wept when he had not seen his mother for a long time and thought she was lost, in the place where he had been left alone? So when it then says, "Take the boy," it does not mean that she should lift him up from the ground as though he were lying there. It means that she should rejoin him and hold him by the hand as her companion from then on, as he already was. People of any age often do this when they walk together.

"It happened at that time that Abimelech said," and so on. When Abraham made a pact with this Abimelech, and the well he had dug was called the well of the oath, one may ask how this fits with the truth. For Hagar, when she had been driven out of Abraham's house with her son, was wandering, as the text says, near the well of the oath. Yet the well is said to have been made by Abraham a good while afterward, for it was there that Abimelech and Abraham swore their oath, which had certainly not yet happened when Hagar and her son were driven out of Abraham's house. How, then, was she wandering near the well of the oath? Should we understand that Abraham's dealings with Abimelech had already happened and were related later by recapitulation? Or perhaps the man who wrote the book long afterward named the region where the mother wandered with her son after the well of the oath, as if to say: she was wandering in the region where the well of the oath was made. The well was made later than her wandering, but long before the writer's time, and when the book was being written the well was still called by the old name Abraham had given it. But if this is the same well that Hagar saw when her eyes were opened, there is no way left to resolve the question except by recapitulation. Nor should it trouble us that Hagar did not know of a well Abraham had dug, if it was dug before she was driven out. It is quite possible that he dug a well for the sake of his flocks far from the house where he lived with his household, and that she did not know of it.

One may ask how Abraham had planted a field at the well of the oath if, as Stephen says, he had received no inheritance in that land, not even room to set his foot. But we should understand by inheritance the one God was going to give him as his gift, not one bought for a price. And the ground around the well is understood to belong to that purchase agreement in which seven ewe lambs were given, when Abimelech and Abraham also swore oaths to each other.

"And God tempted Abraham." People often ask how this can be true, since James says in his letter that God tempts no one. The answer is that in the idiom of the Scriptures "tempts" is often said for "tests." The temptation James speaks of is understood only as the kind by which a person is entangled in sin. Hence the apostle says, "lest perhaps the tempter has tempted you." Elsewhere, too, it is written, "The Lord your God tempts you, to know whether you love him." This "to know" is also the same kind of idiom, as if it said "to make you know," because the strength of a person's love is hidden even from himself unless it becomes known to him through God's testing.

The voice of the angel from heaven to Abraham: "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God." This question too is resolved by a similar idiom. "Now I know that you fear God" means "now I have made you know." This kind of idiom appears plainly in what follows, where it says, "And Abraham called the name of that place 'The Lord saw,' so that they say today, 'On the mountain the Lord appeared.'" "Saw" is put for "appeared," that is, "saw" for "caused to be seen," signifying the effect by naming the cause, just as cold is called sluggish because it makes people sluggish.

"And you have not spared your beloved son for my sake." Did Abraham refuse to spare his son for the sake of an angel and not for the sake of God? Either the Lord Christ is meant by the name of angel, who is without doubt God and is plainly called by the prophet "the angel of great counsel," or else God was in the angel and the angel was speaking in God's person, as also often happens in the prophets. This seems even clearer in what follows, where we read: "And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By myself I have sworn, says the Lord." For it is not easy to find the Lord Christ calling the Father "Lord" as though he were his own Lord, especially at that time, before he took flesh. With respect to his having taken the form of a servant, it does not seem unfitting to say so; thus, in prophecy of this future event, the psalm says, "The Lord said to me, You are my Son." Yet even in the Gospel itself we do not easily find God the Father called "Lord" by Christ in the sense of being his Lord, although we do find him called "God" in the place where he says, "I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God." As for the text "The Lord said to my Lord," it refers to the one who was speaking, that is, "The Lord said to my Lord," namely the Father to the Son. And "The Lord rained from the Lord" was said by the writer, so that we understand that his Lord rained from his Lord, that is, our Lord from our Lord, the Son from the Father.

Among the sons reported to Abraham as born to his brother is named Kemuel, "father of the Syrians." Those who brought the report could certainly not have reported him as father of the Syrians, for the Syrian people descended from him only long afterward. It was said in the person of the writer, who related these things in writing after all those times, just as we said above about the well of the oath.

"Abraham rose and bowed down to the people of the land." One asks how this fits with the text "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone," since Abraham so honored a certain Gentile people that he even bowed down to them. But note that the same commandment does not say "You shall worship the Lord your God alone," as it does say "and serve him alone," which in Greek is λατρεύσεις. That kind of service is owed only to God. This is why idolaters are condemned: they render to idols the kind of service that is owed to God. Nor should it trouble anyone that elsewhere in Scripture an angel forbids a man to bow down to him and tells him to worship the Lord instead. The angel had appeared in such a form that he could be worshiped in place of God, and so the worshiper had to be corrected.

Abraham orders his servant to put his hand under his thigh and so binds him by oath by the Lord God of heaven and the Lord of the earth. This often troubles the unlearned, who do not notice that here a great prophecy about Christ was given: that the Lord God of heaven and Lord of the earth himself would come in the flesh descended from that thigh.

We should ask how unlawful divinations differ from the request for a sign made by Abraham's servant, when he asked God to show him that the future wife of his master Isaac would be the one who, when he asked her for a drink, would say to him, "Drink, and I will water your camels until they have finished drinking." It is one thing to ask for something wonderful that is a sign by its very wonder; it is another to watch for things that happen in such a way that they are not wonderful at all, but are interpreted by soothsayers with superstitious vanity. But whether one should even dare to ask for something wonderful to show what one wants to know is no small question. It bears on the fact that those who do this wrongly are said to tempt the Lord. For the Lord himself, when he was tempted by the devil, cited the testimony of Scripture: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." It was suggested to him, as to a man, that he should use some sign to find out how great he was, that is, how much power he had with God; and whenever that is done, it is done wrongly. What Gideon did when the danger of battle was at hand is to be distinguished from this, for that was consulting God rather than tempting him. This is also why Ahaz, in Isaiah, is afraid to ask for a sign, lest he seem to tempt God, though the Lord urges him to it through the prophet. He thought, I believe, that the prophet himself was testing whether he remembered the commandment by which we are forbidden to tempt God.

Abraham's servant, relating the instructions his master had given him, says that he told him: "You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live in their land, but you shall go to my father's house and to my tribe and take a wife for my son from there," and so on. If one reads how the instructions were actually given to him, the same meaning is found, but not all the words are the same or spoken in the same way. I thought this worth pointing out because of foolish and ignorant people who slander the evangelists on the ground that they do not agree in every word, though they do not differ at all in the facts and the meaning. Certainly one man wrote this book, and he could have looked back at what he had said above when Abraham gave his instructions and set it down in exactly the same way, if he had judged that to matter. But what the truth of a narrative requires is only truth of facts and meanings, so that the intention which the words are meant to convey is made sufficiently clear.

Where the Latin manuscripts, in the servant's account of his master's instructions, read "then you will be free of my oath" or "of my swearing," the Greek reads "of my curse." For ὅρκος means an oath and ἀρά a curse, from which κατάρατος or ἐπικατάρατος means "cursed." So the question arises how that oath can be understood as a curse, unless it is because whoever acts against an oath is cursed.

"If, then, you will show mercy and justice to my master, tell me." These two things that are constantly set together in the other holy Scriptures, and above all in the Psalms, mercy and justice (for "mercy and truth" amounts to the same thing), have already begun to appear here.

"Here is Rebekah before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the Lord has spoken." One asks when the Lord spoke. Either they knew that Abraham was a prophet and recognized that what he had said was spoken prophetically by the Lord, or else they called the sign that the servant said had been given him a speaking of the Lord, for that pointed more specifically to Rebekah. What Abraham had said was not said about Rebekah but about some woman from his tribe or kindred, and it left both possibilities open, so that the servant would be free of his oath if he did not succeed. Such a thing is certainly not said when something is prophesied, for a prophecy ought to be certain.

As for what Rebekah's brothers said to her as she set out, "You are our sister; become thousands of thousands, and may your offspring possess the cities of their enemies as an inheritance": they were not prophets, nor did they wish this out of such enormous vanity; rather, they could not have been unaware of what God had promised Abraham.

As for the text "And Isaac went out to exercise in the field at midday," those who do not know the Greek word used here think it means bodily exercise. But the Greek has ἀδολεσχῆσαι, and ἀδολεσχεῖν refers to an exercise of the mind. It is often counted as a fault, yet in the usage of the Scriptures it is usually meant in a good sense. For this word some of our translators put "exercise," others "garrulousness," in the sense of wordiness, which in Latin usage is seldom if ever found in a good sense. But, as I said, in the Scriptures it is usually used in a good sense, and it seems to me to mean the state of a mind thinking very intently about something and taking delight in the thinking, unless those who understand these Greek words better take a different view.

"Abraham took another wife, named Keturah." This would be a question if it were a sin, especially among the ancients, who devoted themselves to producing offspring. In this case anything should be suspected of so great a man, especially at that age, rather than incontinence. Why he had sons by her when he had fathered a son by Sarah through a miracle has been discussed above. Some, however, maintain that the gift Abraham received, a kind of renewal of his body for begetting children, lasted a long time, so that he could beget others as well. But it is far more straightforward to say that an older man could beget by a young woman, whereas an older man could not beget by an older woman unless God had worked a miracle there, especially because of Sarah's barrenness as well as her age. Indeed, that someone of more advanced age, and, as Scripture puts it, full of days, can be called senior, that is, πρεσβύτης, can be understood from the fact that Abraham was given this name when he died. So every old man (senex) is also a πρεσβύτης, but not every πρεσβύτης is also an old man, since this is usually the name for the age just below old age and bordering on it, and for that reason in Latin it too took its name from old age, so that a πρεσβύτης is called senior. Among the Greeks, however, and especially in the usage of Scripture, people are called πρεσβύτεροι and νεώτεροι even when young men's ages are being compared, as we say "elder" and "younger." Nevertheless, this act of Abraham's, having sons by Keturah after Sarah's death, should not be taken as if it were done merely out of human custom and the wish to have more offspring. People could take what was done with Hagar in the same way, if the apostle did not point out that those things were done prophetically, so that in both women and their sons an allegorical meaning prefigured the two covenants as a foretelling of things to come. So in this act of Abraham's too something of the sort should be sought. Though it does not come readily to mind, I will offer for now what does occur to me. The gifts that the sons of the concubines received seem to me to signify certain gifts of God, whether in sacraments or in various signs, given also to the carnal people of the Jews and to heretics, as to sons of concubines; whereas the gift of the inheritance, which is love and eternal life, belongs only to Isaac, that is, to the children of the promise.

What is meant by the text "These are the names of the sons of Ishmael according to the names of their generations"? It is not very clear why "according to the names of their generations" was added, since only those he fathered are named, not also those fathered by them. Perhaps "according to the names of their generations" means that the nations descended from them are called by their names. Yet in that case those nations are named after these men, rather than these names being after those nations, since the nations came into existence later. So the idiom should be noted, since it is also said of them afterward: "twelve princes according to their nations."

Scripture says that Rebekah went to inquire of the Lord when the children were leaping in her womb, and one asks where she went. For at that time there were no prophets, nor priests according to the order of the Lord's tabernacle or temple. So where she went is a fair question, unless perhaps it was to the place where Abraham had set up an altar. But how answers were given there Scripture says nothing at all. Was it through some priest? That is hard to believe, since, if there was one, he would surely have been named, and no mention at all is made of any priests there. Or perhaps people went there, laid their desires before God in prayer, and slept in the place so as to be instructed through a dream? Or was Melchizedek still alive, a man of such excellence that some doubt whether he was a man or an angel? Or were there other men of God like him even at that time, through whom God could be consulted? Whichever of these it was, or anything else that I may have overlooked and failed to mention, Scripture cannot lie when it says that Rebekah went to inquire of the Lord and that the Lord answered her.

In the Lord's answer to Rebekah, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be separated from your belly; and one people will overcome the other, and the elder will serve the younger," the spiritual sense is that the carnal members of God's people are signified by the elder son and the spiritual by the younger, because, as the apostle says, the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and afterward the spiritual. It is also commonly understood in this way: Esau prefigures the elder people of God, that is, Israel according to the flesh, while Jacob prefigures Jacob himself according to his spiritual offspring. But this answer is also found fulfilled in the literal history, when the people of Israel, that is, Jacob the younger son, overcame the Edomites, that is, the nation descended from Esau, and made them tributary under David. They remained so for a long time, until the reign of the king under whom the Edomites rebelled and threw the yoke of the Israelites off their necks, according to the prophecy of Isaac himself when he blessed the younger in place of the elder. For he said this to the elder when he afterward blessed him too.

"But Jacob was a simple man, dwelling at home." What is called ἄπλαστος in Greek the Latin translators rendered as "simple"; but ἄπλαστος properly means "not feigned." So some Latin translators rendered it "without guile," saying: "Jacob was without guile, dwelling at home." This raises a great question: how did someone who was without guile obtain the blessing through guile? But Scripture put this first in order to signify something great. Here above all we are compelled to look for a spiritual meaning in that passage, since the one who practiced guile was without guile. What we think of it we have said fully enough in a sermon preached to the people.

Regarding the text "There was a famine in the land, besides the famine that had occurred earlier in the time of Abraham; and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar," one asks when this happened. Was it after Esau sold his birthright for a dish of lentils, since this account begins after that one? Or, as often happens, did the narrator go back to these events by recapitulation, after he had gone on about Isaac's sons as far as the episode of the lentils? What raises the question is that this is the same Abimelech who had desired Sarah, for his friend who escorted the bride and the commander of his army, who were mentioned there, are mentioned here too. Could they still have been alive? When he became Abraham's friend, Isaac had not yet been born, though he had already been promised. Let us suppose that happened a year before Isaac was born. Then Isaac had his sons when he was sixty, and they were young men when Esau sold his birthright; let us suppose they were about twenty. That makes Isaac about eighty at the time of his sons' transaction. Let us take it that Abimelech was a young man when he desired Isaac's mother and became Abraham's friend. He could then have been about a hundred if Isaac went to that land, driven by famine, after his sons' transaction. So nothing here forces us to think that Isaac's journey to Gerar is narrated by recapitulation. But since Scripture says that Isaac was there a long time, dug wells, quarreled over them and grew rich, it would be surprising if these things were not being recounted by recapitulation, having been passed over earlier so that the narrative about his sons could first reach the episode of the lentils.

In the text of Scripture about Isaac, "And the Lord blessed him, and the man was exalted, and he went on growing greater until he became very great," what follows shows that this was said with respect to earthly prosperity. For the narrator goes on to describe the very riches by which he became great, and Abimelech, moved by this, was afraid to have him there, lest his power should become a threat to himself. So although these things signify something spiritual, still, with respect to what actually happened, "the Lord blessed him" was put first so that with sound faith we may understand that even these temporal gifts cannot be given by anyone but the one God, nor should they be hoped for from anyone else, even when weaker people seek them. Thus whoever is faithful in the least things is faithful also in great ones, and whoever has been found faithful in unrighteous mammon deserves to receive the true riches as well, as the Lord says in the Gospel. Similar things were said of Abraham too, that God's gifts came to him. So this narrative does much to build up sound faith in those who understand it devoutly, even if no allegorical meaning could be drawn out of these matters.

"Let there be a curse between us and you," that is, an oath that binds by curses which are to fall on whoever breaks it. In light of this we should consider what Abraham's servant also mentioned when he gave his account to those from whom he received a wife for his master Isaac.

What does it mean that when Isaac's servants came and said, "We dug a well and found no water," Isaac named that well "Oath"? Although it really happened, must it not without doubt be taken to have some spiritual meaning, since by the letter there is no sense at all in naming the well "Oath" because no water was found there? Other translators, it is true, say instead that Isaac's servants reported that water had been found. But even so, why was it called "Oath" when no oath had been sworn there?

So great a patriarch as Isaac, before he dies, asks his son for game and the kind of food he loves as a great favor and promises him a blessing. We think this is by no means without prophetic meaning, especially since his wife hurries to have the younger son, whom she loved, receive that blessing. And the rest of the same narrative strongly prompts us to understand, or to search out, greater things.

Where the Latin manuscripts read, "And Isaac was afraid with a very great fear," the Greek read, "And Isaac was struck with a very great ecstasy" (exestē de Isaak ekstasin megalēn sphodra). This conveys a disturbance so great that a kind of withdrawal of the mind followed, which is what is properly called ecstasy. Since this usually happens when great things are revealed, we should understand that in this ecstasy Isaac received a spiritual warning to confirm his blessing on his younger son, with whom he might rather have been angry for deceiving his father. So too with Adam: when the great sacrament that the apostle says concerns Christ and the church is prophesied, "The two shall be one flesh," we are told that an ecstasy came first.

How were Esau's words, in which he threatened to kill his brother, reported or passed on to Rebecca, when Scripture says that he said this in his own thoughts? The only explanation is that we are given to understand from this that everything was revealed to them by God. Hence it belongs to a great mystery that she wanted her younger son to be blessed in place of the elder.

Where the Latin manuscripts have Isaac say to his son, "Go into Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife for yourself from there," the Greek manuscripts do not have "go" but "flee," that is, apodrathi. From this we understand that Isaac too knew what his son Esau had said in his thoughts about his brother.

"And Jacob rose from his sleep and said, 'The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.' And he was afraid and said, 'How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.'" These words belong to prophecy, because the tabernacle that the Lord set up among men in his first people was to be there. And we ought to understand "the gate of heaven" as meaning that from there believers would have access to take possession of the kingdom of heaven.

When Jacob set up the stone he had placed under his head, made it a pillar, and poured oil over it, he did nothing resembling idolatry. For neither then nor afterward did he visit the stone to worship it or to sacrifice to it. Rather, it was set up as a sign within a very clear prophecy, one that concerns anointing; and it is from chrism that the name of Christ comes.

"And Jacob called the name of that place 'House of God'; and Ulammaus was formerly the name of the city." If we understand that he slept beside the city, there is no problem; but if he slept in the city, it seems strange how he could have set up that pillar. As for the vow he made, if he should prosper going and returning, and his promise of tithes to the house of God that was to be in that place, this is a prophecy of the house of God. There, too, on his return he sacrificed to God, calling that stone not God but the house of God, that is, because the house of God was to be in that place.

Rachel came with her father's sheep, and Scripture says that when Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well. Here we should note that Scripture leaves out something we are meant to understand, rather than raise any problem. For we understand that the men Jacob first spoke with were asked who the woman coming with the sheep was, and they told him she was Laban's daughter, whom Jacob certainly did not know. Scripture passes over his question and their answer, but intends us to understand them.

As for what is written, "And Jacob kissed Rachel, and cried out with his voice and wept. And he told her that he was her father's brother and that he was Rebecca's son": it was very much the custom, in the simplicity of the ancients, for kinsmen to kiss their kinswomen, and this is still done in many places today. But one may ask how she accepted a kiss from a stranger, if Jacob only afterward told her of their kinship. We must therefore understand either that he, having already heard who she was, confidently went to kiss her, or that Scripture afterward narrates by recapitulation what had happened first, namely that Jacob told her who he was. In the same way it is told afterward how God laid out paradise, when it had already been said that God planted paradise and placed there the man he had formed; and there are many other things understood to be told by recapitulation.

As for what is written, "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like a few days, because he loved her," we must ask why this was said, since even a short time usually seems long to lovers. It was said, then, with regard to the toil of his service, which love made easy and light.

If the account of this matter is read carelessly, one will think that after Jacob married Leah he then served another seven years for Rachel and only then married her. But this is not so. Laban said to him, "Complete this one's seven, and I will give you this one too, for the work you will do for me for another seven years." When he says, "Complete this one's seven," this refers to the wedding celebration, which was customarily held over seven days. So this is what he means: "Fulfill the seven days of the wedding belonging to the woman you have married, and I will give you this one too, in return for working for me another seven years." Then follows: "And Jacob did so, and fulfilled her seven"—that is, the seven days of Leah's wedding—"and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife. And Laban gave his daughter Rachel his maidservant Bilhah as her maidservant. And he went in to Rachel; and he loved Rachel more than Leah; and he served him another seven years." It is clear, then, that after he married Rachel he served another seven years for her. For it would have been too harsh and very unjust to put off a man who had been deceived for another seven years and only then give him the woman he ought to have given him in the first place. That weddings were customarily celebrated for seven days is also shown by the book of Judges in the case of Samson, when he held a feast for seven days. And Scripture adds that young men were accustomed to do so; and he did this on account of his wedding.

It is not easy to tell which women Scripture calls concubines and which wives, since Hagar was called a wife and afterward is called a concubine, and so too Keturah and the maidservants whom Rachel and Leah gave to their husband. Perhaps in the usage of Scripture every concubine is called a wife, but not every wife a concubine. That is, Sarah, Rebecca, Leah and Rachel cannot be called concubines, whereas Hagar, Keturah, Bilhah and Zilpah are both wives and concubines.

Where the Latin manuscripts have Leah say, when a son was born to her by Zilpah, "I have become blessed" or "happy," the Greek have en tychē [?], which rather means good fortune. This seems to give an opening to those who do not understand well, as if those people worshiped Fortune, or as if the authority of the divine Scriptures had admitted this word into use. But either "fortune" is to be understood of those things that seem to happen by chance—not because it is some divine power, since even the things that seem to happen by chance are given by God through hidden causes. That is why we have words that no one can remove from ordinary speech, namely forte, fortasse, forsitan ("perhaps") and fortuito ("by chance"); and the same seems to echo in Greek, in their word tacha ("perhaps"), as if derived from tychē. Or else Leah spoke this way because she still kept the custom of the Gentiles. For it was not Jacob who said this, so that one might suppose the word was given authority by it.

When Jacob says, "And the Lord has blessed you at my foot," the sense of the Scriptures must be carefully observed and noted, so that no one who speaks this way should seem to be practicing augury. For what he added makes a great difference: "The Lord has blessed you at my foot." He meant it to be understood as "at my coming," and was thereby giving thanks to God.

Concerning what Jacob did when he peeled rods, stripping off the green so that the white would show in a varied pattern, and so the offspring of the flocks would be varied at conception, since the mothers drank at the water troughs and, having seen the rods, conceived that variety: many similar things are said to happen in the offspring of animals. It is even reported of a woman, and found written in the books of Hippocrates, that most ancient and most skilled physician, that she was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery because she had given birth to a very beautiful boy unlike both his parents and their family. But the physician I mentioned solved the problem by telling them to look and see whether there might be some such picture in the bedroom. When one was found, the woman was freed from suspicion. But as regards what Jacob did, what use the joining together of rods from three different trees could have had for multiplying spotted sheep is not at all apparent. Nor does it make any difference to this purpose whether the rods were made varied from a single kind of wood or there were several kinds of wood, since only the variegation of the wood was needed. This, then, compels us to look for a prophecy and some figurative meaning in the matter, which Jacob undoubtedly did as a prophet; and for that reason he is not to be accused of fraud either. For we must believe that he did nothing of the kind except by spiritual revelation. As for what pertained to justice, as other translators tell it more plainly, he did not put the rods at the second conception of the sheep. The Septuagint says this all the more obscurely for saying it so briefly: "for when they had given birth, he did not put them." This is understood to mean "when they had first given birth," so that we understand he no longer used to put them when the sheep were about to give birth a second time, lest he take all the offspring for himself, which would have been unjust.

Laban says, "Why have you stolen my gods?" This is perhaps the source of his having said that he practiced augury, and of his daughter's having named good fortune. And it should be noted that here, for the first time since the beginning of the book, we find gods of the Gentiles; for in the earlier passages of Scripture they named God.

What does Jacob mean when he says to his father-in-law, "And you cheated me of my wages by ten ewe lambs"? Scripture does not tell when and how this happened, but it certainly happened as he recounts. For he said this to his wives as well, when he called them into the field. Complaining about their father, he said among other things, "And he changed my wages by ten lambs." We understand, then, that at each lambing season, when Laban saw that the offspring born were of the kind it had been agreed would belong to Jacob, he fraudulently changed the agreement and said that at the next lambing Jacob would have sheep of other colors as his wages. Then Jacob would not place the variegated rods beneath them, and the lambs were born not spotted but of one color, which Jacob took under the new agreement. When Laban saw this, he again fraudulently changed the agreement, so that the spotted ones would belong to Jacob; then, by placing those rods beneath them, spotted lambs were born. So when Jacob said to his wives, "He changed my wages by ten lambs," and later to Laban himself, "You cheated me of my wages by ten ewe lambs," he did not say it as though the fraud had succeeded for his father-in-law; indeed, he said that God had stood by him against Laban so that it would not succeed. Rather, he put ten lambs or ten ewe lambs for ten seasons in which the sheep he was pasturing gave birth over six years. For they gave birth twice a year. It had happened that in the first year, when they made their agreement and he took on the pasturing of the sheep on the terms of this wage, they gave birth only once, at the end of the year, since when he took them on they had already given birth once. And again in the sixth year, that is, the last, after they had given birth once, the need to depart arose and he left before they gave birth again. Thus, since the first and last years had two lambings under him, that is, one each, and the four middle years two each, they make ten in all. Nor is it surprising that he called these ten seasons by the name of the lambs born in them, just as someone might say, "over so many vintages" or "so many harvests," meaning a number of years. Hence someone says, "after some ears of grain," meaning harvests by ears of grain and years by harvests. And the fertility of the flocks of that region, like those of Italy, is said to be so great that they give birth twice a year.

"And Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar." We must carefully observe how they set up such pillars as witness to some matter—not to worship them as gods, but so that they might signify something to them.

Laban and Jacob named the heap of stones they had set up between them with some difference, Laban calling it "heap of testimony" and Jacob "heap witness." Those who know both Syriac and Hebrew report that this happened because of the peculiarities of each language. For it often happens that what one language says in a single word is not said in one word in another, and a thing is named by something close in meaning. For afterward it is said, "For this reason its name was called 'The heap bears witness.'" This was placed in between, so as to suit both the one who had said "heap of testimony" and the one who had said "heap witness."

What does Laban mean when he says to Jacob, "This heap bears witness and this pillar bears witness; for this reason its name is called 'The heap bears witness,' and the vision, which he said, 'Let God watch between me and you'"? Perhaps the order runs: "And the vision which God spoke, let it watch between me and you"; for God had told him in a vision not to harm Jacob.

What does Laban mean when he says next, "See, no one is with us"? Perhaps no outsider; or else it is on account of God's witness, whom they ought to regard in such a way as if there were no one with them whom they could add to his testimony.

"And Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac." "By the fear," that is, with which he feared God—a fear he also commended earlier when he said, "the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of my father Isaac."
There is no doubt that the camp of God that Jacob saw on his journey was a multitude of angels; for in the Scriptures this is called the host of heaven.

When Jacob was told that his brother was coming to meet him with four hundred men, he was indeed troubled and confused in mind, because he was very afraid; and as seemed best to a man in distress, he divided his company into two camps. Here one may ask how he had faith in God's promises, since he said, "If my brother comes to the first camp and destroys it, the second will be saved." But this too could have happened—that Esau would overthrow his camp—and yet God would stand by him after that affliction, deliver him and fulfill what he had promised.
