And this example should teach us that, although we believe in God, we should still do what men ought to do to protect their safety, so that we do not appear to tempt God by neglecting it. Indeed, we should consider the words Jacob speaks after this: "God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, Lord, who said to me, 'Return to the land of your birth, and I will do you good': you are sufficient for me, out of all the justice and all the truth you have shown your servant. For with this staff of mine I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Rescue me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I fear him, lest he come and strike me down, and the mothers with the children. But you said, 'I will do you good, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for its multitude.'" In these words both human weakness and devout faith are plain enough to see.

Where the Latin manuscripts say of Jacob, "For he said, 'I will appease his face with the gifts going before him,'" we understand that the writer of the book, who in his narrative says of Jacob, "For he said, 'I will appease his face,'" reports Jacob's words up to this point, and that the rest, "with the gifts going before him," he added himself, as if Jacob were saying, "I will appease my brother's face with the gifts that were going before Jacob." So the order of Jacob's words is: "I will appease his face, and after this I will see his face; perhaps he will receive my face." But the writer's words, "with the gifts going before him," have been inserted between.

That Jacob desires to be blessed by the angel he overcame in wrestling is a great prophecy of Christ. For this very fact signals that something mystical is meant, since every man wishes to be blessed by one greater than himself. How, then, did he wish to be blessed by one he had beaten in wrestling? Jacob prevailed over Christ, or rather seemed to prevail, through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified; and yet he is blessed by him in those Israelites who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said, "For I too am an Israelite, of the race of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin." So one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed: lame in the breadth of his thigh, as in the multitude of his race, of whom it was said, "And they limped from their paths"; but blessed in those of whom it was said, "A remnant has been saved by the election of grace."

What does Jacob mean when he says to his brother, "For this reason I have seen your face, as when one sees the face of God"? Did the words of a frightened and troubled mind burst out into such flattery? Or can they be taken in some sense that is without sin? Perhaps, since the gods of the Gentiles, which are demons, are also called gods, these words should not be held against the man of God. For he did not say, "as if I were seeing the face of God," but "as when one sees"; and who that "one" may signify is uncertain. And perhaps his words were tempered so that Esau himself would gratefully accept the great honor paid him, while those who can understand them otherwise would not charge the one who spoke them with any crime of impiety. Or, if these brotherly words were spoken with a kindly mind, since after the warm welcome his fear itself had passed, they could have been spoken in the way that Moses too was called Pharaoh's god, in line with what the apostle says: "Even if there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords"—especially since in Greek it is said without the article, the article being what most clearly signifies the one true God. For he did not say prosōpon tou theou, but prosōpon theou; and those accustomed to hearing and understanding the Greek language easily grasp the difference in what is said.

It is asked whether Jacob made a false promise to his brother when he said that, following at the pace of his people on the journey—for whose sake he would go slowly—he would come to him at Seir. For, as Scripture then relates, he did not do this, but went on by the road that led to his own people. Or perhaps he made the promise in good faith, but later, on reflection, chose otherwise?

How does Scripture say that "Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the land, saw Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and took her and slept with her and humbled her. And he set his heart on Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and loved the virgin, and spoke to her according to the virgin's mind"? How is she called a virgin if he had already slept with her and humbled her? Perhaps in Hebrew usage "virgin" is a term of age. Or rather, is what happened first mentioned afterward by recapitulation? For he could first have set his heart on her, loved the virgin and spoken according to the virgin's mind, and then slept with her and humbled her.

Since shortly before, in speaking with his brother Esau, Jacob indicates that his sons are little children—called paidia in Greek—one may ask how they could have carried out such a slaughter and sack of the city for the sake of their sister Dinah, even though the men killed were laid up in the pain of circumcision. But we must understand that Jacob lived there a long time, until his daughter had become a young woman and his sons young men. For it is written thus: "And Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped facing the city. And he bought the part of the field where he pitched his tent from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs; and he set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel. And Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to get to know the daughters of that region," and so on. It is clear from these words, then, that Jacob did not stay there in passing, as a traveler does, but bought a field, pitched his tent, built an altar, and therefore lived there for quite a long time; and that his daughter, when she reached an age at which she could have friends, wished to get to know the daughters of the townspeople; and so that most bloody slaughter and plundering was carried out on her account—which, I think, no longer presents a problem. For there was no small multitude with Jacob, who had become very rich; but his sons are named in this deed because they were its leaders and instigators.

Jacob, fearing war with his neighbors over the city of Salem, which his sons had sacked, says, "But I am few in number, and they will gather against me and kill me." He called himself few in number in view of wars with many peoples that could arise, not because he had fewer men than would suffice to take that city, since on his journey he had divided his people into two camps.

"And God said to Jacob, 'Arise and go up to the place Bethel and live there; and make there an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.'" Why did he not say, "and make there an altar to me, who appeared to you," but God says, "make there an altar to God, who appeared to you"? Was it the Son who appeared there, and God the Father who says this? Or should it be counted as some figure of speech?

When Jacob is about to go up to Bethel, where he has been commanded to make an altar, he says to his household and to all who were with him: "Put away the foreign gods that are among you," and so on. Then it is said: "And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands, and the earrings that were in their ears." The question is why the earrings too, since if they were ornaments they had nothing to do with idolatry. The answer must be that they are to be understood as amulets of the foreign gods. For Scripture testifies that Rebecca received earrings from Abraham's servant, which would not have happened if they were not permitted to wear earrings as ornaments. So those earrings that were handed over with the idols were, as has been said, amulets of the idols.

"And the fear of God came upon the cities that were around them, and they did not pursue the sons of Israel." Let us begin to take note of how God works in the minds of men. For by whom was the fear of God produced in those cities, if not by him who was safeguarding his promises in Jacob and his sons?

"And Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, that is, Bethel." It should be noted that three names of this city have now been mentioned: Ulammaus, which it was said to have been called earlier, when Jacob had come there before on his way to Mesopotamia; Bethel, the name he himself gave it, which means "house of God"; and Luz, which has just been mentioned. Nor should this seem strange, for it has happened in many places, with cities, rivers and all sorts of lands, that names were added or changed for one reason or another, just as with people themselves.

Again God appeared to Jacob in Luz and said to him: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." See, God says this to him again in a blessing, and the repetition confirms that a great promise lies in this name. For this is remarkable: those to whom such a name was once given were no longer called what they had been called but what the new name imposed on them, and were never again called anything but the name imposed on them; yet this man, to whom God had once said, "You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name," was called Jacob throughout his whole life and afterwards, after his life. Clearly, then, this name is rightly understood to belong to that promise in which God will be seen as he was never seen before by the fathers. For there the old name will not exist, since nothing of oldness will remain even in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the supreme reward.

Among the promises to Jacob it is said: "Nations and assemblies of nations shall come from you." Are the "nations" meant according to the flesh, and the "assemblies of nations" according to faith? Or is each said with reference to the faith of the Gentiles, since the one nation of Israel according to the flesh cannot be called "nations"?

"And God went up from him from the place where he had spoken with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone; and he poured a drink offering upon it and poured oil upon it. And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him there 'Bethel.'" Was what had been done before done again in this place, or is it being recounted again? But whichever of these it is, Jacob poured the drink offering upon the stone; he did not pour it out to the stone. It is not, then, the way idolaters are accustomed to set up altars before stones and pour out offerings to stones as if to gods.

The twelve sons of Israel who were born to him are counted up, and it is said: "These are the sons of Israel who were born to him in Mesopotamia," although Benjamin was born long afterwards, when they had already passed Bethel and were approaching Bethlehem. Some, trying in vain to resolve this question, have said that we should read not "were born," as most Latin manuscripts have it, but "came to be" — for the Greek has ἐγένοντο [?] — meaning that Benjamin too, though he was not born there, nevertheless came to be there, because he had already been conceived in the womb, so that Rachel is believed to have been pregnant when she left. But in this way, even if "were born" were read, they could say: he was already born in the womb, because he had been conceived; just as it was said to Joseph about holy Mary: "For what is born in her is of the Holy Spirit."

But something else stands in the way of this solution to the question. If Benjamin had already been conceived there, then the sons of Jacob who were oldest when they left that place could hardly have been twelve years old. For Jacob completed twenty years there, and for the first seven of them he was unmarried, until he earned his wife by his service. So even if a son was born to him in the first year after he took a wife, the firstborn could have been twelve years old when he set out from there. Accordingly, if Benjamin had already been conceived, that whole journey, and everything written about Jacob on the way, was completed within ten months. It would follow that his sons, still such small children, wrought such slaughter for their sister Dinah, killed so many men, and stormed a city in this way. Among them Simeon and Levi, who were the first to gird on their swords, went in against those men and slew them, and one of them would turn out to have been eleven years old and the other ten, even if she had borne a child every single year without a break. It is surely incredible that boys of that age could have done all those things, when Dinah herself was still scarcely six years old.

The question must therefore be solved in another way, so that, after the twelve sons have been listed, the words "These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria" are understood to have been said because, of all those many sons, only one was not born there, and yet he owed his birth to that place, since it was there that his mother was joined to his father. But this solution of the question needs to be confirmed by some example of a similar expression.

Yet no solution to this question is easier than to take it as a synecdoche. For where one part is the greater or the more important, its name commonly includes also what does not properly belong under that name. Thus Judas no longer belonged to the twelve apostles; he was in fact already dead when the Lord rose from the dead. And yet the apostle kept the name of the number twelve in his epistle, where he says that the Lord appeared to the twelve. The Greek manuscripts have this with the article, so that it cannot be understood as any twelve whatever, but as those distinguished by that number. In the same manner of speaking, I think, the Lord also said, "Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil," so that Judas does not seem to belong to the election as well. For the name "elect" is not easily found applied to evil, except when the wicked are chosen by the wicked. But if we suppose that Judas too was chosen, so that the Lord's passion might be accomplished through his betrayal—that is, that his wickedness was chosen for a purpose, since God makes good use even of evil things—let us consider another passage, where he says, "I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen." There he makes clear that only the good belong to the election. And so the words "I chose you twelve" were spoken by synecdoche, so that under the name of the greater and better part he might also include what does not properly belong under that name.

This same figure occurs in this very book, where Hamor, on behalf of his son Shechem, so that he might receive Dinah the daughter of Jacob, went out to speak with Jacob, and Jacob's sons, who had been away, also came; and Hamor says to them all, "My son Shechem has set his heart on your daughter; give her to him, then, as his wife." Because the father's person was the more important, by saying "your daughter" he included under this name, by synecdoche, the brothers as well, whose daughter she was not. Hence also this: "Go to the flock and bring me two kids from there." For the sheep and the kids were pastured together; and because sheep are the more important, he included the herd of goats as well under their name. In the same way, because the eleven sons of Jacob born in Mesopotamia formed the greater number, Scripture included in its mention of them Benjamin too, who was not born there, and said, "These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria."

The account of the wives Esau took and the sons he fathered comes after the account of Isaac's death. It must be understood as a recapitulation, for these things did not begin to happen only after Isaac's death, when Esau and Jacob were already a hundred and twenty years old. Isaac fathered them when he was sixty, and he lived a hundred and eighty years in all.

The question is how Scripture can say that after the death of his father Isaac, Esau left the land of Canaan and settled on Mount Seir, when we read that he was already living there when his brother Jacob came back from Mesopotamia. It is easy to think of what could have happened so that Scripture need not be thought either mistaken or misleading. After his brother left for Mesopotamia, Esau did not want to live with his parents. Perhaps this was because he was still upset and resented being cheated of the blessing. Perhaps it was because of his wives, whom he saw his parents disliked, or for some other reason. So he began to live on Mount Seir. Then, after his brother Jacob returned and the two were reconciled, he too came back to his parents. When they had buried their dead father together, the land, as Scripture says, could not hold them, for both had grown very rich. So he left again for Seir, and there he founded the nation of the Idumaeans.

The words "These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir, in the land of Edom" refer to the time in which the writer was living. When Seir, who fathered these men, lived there, Esau had not yet come into that land, and so it was certainly not yet called the land of Edom. The land took that name only from Esau himself, since the same man was called both Esau and Edom, and from him came the Idumaeans, that is, the nation of Edom.

The words "And these are the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned in Israel" should not be taken to mean that all the kings are named down to the time when the kings of Israel began, the first of whom was Saul. There were many kings in Edom up to the time of Saul, including the time of the judges, who came before the kings. But of these many, Moses could record only those who lived before his own death. Nor is it surprising that we find more generations when we count from Abraham through Esau, father of the nation of Edom, then through Reuel son of Esau, Zerah son of Reuel and Jobab son of Zerah (Jobab was succeeded as king by Balak, who is recorded as the first king in the land of Edom), down to the last king Moses could name, than when we count from Abraham through Jacob down to Moses. On that side we find about twelve generations, but on this side only about seven down to Moses. More could be named there because they died sooner, so that more of them succeeded one another. In the same way Matthew, following one line, counts forty-two generations from Abraham to Joseph, while Luke, counting along another line, through Nathan rather than through Solomon as Matthew does, lists fifty-five from Abraham to Joseph. In the line where more generations are counted, the men died sooner than in the line where fewer are counted. Someone might be troubled that Balak son of Beor is listed among the kings of Edom, and might think from the likeness of the name that he was the Balak who opposed Moses as he led the people of Israel. Let him know that that Balak was a Moabite, not an Idumaean, and was the son of Zippor, not the son of Beor. There was indeed a son of Beor on that occasion too, but he was Balaam, not Balak: the Balaam whom that same Balak hired to curse the people of Israel.

Scripture seems to tell its story in order, as though Isaac died when his grandson Joseph was seventeen. But however one turns the matter, it is hard to see how that could be. I do not want to say it cannot be solved, in case something has escaped me that has not escaped someone else. If Joseph was seventeen after his grandfather Isaac's death, when his brothers sold him into Egypt, then his father Jacob must have been a hundred and twenty in his son Joseph's seventeenth year. For Isaac fathered Jacob and Esau when he was sixty, as Scripture says. Isaac therefore lived a hundred and twenty years after that, since he died at a hundred and eighty. So he left his sons a hundred and twenty years old and Joseph seventeen. Now Joseph was thirty when he appeared before Pharaoh, and then came seven years of plenty and two of famine before his father came to him with his brothers. So Joseph was in his thirty-ninth year when Jacob entered Egypt. At that time Jacob was in his hundred and thirtieth year, as he tells Pharaoh with his own mouth. Yet on this reckoning Jacob was a hundred and twenty when Joseph was seventeen, and that cannot possibly be true. If Jacob was a hundred and twenty in Joseph's seventeenth year, then in Joseph's thirty-ninth year Jacob would have been not a hundred and thirty but a hundred and forty-two. And if Joseph was not yet seventeen on the day Isaac died, but reached his seventeenth year some time after his grandfather's death (the year in which, as Scripture testifies, his brothers sold him into Egypt), then his father must have been even older than a hundred and forty-two when he followed his son into Egypt. For after Scripture has told of Isaac's last year of life, his hundred and eightieth, and of his death and burial, it records how Esau left his brother and went from the land of Canaan to Mount Seir. It then adds a list of the kings and chiefs of the nation in which Esau settled, or which he founded. After this it introduces the story of Joseph in these words: "Jacob lived in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen years old, tending the sheep with his brothers." Then it tells of the dreams, and how they made his brothers hate him and sell him. So he came into Egypt either in that same seventeenth year or when he was somewhat older. Either way, the question remains. If he was seventeen after his grandfather's death, when his father was a hundred and twenty, then in Joseph's thirty-ninth year, when Jacob came into Egypt, Jacob must have been a hundred and forty-two. But Jacob was in fact a hundred and thirty at that time. It follows that if Joseph was sold into Egypt at seventeen, he was sold twelve years before his grandfather died. He could only have been seventeen twelve years before Isaac's death, in the hundred and eighth year of his father Jacob's life. If we add to these the twenty-two years Joseph spent in Egypt before his father arrived, Joseph's age comes to thirty-nine and Jacob's to a hundred and thirty, and there is no problem at all. But because Scripture tells these things after Isaac's death, Joseph is thought to have been seventeen after that same grandfather's death. We should therefore understand that Scripture said nothing more of Isaac's life, since he was now very old and frail, because it was already speaking of Jacob and his sons. But Isaac was still alive when Joseph turned seventeen.

Jacob says to Joseph: "What is this dream you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers really come and bow down to the ground before you?" Unless this is taken as said in some mystery, how can it be understood of Joseph's mother, who was already dead? So we should not think it was fulfilled in Egypt when Joseph was raised to power, since his father did not bow down to him when he came to him in Egypt, and his mother, long dead, could not. But in the person of Christ it is easily understood, even of the dead, according to what the apostle says: that God gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

It is asked why Scripture calls the Ishmaelites, to whom Joseph's brothers sold him, Midianites as well, since Ishmael was Abraham's son by Hagar, while the Midianites came from Keturah. Is it that Scripture had said of Abraham that he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, namely Hagar and Keturah, and sent them away from his son Isaac to the land of the east? Are we to understand that they had become a single nation?

It is written of Jacob, when he was mourning Joseph: "All his sons and daughters gathered and came to comfort him." What daughters were these, besides Dinah? Or does it speak of sons and daughters counting grandsons and granddaughters too? His older sons could already have had children.

"And he refused to be comforted, saying, 'I will go down to my son in hell, mourning.'" It is usually a great question how hell is to be understood: whether only the wicked go down there when they die, or the good as well. If only the wicked, how can Jacob say that he wants to go down mourning to his son? He does not believe that his son is in the torments of hell. Or are these the words of a man distraught and grieving, who makes his misfortune seem even greater in this way too?

"And they sold Joseph into Egypt to Potiphar, a eunuch, the chief of the cooks." Some do not want to translate the Greek word archimageiros as "chief of the cooks" but as "chief of the soldiers," one who had the power to put men to death. For the man whom Nebuchadnezzar sent was also given this title, and he is found rather to have held the chief military command.

"It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers [?] to a certain man of Adullam named Hirah. There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua, and he took her and went in to her. She conceived and bore a son," and so on. It is asked when these things could have happened. If they happened after Joseph came into Egypt, how could Judah's sons all have reached an age to marry within about twenty-two years? (That is how much time can be reckoned to have passed before they came with their father to their brother Joseph in Egypt.) For when his firstborn died, Judah gave his daughter-in-law Tamar to his second son. When that son also died, she waited for the third to grow up. When he had grown up, Judah did not give her to him either, for fear that he too would die. That is why she gave herself to her father-in-law. So it rightly raises a question how all these things could have happened within so few years. The answer may be that Scripture, as it often does, wants us to understand by way of recapitulation that this began to happen some years before Joseph was sold, since the passage is introduced with the words "It happened at that time." But here too it is asked how old Judah, the fourth son of Jacob, could have been if Joseph was seventeen when he was sold, since even Reuben, the firstborn, could have been at most five or six years older than his brother Joseph. Scripture plainly says that Joseph was thirty when he became known to Pharaoh. Since he is believed to have been sold in his seventeenth year, he had spent thirteen years in Egypt unknown to Pharaoh. To these thirteen years were added the seven years of plenty, making twenty. Add two more, since Jacob entered Egypt with his sons in the second year of the famine, and we find twenty-two years during which Joseph was away from his father and his brothers. It is hard to work out how everything told about Judah's wife, sons and daughter-in-law could have happened in that period. Perhaps we should believe (for this too could have happened) that as soon as Judah began to grow into a young man, he fell in love with the woman he married, before Joseph had yet been sold into Egypt.
"And she took off her widow's garments." This suggests that even in the time of the patriarchs widows had their own particular garments, different from those of married women.

When it says again, "Joseph was taken down into Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh's eunuch, bought him," Scripture returns to the point in the story from which it had turned aside to tell the events set out above.

Some Latin manuscripts read "three baskets of groats," where the Greek has chondritōn, which those who know that language take to mean common bread. But it is puzzling how Pharaoh could have had common bread among his food. For the baker says that the top basket held all kinds of baked goods that Pharaoh ate. But we should understand that this basket also held common bread, since it says "three baskets of chondritōn," and that on top, in the same top basket, were all those kinds of baked goods.

Pharaoh thought he was standing "over the river," in the same way that Abraham's servant said, "See, I am standing over the spring of water." There too the Greek has epi tēs pēgēs, just as here it has epi tou potamou. If this way of speaking is understood in the psalm where it is written, "who founded the earth over the water," people will not be forced to think that the earth floats on the water like a ship. By this way of speaking it is rightly understood that the land is higher than the water, for it is raised up above the waters so that land animals can live there.

The words "and they will forget the plenty that is to come in all the land of Egypt" do not mean plenty still to come for those who suffer the famine, as though plenty would come to them afterward. The plenty was still to come at the time he was speaking. It is as if he said: in the famine signified by the bad cows and the bad ears of grain, people will forget this plenty, which the good cows and the good ears of grain signified was to come.

"Can we find a man like this, who has the Spirit of God in him?" Here, unless I am mistaken, the Spirit of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, is mentioned to us for the third time in this book. The first was where it says, "And the Spirit of God was moving over the water." The second was where God said, "My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." The third is now, where Pharaoh says of Joseph that the Spirit of God is in him. But we have not yet read the words "Holy Spirit."

"And Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Psonthomphanech." This name is said to mean "he revealed hidden things," no doubt because he explained the dreams to the king. But they say that in the Egyptian language this name means "saviour of the world."

"And he gave him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of the City of the Sun, as his wife." People often ask which Potiphera this was: the one whose slave Joseph had been, or another. It is thought more likely that he was another. There are many difficulties in believing it was the former. First, Scripture does not mention it, and it seems unlikely it would have passed over something that brought no small glory to the young man, namely that he married the daughter of the man whose servant he had been. Second, how could a eunuch have a daughter? But the reply is: how could he have a wife? He is thought to have been castrated later, either through some accidental wound or by his own choice. A further difficulty is that he is not given the title he usually has, archimageiros, which the Latin translators rendered "chief of the cooks," though some want it understood as "chief of the soldiers." But the reply here too is that he held two offices, the priesthood of the Sun and the chief military command. Elsewhere it was fitting to mention the office that suited the actions described. Here, however, after no small divinity had appeared in Joseph, it was right to name the office of his father-in-law that, in the opinion of the Egyptians, related to no small divinity, namely the priesthood of the Sun. But in all this, since he was also in charge of the prison, it is very hard to believe that a priest was put in charge of such a task. Moreover, he is not simply called a priest of the Sun but a priest of the City of the Sun, which is called Heliopolis. It is said to be more than twenty miles from the city of Memphis, where the Pharaohs, that is, the kings, mostly lived. How then could he have left the duties of his priesthood and served the king diligently as chief of the soldiers? There is also the fact that Egyptian priests are said to have served only in the temples of their gods and never to have held any other office. But if things were perhaps different at that time, let each believe what he likes. In any case, this is not a question that has no way out, whether there was one Potiphera or two. Whichever view one holds, it is neither dangerous to the faith nor contrary to the truth of God's Scriptures.

"And Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, a very great amount, until it could not be counted, for there was no number." "For there was no number" is said because that abundance went beyond every number in common use, and no word could be found for it. For how could any multitude, however great, if it is still finite, have no number? It may also have been said as hyperbole.

"And Joseph remembered his dreams, which he had seen, for his brothers had bowed down to him." But we must look for something more exalted in those dreams. For they cannot be fulfilled in this way with respect to his father and his mother, who was already dead. When he had seen the sun and the moon, he heard of them from his father, who was alive and rebuked him.

Joseph was so wise a man, praised not only by the testimony of the people among whom he lived but by the testimony of Scripture itself. Why then does he swear by the life of Pharaoh that his brothers will not leave Egypt unless their youngest brother comes? Did Pharaoh's life count for little even to a good and faithful man, who kept faith with him in everything as he had earlier with his master? He would surely do so all the more for the man who had raised him to such high honour, if he had done so for the man who owned him as a slave he had bought. And if he cared nothing for Pharaoh's life, should he not have avoided perjury, whatever man's life he swore by? Or is it not perjury? He did keep one of them until Benjamin came, and so what he had said came true: "You shall not leave here unless your brother comes." What he said could not apply to all of them, for how could Benjamin come unless some of them went back to bring him? But what follows presses the question harder, where he swore again, saying: "Send one of you and bring your brother, and you will be held in custody until your words are shown to be true or not. If not, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies." That is: if you are not telling the truth, you are spies. He added an oath to this statement because, if they had not told the truth, they would be spies, that is, they would deserve the punishment of spies. Yet he knew they were telling the truth. No one commits perjury if he says to a man he knows to be perfectly chaste, "If you have committed this adultery of which you are accused, God condemns you," and adds an oath to these words. What he swears is entirely true, for there is a condition in his words, "if you have done it," though he is certain the man has not done it. But someone may say: it is true that if he has committed adultery, God condemns him; but how is it true that "If you are not telling the truth, you are spies," since even if they were lying they would not be spies? The answer is what I said: "you are spies" was said as though it meant "you deserve the punishment of spies," that is, "you will be counted as spies because of your lie." Countless similar expressions show that "you are" could be said for "you will be held to be" or "you will be counted." Hence Elijah's saying: "Whoever answers by fire, he shall be God." He would not become God then, but would be held to be God then.

The sons of Israel, filled with remorse, were saying among themselves that they had treated their brother Joseph badly, and that this was being paid back to them by divine judgment, since they saw themselves in danger. Why does Scripture add: "They did not know that Joseph was listening, for an interpreter was between them"? We are to understand that they thought he did not hear because they saw that the interpreter who stood between them told him nothing of what they were saying. They thought the interpreter was there for no other reason than that Joseph did not know their language. And the interpreter had no reason to report to the man who had appointed him what they were saying among themselves rather than to him.
"And he came back to them and spoke to them." It does not add what he said to them. From this we understand that he said the same things he had said before.

"And you will bring my old age down to hell in sorrow." Is it "to hell" because it is "in sorrow"? Or does he say this as one who would go down to hell when he died even if there were no sorrow? Hell is a great question, and we must note what Scripture means by it in every place where it happens to be mentioned.

They hear from the steward of the house: "Your God and the God of your fathers has given you treasure in your sacks; as for your silver, I have it, and it is tested." This seems to be a lie, but we must believe it signifies something. For silver that is both given away and not diminished (it is also called "tested") must surely be understood as the silver of which we read elsewhere: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire, tested in the earth, purified seven times," that is, perfectly.

"And they drank and were made drunk with him." Drunkards tend to cite this passage in their own defence, not because of those sons of Israel, but because of Joseph, who is praised as exceedingly wise. But anyone who pays careful attention will find in many places that in the Scriptures this word is also commonly used to mean being satisfied. Hence that saying: "You have visited the earth and made it drunk; you have greatly enriched it." Since this is said in praise of a blessing and recalls a gift of God, it is clear that this drunkenness signifies being filled. For to be made drunk in the way drunkards are made drunk is of no use even to the earth, since it is spoiled by more moisture than is needed to satisfy it, just like the life of drunkards, who do not fill themselves to satisfaction but drown themselves in a flood.

Joseph said to his brothers: "Do you not know that a man such as I practises divination?" He had also ordered his steward to speak to them about this divination. People usually ask what this means. Since, as the outcome showed, it was said in jest and not in earnest, should it not be counted as a lie? Liars tell their lies in earnest, not in jest; and when things that are not so are said as a kind of joke, they are not reckoned as lies. But what is more puzzling is the meaning of this conduct of Joseph, by which he made sport of his brothers so many times, until he revealed to them who he was, and kept them hanging in such suspense. The more unexpected this is for those with whom he is dealing, the more delightful it is to read. Even so, given the seriousness of his wisdom, unless something great were signified by this game, as it were, he would not have done it, nor would it be contained in that Scripture which carries such authority of holiness and is so intent on prophesying things to come. We have not undertaken to work this out in an exposition now; we only wanted to point out what ought to be investigated here. For I do not think it is without purpose that he does not say, "I practise divination," but, "a man such as I practises divination." If this is a manner of speaking, something similar should be found elsewhere in the body of Scripture.

I think we should consider with some care how Joseph kept his brothers in such misery and distress for as long as he wished, and drew it out with as much delay as he wished. He was certainly not making them wretched, since he was thinking of how it would end in their own great joy to come. All that he did to postpone their gladness, he did so that the delay would heap it higher, as though the sufferings they endured through all that time of distress were not worthy to be compared with the coming glory of exultation that was to be revealed in them when they recognized the brother they thought they had destroyed.

In Judah's account many things are told differently from the way Joseph had dealt with them, even though he was speaking in Joseph's presence. For instance, nothing at all is said about the charge that they were spies. It is not clear whether this was left out on purpose or whether the confusion of the moment made him forget it. For they also said that Joseph himself had asked them about their father and their brother, and that they had told him in answer to his questions. It would be surprising if this account could match what happened even in substance, so that it could be shown to be truthful. Yet even if some things in it are false, Judah could more probably have been mistaken through forgetfulness than have dared to lie, especially to the very man to whom he was speaking. For he was not speaking to him as to someone who did not know; he included in his account things he knew Joseph also knew, in order to move him to mercy.

What does Joseph mean when he says: "For God sent me before you to preserve a remnant of you upon the earth, and to keep alive a great remnant of you"? It does not quite fit to take the remnant, or the great remnant, as Jacob and his sons, since they were all alive and well. Or does it perhaps signify, by a deep and hidden mystery, what the Apostle says: "A remnant has been saved by the election of grace," since the prophet had foretold: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved"? For Christ was killed by the Jews and handed over to the Gentiles, as Joseph was handed over by his brothers to the Egyptians, for this very purpose, that the remnant of Israel too might be saved. Hence the Apostle says: "For I too am an Israelite," and: "that the fullness of the Gentiles might come in, and so all Israel would be saved"; that is, out of the remnant of Israel according to the flesh, and out of the fullness of the Gentiles, who are Israel according to the spirit in the faith of Christ. Or else, if a fullness of faith still remains for that Israelite nation too, from which came the remnant, the remnant in which the apostles themselves were saved at that time, then this is signified by that full deliverance of Israel by which they were freed from Egypt through Moses.

"Jacob and all his offspring entered Egypt, his sons and his sons' sons, his daughters and his daughters' daughters with him." We must ask how he can say "daughters and daughters' daughters with him," when we read that he had only one daughter. We said earlier that his daughters could be taken to mean his granddaughters, just as the whole people descended from him are all called sons of Israel. But now, when it says "daughters' daughters" because of Dinah alone, the plural is used for the singular, just as the singular is often used for the plural. Unless, of course, someone claims that his daughters-in-law could have been called his daughters.

Scripture says that Leah bore so many souls, or that so many souls came out of Jacob's thighs. We must see how to answer those who try to use this text to prove that souls are passed on from parents together with bodies. No one doubts that "souls" is said for "human beings," by a figure of speech in which the part stands for the whole. But if we are to separate that very part by which the whole is named, that is, the soul, whose name stands for the whole human being, from the statement "they came out of his thighs," so as to understand that only the flesh was born of him even though only the souls are named, then we must look into the ways Scripture uses language.

"These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria, and Dinah his daughter. All the souls, sons and daughters, were thirty-three." Were all these thirty-three souls born of Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria? There were in fact six sons and one daughter, and the grandsons listed are descended from them. Now a question had already arisen about Benjamin alone, when the twelve sons of Jacob were counted and named one by one, and it was said: "These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria." How much greater, then, is the question now, how thirty-three souls were born of Leah in Mesopotamia of Syria! Unless this confirms that manner of speaking by which all are said to have been born in a place where their parents were born. And then it is no longer in doubt that, in the case of the one daughter, "daughters" are named, the plural being put for the singular.

We read that sixty-six souls entered Egypt with Jacob, not counting, of course, the sons of Joseph; then, once they are added, it continues: "There were seventy-five souls with whom Jacob entered Egypt." This must be understood as meaning those who were in Jacob's household when he entered Egypt, for he certainly did not enter with those he found there. But when the truth is examined more carefully, it turns out that only two had already been born when he entered, Ephraim and Manasseh. Not only are the Hebrew manuscripts said to have this in this place, but the Septuagint version itself makes it clear in Exodus. Yet I do not think the Septuagint translators made a mistake here. Because of some mystical meaning, with what we might call prophetic freedom, they wanted to fill out this number, on the supposition that those people were descended from the two sons Manasseh and Ephraim while Jacob was still alive, and so they judged that they should be counted as part of Jacob's household. But since Jacob is found to have lived seventeen years in Egypt, there is no way to see how Joseph's sons could have had even grandsons while he was alive. For Jacob entered Egypt in the second year of the famine, and Joseph's sons were born in the years of plenty. Whichever years of plenty they are thought to have been born in, from the first year of plenty to the second year of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, is nine years. Add the seventeen years Jacob lived there, and the total is twenty-six years. How then could young men less than twenty-six years old have had even grandsons? Nor is this question solved by the Hebrew original. For how could it have come about that Jacob had so many grandchildren before he entered Egypt, including through Benjamin, who came to his brother at the age he did? Scripture records not only that Benjamin had sons, but grandsons and great-grandsons as well, all of whom are counted among the sixty-six people with whom, even according to the Hebrew original, Jacob is said to have entered Egypt. We must also consider what it means that, though no more than eight are listed for Joseph and his sons, and eleven in all are found for Benjamin and his sons, the total given is not nineteen, which is eight and eleven, but eighteen; and afterwards Joseph and his sons are said to have been not eight souls but nine, though only eight are found. All these things, which seem impossible to resolve, undoubtedly contain some great meaning. But I do not know whether they can all agree in the literal sense, especially in the numbers. From certain numbers whose meaning we have been able to learn, we most rightly believe that the numbers in Scripture are most sacred and full of mysteries.

The patriarchs are commended for having been keepers of livestock from their youth and from their fathers' time. And rightly so: for without any doubt this is a just servitude and a just lordship, when livestock serve man and man rules over livestock. For so it was said when he was created: "Let us make man in our image and likeness; and let him have power over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and all the livestock that are upon the earth." This suggests that reason ought to rule over irrational life. But it is either wickedness or misfortune that has made one human being the slave of another. Wickedness, as when it was said: "Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a slave to his brothers"; misfortune, as happened to Joseph himself, who was sold by his brothers and became the slave of a foreigner. So it was wars that made the first slaves, to whom this name was given in the Latin language. For a man defeated by another man could be killed by the law of war; because he was spared (servatus), he was called a slave (servus). From this too comes the word mancipia, because they were taken by hand (manu capta). There is also a natural order among human beings, by which women serve men and children serve parents, because there too it is just that the weaker reason should serve the stronger. This, then, is the plain justice in lordship and servitude: that those who excel in reason should excel in rule. When this order is disturbed in this world, whether through human wickedness or through the differences of bodily natures, the righteous endure this temporary perversion, and in the end they will have a happiness that is perfectly ordered and everlasting.

"For every shepherd of sheep is an abomination to the Egyptians." Rightly is every keeper of livestock an abomination to the Egyptians, who are a figure of this present world, in which wickedness abounds; for a righteous man is an abomination to the wicked.

"And Jacob and his sons came into Egypt to Joseph; and Pharaoh king of Egypt heard of it. And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying: Your father and your brothers have come to you. See, the land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best land." This repetition is not of something passed over, to which Scripture often returns obscurely by way of recapitulation; it is perfectly plain. For Scripture had already told how Joseph's brothers came to Pharaoh, and what he said to them and heard from them. But now it repeats this as if from the beginning, so as to continue the narrative from the words that Pharaoh spoke to Joseph alone. In all this, in the Greek manuscripts copied out by the more careful scribes, some passages have obeli, which mark what is found in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew, and some have asterisks, which mark what the Hebrew has but the Septuagint does not.

What does Jacob mean when he says to Pharaoh: "the days of the years of my life, which I sojourn"? For that is what the Greek has, where the Latin has "I spend" or "I have," or something else. Did he say "which I sojourn" because he was born in a land that the people had not yet received by God's promise of inheritance, so that living there he was in fact in a foreign land, not only when he was away abroad, as in Mesopotamia, but even when he was in the place where he was born? Or should it rather be understood in line with what the Apostle says: "As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord"? In this sense we also understand what is said in the psalm: "I am a lodger on the earth and a sojourner, like all my fathers." For again he says of these days of his life: "They have not reached the days of the years of the life of my fathers, the days they sojourned." Here he meant nothing other than what the Latin manuscripts render as "they lived"; and so he indicated that this life is a sojourning on earth, that is, the dwelling of a pilgrimage. But I believe this fits the saints, to whom the Lord promises another, eternal homeland. So we must consider how it is said of the wicked: "They will sojourn and hide; they will watch my heel." This is more fittingly understood of those who sojourn in order to hide, that is, in order to lie in wait for the sons; they do not remain in the house forever.

"And he gave them a possession in the best land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded." We must ask whether the land of Rameses is the same as Goshen. For that was the land they had asked for, and that was the land Pharaoh had ordered to be given them.

"And Joseph measured out grain for his father." And yet his father did not bow down to him, either when he saw him or when he received grain from him. How then are we to think that Joseph's dream was fulfilled at this point, and not rather that it contains a prophecy of something greater?
"And Joseph brought all the money into Pharaoh's house." It was Scripture's concern to commend the faithfulness of God's servant in this matter too.

Joseph said to them: "Bring your livestock, and I will give you bread in exchange for your livestock, if your money has run out." It may be asked: since Joseph had gathered grain for people to live on, what did the livestock live on while so severe a famine prevailed? Especially since Joseph's brothers had said to Pharaoh: "For there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, because the famine has grown severe in the land of Canaan," and they had mentioned that they had come partly because of this lack of pasture. So if the pastures had failed in the land of Canaan in this famine, why had they not failed in Egypt, when the same famine prevailed everywhere? Is it, as those who know the region report, that in the many marshes of Egypt there could be no lack of pasture even when there was a famine of grain, which usually comes from the flooding of the Nile? For those marshes are said to produce pasture more abundantly when the Nile's waters rise less.

When Jacob is about to die, he says to his son Joseph: "If I have found favour in your sight, put your hand under my thigh, and you will show me mercy and truth." He binds his son with the same oath with which Abraham had bound his servant: Abraham when giving instructions about where a wife was to be taken for his son, Jacob when entrusting the burial of his body. In both cases, however, the same two things are named which must be highly regarded and weighed throughout the Scriptures, wherever they are found scattered: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth; for in one place it is written: "All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth." So these two things, being much commended, deserve much consideration. Abraham's servant had said: "If you will show mercy and justice to my master," just as Jacob says to his son: "and you will show me mercy and truth." But why should so great a man be so anxious in giving instructions about his body, that it not be buried in Egypt but in the land of Canaan beside his fathers? If we measure this by human custom, it seems strange and almost absurd, and unworthy of so excellent a prophetic mind. But if we seek sacred mysteries in all these things, the joy of greater wonder will arise for whoever finds them. For there is no doubt that in the Law the corpses of the dead signify sins, since people are commanded to purify themselves, as if from uncleanness, after handling them or touching them in any way. From this comes that saying: "If someone is washed after touching a dead body and touches it again, what has his washing gained him? So it is with one who fasts for his sins and goes off and does the same things again." The burial of the dead, then, signifies the forgiveness of sins, in keeping with the words: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered." Where, then, should the corpses of the patriarchs, which signified this, have been buried, if not in the land where he was crucified by whose blood the forgiveness of sins came about? For in the deaths of the patriarchs the sins of mankind were prefigured. It is said, moreover, that the place called Abrahamium, where these bodies lie, is about thirty miles from the place where the Lord was crucified, so that the number itself may be understood to signify him who, at his baptism, appeared at about thirty years of age. And whatever else may be understood about so great a matter, whether in this way or in a more exalted one, let us only not think that such great men of God took such care over the burial of their bodies for nothing. For the faithful have, and ought to have, this assurance: wherever their bodies are buried, or even if they are left unburied by the fury of their enemies, or torn apart and destroyed as their enemies please, their resurrection will not for that reason be any less complete or any less glorious.

Where the Latin manuscripts have "and he worshipped upon the top of his staff," meaning Joseph's, some correctors have "he worshipped upon the top of his own staff," or "at the top of his own staff," or "toward the tip" or "upon the tip." They are misled by the Greek word, which is written with the same letters whether it means "his" or "his own"; but the accents differ, and those who understand these things do not disregard them in the manuscripts, for they make a great difference. Besides, if it meant "his own," it could also have one more letter, so that it would be not αὐτοῦ but ἑαυτοῦ. So it is rightly asked what the saying means. For it is easy to understand that the old man, who carried a staff as people of that age usually carry a stick, did this upon the tip of his own staff when he bowed down to worship God: he held it in such a way that he could worship God by bowing his head over it. What then does "he worshipped upon the top of his staff," that is, his son Joseph's, mean? Had he perhaps taken the staff from him when his son was swearing the oath to him, and while he was holding it, before he had given it back, did he immediately worship God after his son had spoken the oath? For he was not ashamed to carry for a while the emblem of his son's power, since in it a figure of a great thing to come was being foreshadowed. Yet the Hebrew is said to offer a very easy solution to this question, for they report that it is written there: "And Israel worshipped at the head of the bed," the bed on which the old man was lying and which he had arranged so that he could pray on it without effort whenever he wished. Still, we should not therefore think that what the Septuagint translated has no meaning, or only a trivial one.

Here too, when Jacob recalls the promises God made to him, he says that he was told: "I will make you into assemblies of nations." By these words he signifies the calling of the faithful rather than the spreading of a physical lineage.

Jacob says of Ephraim and Manasseh: "Now, then, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt are mine, Ephraim and Manasseh; they shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon are. But the children whom you may beget afterwards [?] they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their allotments." This sometimes misleads readers into thinking it was said as if Jacob were commanding that, if Joseph had other sons, they should be called by the names of these two. That is not so. The order of the words runs like this: "Now, then, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt are mine, Ephraim and Manasseh; they shall be mine as Reuben and Simeon are; they shall be called by the name of their brothers in their allotments." That is, they will receive their inheritance together with their brothers, so that they will be called sons of Israel together with them. For these two tribes were added so that, leaving aside the tribe of Levi, which was the priestly tribe, there would be twelve to divide the land and pay tithes. What he said about other sons of Joseph, should any be born, was put in parenthetically.

Jacob wanted to tell his son Joseph, as though he did not know, where and when he had buried his mother, though Joseph himself had been there with his brothers. Even if he was then so young that he could not have paid attention to it or remembered it, what made it necessary to say it now? Unless perhaps it was to the point to record that Joseph's mother was buried in the place where Christ was to be born.

Israel blesses his grandsons by laying his right hand on the younger and his left on the elder. When his son Joseph tries to correct him, as though he were making a mistake without knowing it, he answers: "I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people, and he too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations." This is to be understood of Christ to the same extent as what was said of Jacob himself and his brother, "The elder shall serve the younger." For by doing this Israel was prophetically signifying that the later people, which was to come into being through Christ by a spiritual generation, would surpass the earlier people, which gloried in its fleshly descent from the fathers.

Jacob says that he is giving Shechem to his son Joseph as a special portion, and he adds that he took possession of it with his sword and his bow. One may ask how this can fit the literal sense. For he bought that property for a hundred lambs; he did not take it by right of victory in war. Is it because his sons stormed Salem, the city of the Shechemites, and it could have become his by right of war, so that the war waged against them might be considered just, since they had first done him so great a wrong in defiling his daughter? Then why did he not give that land to those who did the deed, that is, to his elder sons? Further, if he is now giving that land to his son Joseph because he glories in that victory, why was he displeased at the time with the sons who committed the act? And finally, why even now, as he was blessing them, did he recall it among their deeds as a reproach? Beyond doubt, then, some prophetic mystery lies hidden here. Joseph prefigured Christ in a special way, and to him is given the land where Jacob had done away with the foreign gods by burying them, so that we may understand that Christ was to possess the nations that renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in him.

We must consider what Scripture means when it says, as it constantly does of the dead, "And he was gathered to his fathers," or, "He was gathered to his people." For here this is said of Jacob when he was already dead but not yet buried, and it is not easy to see to what people he was gathered. For the earlier people, called the people of Israel, is born from him; while those righteous men who preceded him are so few in number that we hesitate to call them a people. If it had said, "He was gathered to his fathers," there would be no question. Or is the people perhaps not only the people of holy men but also of the angels of that city of which the Letter to the Hebrews says, "But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of God, Jerusalem, and to thousands of rejoicing angels"? To this people are gathered those who end this life pleasing to God. For they are said to be gathered at the point when no anxiety about temptations and no danger of sin any longer remains. With this in view Scripture says, "Praise no man before his death."

The forty days of burial that Scripture records perhaps signify something about repentance, by which sins are buried. For it is not without reason that forty days of fasting were also established, the days on which Moses and Elijah and the Lord himself fasted; and the church calls its chief observance of fasting Quadragesima, the Forty Days. This is also why they report that in the Hebrew text of the prophet Jonah it is written of the Ninevites, "Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown," so that we may understand that over that many days, days evidently suited to the humbling of penitents, they wept for their sins with fasting and obtained God's mercy. Yet we must not think that this number befits only the mourning of penitents; otherwise the Lord would not have spent forty days with his disciples after the resurrection, going in and out with them, eating and drinking, and those were certainly days of great joy. Nor should we believe that the Seventy translators, whom the church is accustomed to read, made a mistake in saying not "forty days" but "three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." For, endowed with an authority greater than the task of translators requires, the prophetic Spirit, by which they are also affirmed to have agreed as with one voice in their translations (which was a great miracle), they put "three days," though they were not unaware that "forty days" was the reading in the Hebrew manuscripts. They did so in order that sins might be understood to be dissolved and abolished in the glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it was said: "Who was handed over for our offenses and rose again for our justification." Now the glorification of the Lord is recognized in his resurrection and his ascension into heaven. That is why he also gave the Holy Spirit twice, though it is one and the same Spirit: first after he rose again, and again after he ascended into heaven. And since he rose again after three days but ascended after forty days, the Hebrew manuscripts indicate by the number of days the one of these events that came later, while the Seventy chose to record the other, the three days, which also bears on the same matter, not out of servitude to translation but by the authority of prophecy. Let us not say, then, that one of these is false, nor quarrel on behalf of some translators against others. For those who translate from the Hebrew prove to us that what they translate is written there, while the authority of the Seventy translators, commended by so great a miracle wrought by God, is confirmed by such long-standing use in the churches.

Joseph instructed the great men of Egypt to say to Pharaoh in his name: "My father made me swear, saying, 'In the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.'" One may ask how this is true, since these words of his father are not read where he gave instructions about his burial. But we ought to refer words to their meaning, as we have pointed out above in other cases where words or narratives are similarly repeated. For words ought to serve the purpose of expressing a person's will and making it known. Nowhere earlier in the Scriptures, moreover, do we read that Jacob dug a tomb for himself; but unless he had done so while they were living in those lands, it would not be said now.

What does Scripture mean when it says that, as they were on their way to bury Jacob, "they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan"? For they went past the place where the dead man was to be buried by more than fifty miles, as those who know the area report; that is roughly the distance from the place where the patriarchs, Jacob among them, were buried to the place they are said to have reached. For after the great mourning and lamentation held there, they crossed the Jordan again and returned to the place they had passed. Unless perhaps someone says that, to avoid certain enemies, they traveled with the body through the wilderness, the way by which the people of Israel was also led by Moses after being freed from Egypt. For that route makes a very long detour and reaches Abrahamium, where the bodies of the patriarchs lie, that is, the land of Canaan, by way of the Jordan. But however it came about that they went so far beyond those places toward the east and then came to them across the Jordan, we must believe that it was done for the sake of a sign, because Israel was later to come into those lands across the Jordan in the persons of his sons.

"And he mourned for his father seven days." I do not know whether one can find in the Scriptures that a nine days' mourning, what the Latins call the novendial, was held for any of the saints. So it seems to me that any Christians who observe this number for their dead should be forbidden this custom, which belongs rather to the custom of the pagans. The seventh day, however, has authority in the Scriptures. Hence it is written elsewhere: "Mourning for the dead is seven days, but for a fool all the days of his life." The number seven, because of the mystery of the sabbath, is above all a sign of rest; so it is fittingly given to the dead as to those who are at rest. Yet in the mourning for Jacob the Egyptians multiplied this number tenfold, for they mourned him seventy days.

"And Joseph lived one hundred and ten years. And Joseph saw Ephraim's children to the third generation; and the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph's knees." Since Scripture says that Joseph lived to see these sons of his sons, or grandsons of his sons, how does it count them among those seventy-five persons with whom it says Jacob entered Egypt? For Joseph reached old age before he saw them born, whereas when Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph was young, and when his father died he left him at about fifty-six years of age. It is clear from this that Scripture meant to commend that number, seventy-five, for the sake of some mystery. But if anyone demands to know how it can also be true according to historical fact that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy-five souls, we must understand his entry not as that single day on which he came. Rather, since Jacob is very often named in the person of his sons, that is, of his descendants, and since it is clear that he entered Egypt through Joseph, his entry is to be taken as lasting as long as Joseph lived, through whom it came about that he entered. For during that whole period all those who are listed could have been born and lived, so that the seventy-five souls are completed down to the grandsons of Benjamin. For Scripture says, "These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria," speaking even of those who had not yet been born, because she had borne there the parents from whom they were born; it declares them born there because the cause of their being born was born there, that is, their parents, whom Leah bore there. In the same way, since Jacob's reason for entering Egypt lay in Joseph, the whole time that Joseph lived in Egypt was Jacob's entry into Egypt through his offspring, which kept increasing while Joseph was alive, through whom it came about that he entered.
BOOK TWO. QUESTIONS ON EXODUS.

(At the end, a description of the tabernacle.) QUESTION 1. Concerning the lie of the midwives, by which they deceived Pharaoh so as not to kill the Israelite males at birth, when they said that the Hebrew women did not give birth as the Egyptian women did, people often ask whether such lies have been approved by divine authority, since it is written that God dealt well with the midwives. But whether he pardoned the lie on account of their mercy, or judged the lie itself worthy of reward as well, is uncertain. For the midwives did one thing in keeping the little infants alive, and another in lying to Pharaoh. In keeping them alive there was a work of mercy; but they used that lie for their own sake, so that Pharaoh would not harm them, and this could belong not to praise but to pardon. Nor does it seem to me that this sets up any authority for lying for those of whom it was said: "And no lie was found in their mouth." For if the life of certain people, far below the profession of the saints, contains such sins of lying, they are borne with on account of their very progress and promising disposition, especially if they do not yet know how to look for heavenly things as God's benefits but are occupied with earthly ones. But those who live in such a way that their citizenship, as the apostle says, is in heaven, ought not, I think, to shape the measure of their tongue, as far as it concerns speaking the truth and avoiding falsehood, by the example of those midwives. But this question must be discussed more carefully because of other examples found in the Scriptures.

Concerning what Moses did when he killed the Egyptian to defend his brothers, we have discussed sufficiently in the work we wrote against Faustus on the life of the patriarchs. The question was whether there was a praiseworthy disposition in him through which he committed this sin, just as rich soil is often praised even before it receives useful seed, for a certain fertility in weeds, however useless; or whether the deed itself is to be justified outright. It does not seem so, because he did not yet hold any lawful authority, either received from God or ordained by human society. Yet, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, he supposed that his brothers understood that God was giving them salvation through him; so by this testimony Moses may seem to have been already prompted by God — about which Scripture is silent in that passage — and thus able to dare this.

"The Lord called him from the bush." Was it the Lord in an angel? Or was the Lord that angel who is called "the angel of great counsel" and is understood to be Christ? For above it said: "An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the bush."

"To bring them out of that land into a good and large land, into a land flowing with milk and honey." Should we take "a land flowing with milk and honey" spiritually, since in the proper sense of our words this is what the land given to the people of Israel was? Or is it a manner of speaking, by which it refers to the praise of its richness and sweetness?
"And now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to me" — not like the cry of Sodom, by which iniquity without fear and without shame is signified.

As for the Lord's command to the Hebrews through Moses that they should take from the Egyptians vessels of gold and silver and clothing — to which he added, "and you shall plunder them" — the judgment behind this command cannot be unjust. For it is a command of God, which was not to be judged but obeyed. He knows how justly he commanded it; the servant's part is to do obediently what he has commanded.

When Moses says to the Lord, "I pray, Lord, I have not been eloquent before yesterday or the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant," he is understood to believe that by God's will he could suddenly become eloquent. When he says, "nor since you began to speak to your servant," it is as if he were showing that it could have happened that one who had not been eloquent before yesterday and the day before should suddenly become so from the moment the Lord began to speak with him.

"Who made the dumb and the hearing, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?" There are some who slander God, or rather the Scripture of the Old Testament, because God said that he himself made the blind and the dumb. What then do they say of the Lord Christ, who says openly in the Gospel: "I came that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind"? Who but a fool would believe that anything could happen to a man by way of bodily defects that God does not will? But no one doubts that all he wills, he wills justly.

The Lord says to Moses: "But now go, and I will open your mouth and instruct you in what you are to say." Here it is quite clear that not only the instruction of the mouth but also its very opening belongs to God's will and grace. For he does not say, "You open your mouth and I will instruct you," but he himself promised both: "I will open and I will instruct." Elsewhere, however, he says in a psalm: "Open your mouth wide and I will fill it" — where he signifies in man the will to receive what God gives to one who wills, so that "open your mouth wide" belongs to the beginning of the will, and "and I will fill it" to God's grace — but here: "and I will open your mouth and instruct you."

"And the Lord, angry with anger, said." How God can be understood to be angry — not as a man is, through irrational disturbance — must be held to throughout, wherever Scripture says something of this kind, so that the same things need not often be said about it. But it is rightly asked why here, being angry, he spoke of Moses' brother, saying that he would speak for him to the people. For it seems that, because Moses was distrustful, God did not give him the very full capacity he was going to give, and willed that something be done through two that could have been done through one, had he believed. Yet when all these same words are considered more carefully, they do not indicate that the angry Lord gave Aaron by way of punishment. For he says: "Is not Aaron your brother the Levite here? I know that he will speak readily." By these words God is shown rather to have rebuked him: why was he afraid to go because he himself was less fit, when he had a brother through whom he could say to the people whatever he wished, since he himself had a thin voice and a slow tongue — although he ought to have hoped for everything from God? Then, after he was angry, he says the very same things he had promised a little before. He had said, "I will open your mouth and instruct you"; now he says, "I will open your mouth and his mouth and instruct you in what you are to do." But since he added, "and he shall speak for you to the people," it seems that the opening of the mouth was granted because Moses said he was slow of tongue; as for the thinness of his voice, however, the Lord did not wish to grant him anything, but for that reason added the help of his brother, who could use a voice sufficient for teaching the people. So when he says, "and you shall put my words in his mouth," he shows that he would give them to be spoken; for if they were only to be heard, as by the people, he would have said "in his ears." Then when he says a little later, "and he shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth," here too "to the people" is understood. And when he says, "he shall speak for you to the people," he indicates clearly enough the chief authority in Moses and the ministry in Aaron. Then when he says, "but you shall be to him in the things that pertain to God," perhaps a great mystery is to be searched out here: of whom Moses bears the figure, standing as it were in the middle between God and Aaron, and Aaron in the middle between Moses and the people.

In what is written — "And it came to pass on the way, at the lodging place, that an angel met him and sought to kill him. And Zipporah took a stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: The blood of my infant's circumcision has stopped. And he departed from him, because she said: The blood of circumcision has ceased" — the first question is whom the angel wanted to kill. Was it Moses, since it is said, "an angel met him and sought to kill him"? For whom will he be thought to have met but the one who was at the head of his whole company and by whom the others were being led? Or did he seek to kill the boy, whom his mother rescued by circumcising him, so that it is to be understood that he wished to kill the infant because he was not circumcised, and thus to ratify the precept of circumcision by the severity of punishment? If so, it is unclear at first of whom it says "he sought to kill him," since we do not know whom unless it is discovered from what follows — a remarkable and unusual way of speaking indeed, to say first "he met him and sought to kill him" of someone about whom nothing had been said before. But there is such an expression in the psalm: "Its foundations are on the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion." For the psalm begins there, and had said nothing earlier about the one, whether he or she, whose foundations it meant to be understood when it said, "Its foundations are on the holy mountains." But since there follows, "The Lord loves the gates of Zion," the foundations are therefore either the Lord's or Zion's, and for the easier sense rather Zion's, so that they are taken as the foundations of the city. But because in this pronoun eius the gender is ambiguous — for this pronoun serves every gender, that is, masculine, feminine and neuter — whereas in Greek the feminine is autēs and the masculine and neuter autou, and the Greek codex has autou, we are compelled to understand not the foundations of Zion but the foundations of the Lord, that is, those which the Lord laid, of whom it is said: "The Lord builds up Jerusalem."
