Yet it had named neither Zion nor the Lord beforehand when it said, "Its foundations are on the holy mountains." So here too, before the infant is named, it is said, "he met him and sought to kill him," so that we may recognize from what follows of whom it was said. And yet if anyone wishes to take it of Moses, there is no need to resist strongly. Rather, let us understand, if possible, what follows: what it means that the angel withdrew from killing whichever of them it was because the woman said, "The blood of my infant's circumcision has stopped." For it does not say "he departed from him" because she circumcised the infant, but because the blood of circumcision stopped: not because it flowed, but because it stopped — a great mystery, unless I am mistaken.

It was said above that Moses set his wife and his children on beasts of burden in order to go with them into Egypt; but later Jethro his father-in-law came to meet him with them, after he had led the people out of Egypt. It may be asked how both can be true. But it must be understood that after that killing of Moses or of the infant, which the angel was about to carry out, she went back with the little ones. Indeed some have thought that the angel struck terror for this very reason: so that the female sex should not accompany Moses as a hindrance to the ministry that God had laid upon him.

It is asked how it can be said to the people that God had commanded that he would bring them out of Egypt into the land of Canaan, while to Pharaoh it is said that they wished to go out a three days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to their God at his command. But it must be understood that, although God knew what he would do, since he foreknew that Pharaoh would not consent to let the people go, he first said what would also have happened first if Pharaoh had let them go. For that everything should happen as the following Scripture testifies was what the obstinacy of Pharaoh and his people deserved. Nor does God command deceitfully what he knows the one commanded will not do, so that a just judgment may follow.

The words Moses says to the Lord — "Why have you afflicted this people? And why did you send me? For since I went in to Pharaoh to speak in your name, [?] this people, and you have not delivered your people" — are not words of defiance or indignation but of inquiry and prayer, as is clear from what the Lord answered him. For he does not reproach his unbelief, but reveals what he is going to do.

There is no doubt that this passage holds a mystery: Scripture, wishing to show the origin of Moses, since his activity now required it, began the genealogy from Jacob's firstborn, that is, Reuben, then went on to Simeon, then to Levi, and went no further, because Moses was from Levi. Those mentioned here are the ones who had already been mentioned among the seventy-five with whom Israel entered Egypt. For God willed that not the first nor the second but the third tribe, that is, the Levitical tribe, should be the priestly one.

When Moses says, "Behold, I have a thin voice, and how will Pharaoh listen to me?" he seems to excuse himself on account of the thinness of his voice not only because of the size of the people but even because of one man. It would be strange if his voice was so thin that he could not be heard even by one man. Or perhaps royal haughtiness did not allow them to speak at close quarters? But it is said to him: "Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet."

It should be noted that when he was being sent to the people, it was not said to him, "Behold, I have made you a god to the people and your brother shall be your prophet," but rather, "Your brother," he says, "shall speak for you to the people." It was also said, "He shall be your mouth, and you shall be to him in the things that pertain to God"; it was not said, "You shall be a god to him." But to Pharaoh Moses is said to be given as a god, and by analogy Aaron is a prophet to Moses, but in relation to Pharaoh. Here it is suggested to us that the prophets of God speak what they hear from him, and that a prophet of God is nothing other than one who announces the words of God to men who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God.

God says repeatedly, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart," and he adds what seems to be the reason why he does this. "I will harden," he says, "Pharaoh's heart, and I will fulfil my signs and my wonders in Egypt," as though the hardening of Pharaoh's heart were necessary for God's signs to be multiplied or fulfilled in Egypt. God, then, makes good use of evil hearts for what he wishes to show to the good, or to those whom he will make good. And although the character of each heart in its wickedness — that is, what sort of heart it has toward evil — comes about through its own fault, which has grown into it from the choice of the will, yet as for that evil character being moved this way or that, since whichever way it moves it moves badly, this comes about through causes by which the mind is driven. Whether these causes exist or do not exist is not in man's power, but they come from the hidden providence of God, who is wholly just and wholly wise as he orders and governs the whole universe he created. That Pharaoh had such a heart, one that was moved by God's patience not to piety but rather to impiety, was his own fault; but that those things were done by which his heart, malignant through its own fault, resisted God's commands — for this is what is meant by "hardened," since it did not consent pliably but resisted inflexibly — belonged to the divine dispensation, by which a punishment not only not unjust but evidently just was prepared for such a heart, by which those who fear God might be corrected. For example, when some gain is set before people, for the sake of which a murder might be committed, the greedy man is moved one way and the man who despises money another: the one to commit the crime, the other to guard against it. Yet the setting forth of that gain was not in the power of either of them. So causes come to evil men which are indeed not in their power, but which make of them what they found them already made by their own vices from their past will. One must indeed consider whether "I will harden" can also be taken as if he were saying, "I will show how hard it is."

"If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, 'Give us a sign or a wonder,' then you shall say to Aaron your brother: Take the rod and throw it down before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it shall become a serpent." Here surely there was no need for the service of a voice, for which Aaron seemed to have been given as if out of necessity because of the thinness of Moses' voice; rather the rod was to be thrown down so that it might become a serpent. Why then did Moses not do this himself, unless this mediation of Aaron between Moses and Pharaoh bears the figure of some great reality?

This too should be noted: when that sign was performed before Pharaoh, it is written, "And Aaron threw down his rod." Had it perhaps said only "threw down the rod," there would be no question; but the addition of "his," when Moses had given it, was perhaps not said without purpose. Or was that rod common to both, so that whichever of them it was said to belong to, the truth would be told?

"And Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods." Had it said, "Aaron's serpent swallowed up their rods," it would be understood that Aaron's true serpent did not swallow those illusory figments but the rods. For it could swallow what they were, not what they seemed to be and were not. But since it said, "Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods," — though it was surely a serpent, not a rod, that could swallow rods — the thing is called by the name of what it was changed from, not what it was changed into, because it was also changed back into that; and therefore it ought to be called what it principally was. What then are we to say about the magicians' rods? Had they too become true serpents, but were called rods for the same reason as Aaron's rod? Or did they rather seem to be what they were not, through sorcerous trickery? Why then are both sides spoken of as rods and as serpents, so that the manner of speaking makes no difference in the case of those figments? But it is difficult to show how, even if true serpents were made from the magicians' rods, neither the magicians nor the evil angels through whose agency these things were worked were the creators of serpents. For in bodily things, throughout all the elements of the world, there are certain hidden seminal principles, which, when the right opportunity of time and cause is given, burst forth into their proper forms according to their own modes and limits. And so the angels who do these things are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops or trees or of anything that grows in the earth, even though they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for these things to come forth. What farmers do visibly, angels do invisibly; but God alone is the one Creator, who implanted those very causes and seminal principles in things. The matter has been stated briefly; if it were to be explained with examples and ample discussion so as to be more easily understood, a long discourse would be needed, from which the need for haste in our work excuses us.

"And the enchanters of the Egyptians also did likewise with their sorceries; and Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said." When this is said, it seems that Pharaoh's heart was hardened because the enchanters of the Egyptians also did similar things; but what follows will show how great that hardening was, even when the enchanters failed.

"And the enchanters of the Egyptians also did likewise with their sorceries and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt." It is asked from where, if this had already happened everywhere. But there is a similar question as to where they got the water they turned into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood. We must therefore understand that the region where the children of Israel lived was not struck by such plagues, and that from there the enchanters could either draw water to turn into blood or bring up some frogs merely to display their magical power. Although they could also have done it after those plagues had been checked; but Scripture, narrating quickly, joined together what could also have happened later.

"And Pharaoh saw that there was relief; and his heart was made heavy, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said." Here it appears that the causes of the hardening of Pharaoh's heart were not only that his enchanters did similar things, but also God's very patience, by which he spared him. God's patience, according to the hearts of men, is useful to some for repentance, and useless to others, who use it to resist God and persist in evil; yet it is not useless in itself, but according to the evil heart, as we have already said. The apostle says this too: "Do you not know that God's patience leads you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works." And elsewhere, when he said, "We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place," he also added, "both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing." He did not say that he was the good fragrance of Christ to those who are being saved but a bad one to those who are perishing; he said only that he was a good fragrance. But they are such that they perish even by a good fragrance, according to the character of their heart, as has often been said, which must be changed by a good will in the grace of God, so that the judgments of God, which harm evil hearts, may begin to benefit them. Hence the one whose heart had been changed for the better sang: "My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments will help me." He did not say "your gifts" or "your rewards," but "your judgments." It is a great thing, however, to be able to say with sincere confidence: "Prove me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart." And lest he should seem to have attributed anything to his own strength, he at once added: "For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been well pleased in your truth." He recalls the mercy shown to him, so that he may be well pleased in the truth, since "all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth."

The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God," because they could not bring forth gnats. Knowing the power of their wicked arts, they surely saw that their efforts had not been thwarted by arts of that kind, as if Moses were more powerful in them, so that they could not bring forth gnats. They saw that they had been thwarted by the finger of God, who was plainly working through Moses. And the finger of God, as the Gospel states most clearly, is understood to be the Holy Spirit. For while one evangelist reports the Lord's words as "If I cast out demons by the finger of God," another evangelist, reporting the same saying, wished to explain what the finger of God is, and says, "If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." So the magicians, in whose power Pharaoh trusted, confessed that the finger of God was in Moses, and that by it they were overcome and their sorceries came to nothing. Even so, Pharaoh's heart was hardened, now with a hardness that is truly astonishing. Why the magicians failed at this third plague is hard to perceive and to explain. (The plagues began when the water was turned into blood.) They could have failed at the first sign, when the rod was turned into a serpent, and at the first plague, when the water was changed into blood, and at the second, of the frogs, if the finger of God, that is, the Spirit of God, had so willed. For who would be so utterly mad as to say that the finger of God could block the magicians' efforts at this sign but was unable to do so at the earlier ones? There is, then, a definite reason why they were allowed to do those things up to this point. Perhaps the Trinity is being commended to us. And it is true that the greatest philosophers of the gentiles, so far as can be traced in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Spirit, though they did not keep silent about the Father and the Son. Didymus also mentions this in the book he wrote on the Holy Spirit.

"Behold, I will send the dog-fly upon you and your servants, your people and your houses, and the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with the dog-fly, so that you may know that I am the Lord, the God of all the earth. And I will set a separation between my people and your people." Scripture has made this plain here so as not to have to say it everywhere, and we should understand that in both the later and the earlier signs it came about that the land where the people of God lived was not troubled by any such plagues. It was fitting for this to be stated openly at this point, where the signs begin that the magicians did not even attempt to imitate. For there is no doubt that the gnats had been everywhere in Pharaoh's kingdom but not in the land of Goshen. So the magicians tried to do the same there, and they could not do it at all. Up to the point of their failure, then, nothing was said about the setting apart of that land. It was said only from the point where those signs began to be done that the magicians no longer dared even to attempt to imitate.

Where the Latin versions have "Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land," the Greek has "Come, sacrifice to the Lord your God in the land." Pharaoh did not want them to go where they said they were going. He wanted them to sacrifice there in Egypt. The words of Moses that follow show this, for he says that it cannot be done because of the abominations of the Egyptians.

Moses says, "It cannot be done so, for we shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God." That is, we are going to sacrifice the things that the Egyptians abhor, and for that reason we cannot do it in Egypt. The words he adds make this clear: "For if we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians before their eyes, we shall be stoned." Some of our translators did not understand this and rendered it as "It cannot be done so. Shall we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God?" But what Scripture actually says is that they are going to sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians. Other Latin versions read: "It cannot be done so, since we shall not sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God." Adding the negative particle produces the opposite sense, for Moses said, "It cannot be done so, for we shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God." That is why they said they wanted to go into the wilderness, where the Egyptians would not see the things they abhorred. This should be understood as having a mystical meaning. We said the same about the shepherds, who were abhorrent to the Egyptians, which is why the Israelites received a separate land when they came into Egypt. For in the same way the sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, as the life of the righteous is to the wicked.

When the locusts had been taken away, it was said of Pharaoh: "And Pharaoh made his heart heavy at this time also, and would not let the people go." Certainly it is not said here, "Pharaoh's heart was made heavy," but "Pharaoh made his heart heavy." And so it is, surely, in all the plagues. For the origin of vices lies in the will of man. But human hearts of one kind are moved by causes in one way, and hearts of another kind in another way. Often they are moved in different ways even by the same causes, according to their own qualities, which come from their wills.

"And when Pharaoh saw that not one of the cattle of the children of Israel had died, Pharaoh's heart was made heavy." How did this heaviness of Pharaoh's heart arise from causes that pointed the opposite way? If the cattle of the Israelites had also died, there would seem to be a fitting cause for his heart to grow heavy in contempt of God, as if his magicians had made the Israelites' cattle die too. But as it is, his heart grew heavy from the very thing that ought to have moved him to fear or to believe, when he saw that not one beast of the Hebrews' cattle had died. That is, this heaviness had progressed even this far.

What does God mean when he says to Aaron and Moses, "Take handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh and before his servants, and let it become dust over all the land of Egypt"? The earlier signs were done with the rod, which not Moses but Aaron either stretched out over the water or struck the earth with. But now, after two intervening signs, the dog-fly and the death of the cattle, in which neither Aaron nor Moses did anything with his hand, Moses is told to scatter ashes from the furnace toward heaven. Both are ordered to take the ashes, but Moses is to scatter them, and not on the earth but toward heaven. It is as though Aaron, who had been given to the people, was to strike the earth, or stretch out his hand over the earth or the water, while Moses, of whom it was said, "You shall be for him [?] in the things that pertain to God," is ordered to scatter the ashes toward heaven. And what of those two preceding signs, in which neither Moses nor Aaron does anything with his hand? What does this variety mean? For it does not mean nothing.

"And for this very reason you have been preserved, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." The apostle also cited these words of Scripture when he was dealing with this same very difficult passage. There he also says: "But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath"—by sparing, of course, those he foreknew would be wicked; these are the vessels he calls "fitted for destruction"—"and in order," he says, "to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy." Hence the voice of the vessels of mercy in the Psalms: "My God, his mercy will go before me; my God will show me [his will] among my enemies." God, then, knows how to make good use of the wicked. In them he does not create human nature for wickedness, but he bears with them patiently for as long as he knows he should. He does not do this to no purpose, but uses them to admonish or to train the good. For see: that the name of God should be proclaimed in all the earth is certainly of benefit to the vessels of mercy. So it was for their benefit that Pharaoh was preserved, as both Scripture testifies and the outcome shows.

Why did God, when he threatened to send a great hail, instruct Pharaoh to hurry and gather in his cattle and whatever he had in the field, so that they would not perish in the hail? He seems to give this warning less in anger than in mercy. But that raises no question, since God tempers punishment even when he is angry. What rightly troubles us is this: for which cattle is he now taking thought, if all of them had died in the previous plague? For it is written there that God distinguished between the cattle of the Hebrews and those of the Egyptians, so that none died on the Hebrews' side, while all the cattle of the Egyptians died. Is the question perhaps solved by this, that he had foretold the death of the cattle that were in the field, so that "all" refers to these, and we should understand that the cattle in the houses escaped? Those doubtful whether what Moses had foretold that the Lord would do might be true could have gathered them in and kept them indoors. And some of these could have been in the fields again, the ones he now warns them to gather into their houses so that they would not perish in the hail. This is especially likely because Scripture goes on to say: "Whoever among Pharaoh's servants feared the word of the Lord gathered his cattle into the houses, but whoever did not set his mind on the word of the Lord left his cattle in the field." So this could also have happened when God threatened the death of the cattle, though Scripture says nothing about it.

"And the Lord said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and there will be hail in all the land of Egypt.'" Here again Moses is ordered to stretch out his hand not toward the earth but toward heaven, as with the ashes earlier.

Pharaoh, terrified by the crashing of the sky, which was violent during the hail, asked Moses to pray for him and confessed his own wickedness and that of his people. Moses said to him, "As for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the Lord." What sort of fear was Moses looking for, if this fear was not yet the fear of the Lord? It is easy to fear punishment, but that is not fearing God. He meant, of course, the fear that belongs to piety, which Jacob speaks of when he says, "Unless the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had been with me, you would now have sent me away empty."

"The Lord said to Moses, 'Go in to Pharaoh, for I have made his heart heavy, and the hearts of his servants, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in order.'" He says, "For I have made his heart heavy, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in order," as if God needed anyone's wickedness. But it should be understood as if he had said, "For I have been patient with him and his servants, not taking them away, so that my signs may come upon them in order." Because a wicked mind was growing more obstinate through God's patience, "I have made his heart heavy" is said in place of "I have been patient with him."

"And not a single locust was left in all the land of Egypt. And the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart." Scripture has clearly recorded God's kindness in taking away the locusts, and then goes on to say that the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. He did so, of course, by his own kindness and his own patience, through which that obstinacy grew while Pharaoh was being spared. In the same way, all wicked human hearts grow hard by misusing the patience of God.

For the third time Moses is told, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven," so that the plague of darkness might also come about. But his brother Aaron was never told to stretch out his hand toward heaven. As for Moses being told, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, and let the locusts come up over the land," I believe this signifies that one who can do the greater can also do the lesser, but that one who is granted the lesser cannot by that fact do the greater.

God says to Moses: "Speak, then, secretly in the ears of the people, and let each man ask of his neighbor, and each woman of her neighbor, vessels of silver and gold, and clothing." No one should think he may take this as an example for despoiling his neighbor in this way. For God commanded this, and he knew what each person ought to suffer. The Israelites did not commit theft; they performed a service at God's command. It is like an officer of a judge who kills a man whom the judge has ordered to be killed. If he did it of his own accord, he would certainly be a murderer, even if he killed a man he knew the judge ought to have sentenced to death. There is also some question here. If the Hebrews lived apart in the land of Goshen, where the plagues that afflicted Pharaoh's kingdom did not occur, how could each of them ask a neighbor, man or woman, for gold, silver and clothing? This is especially puzzling because, where this is first commanded through Moses, it is put this way: "and the woman from her neighbor and her fellow-lodger"—concellaria or concellanea, if one may use such a word—"or her housemate." From this we should understand that the Hebrews were not the only people living in the land of Goshen; some Egyptians lived there alongside them. Those divine benefits could rightly reach these Egyptians too, for the Hebrews' sake, so that these Egyptians who lived among them came to love them and readily lent them what they asked for. Yet God did not judge these Egyptians to be so far removed from the wrongs and afflictions that God's people had suffered that they should escape even this loss, since they had not been struck by those plagues because that land was being spared.

"And the Lord said to Moses, 'Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.'" It is as though his disobedience were needed for those signs to be multiplied. They served a useful purpose in striking fear into the people of God and, by the very distinction made between them and the Egyptians, in forming them in piety. But this was the work of God, who made good use of the wickedness of that heart, not of Pharaoh, who misused the patience of God.

"Whatever is left of it until morning you shall burn with fire." One may ask how anything could be left over, since they had been told beforehand that if a household did not have enough people to eat the animal, neighbors should be brought in. But because it was said, "You shall not break a bone of it," we understand that the bones at least would remain, and these were to be burned with fire.

"You shall have a lamb that is perfect, a male, a year old." This way of speaking may trouble someone, as if a lamb could be anything other than male, if he does not know why it had to be translated this way. The word ought to have been translated "sheep," because the Greek has probaton. But probaton is neuter in Greek, so all the words that follow could agree with it, as if one said, "You shall have a beast that is perfect, male, a year old." In Latin one could have said "male beast" (masculum pecus) in the neuter, as one speaks of "male frankincense" (mascula tura). But one could not say ouis masculus, because ouis, "sheep," is feminine, and ouis mascula would be even more absurd. If pecus, "beast," had been used, something else might also have been understood, and the mystery would not have been preserved. For although Scripture is speaking of a sheep, it afterwards says, "You shall take it from the lambs and the kids." Christ is rightly understood to be signified in this. For why would there have been any need to direct that a sheep or a lamb be taken from the lambs and the kids, unless it prefigured him whose flesh descended not only from the righteous but also from sinners? The Jews, it is true, try to understand that a kid too may be taken to celebrate the Passover. They think "take from the lambs and the kids" means that one should take a lamb from the lambs or, if there is none, a kid from the kids. Yet now that these things have been fulfilled in Christ, it is clear what that commandment prefigured.

Scripture says, "And you shall keep this day throughout your generations as an eternal ordinance," or "an everlasting one" [?]; the Greek word is aiōnion. This should not be taken as if any of these passing days could be eternal. What is eternal is what this day signifies. In the same way, when we say that God himself is eternal, we are certainly not saying that the syllables of the word "God" are eternal, but the one they signify. Still, we must examine carefully how Scripture usually uses the word "eternal." Perhaps it calls "eternal," in a formal sense, something that they would hold it sacrilege to omit or to change of their own accord. For it is one thing when something is commanded with a limit on how long it is to be done, as when the ark was commanded to go around the walls of Jericho seven times. It is another when something is commanded to be observed with no end set to its observance, whether daily, or monthly, or solemnly every year, or at fixed intervals of many years or of a few. So either Scripture called it "eternal" because they were not to dare stop celebrating it of their own accord, or, as I said, so that we would understand that what is eternal is not the signs themselves but the realities they signify.

"And there was a great cry in the land of Egypt, for there was no house in which there was not one dead." Could there not have been some house that had no firstborn? Since only the firstborn died, how was there no house without a dead person? Or had this too been arranged by God's foreknowledge, so that there were firstborn in absolutely every house where Egyptians were to be struck? We certainly should not think that the Egyptians who lived in the land of Goshen were spared this plague. For this plague fell on human beings and animals, not on the land. That is, firstborn humans and animals died by a hidden blow from an angel. Nothing had been done on the earth or in the sky, such as the frogs, the locusts or the darkness, to afflict those who lived there. Since the land of Goshen had been free of such plagues, the benefit no doubt reached the Egyptians who lived in that land with the Hebrews. But in this plague all their firstborn were struck.

"And the children of Israel did as Moses had commanded them, and they asked the Egyptians for vessels of gold and silver, and clothing. And the Lord gave his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and they lent to them; and they plundered the Egyptians." This had already happened before the death of the Egyptians' firstborn, but now it is repeated by way of recapitulation. For it was narrated at the time when it happened. How could the Egyptians have lent these things to the children of Israel now, in such great mourning over the deaths of their own? Unless perhaps someone says that the Egyptians who lived with the Hebrews in the land of Goshen were not struck by this plague either.

What does it mean when it says, "You shall take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood that is by the door, and smear it on the lintel and on both doorposts"? The question is which blood he means by the blood "by the door," since he surely wants us to understand the blood of the lamb by whose sacrifice the Passover is made. Is he implying, though he does not say so, that the lamb is to be killed by the door? Or, which is more credible, did he say "from the blood that is by the door" because whoever was going to smear the lintel and doorposts would of course set the vessel in which he had caught the blood by the door, so as to have it at hand when he dipped the hyssop?

"And the children of Israel set out from Rameses to Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the baggage," or "property," if that is a correct way to translate the Greek word aposkeuē. Scripture shows that this word signifies not only movable goods but also living things that move. Judah, speaking to his father, says: "Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, so that we may live and not die, both we and you and our substance." There the Greek has aposkeuē where the Latin translator rendered "substance." Our translators sometimes render it "property," just as we chose to say "baggage" here, provided that by this word both human beings and beasts of burden, or all kinds of livestock, are understood. Whether wives too can be understood there I do not know. But Scripture mentions six hundred thousand men on foot and adds, "apart from the baggage," or "property," or "substance," or whatever other word better translates aposkeuē. So it is clear that people were also signified by it, whether slaves, or women, or those whose age made them unfit for military service. Thus we are to understand the six hundred thousand men on foot as only those who could be armed as a military force.

It is often asked whether the Hebrews could have reached so great a number during the years in Egypt that a careful reckoning of the numbers in the scriptures can show. First of all, how many years there were is no small question. For God says to Abraham, when that sacrifice of the three-year-old heifer, the she-goat, the ram, the turtledove and the pigeon had been offered, before not only Isaac but even Ishmael had been born: "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will reduce them to slavery and do them harm for four hundred years." If, then, we take these four hundred years to mean years spent in slavery under the Egyptians, it was no short span of time for the people to multiply as they did. But scripture testifies by the clearest evidence that there were not so many years.

Some think that four hundred and thirty years should be counted from the time Jacob entered Egypt until the people were set free from there through Moses, since it is written in Exodus: "The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was four hundred and thirty years." They hold that the years of their slavery were four hundred, because it is written in Genesis: "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will reduce them to slavery and do them harm for four hundred years." But since the years of slavery are counted from the death of Joseph (for while he was alive they not only were not slaves there but even ruled), we must consider how four hundred and thirty years in Egypt are to be reckoned. Jacob entered Egypt in the thirty-ninth year of his son, since Joseph was thirty years old when he appeared before Pharaoh and began to rule under him; and after the seven years of plenty had passed, in the second year of the famine, Jacob entered Egypt with his other sons. So Joseph was then thirty-nine years old, and he died when he had completed one hundred and ten years of life. He therefore lived in Egypt seventy-one years after his father came to him. If we subtract these from four hundred and thirty, the remaining years of slavery, that is, after Joseph's death, will be not four hundred but three hundred and fifty-nine. And if we think we ought to count from the time Joseph began to rule under Pharaoh, so that Israel may in a sense be understood to have entered Egypt when his son was raised to such power there, even then there will be three hundred and fifty, which Tyconius would have us take as four hundred, the part being understood from the whole—that is, a part of fifty from a whole hundred—and he proves that scripture habitually uses this rule of speech. But if, as can be said with somewhat more probability, we take Israel to have entered Egypt when Joseph, having been sold, first came to be there, we shall have to subtract a further thirteen years, so that we take three hundred and thirty-seven years for four hundred. But scripture records that Kohath, the son of Levi and grandfather of Moses, entered Egypt with his grandfather Jacob, and says that he lived one hundred and thirty years; that his son Amram, the father of Moses, lived one hundred and thirty-seven; and that Moses was eighty years old when he freed the people from Egypt. Even if Kohath had begotten Moses' father in the year he died, and Amram too had begotten Moses in the last year of his life, the years added together—one hundred and thirty, one hundred and thirty-seven and eighty—make three hundred and forty-seven years, not four hundred and thirty. And if someone should say that Kohath son of Levi was born in the last year of Joseph's life, about seventy years can be added to that sum, since Joseph lived seventy-one years in Egypt after his father came. Yet even so, the seventy years of Joseph's life from Jacob's entry into Egypt to the birth of Kohath (if he is claimed to have been born then), plus Kohath's own one hundred and thirty years, plus the one hundred and thirty-seven of his son Amram, Moses' father, plus Moses' own eighty, make four hundred and seventeen years, not four hundred and thirty.

Accordingly, the reckoning that Eusebius followed in his Chronicle is plainly supported by evident truth. For he counts the four hundred and thirty years from the promise by which God called Abraham to leave his own land for the land of Canaan. The apostle too, when he praised and commended Abraham's faith in that promise in which he wants Christ to be understood as foretold—that is, in which God promised Abraham that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in him—says: "This is what I mean: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promises void." So the apostle says that the law was given four hundred and thirty years after the promise by which Abraham was called and believed God, not after the time when Jacob entered Egypt. Moreover, the text of Exodus itself indicates this clearly enough. For it did not say, "The sojourning of the children of Israel, which they sojourned in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years," but said plainly, "which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers." From this it is evident that we must also count the time of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, from when Abraham began to sojourn in the land of Canaan—that is, from that promise in which the apostle praises his faith—up to the time when Israel entered Egypt. For throughout all that time the fathers sojourned in the land of Canaan, and afterward the offspring of Israel in Egypt. And so the four hundred and thirty years were completed from the promise to the exodus of Israel from Egypt, when the law was given on Mount Sinai, the law which does not annul the covenant so as to make the promises void.

So in the seventy-fifth year of his life, as scripture says, Abraham went out into the land of Canaan, and he begot Isaac when he was a hundred years old. Thus there are twenty-five years from the promise to the birth of Isaac. To these are added all the years of Isaac's life, that is, one hundred and eighty, making two hundred and five. At that time Jacob was one hundred and twenty years old, for he and Esau were born as twins when their father was sixty. Ten years later Jacob entered Egypt, at the age of one hundred and thirty, when Joseph was thirty-nine. So there are two hundred and fifteen years from the promise to Jacob's entry into Egypt. Joseph, from the thirty-ninth year of his age, in which his father found him in Egypt, lived seventy-one years, since the whole span of his life was one hundred and ten years. When seventy-one is added to two hundred and fifteen, the total is two hundred and eighty-six years. There remain one hundred and forty-four, or forty-five, years, during which the people of Israel are understood to have been slaves in Egypt after the death of Joseph. If one considers human fertility, with the help of him who willed them to multiply greatly, it is found to be no wonder how much they could have multiplied in these years, so that the people went out of Egypt six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the rest of the company, which included slaves, women, and those too young or old for war.

So when God said to Abraham, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own, and they will reduce them to slavery and do them harm for four hundred years," this is not to be taken as though the people of God were in that harshest slavery for four hundred years. Rather, since it is written, "In Isaac shall your offspring be named," four hundred and five years are counted from the year of Isaac's birth to the year of the departure from Egypt. When you subtract from four hundred and thirty the twenty-five years from the promise to the birth of Isaac, it is no wonder if scripture chose to call four hundred and five years by the round sum of four hundred, since it customarily names periods of time in such a way that whatever slightly exceeds or falls short of a more complete number is not counted. So the words "they will reduce them to slavery and do them harm" are not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they had been held in slavery for that many years. Rather, the four hundred years are to be referred to what was said, "your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own," because whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that offspring was a sojourner until they received the land as an inheritance according to God's promise, which happened after they were freed from Egypt. Thus a hyperbaton is to be understood here, and the order of the words is: "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not their own for four hundred years," while the words "and they will reduce them to slavery and do them harm" are to be understood as inserted, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For it was in the last part of this total span of years, that is, after Joseph's death, that the people of God came to endure harsh slavery in Egypt.

What does it mean when he says, in giving the command about the Passover, "And it shall be for you as a sign upon your hand"? Is it to be understood as "upon your works," that is, something you ought to place before your works? For the Passover, because of the slaughter of the sheep, relates to faith in Christ and to the blood by which we have been redeemed. This faith is to be placed before works, so that it is in a certain way "upon the hand," against those who gloried in the works of the law. The apostle speaks of this and deals with it at length; he wants faith to be put before works in such a way that good works depend on it and are preceded by it, not so that faith itself should seem to be given as a reward for the merits of good works. For faith belongs to grace; "but if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace."

"Now when Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the road of the land of the Philistines, although it was near. For God said, 'Lest the people perhaps repent when they see war, and return to Egypt.'" Here it is shown that everything that can rightly be done by prudent planning ought to be done to avoid adversity, even when God is most plainly our helper.

"And in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt." Does he want a generation to be reckoned as a hundred years, so that it says "in the fifth generation" because it was after four hundred and thirty years? Or should this rather be understood in terms of the generations of men, from Jacob himself, who entered Egypt, down to Moses, who went out with the people? For Jacob is found to be the first, Levi the second, Kohath the third, Amram the fourth, and Moses the fifth. The Latin translator calls them progenies; the Greeks call them geneai, and in the Gospel they are called generationes, and they are counted only by the succession of men, not by a number of years.

"And Moses said, 'Take courage, stand firm, and see the salvation that comes from the Lord, which he will work for you today. For as you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall never see them again for all time.'" How are these words to be taken, since the Israelites did see Egyptians afterward? Is it because those who saw them then did not see them any more, since both the pursuers died and these men all died too, each on the day of his death? For their descendants did see the descendants of the others. Or is "you will not see them as today" to be understood as "not as today, pursuing you as enemies and coming after you in so great an army"? In that case there is no problem at all, not even about the "for all time" that he put here; for even though both peoples will see each other at the time of the resurrection, they certainly will not see each other as they did that day.

What does it mean that the Lord said to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me?" when Scripture has said nothing of Moses' words, nor mentioned him praying? Unless it wanted us to understand that he did this in the silence of his voice, crying out with his heart.

"And you, lift up your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea." This is the rod by which the wonders were done, which is now said to be Moses'; earlier, however, it was said to be his brother's, when he himself was working through it.

"You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them." It is not surprising that "earth" is put for water. For this whole outermost or lowest part of the world is reckoned under the name of "earth," according to the frequent phrase, "God who made heaven and earth." And in that psalm's arrangement, after the heavenly things have been mentioned, it says, "Praise the Lord from the earth," and goes on to name in that praise things which also belong to the waters.

"You sent your spirit, and the sea covered them." See, now the Spirit of God is mentioned for the fifth time, if we count in this number also the saying, "This is the finger of God." The first is where it is written, "The Spirit of God was moving over the waters"; the second, where it is said, "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh"; the third, where Pharaoh says to Joseph, "For the Spirit of God is in you"; the fourth, where the Egyptian magicians say, "This is the finger of God"; the fifth in this song: "You sent your spirit, and the sea covered them." We should remember, moreover, that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only for benefits but also for punishment. For what else did he say above: "And by the spirit of your wrath the water was divided"? So this Spirit of God was the spirit of his wrath toward the Egyptians, whom the division of the waters harmed, since it let them go in so that they could be overwhelmed when the waters returned; but for the children of Israel, whom the division of the water benefited, it was not the spirit of God's wrath. This shows that the Spirit of God is called by different names because of its different operations and effects, though it is one and the same Spirit, who is also understood to be the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Trinity. Accordingly, I do not think that any other but the same Spirit is meant where the apostle says, "For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, 'Abba, Father,'" because by the same Spirit of God, that is, the finger of God, by which the law was written on the tablets of stone, fear was struck into those who did not yet understand grace, so that through the law they might be convicted of their weakness and sins, and the law might become their tutor, to lead them to the grace that is in faith in Jesus Christ. And of this Spirit of adoption and grace, that is, of this work of the Spirit of God by which grace and rebirth into eternal life are bestowed, it is said, "But the Spirit gives life," after it had been said just before, "The letter kills," that is, the written law that only commands, without the help of grace.

"And they came to Marah, and they could not drink from Marah, for it was bitter." If the name of the place was called "bitterness" because they could not drink the water there, since it was bitter (for Marah means "bitterness"), how did they come to Marah? Only because Scripture called the place they came to by the name it already bore when these things were being written; for of course they were written later than they happened.

"And the Lord showed him a tree, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet." Was it a kind of wood that had this power, or could God, who was doing such great wonders, do this with any wood whatever? The words "he showed him" seem to indicate that it was already a wood of such a kind that this could be done by it. Unless perhaps it was a place where no wood at all was to be found, so that the very fact that the Lord showed him a piece of wood where there was none was itself part of the divine help, and he made the waters sweet through wood, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even if the wood had such a nature, who is to be praised but the one who created it and pointed it out?

"And the Lord said to Moses, 'Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion each day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.'" This testing is a proving, not an enticement to sin; nor is it a proving so that God may know, but so that he may show men to themselves, that they may become humbler in asking for help and in acknowledging the grace of God.

Moses and Aaron say to the people, among other things: "Because the Lord has heard your murmuring, which you murmur against us. But what are we? For your murmuring is not against us, but against God." They did not mean by this that they had as much power as God (for they said, "What are we?"), but that the people should know they had murmured against him who had sent these men and was working through them. Nor is this like the statement where Peter says to Ananias, "Did you dare to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God." For he did not say, "Did you dare to lie to me? You have not lied to me, but to God"; had he said that, it would have been similar. Nor did he say, "Did you dare to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to the Holy Spirit, but to God"; for by speaking thus he would have denied that the Holy Spirit is God. But as it is, having said, "Did you dare to lie to the Holy Spirit?" when Ananias thought he had lied to men, he showed that the Holy Spirit himself is God by adding, "You have not lied to men, but to God."

God commands the people through Moses: "In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread." Notice that "bread" is not used here for every kind of food. For in that case the name would have included meat too, since it also is food. Yet neither does he here call "bread" what is made from grain (which is what we usually call bread in the proper sense); rather, he calls the manna by the name of bread. And it is not without meaning that he says he will give meat in the evening and bread in the morning. Something of the sort was also signified in Elijah's case, when the raven brought him food. Or perhaps by the meat in the evening and the bread in the morning is signified he who "was handed over for our sins and rose again for our justification"? For in the evening he died in weakness and was buried, and in the morning he appeared to his disciples, having risen in power.

"And Moses said to Aaron, 'Take one golden jar and put a full omer of manna in it, and you shall lay it up before God, to be kept for your generations, as the Lord commanded.'" One may ask where Aaron was to lay it up before God, when there was no image, and the ark of the covenant had not yet been made. Did he perhaps say "you shall lay it up" in the future tense, so that it would be understood that it could be laid up before God at the time when the ark would exist? Or was "before God" said rather of what is done in the very devotion of offering, wherever it might be placed? For where is God not? But what he adds, "And Aaron laid it up before the testimony to be kept," supports the first sense more. For in this way Scripture spoke by prolepsis of what was done later, when the tabernacle of the testimony came into being.

"And the children of Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land; they ate manna until they came to the region of Phoenicia." Scripture indicated by prolepsis, that is, by mentioning here what also happened later, that the children of Israel ate nothing but manna in the desert. For this is what it means by "until the inhabited land," that is, land that is no longer desert; not that they stopped eating manna as soon as they came to habitable land, but that they did not stop before then. For the manna is said to have ceased after they had crossed the Jordan, where they ate the bread of the land. So when they had entered habitable land, before they crossed the Jordan, they could either eat manna only or both foods; this can be understood, since the manna is not said to have ceased until the Jordan had been crossed. But why, in that scarcity of the desert, they also craved meat, when they had come out of Egypt with very many flocks of their own, is a great question. Unless perhaps it is said that, since the pastures in the desert were not so plentiful and the increase of the flocks seemed likely to be smaller as a result, they spared their animals, lest if they all ran out they would lack even what was needed for sacrifices; or whatever else may be said to solve this question. It is more fittingly believed, however, that they did not crave the meat they could have had from their flocks, but the meat they lacked, namely from the waters; for they did not find that in the desert. Hence they were also given the ortygometra, that is, birds which many have translated into Latin as "quails," though the ortygometra is a different kind of bird, albeit not altogether unlike quails. For God knew what they craved and with what kind of meat to satisfy their craving. But because Scripture had said that they craved meat and had not specified what kind of meat, the question arose.

"They ate manna until they came to the region of Phoenicia." He had already said, "until they came to an inhabited land"; but because he had not stated specifically which land he meant, by the repetition he seems to have specified it more precisely by saying "to the region of Phoenicia." But we must believe that this land was so called at that time, for it is not called that now. For the region called Phoenicia is a different one, that of Tyre and Sidon, through which we do not read that they passed. Yet perhaps Scripture could have called it the land of Phoenicia where palm trees had begun to appear after the waste of the desert, since the palm is called by that name in Greek. For at the beginning of their journey they found a place where there were seventy palm trees and twelve springs; but afterward the long stretch of desert received them, where there was nothing of the kind, until they came to cultivated places. But the more probable sense is that we should believe the land was so called at that time. For the names of many lands and places, as of rivers and cities, have changed over the ages for definite reasons.

"And the Lord said to Moses, 'Go on ahead of the people, and take with you some of the elders of the people; and take in your hand the rod with which you struck the river.'" We read that it was Aaron, not Moses, who struck the river with the rod; for Moses divided the sea with that same rod, not a river. What, then, does "Take the rod with which you struck the river" mean? Did he perhaps call the sea a river? If so, an example of this manner of speaking should be looked for. Or was what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses, because God commanded through Moses what Aaron should do, and the authority lay with Moses, while the ministry lay with Aaron? Indeed, in his very first words God said this to him about his brother: "He shall be for you to the people, and you shall be for him in the things that pertain to God."

"And behold, I will stand on the top of the hill, with the rod of God in my hand," says Moses to Joshua son of Nun when he ordered him to fight against Amalek. So now it is called the rod of God, which was first called the rod of Aaron and afterward the rod of Moses. Just as the spirit of Elijah is spoken of, which is the Spirit of God of whom Elijah was made a partaker, so it could be with the rod. Likewise we speak of the righteousness of God, which is ours but given by God; speaking of it, the apostle rebukes the Jews, saying, "Being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own righteousness," that is, as though it were acquired by themselves for themselves. Against such people he says, "For what do you have that you did not receive?"

"And Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God," or, as other manuscripts have it, "in the presence of God," which in Greek is written enantion tou theou. It is asked where "before God" was, when there was as yet neither the tabernacle nor the ark of the covenant, which were established later. For here we cannot take it as said of the future, as was said about the manna that was placed in the golden jar. So we must take it that what was done in honor of God was done "before God"; for where is God not?

Moses says to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to seek judgment from God; for when a dispute arises among them and they come to me, I judge each one and instruct them in the commandments of God and his law." One may ask how Moses said this, when no law of God had yet been written down. Unless it is because the law of God is eternal, which all devout minds consult, so that whatever they find in it, they either do or command or forbid, according to what it has prescribed by its unchangeable truth. For are we to believe that Moses, even though God spoke with him, used to consult God on every single point that arose in the disputes of so great a multitude, which kept him occupied in this business of judging from morning until evening? And yet, unless he consulted the Lord presiding over his mind and wisely attended to his eternal law, he would not have found what most just judgment he could give between the disputants.

Concerning Jethro's advice to his son-in-law Moses, that he should not be so taken up with judging the people that both he and the people would be worn out with an unbearable weariness, the first question is why God allowed his servant, with whom he himself spoke of things so great and so many, to be advised by a foreigner. In this Scripture teaches us that counsel of truth, by whatever person it is given, ought not to be despised. We should also consider whether God perhaps wished Moses to be advised by a foreigner in a matter where pride could also tempt him; for he was sitting alone in the loftiness of a judge, while the whole people stood. Jethro himself points to this sense when he directs that those chosen to judge the people's cases should be men who hate pride. Next, how much we ought to heed what Scripture says elsewhere, "My son, let not your activities be many," is quite evident here as well. Then the words of Jethro as he gives Moses advice must be considered; for he says, "Now therefore listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you." Here it seems to me to be signified that a mind too intent on human affairs is in a certain way emptied of God, with whom it is filled the more fully, the more freely it reaches out toward heavenly and eternal things.

And when he goes on to say, "Be for the people in the things that pertain to God, and bring their words to God; and you shall testify to them the commandments of God and his law, and show them the ways in which they are to walk and the works they are to do," he shows that these things are to be done with the whole people. For he does not say, "Bring the words of each individual to God," but "their words," after saying above, "Be for the people in the things that pertain to God." After this he advises that the affairs of individuals, which they have among themselves, should not be neglected, but should be handed over, that is, to chosen men, able, God-fearing, just, and hating pride, whom he should set over thousands, others over hundreds, others over fifties, and others over tens. In this way he both removed burdensome and dangerous occupations from Moses himself and did not overburden these men, since a thousand would have one over them, and under him ten others, and under them twenty others, and under these a hundred others, so that hardly anything would reach each of these officers that they would need to judge. Here too an example of humility is conveyed, in that Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or despise the advice of his foreign father-in-law. And yet it is rightly asked whether Jethro himself, though he was not an Israelite, should be counted among the men who worshiped the true God and were religiously wise, as Job was, though he did not belong to that people; indeed, it is held to be quite credible. For the words are ambiguous as to whether he sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law, and whether Moses himself bowed down to him; though even if the bowing down had been stated explicitly, it would seem to be honor paid to a father-in-law, in the way fathers customarily show it to men as a mark of respect, just as it is written of Abraham that he bowed down to the sons of Heth. But whom he means by grammatoeisagogeis, after the commanders of tens, cannot easily be known, since we have no such name in use for any office or post. Some have translated it "teachers," meaning, of course, teachers of letters, who introduce people to letters, as the Greek word suggests. Here, certainly, it is indicated that the Hebrews had letters before the law was given; but whether it can be traced when these began, I do not know. For some think that they began with the first men and were handed down to Noah, and from there to Abraham's forebears, and from there to the people of Israel; but how this could be proved, I do not know.

"In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the desert of Sinai. And they set out from Rephidim and came into the desert of Sinai, and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain. And Moses went up to the mountain of God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain, saying, 'Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel,'" and so on. Then a little later: "Go down and charge the people, and purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people." On this day, as what follows shows, we find that the law was given which was written on tablets of stone by the finger of God. And this third day is evidently that of the third month after Israel's departure from Egypt. So from the day on which they kept the Passover, that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth of the first month, up to this day on which the law is given, fifty days are counted: namely seventeen of the first month, the remaining days counted from the fourteenth itself; then all thirty of the second month, which makes forty-seven; and the third of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the feast of the slain lamb. And thus, in this shadow of what was to come, just as the law written by the finger of God was given on the fiftieth day after the feast of the sacrificed lamb, so in the very truth of the New Testament fifty days are counted from the feast of the spotless Lamb, Christ Jesus, until the Holy Spirit was given from on high. That the finger of God is the Holy Spirit we have already said above, on the testimony of the Gospel.

The question is how the ten commandments of the law are to be divided: whether there are four up to the commandment about the sabbath, which concern God himself, and the remaining six, the first of which is "Honor your father and mother," which concern human beings; or whether there are rather three of the former and seven of the latter. For those who say that there are four of the former separate the words "You shall have no other gods besides me," so that "You shall not make yourself an idol," and so on, where the worship of fashioned images is forbidden, is another commandment. But they want "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, you shall not covet your neighbor's house," and everything to the end, to be one commandment. Those, on the other hand, who say that there are three of the former and seven of the latter want whatever is commanded about worshiping the one God, so that nothing else besides him be worshiped as God, to be one commandment; but they divide these last words into two, so that "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife" is one commandment and "You shall not covet your neighbor's house" another. Yet neither side doubts that there are ten commandments, since Scripture bears witness to this.

To me, however, it seems more fitting to take the former as three and the latter as seven, because to those who look more carefully the commandments that concern God seem to point to the Trinity. And in fact the words "You shall have no other gods besides me" are explained more fully when the worship of man-made images is forbidden. Moreover, coveting another man's wife and coveting another man's house are so different as sins that other things are added to "You shall not covet your neighbor's house," for Scripture goes on: "nor his field, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his beast of burden, nor any of his livestock, nor anything that is your neighbor's." It seems, then, that Scripture set coveting another man's wife apart from coveting anything else that belongs to another, since it began each of them in the same way: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife"; "You shall not covet your neighbor's house," and it was to the latter that it began to attach the rest. It did not, after saying "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife," link other things to it by saying "nor his house, nor his field, nor his servant," and so on. Rather, it is quite plain that the things which seem to be contained in one commandment belong together, and are distinct from the commandment in which the wife is named. As for the words "You shall have no other gods besides me," it is plain that what follows is a more detailed working-out of this very point. For what do the words "You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above or on the earth below or in the water under the earth; you shall not bow down to them or serve them" refer to, if not to what was said: "You shall have no other gods besides me"?

But again it is asked how "You shall not steal" differs from what is commanded a little later about not coveting your neighbor's possessions. Certainly not everyone who covets his neighbor's property steals; but everyone who steals does covet his neighbor's property. So what concerns theft could also have been included in that general commandment about not coveting your neighbor's property. In the same way it is also asked how "You shall not commit adultery" differs from what is said a little later: "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife." For that too could have been understood within "You shall not commit adultery." Unless perhaps in the two sins of adultery and theft it is the deeds themselves that are marked out, while in these last ones it is the coveting itself. And these differ so much that sometimes a man commits adultery who does not covet his neighbor's wife but has intercourse with her for some other reason, and sometimes a man covets her but does not have intercourse with her because he fears punishment. And perhaps the law wished to show this: that both are sins.

Likewise it is often asked whether fornication is also covered by the term "moechia" (adultery). For this is a Greek word, which Scripture now uses in place of the Latin; yet in Greek "moechoi" means only adulterers. But surely this law was given not only to the men among the people but also to the women. For a woman must not think, just because it was said "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife," that nothing is commanded to her here, and that she may lawfully covet her neighbor's husband, so to speak. If, then, it is understood here from what was said to the man that the command also applies to the woman, even though this is not stated, how much more are both sexes bound by "You shall not commit adultery," since this very commandment can be applied to either, just like "You shall not kill," "You shall not steal," and the others which, not naming one sex in particular, seem to speak to both alike! Yet where one sex is named, it is of course the more honored one that is named, that is, the male, so that from this the woman too may understand what is commanded to her. And so, if a woman who has a husband is an adulteress by lying with a man who is not her husband, even if he has no wife, then surely a man who has a wife is also an adulterer by lying with a woman who is not his wife, even if she has no husband. But it is rightly asked whether a man who has no wife, or a woman who has no husband, is guilty of breaking this commandment if they do this. For if they are not, then fornication is not forbidden in the Decalogue, but only moechia, that is, adultery, although every act of adultery is understood also to be fornication, as the Scriptures speak. For the Lord says in the Gospel: "Whoever divorces his wife, except on the ground of fornication, makes her commit adultery." Here he certainly called it fornication if a woman who has a husband sins with another man, which is moechia, that is, adultery. So in the Scriptures every act of adultery is also called fornication. But whether every act of fornication can also be called adultery, I have not as yet come across an example of that usage in the same Scriptures. And if not every act of fornication can be called adultery, I do not know whether it can be found where in the Decalogue that fornication is forbidden which men who have no wives commit with women who have no husbands. But if the term "theft" is rightly understood to include every unlawful seizure of another's property—for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery; rather, he certainly wanted the whole to be understood from the part, namely whatever is unlawfully taken from a neighbor's possessions—then surely by the term "adultery" too every unlawful intercourse and every illegitimate use of those members ought to be understood as forbidden.

And as for the words "You shall not kill," it must not be thought that this commandment is broken when the law puts someone to death or when God commands someone to be killed. For the one who commands is the one who does it, when it is not lawful to refuse the service.

Concerning the words "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor," it is often asked whether every lie is forbidden, or whether perhaps this commandment is not aimed at those who say that one ought to lie when the lie benefits someone and does no harm to the person you are lying to. Such a lie, of course, is not "against your neighbor"; so it might seem that Scripture added this phrase for that reason, when it could have said briefly, "You shall not bear false witness," just as it said "You shall not kill," "You shall not commit adultery," "You shall not steal." But this is a great question, and it cannot be properly worked out by people in a hurry: how we are to take "You will destroy all who speak a lie," and "Do not wish to tell any lie," and other sayings of this kind.

"And all the people saw the voice and the torches and the voice of the trumpet and the mountain smoking." It is often asked how the people saw the voice, since a voice seems to belong not to sight but rather to hearing. But just as I have just said "seems" about everything I have said, so "see" is commonly used for perception in general, not only of the body but also of the mind. Hence also the saying "When Jacob saw that there was food in Egypt," though of course he was far away from it. Some, however, have thought that "seeing" the voice means nothing other than "understanding," which is the sight of the mind. But since the matter had to be put briefly here—that the people saw the voice and the torches and the voice of the trumpet and the smoking mountain—a greater question would have arisen if it had said they heard the torches and the smoking mountain, which belong to the sense of sight. Unless someone would say that it should not have been put so briefly, but the whole should have been spelled out: "they heard the voice and saw the torches and heard the voice of the trumpet and saw the smoking mountain." For there were two kinds of voice: one from the clouds, like thunder, and one from the trumpet—if indeed by "voice" he meant the one that came from the clouds. And so, since Scripture wanted to take in the whole briefly, it was better to apply the general sense, that is, sight, to the things that belonged to hearing, than to have hearing understood in the things that belong to sight: that is not a way we usually speak. For we often say "see what it sounds like," but we do not say "hear what it shines like."

"You speak to us, and do not let God speak to us, lest we die." This signifies strongly and firmly that fear belongs rather to the Old Testament, just as love belongs to the New, although the New lies hidden in the Old and the Old is laid open in the New. But how such a people could be credited with seeing the voice of God, if this is to be taken as "understanding," when they are afraid that God will speak to them and they will die, is not entirely clear.

"And Moses said to them: Be steadfast; for God has come to you to test you, so that his fear may be in you, that you may not sin." In this way they had to be held back from sins, namely by fear of suffering bodily punishments, because they were not yet able to love righteousness. And in this lay their testing by the Lord, by which they were proved, so that it might become plain what kind of people they were—not so that they might become known to God, from whom it was not hidden what they were, but to one another and to themselves. Yet in these terrors the distinctive character of the Old Testament is strongly brought out, as is also said very plainly in the Letter to the Hebrews.

"But Moses entered into the cloud where God was"—that is, where clearer signs were being given by which God might be known. For how was he in a cloud, he whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain? Only in the way that he who is in no place is nowhere absent.

"You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves." What was impressed in the first commandment is repeated; and by gods of silver and gold all images are of course to be understood, as also in that psalm: "The idols of the nations are silver and gold."

As for what is commanded about the Hebrew slave, that he should serve six years and be let go free without payment: so that Christian slaves would not demand this of their masters, apostolic authority commands slaves to be subject to their masters, lest the name of God and his teaching be blasphemed. For it is clear enough that this was commanded as a mystery, from the fact that God also commanded that the ear of a slave who refused that freedom be pierced with an awl against the doorpost.

"If anyone sells his daughter as a maidservant, she shall not go out as the female slaves depart. If she does not please her master, who has not named her as his, he shall compensate her. But he is not master to sell her to a foreign nation, since he has slighted her. If he names her for his son, he shall deal with her according to the right of daughters. If he takes another for him, he shall not defraud her of what she needs, her clothing and her companionship. And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out free without price." Unusual words and expressions have made this passage so very obscure that our translators could hardly find a way to explain it. Even in the Greek itself what is said here is very obscure. Nevertheless, I will set out, as best I can, what seems to be meant.

"If anyone," it says, "sells his daughter as a maidservant"—that is, to be a maidservant, which the Greeks call [?]—"she shall not go out as the female slaves depart." This is to be understood as: "she shall not depart in the way Hebrew female slaves depart after six years." For we must understand that the law given for males also applies to a Hebrew woman. Why, then, will this woman not depart in the same way, unless because she is understood to have been humbled in that service by her master having had intercourse with her? This becomes somewhat clearer in what follows. For it goes on to say: "If she does not please her master, who has not named her as his"—that is, has not made her his wife—"he shall compensate her"; this is what it said above: "she shall not go out as the female slaves depart." For it is just that she receive something for having been humbled, since he did not have intercourse with her in such a way as to make her his wife, that is, to name her as his own. Where we have said "he shall compensate her," some translators have said "he shall redeem her"; but if that were what was said, the Greek would have been written ἀπολώσεται [?], as it is written: "And he himself will redeem Israel"; for there ἀπολυτρώσεται is written. In this place, however, we read ἀπολυτρώσει, where it is understood that she receives something, rather than that something is paid for her so that she may be redeemed. For to whom would her master pay, to redeem a woman whom he himself owns as a maidservant? "But he is not master to sell her to a foreign nation, since he has slighted her"—that is, it is not because he has slighted her that he is master to sell her; in other words, he will not have such power over her that he may lawfully sell her even to a foreign nation.
