"He has slighted in her" is the same as "he has slighted her"; and "he has slighted her" means "he has humbled her," that is, by lying with her and not making her his wife. The Greek has ἠθέτησεν, which we have rendered "slighted": a word Scripture uses in Jeremiah: "As a woman slights the man with whom she has intercourse."

Then it goes on to say: "If he names her for his son, he shall deal with her according to the right of daughters." Here it begins to become clear what was meant above by "who has not named her as his." For what else does "if he names her for his son" mean but "if he joins her to his son as a wife"? For it says: "he shall deal with her according to the right of daughters," that is, "he shall give her away as though she were a daughter," namely by providing her with a dowry. Then it adds: "If he takes another for him"—that is, if he does not assign this woman as a wife to his son but takes another for him—"he shall not defraud her of what she needs, her clothing and her companionship"; he shall give her what is due by the same rule, since she did not remain his son's wife, just as he would give to her if he had not named her as his own and yet had humbled her by lying with her. Where we have said "he shall not defraud her of her companionship," the Greek has ὁμιλίαν, that is, "speech," a word by which Scripture is understood to refer more decently to intercourse. And what does "he shall not defraud her of the intercourse" mean but "he shall pay her a fee for the intercourse"? For in Daniel, the elders who bore false witness against Susanna say: "A young man, who had been hidden in concealment, came to her and lay with her." And Daniel, questioning them about this very thing, says: "Under what tree did you see them talking together?"—for what they had said: "he lay with her." Then, refuting and convicting the other, he said: "Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you and lust has perverted your heart; this is how you used to treat the daughters of Israel, and they in fear consented to you." But the Greek has ὠμίλουσαν ὐμῖν, which could be put in Latin word for word as "they spoke with you," by which intercourse would be signified. Again, where he says: "Under what tree did you catch them?" the Greek has: "did you catch them talking with each other?" And there too intercourse is signified.

So when Scripture adds about this woman under discussion: "And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out free," it is understood to mean this: if he has not himself humbled her by intercourse, nor joined her to his son, nor cast her off when his son has married another, she shall go out free—that is, it is enough for her not to be held in slavery; for she shall go out receiving nothing, like a Hebrew slave. For her master is not allowed to unite her to a man who is not a Hebrew, since she may not be handed over to a foreign nation. But if he has united her to a Hebrew slave, it is surely understood that she will go out free with him, and by no means be separated from her husband.

"If anyone strikes a man and he dies, let him surely be put to death. But if he did not intend it, but God delivered him into his hands, I will give you a place to which he may flee." The question here is why it says, "But if he did not intend it, but God delivered him into his hands," as if a man who kills intentionally could kill unless God delivered the victim into his hands. It is to be understood, then, that when someone is killed by a person who did not intend it, God alone has done it; and because God alone did it, it is said, "but God delivered him into his hands." When a man kills intentionally, however, both he kills and God delivered the victim into his hands. The difference, then, is this: in the one case God alone acted; in the other both God and the man acted, the man because of the will of the one doing it, but not in the same way as God. For God acts only justly, whereas the man deserves punishment, not because he killed someone whom God did not want killed, but because he did it through wickedness. He did not render service to God's command; he served his own malicious desire. In one and the same deed, therefore, God is praised for his hidden justice and the man is punished for his own wickedness. For it is not the case that, because God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, Judas, who delivered that same Christ to death, is therefore excused.

"But if two men quarrel and strike a woman who is with child, and her infant comes forth not yet formed, he shall suffer a penalty: as much as the woman's husband imposes, and he shall pay it with a request." It seems to me that these things are said for the sake of some figurative meaning rather than because Scripture is concerned with deeds of this kind. For if it were attending to this, that a pregnant woman should not be struck and driven to miscarry, it would not posit two men quarrelling, since this could also be committed by one man who had quarrelled with the woman herself, or even had not quarrelled but did it from a wish to harm another man's offspring. But in refusing to count an unformed fetus as a matter of homicide, it plainly did not regard what is carried in the womb in that state as a human being. Here the question about the soul is commonly raised: whether what is not formed cannot even be understood to be ensouled, and is therefore not homicide, because it cannot be said to have been deprived of soul if it did not yet have one. For it goes on to say: "But if it was formed, he shall give life for life." What else is to be understood here but "he himself shall die"? For on this occasion it goes on to lay down the same for other cases as well: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise" — that is, by the equity of retaliation. The law established this in order to show what punishment is owed. For unless it were known through the law what punishment was owed, how would it be known what pardon remits, so that one could say, "And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors"? Debtors, then, are pointed out by the law, so that when pardon is given it may be clear what is being forgiven. For we would not forgive debts unless we learned, with the law as our informant, what was owed to us. If, then, that unformed fetus already existed but was still in some way ensouled in an unformed manner — for the great question about the soul must not be rushed into with the rashness of an unexamined opinion — the law refused to count it as homicide because a living soul cannot yet be said to be in a body that lacks sensation, if the soul is such in flesh not yet formed and therefore not yet endowed with senses. But what it means by "and he shall pay it with a request" — the amount the woman's husband had set to be paid when the unformed fetus was expelled — is not easy to understand. The word the Greek has, axioma, can be understood in several ways, and "with a request" is a more tolerable rendering than anything else would be. Perhaps he will ask to be allowed to pay, so as in this way to make satisfaction to God, even if the husband or the woman does not demand it.

"But if a bull gores a man or a woman with its horn and they die, the bull shall be stoned with stones and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull shall be innocent." It belongs to justice that an animal harmful to human beings should be destroyed. And what is laid down about the bull is to be understood as a part standing for the whole: whatever among the beasts made subject to human use is dangerous to people. But if it must be killed, must it be stoned? What does it matter by what death an animal that is to be done away with is done away with? And then the addition that its flesh is not to be eaten — what is its point, unless all these things signify something, which is what Scripture chiefly has in view?

"But if someone's bull gores his neighbor's bull with its horn and it dies, they shall sell the living bull and divide its price, and they shall divide the bull that died." Is this ordinance to be observed only in the case of a bull, and not in such a case with any beast? So this too must be understood as a part standing for the whole; but with regard to the flesh of the slain animal this cannot be done in the case of animals that are not eaten.
What sort of ordinance is it that five should be repaid for one calf and four for a sheep, unless it is understood to signify something?

"But if a thief is found breaking in and is struck and dies, it is not homicide for the one who struck him; but if the sun has risen upon him, he is guilty; he shall die in return for the death." It is understood, then, that it does not count as homicide if a thief is killed at night, but that it does if he is killed by day; for that is what it means by "if the sun has risen upon him." For then it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore he ought not to be killed. This is also found in the ancient secular laws — though this law is older than they — that a thief by night may be killed with impunity in any manner, but a thief by day only if he defends himself with a weapon, for then he is already more than a thief.
What does it mean: "Whoever is convicted through God shall restore double"? Only that God wills at times to expose a perjurer by giving a sign.

"You shall not curse gods." The question is whom it calls gods. Does it mean the rulers who judge the people, as it was said of Moses that he was given as a god to Pharaoh, so that what follows is said by way of explanation, as if to show whom it called gods, when it says, "and you shall not curse the ruler of your people" (where the Greek has "you shall not speak evil of")? Or is it to be taken in line with what the apostle says: "For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords"? For by adding "as indeed there are" he wanted those to be understood who are also called so fittingly. This is certainly so, but on the understanding that what the Greeks call latreia, which is translated in Latin as servitus (service) — but service understood as belonging to religion — is owed to none but the one true God, who is our God. As for those who are called gods, even if there are some who are rightly so called, we are forbidden to curse them, but we are not commanded to honor them with sacrifices or with any acts of worship (latreia).
"You shall not be with the many in wickedness." That is, let no one defend himself on the ground that he did it along with many, or think that it is therefore not a sin.

"And you shall not show pity to a poor man in judgment." Had it not added "in judgment," there would be a great question. But it would have had to be understood even if it had not been written; for it had said just before: "You shall not join with the multitude to turn aside with the many so as to pervert judgment." And so "and you shall not show pity to a poor man" could have been understood as "in judgment." But since this is added, there is no question that the command is this: that when we are judging and see that justice is on the side of the rich man against the poor, we should not think we are acting rightly if we favor the poor man against justice for the sake of mercy. Mercy, then, is good, but it must not be against judgment — and by judgment Scripture of course means what is just. But lest anyone suppose on account of this statement that God forbids mercy, what follows follows most fittingly: "But if you come upon your enemy's ox or his beast of burden straying, you shall lead it back and return it to him." So that you may know you are not forbidden to show mercy, show it even toward your enemies when your authority is free from the office of judging. For when you lead back your enemy's straying ox and return it, you are not sitting as judge between parties.

"For six years you shall sow your land and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year you shall grant it release and give it rest, and the poor of your nation shall eat; and what remains the wild beasts shall eat. So you shall do with your vineyard and your olive grove." It may be asked what the poor are to gather, if in the seventh year the land is so spared that it is not even sown — for the words "the poor of your nation shall eat" do not refer to the vineyard and the olive grove — since they can take nothing from unsown land, where crops cannot grow. As for the vineyard and the olive grove, it says afterwards that the same is to be done with them; and therefore the former is understood of the fields that serve for grain. Or is it to be taken thus: "For six years you shall sow your land and gather its fruit," that is, for six years you shall sow and gather; but in the seventh you shall not gather — so that "you shall sow" is understood even though it is not said, sowing and gathering belonging to the six years, while to the seventh belongs leaving alone what has been sown? For otherwise what will the poor have from it, whose leftovers he has even given to the wild beasts — those, that is, which can feed on such produce, like boars and deer and any others of that kind? This, however, would not be said except for the sake of some figurative meaning. For if, so far as the commandments given to human beings are concerned, God does not care for oxen — which is not to be understood as though he does not himself feed the creatures that neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, but that it is not his concern to instruct a man by commandment on how to look after his ox — how much less is it his concern to give commandments about wild beasts, as to how human beings should look after them, since he himself feeds them from the riches of a nature fruitful everywhere, and feeds them also during the other six years, when what is sown is gathered!

"You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk": I do not know whether any way can be found to understand this according to the literal sense of the words. For if we take it that cooking a lamb in milk was forbidden for the sake of some figurative meaning, there is no practice of cooking it that way. And if it means during the days when it is suckling, which of the Jews ever made it an observance not to cook a lamb until it had stopped sucking? And what does "in its mother's milk" mean? As if, even on this understanding, it could be cooked without transgressing this commandment if its mother died after it was born and it was suckled by another ewe! No one doubts, surely, that the commandment exists for the sake of signifying something. Yet even those commandments that can actually be carried out in observance were not given so without reason; they too signify something. But how this one could be observed according to the literal sense of the words either is not possible or is not clear. I do approve, however, the interpretation concerning Christ: that this prophecy foretold that as an infant he would not be killed by the Jews, when Herod sought him to kill him and did not find him — so that "you shall cook" refers to the fire of suffering, that is, tribulation. Hence it is said: "The furnace tests the potter's vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just men." Because, then, he did not suffer as an infant, when Herod sought him and danger of this kind seemed to threaten, it was foretold in these words: "You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk" — "you shall not kill Christ"; for the prophecy appears to be warning the good Israelites not to join the wicked Jews by whom Christ suffered. For the tribulation of suffering is like fire. Hence it is written: "Like gold in the furnace he tested them, and like a whole burnt offering he accepted them." The Lord also bears witness to this meaning when he says, "I have a baptism to be baptized with, which you do not know"; for he said this after saying, "I came to cast fire upon the world." And John says: "He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire," which is understood both of the cleansing of sanctification and of the testing of tribulation. He himself also signified this same fire when he was being led to his passion, when he told those who were lamenting him that they ought rather to lament for themselves. For he concluded by saying: "If they do this in the green wood, what will they do in the dry?" The good, then, are warned not to consent with the wicked in crucifying Christ. For he is called the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. So, "You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk": you shall not bring the fire of suffering upon Christ on the day on which he was conceived. For tradition holds that he also suffered on that day, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], from which day to the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December], the day his birth is celebrated, nine months are counted, the tenth having begun. And women's breasts are said to gather milk from the day of conception. But there is another, easier sense. "You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk": one still little and suckling — such as those to whom the apostle says, "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food" — you shall not send into premature suffering. It is as if this were said to Christ, who spared his disciples while they were still of this kind, offering himself for them and saying, "If, then, you are seeking me, let these go." And so that it might be understood that they were still weak and not yet fit for suffering, like lambs in their mother's milk, the evangelist went on to say: "so that the word which he spoke might be fulfilled: Of those whom you gave me I have not lost a single one." From this it is clear that if they had suffered then, they would have perished; for they did not suffer then what they suffered later, when they were no longer lambs in milk but rams in the flock. Nor perhaps is what others say absurd: that this was commanded through the prophet so that the good Israelites should not join the wicked Jews by whom Christ suffered like a lamb in its mother's milk, that is, at the time at which he was conceived. For women are said to gather milk from the time they conceive; and that Christ was both conceived and suffered in that month is shown both by the observance of Easter and by the day of his birth, so well known to the churches. For one who was born in the ninth month, around the eighth day before the Kalends of January, was surely conceived in the first month, around the eighth day before the Kalends of April. That was also the time of his passion — "in his mother's milk," that is, in the days of his mother's milk.

"Behold, I send my angel before your face, to keep you on the way, to bring you into the land which I have prepared for you. Take heed to yourself and listen to him. Do not fail to believe him; for he will withhold nothing from you; for my name is upon him." This is undoubtedly to be understood of the one whose name was changed so that he was called Jesus — that is, Joshua; for it was he who brought the people into the land of promise.

"And you shall serve the Lord your God, and I will bless your bread and your wine and your water, and I will turn sickness away from you. There shall be none who does not bear, nor any barren one, in your land. I will fill up the number of your days. And I will send fear to go before you, and I will drive mad all the nations into which you will enter," and so on. Although these promises can also be understood spiritually, nevertheless when they are understood in terms of people's temporal happiness, they belong to the Old Testament. There, although the commandments pertaining to good conduct are found to be the same — apart from those that signify something as sacraments — the promises are carnal and earthly. That is why in the seventy-second psalm the man of God says that his steps had nearly slipped and given way, when he was envious of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners. For he saw the ungodly abounding in the very things which he himself, according to the Old Testament, was expecting from the Lord God, whom he served for this reward. And when an ungodly thought had begun to creep in on him from this — that he supposed God did not care about human affairs — he says that he was set right, since he did not dare to reject the authority of the saints, and undertook to understand, and said: "This is a toil before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand the last things." For there the rewards belonging to the New Testament will be given, which the ungodly will not receive; and then will come the punishments of the ungodly, which none of the godly will feel.

"And I will send wasps before you, and they will drive out the Amorites and the Hivites and the Canaanites and the Hittites from before you." The question is what is to be understood by these wasps. For God both promises this and the book of Wisdom says it was fulfilled, where it says: "And he sent wasps as forerunners of his army." Yet we do not read that it happened, either in the time of Moses, or under Joshua son of Nun, or under the judges, or under the kings. And so these wasps are perhaps to be understood as the stings of fear by which the nations mentioned were driven to give way to the children of Israel. For it is God who speaks, and if something is said figuratively in his speech which was not fulfilled literally, this does not impair the trustworthiness of the history, in which the truth of the narrative is plain to see — just as the narrative of the evangelists is not impaired in its literal sense if something is said figuratively by Christ.

"If you serve their gods, they will be a stumbling block to you." Here the Greek has douleusēs, not latreusēs. From this it is understood that douleia (service) is owed to God as Lord, but latreia (worship) is owed only to God as God.

"And he said to Moses: Come up to the Lord, you and Aaron and Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, and they shall worship the Lord from afar. And Moses alone shall approach the Lord, but they shall not approach; and the people shall not go up with them. And Moses went in and told the people all the words of God and the ordinances. And all the people answered with one voice, saying: All the words which the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear." Up to this point in Scripture are understood to be the ordinances that were given to the people to observe. They begin, as far as the words of Scripture themselves indicate — that is, the point from which this term "ordinances" begins — with the Hebrew slave whose ear is pierced at the doorpost. In all these ordinances one must consider what can be drawn from them for the conduct of life and the preservation of good morals. For there are many sacraments in them that signify something rather than instruct our life. The Latin translators, of course, have called "ordinances" what the Greeks call dikaiōmata.

It should be noted that the people again answer thus: "All the words which the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear," when the natural order would seem to require "we will hear and we will do." But it would be surprising if some meaning did not lie hidden here. For if "we will hear" is put for "we will understand," then one must first render to God's words the service of doing them, so that he himself may lead us to understand the things that are done at his command, by the merit of the devotion with which they were not scorned but done. But we must consider whether this people is not found to resemble that son who said to his father's command, "I will go into the vineyard," and did not go. For the Gentiles, who had utterly scorned the Lord, were afterwards justified through the obedience of one; they who did not pursue righteousness have attained righteousness.

It should be noted that Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain, with twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. For the altar built of twelve stones is understood to have signified that the people itself is the altar of God, just as it is the temple of God.

"And they sacrificed a victim of salvation to God." It did not say "a saving victim" but "a victim of salvation," for the Greek has sōtēriou. So too in the psalm it says, "I will take the cup of salvation," not "the saving cup." Here we must consider whether he is perhaps signified of whom Simeon said, "For my eyes have seen your salvation." For the psalm too commends him, where we read: "Proclaim well, day from day, his salvation." For if we attend more carefully, what else does "day from day" mean but light from light, that is, God from God, which is the only-begotten Son?

"And Moses took half of the blood and poured it into a bowl, and the rest of the blood he poured out against the altar. And taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people." It should be noted that this is the first time Scripture plainly says that Moses offered sacrifice since the people were brought out of Egypt. For earlier it had been said of Jethro, his father-in-law, though with some ambiguity, that he sacrificed to God. And it should be observed that the book of the covenant is read along with the blood of the victim; in this book we should take it that those ordinances were written down. For it was made clear later that the Decalogue of the law was written on tablets of stone.
"And they said: All that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear." See, now for the third time they answer in no other way.

"And Moses and Aaron and Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the place where the God of Israel had stood." It is agreed among those who understand rightly that God is contained in no place and does not dispose his limbs in any bodily posture, as our bodies do — sitting, lying, standing, and anything of that kind. For these belong only to bodies, but God is spirit. When, therefore, he shows himself in bodily form or through signs expressed in bodily ways, it is not his substance that appears, by which he is what he is; rather, the assumption of visible forms is subject to his omnipotence.

And of the chosen of Israel not even one was out of accord; and they appeared in the place of God, and they ate and drank. Who would doubt that those whom it named one by one, together with the seventy elders, are now called the chosen of Israel? Beyond doubt they represented those who are chosen among the people of God. For not all have faith, and the Lord knows those who are his; and in a great house there are some vessels for honor and others for dishonor. Since, then, those whom he foreknew he also predestined, and those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified, it is certain that of the chosen of Israel not even one was out of accord. They are signified by the number four in Moses, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, because of the four Gospels and the promise to the whole world, which is divided into four parts; and by the seventy of the elders of Israel, that is, the number seven multiplied by ten, which serves to signify the Holy Spirit. The sapphire signifies the heavenly life, above all because it is said: "like the appearance of the firmament." And who does not know that the firmament is called heaven? The form of the brick in that same sapphire figures squareness itself, or stability, or the mystery of that same number four. That they eat and drink in the place of God signifies the sweetness and fullness in that kingdom of eternity. For blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Hence the Lord too says that many will come—who, indeed, if not the chosen, the foreknown, the predestined, the called, the justified, the glorified?—and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. For in another place he himself promises this to his faithful: that he will make them recline, and will pass by and serve them.

What does it mean that Joshua son of Nun, who was not mentioned among those four, suddenly appears with Moses and goes up with him onto the mountain to receive the tablets of the law; and then suddenly Joshua is hidden again, that is, passed over in silence; and Moses receives the law on two tablets, and Joshua appears with him again? Does it perhaps signify, under the name of Joshua—that is, Jesus—the New Testament, which is both hidden in the law and at some point appears to those who understand? As for his already being called Joshua, when Scripture testifies in the book of Numbers to the time he received that name, when they were already close to entering the land of promise: this is by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, Scripture anticipating what was done later. For all these things were written after they were done; and so, when the event now being recounted took place, he was not yet called Joshua, but when it was written he was already called so.

And you shall make on it twisted golden moldings all around. By "moldings" it means those that stand out around the square on all four sides, as is usually done on square tables. Nor should we take "twisted" to mean movable—for they are fixed, as I said tables usually have them—but by "twisted" it meant "wreathed," what in Greek are called strepta, either fluted, like twisted columns, or made of two rods wound together like a rope, as necklaces are also commonly made. And as for its saying: And you shall make for it four golden rings and put them on the four sides: two rings on one side and two rings on the other side, the four rings fall at the four corners, one at each, and by the number of corners it comes about that what is placed on two sides is placed on all four. For one corner is common to two sides; otherwise it would not work out that two rings are placed on each of four sides when there are four rings; there would have had to be eight, if it were understood otherwise than as I have said, according to the number of corners. For the rings are placed at the corners in order that the carrying poles, or bearing poles, may be put through them, by which the ark is carried by four men, from this side and that.

People often ask what is meant by the mercy seat to be placed on top of the ark. But since it orders it to be made of gold, and specifies its length and breadth as the same as those stated for the ark itself, without doubt it commands that a kind of golden plate of that size be made, by which the ark would be covered, with two cherubim on the mercy seat itself, on either side, facing each other, so that their faces were toward the mercy seat and they overshadowed the mercy seat with their wings. This is a great mystery. For gold signifies wisdom, and the ark signifies the secret of God. In the ark were to be placed the law, the manna and the rod of Aaron: in the law are the commandments; the rod signifies power, the manna grace, because without grace there is no power to do the commandments. Yet because the law is not fulfilled in every part by anyone, however far he advances, the mercy seat is on top: for this is needed, that God be merciful; and it is placed on top because mercy triumphs over judgment. The two cherubim overshadow the mercy seat with their wings, that is, they honor it by veiling it, since those mysteries are there; and they face each other, because they are in harmony—for the two testaments are figured there—and their faces are toward the mercy seat, because they strongly commend the mercy of God, in which alone is hope. Accordingly God promised that he would speak to Moses from there, from between the cherubim above the mercy seat. Further, if the rational creature in the fullness of knowledge—since this is the interpretation of "cherubim"—is signified by these two living beings, then they are two in order to commend the fellowship of love; they overshadow the mercy seat with their wings because they attribute their wings to God, not to themselves, that is, they honor God with the virtues in which they excel; and their faces are turned only toward the mercy seat, because for any progress toward the fullness of knowledge there is no hope except in the mercy of God.

As for its saying: the rings shall be in the sheaths for the carrying poles, to lift the table, this is to be understood as meaning that the rings were like sheaths for the carrying poles; that is, the carrying poles are put through them as into sheaths. For "they shall be in the sheaths" is said as if it were said: they shall serve as sheaths.

He orders the tabernacle to be made of ten curtains, since the law is a decalogue. The curtains signify breadth, by reason of ease. For love is the fulfillment of the law, and the commandments are easy only for love. Hence this very enlarging is commended when it is said: You have enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footsteps have not been weakened. But since this enlarging comes about through the grace of God—for the love of God has been poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us—therefore the very number that also pertains to the Holy Spirit, through whom the law can be fulfilled, is mystically commended here as well. For it is said that a curtain should have a length of twenty-eight cubits. And that this number is to be divided by seven it indicated when it gives the breadth of a curtain as four cubits. For four times seven makes twenty-eight. This number is also perfect, because, like the number six, it is made up of the sum of its parts. And when it says so often: You shall make them with cherubim, the work of a weaver, what else does it commend in all these things than the fullness of knowledge, which is the meaning of "cherubim"?

And you shall make curtains of hair to cover the tabernacle; you shall make eleven curtains. These curtains of hair, that is, of goats' hair cloth, are said to be eleven. For in sins there is transgression, and transgression is signified by the number eleven, since it goes beyond ten, that is, the law. Therefore these eleven multiplied by seven make seventy-seven, by which the Lord signified the complete remission of sins when he said: not only seven times but even seventy-seven times; for that is how many generations are found when Luke, counting upward from the Lord's baptism, ascends through Adam all the way to God. For the purpose of signifying sins in these curtains is that they may be expressed through confession and abolished, that is, covered, through the grace given to the Church: whence it is said: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Next he orders those curtains to be covered with rams' skins dyed red. And to whom does a ram dyed red not call to mind Christ, bloodied by his passion? These also signify the holy martyrs, by whose prayers God is made propitious toward the sins of his people. Finally, over these are laid skins of hyacinth blue, to signify eternal life by their freshness, as by unfailing vigor.

You shall make two brackets for each column, set opposite each other, that is, one on this side and one on that side of the column. By "brackets" (anconisci) it means what we commonly call ancones, such as there are on the columns of wine cellars, on which rest the beams that bear the casks. The word is drawn by analogy from the elbows, where the arms bend, on which people lean when reclining; in Greek these are called ankones.

Two bases for each column. Scripture seems to call bases not only those by which columns are supported from below but also the upper ones, which we call capitals. That is why it says: two bases for each column, at both its ends. For what are both its ends, if not the upper and the lower?

As for Scripture's speaking of eight columns and their sixteen bases, according to the reckoning given above, at the rear of the tabernacle, though earlier it had said six, it is understood that by adding the two corner columns they make eight.

And the veil shall divide for you between the holy place and the holy of holies: that is, this veil of which it now speaks, stretched upon four columns, is to be between the holy place and the holy of holies. The Epistle to the Hebrews speaks of this distinction between the holy place and the holy of holies: where the ark of the testimony is, there is the holy of holies, that is, inside, beyond the veil; while outside, the table and the lampstand and the other things whose making it described a little earlier are called the holy things, and not the holy of holies. The outside signifies the Old Testament, and the inside the New, although both are in the reading of the Old Testament, the one expressed in works, the other figured in signification. And so in the holy place there is a figure of a figure, because it is a figure of the Old Testament; but in the holy of holies there is a figure of the truth itself, because it is a figure of the New Testament. For the whole Old Testament, in these things and rites that are commanded to be observed in this way, is a figure.

Concerning the altar, the question is asked how he could have wanted it to be three cubits high, since that is about the height of a man's stature. How then was the altar served, when in another place he forbids the altar to have steps, saying: lest you uncover your nakedness upon it? But there he was speaking of an altar to be built of earth or stones, where the steps, built together with it, would certainly belong to the body of the altar; whereas here he commands the altar to be made of boards, so that if something were set beside it for the hour of service, on which the minister of the altar could stand, and were removed when the service was finished, it would certainly not belong to the body of the altar. It is also asked how the sacrifice offered on a wooden altar could be burned, especially since he orders it to be made hollow and a grate of network to be placed down to its middle, that is, to the middle of its hollow. Is it perhaps that, since he said: and you shall make horns at the four corners; the horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay them with bronze, the words "you shall overlay them with bronze" are to be referred not only to the horns but to everything he was speaking of in giving instructions for building the altar?

And you shall speak to all who are wise in mind, whom I have filled with the spirit of understanding. The Greek indeed has αἴσθησις, which in Latin we usually render "sense," not "understanding"; but Scripture is accustomed to speak in this way of the inner sense, which we call understanding, as in Hebrews: but solid food is for the mature, for those who through practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil. For there, where it put "senses," the Greek has αἰσθήσεως. What spirit, then, ought we to take this to be, if not the Holy Spirit?

And the robes that they shall make: a breastpiece, a shoulder-piece, a full-length tunic, and a tunic with clusters. Note that these are called robes, and the rest too, although earlier he had proposed that a single robe was to be made. As for "a tunic with clusters," the Latin translators thought this a more seemly way to put it than if they had said "with tufts"; well-arranged tufts usually serve as an ornament to garments.

What does he mean by the aspidiscae on the priestly garment? Little shields, named in Latin from scutum, "shield," since the Greeks too call a shield aspis [?]? Or does he say aspidiscae from the asp, the serpent, because of how carefully they are to be fastened together, just as certain ornaments are also called "morays"? A span its length and a span its breadth. Some Latin translators have rendered this as "the measure of the outstretched hand from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger." And the stones are to bear the names of the sons of Israel according to their births, that is, in the order in which they were born.

And you shall make on the rationale fringes that interlock, chain-work of pure gold. That the Latins translated this as "rationale" was due to the poverty of the language. For the Greek has λόγιον, not λογικόν. What we usually call rationale, "rational," is what the Greeks call λογικόν. But since λόγος in the Greek language is ambiguous, meaning either "word" or "reason," being the name for both things, where λόγιον was thought to be derived from "word" our translators rendered it "utterance"; for where we have: The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, the Greeks have λόγια. Here, however, in the priestly garment, there was commanded to be made, of gold and blue and purple and doubled twisted scarlet and doubled twisted fine linen, a doubled square that was to lie on the priest's breast and be called λόγιον; and since it was uncertain whether this was derived from "reason" or from "word," our translators, thinking it named rather from reason, called it "rationale."

And you shall put upon the rationale of judgment the manifestation and the truth. What this means, or in what material or metal the manifestation and the truth were to be placed on the rationale, is hard to discover, since he says that such things were made in the priest's garment as are made physically. Some, however, tell the story that it was a stone whose color would change toward adversity or toward prosperity when the priest entered the holy place, and that this is what he means when he says: and Aaron shall bear the judgments of the sons of Israel upon his breast, showing, that is, in that manifestation and truth what the Lord had judged concerning them. Yet it could also be understood that the manifestation and the truth were placed on the λόγιον in letters.

And you shall make a full-length tunic of blue, that is, one hanging down to the ankles. And there shall be a neck-opening from it in the middle (that is, where the head is put through, for this is what the Greeks call περιστόμιον), having a border all around the neck-opening, the work of a weaver, a <seam> woven together, that is, so that the border itself is not sewn on from outside; this seems to be what he means by "a seam woven together." Hence he also added: from the garment itself, so that it may not tear, that is, so that the border itself is woven together with the garment out of the garment itself.

And Aaron, when he begins to perform the priesthood, his voice shall be heard as he goes into the holy place before the Lord and as he comes out, so that he may not die. He said that the voice of the one entering and leaving is heard from the little bells, and he laid such weight of observance on this as to say: so that he may not die. He wished, then, certain testimonies to be signified by these bells in the priestly garment, by which the Church is certainly signified, so that the priest's way of life might be known, as the apostle says: Show yourself in all things an example of good works, or this: What you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these same things to faithful men who are fit to teach others also. Or is something else meant? Whatever it is, it is something great. "As he goes in" and "as he comes out," in the dative, is an idiom for "of the one going in and coming out." And "voice" stands for "sound"; for little bells have a sound rather than a voice.

And you shall make a plate of pure gold, and you shall form on it the impression of a seal: Holiness of the Lord. And you shall put it upon a doubled twisted blue cord, and it shall be upon the miter; it shall be on the front of the miter. And it shall be upon Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel shall sanctify, of every gift of their holy things. I do not see how "Holiness of the Lord" could be formed on the plate except by some letters, which some say were four Hebrew letters, because they believe that the τετραγράμματον, as the Greeks call it, was, or is to this day, the ineffable name of God. But whatever those letters were or however they stood, as I said, I would believe that the holiness of the Lord, or the sanctification, if that is the better word, since the Greek has ἁγίασμα, could only have been formed on the gold in letters. There, moreover, he says that the priest takes away the sins of the holy things. Whatever the sons of Israel shall sanctify, he says, of every gift of their holy things: I think this is said of those sacrifices which they offer for their sins, so that we are to understand not "of holy men" but "of holy things," in the sense that what is offered for sins is holy. So having spoken of the plate, he added: and Aaron shall take away the sins of the holy things, whatever the sons of Israel shall sanctify, of every gift of their holy things; that is, the priest shall take away whatever they offer for their sins, which are called both "holy things," because they are sanctified, and "sins," because they are offered for sins, just as scripture plainly states this very thing in many places. But when he adds: and it shall always be upon Aaron's forehead, acceptable for them before the Lord, he returns to that plate, in which the ornament of the forehead is understood, the confidence of a good life. Only one who is a priest truly and perfectly, not in a sign but in truth, has this; he alone can take away sins, and he has no need to offer for his own.

When he spoke to Moses giving instructions about Aaron and Aaron's sons, how they were to be clothed and anointed, what does he mean by saying: and you shall fill their hands, so that they may perform the priesthood for me? Perhaps with gifts that are to be offered to God?

And you shall make for them linen breeches to cover the shame of their skin; they shall reach from the loins to the thighs. Since such an amount of clothing covers the whole body, what does he mean by saying: you shall make linen breeches to cover the shame of their skin, as though it could show when so much clothing was put on over it? Unless he wished this to be a sign of chastity or continence, which is signified by a garment precisely so that it may be understood as not possessed of oneself but given.

When speaking of Aaron's sons he says: and you shall clothe them with tunics and gird them with sashes and put cidares around them. What he means by cidaris or cidares is unknown, since it has not been translated and is not in use now. I think, however, that it is not a head-covering, as some have thought. For he would not say "you shall put around them" unless it were something of a kind that served not for the head but for the body.

And the priesthood shall be theirs for me forever. How he says "forever" of these signifying things we have often explained above. For this priesthood was certainly changed, so that it might be theirs for eternity according to the order of Melchizedek, not according to the order of Aaron. For there we have both an oath and no repentance on God's part, by which the change is signified. For the Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are, he says, a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Of the order of Aaron, "forever" was indeed said, either because no time was prescribed for how long it was to be observed, or because it signified eternal things; nowhere, however, was it said of Aaron's priesthood that the Lord swore and will not repent. And so it was said of that priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek: he will not repent, to signify that he did repent of the priesthood of Aaron, that is, he changed it.

What does this mean: and you shall complete the hands of Aaron and the hands of his sons? Did he signify power by "hands," so that they too could consecrate something, while that power itself was being completed by the sanctification with which they were commanded to be sanctified by Moses?

And you shall bring the calf to the door of the tabernacle of testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands upon the calf's head before the Lord. See, this is why it was said above that their hands were to be completed, that is, their power was to be brought to completion, so that they too might sanctify; this happens now, when they lay their hands on the calf to be sacrificed.

When the sacrifice of animal victims is often called in the holy scriptures a sweet odor to the Lord, it is certainly not that God delights in the odor of that smoke; rather, only what is signified spiritually by these things delights God when it is offered spiritually, since God's very sense of smell is understood spiritually. For he does not draw in odor through bodily nostrils as we do. As, then, he smells, so these things signify.
And you shall take the breast of the ram of completion, which is Aaron's, that is, which belongs to this Aaron. For he wished this to belong to the high priest.

And it shall be for Aaron and his sons a perpetual ordinance from the sons of Israel, he says, speaking of the breast and the shoulder of the victims. So he said "perpetual" in the sense we have often noted above.

And the robe of the holy one, which is Aaron's, shall be for his sons after him, to anoint them in them and to complete their hands. For seven days the priest who succeeds him from among his sons shall clothe himself in them, he who shall enter the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the holy places. These words raise many questions. First it should be noted here how, after saying "the robe of the holy one," he then speaks in the plural: to anoint them in them, as though in robes. For above, too, he had spoken of many robes, of which the one robe was made up. Although it is ambiguous whether "in them" refers, in the neuter gender, to all the things of which that robe, that is, the priestly garment, is composed; and this is rather to be supposed from what he says next: For seven days the priest who succeeds him shall clothe himself in them, namely in all the things he listed when describing the priestly garment. He repeated, to be sure, what he had said above: to complete their hands; I have explained what I thought of that. But when he says: For seven days the priest shall clothe himself in them, will he not clothe himself in them on other days? But he wished us to understand those seven continuous days on which his priesthood is in a manner dedicated, and there is a week-long festival at its beginning. He calls Aaron's successor the one who enters the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the holy places, meaning, of course, the one who could only be a single man, not the kind of priests Aaron's sons were while their father was alive, but the kind of man who was Aaron's own successor. How, then, does he say it is peculiar to this one man "to enter the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the holy places," when the things outside the veil, by which the holy of holies is veiled, are also called holy, and that place where the holy things are, namely the table and the lampstand, is also called the tabernacle of testimony? Since the subordinate priests also minister there, at the table and the lampstand and the altar itself, how can he speak of one Aaron who enters the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the holy places? If he had said "to minister in the holy of holies," there would be no question. For into that place, where the ark of testimony is, the one high priest alone entered, as is also set forth most carefully in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Unless perhaps, by the very fact that he says one man enters the tabernacle of testimony to minister in the holy places, he wishes us to understand only the holy of holies, since that too is certainly called holy. For not all things that are holy can also be called holy of holies; but those that are holy of holies are beyond doubt also holy. And that this one man, who entered the holy of holies once a year, signified the Lord Christ is set forth most plainly in the aforementioned Epistle to the Hebrews. Now what was prefigured in the holy of holies, that over the ark, which held the law, there should be the mercy seat, by which we are to understand God's mercy to be signified, by which he becomes merciful toward the sins of those who do not fulfill the law, this seems to me to be signified also in the priest's garment itself; for what else does that garment signify but the sacraments of the Church? For he placed judgments in the λόγιον, that is, the rationale set on the priest's breast, but sanctification and the offering for sins in the plate, as though the rationale on the breast were like the ark in which the law was, and that plate on the forehead like the mercy seat which was over the ark, so that in both what is written might be kept: Mercy triumphs over judgment.

Why does he say that the altar, once purified and sanctified for seven days, will be "holy of holy"? He does not call the altar "holy of holies," as he does the place separated off by the veil, where the ark of the testimony is. Still, he says that this altar too, though placed outside the veil, becomes "holy of holy" through the seven days of sanctification rather than through anointing. And he adds: "Everyone who touches the altar will be sanctified."

Speaking of the rings of the altar of incense, an altar he ordered to be overlaid not with bronze but with gold, he says: "And you shall make two rings of pure gold under its twisted crown; you shall make them into the two sides, on the two sides." The Greek has: εἰς τὰ δύο κλίτη ποιήσεις ἐν τοῖς δυσὶ πλευροῖς. Both κλίτη are sides and πλευρά are sides. So some Latin translators rendered it this way: "You shall make them into two parts, on the two sides." But the Greek does not say μέρη, which means "parts," but κλίτη, which means "sides." This is the word used in the psalm where it is written: "Your wife like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house." So the only difference is the case: first he used the accusative and then the ablative: "You shall make them into the two sides, on the two sides." What the meaning is, however, is hard to grasp, unless perhaps, since Scripture likes ellipsis, where something is left out and has to be understood, here too "they will be" is to be understood, so that the sense is: "You shall make them into the two sides; they will be on the two sides," that is: "You shall make the rings for the two sides, since they will be on the two sides."

"And they shall be arches for the poles, so that it may be carried by them." What he had called rings he now calls arches, for he used "rings" to mean round handles. And what else is a ring or a circle but an arch on every side? So some, not wanting to say "arches," translated it as "sheaths" into which the poles were to be inserted, saying: "And they shall be sheaths for the poles"—as if the Greek could not have said this, when "theca" is itself a Greek word. But he said ψαλίδες, which are translated "arches."

"He shall burn on it the incense of continuance before the Lord throughout their generations." He calls it "incense of continuance" because it was to be offered continually, that is, no day was to be skipped. When he was giving instructions about the altar of incense, that is, the altar on which only incense was to be placed, and no burnt offering, no sacrifice, no libation, he had already said that this incense must be placed on it daily. But now he says: "And Aaron shall make propitiation," or "make entreaty," "upon its horns once a year with the blood of the purification of sins, of propitiation." "Of propitiation" comes from "propitiation," which in Greek is called ἐξιλασμός. From this we should understand that what he orders to be done once a year to make God propitious on the horns of the altar of incense, namely that the horns of the altar of incense are to be touched once a year with the blood of the purification of sins (that is, of the victims offered for sins), has nothing to do with the placing of incense that he had ordered to be done daily. That was done with spices, not with blood, and daily, not once a year. So we are not to understand that the priest used to enter the holy of holies only once a year, but that he entered with blood once a year. He used to enter daily without blood to put on the incense, but with blood once a year, especially since the text goes on to say: "Once a year he shall purify it; it is holy of holies to the Lord." So he will not put incense there once a year, since that was ordered to be done daily; rather, once a year he will purify it, which was commanded to be done with blood. And after this he adds: "It is holy of holies to the Lord." Therefore, if the holy of holies was not outside but inside the veil, then surely the altar now under discussion, which he ordered to be placed facing the veil, he ordered to be placed inside.

What does he mean when he says: "If you take a count of the children of Israel when they are visited," if not that he orders them at some time to be visited and counted, that is, numbered? From this we should understand that this was punished in David's case because God had not ordered it.

We should take careful note of how he ordered everything to be anointed with the ointment of chrism, namely the tabernacle and everything in it, "and then they will be holy of holies." That is, once all things have been anointed, they will be holy of holies. What difference there will then be between the inner things covered by the veil and the rest, if all things once anointed will be holy of holies, must be investigated more carefully; but we thought these points worth noting. Let us also remember this: just as it was said of the altar of sacrifices, which he wished to be called "holy of holy" after its anointing, "Everyone who touches it will be sanctified," so too of all the things afterward that, anointed with that ointment, were called holy of holies, the same statement followed: "Everyone who touches them will be sanctified." This can be understood in two ways: either he will be sanctified by touching, or he will be sanctified so that he may be allowed to touch—if, that is, the people were not allowed to touch the tabernacle when they brought victims or whatever they brought to be offered to God. For he goes on to direct that what he says to Moses is to be told not only to the priests or only to the Levites: "And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying"—and the children of Israel were, of course, that whole people, and he orders this to be said to them—"This oil for smearing in anointing shall be holy to you throughout your generations. It shall not be smeared on human flesh, and you shall not make any like it for yourselves according to this recipe; it is holy, and it shall be a sanctification to you. Whoever makes any like it, and whoever gives any of it to someone of a foreign nation, shall perish from his people." So he commands not just the priests but the whole people of Israel not to make such an ointment for human use. This is what he means by "It shall not be smeared on human flesh." He therefore forbids anything like it to be made for their own use, and threatens death if anyone makes something similar, that is, makes a similar ointment for his own use or gives some of it to anyone of a foreign nation. And so, when he says "It shall be a sanctification to you," and orders this to be said to the whole people of Israel, I do not see how to understand it except that they were allowed to touch the tabernacle when each of them came with his gifts, and by touching it they were sanctified because of the oil with which everything had been anointed. Hence it was said: "Everyone who touches will be sanctified"—though not in the same way as the priests, who were also anointed with it so that they might exercise the priesthood.

When he prescribes the spices from which the thymiama, that is, the incense, is to be made, and says it is to be "compounded in the manner of a perfumer, the work of a perfumer," we should not therefore think that an ointment is being made, that is, something to anoint with. Rather, as was said, it is thymiama or incense to be placed on the altar of incense, on which no sacrifice was permitted and which stood inside in the holy of holies.

"And you shall beat some of it fine and place it before the testimonies, from where I will make myself known to you there. The incense shall be holy of holies to you." Notice that once again this incense is called holy of holies, because it was placed inside, on the altar of incense, which was inside. And "the tabernacle of testimony" properly refers to that inner part itself where the ark was, a distinction certainly being made when he says: "from where I will make myself known to you there." For that is how he had spoken earlier about the propitiatory, which is of course inside, that is, within the veil, above the ark.

Why is it that, when God ordered Bezalel to be employed in making the works of the tabernacle, he said he had filled him with the divine spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge, to devise in every work and to act as master builder, and so on? Are even these works, which seem to belong to craftsmanship, to be attributed to the gift of the Holy Spirit? Or is this too said figuratively, so that the things these works signify belong to the divine spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge? Yet even here, though he is said to be filled with the divine spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge, we do not yet read the words "Holy Spirit."

What does it mean that, when giving the command to keep the sabbath, he says: "an eternal covenant in me, and for the children of Israel"? He does not say "between me and the children of Israel." Is it because the sabbath signifies rest, and there is no rest for us except in him? For by "the children of Israel" he certainly means his whole people, that is, the seed of Abraham. And there is an Israel according to the flesh and an Israel according to the spirit. If no one were to be called Israel except by fleshly descent, the apostle would not say, "Consider Israel according to the flesh." There he certainly indicates that there is an Israel according to the spirit, the one who is a Jew inwardly, by circumcision of the heart. So perhaps it is better to divide the text like this: "an eternal covenant in me," and then a separate clause, "and for the children of Israel it is an eternal sign," that is, a sign of an eternal thing, in the way that the rock was Christ, because the rock signified Christ. So it should not be joined like this: "an eternal covenant in me and the children of Israel," as though this covenant were in God and in the children of Israel. Rather: "an eternal covenant in me"—because eternal rest is promised in him—"and for the children of Israel it is an eternal sign," because the children of Israel received a sign to observe by which eternal rest is signified for the true Israelites, that is, for the children of the promise, who will see God face to face as he is.

"And as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone written with the finger of God." Although God said so much, only two stone tablets are given to Moses, which are called the tablets of the testimony that were to be kept in the ark. Clearly, all the other things God commanded are understood to hang on those ten commandments written on the two tablets, if they are carefully examined and rightly understood, just as these ten commandments in turn hang on those two, namely the love of God and of neighbor, on which the whole law and the prophets hang.

As for Aaron ordering the earrings to be taken from the ears of their wives and daughters so that he could make gods for them out of them, it is not unreasonable to understand that he meant to demand something difficult, in order to call them back from their purpose that way. Yet that very difficult thing was done, so that there was gold for making the idol. I thought this worth noting for the sake of those who are saddened if anything of the kind is ordered by God, for the sake of eternal life, to be done or to be borne with patience.

When the Lord tells Moses what the people had done about the calf, that is, about the idol they had made from their gold, he says they said: "These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt." We do not read that they said this, but God shows that this was their state of mind. They were carrying in their hearts the meaning of these words, which could not be hidden from God.

"And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil he said he would do to his people." Here he meant "evil" to be understood as punishment, as in: "And their departure was reckoned an evil." In this sense good and evil alike are said to come from God, not in the sense of the evil by which people are evil. For God is not evil; but he brings evils upon the evil, because he is just.

Moses seems to have smashed and broken the tablets of the testimony written by the finger of God because he was angry; yet by a great mystery this prefigured the renewal of the covenant, since the old was to be abolished and the new established. We should certainly note how hard he labored in supplication to God for the people, he who showed himself so severe in punishing them. As for his throwing the molten calf into the fire, grinding it to powder, scattering it on water, and giving it to the people to drink, I have already written elsewhere, in the work against Faustus the Manichaean, what I think it signifies for us.

"And they gave it to me; and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf." He spoke in shorthand, not saying that he himself had shaped it so that a molten calf came out. Or did he lie out of fear, to excuse himself, as if he had thrown the gold into the fire to be destroyed and the shape of a calf had come out without his doing anything? We should not believe that he said this with that intent, because Moses could not have failed to see what was in the man—Moses with whom God spoke—and yet he did not rebuke his brother for lying.

"And when Moses saw the people, that they were scattered; for Aaron had scattered them, so that they became a source of joy to their enemies." We should note how all the evil the people did is attributed to Aaron himself, because he consented to do for them what they had wickedly asked. It is said "Aaron scattered them," because he gave in to them, rather than that they scattered themselves, though it was they who demanded such great evil.

When Moses says to the Lord: "I beg you, Lord, this people has sinned a great sin, and they have made themselves gods of gold. And now, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of your book that you have written," he said this with confidence, so that the argument might draw its conclusion from what follows: that is, since God would not blot Moses out of his book, he would forgive the people that sin. Still, we should notice how great an evil Moses saw in that sin, since he believed it had to be expiated by so great a slaughter, he who loved them so much that he poured out those words to God on their behalf.

It is fair to ask why, since Aaron was said above to have scattered the people, no punishment fell on him, either when Moses ordered the death of everyone who met the armed Levites as they went to the gate and back, or later when what Scripture describes took place: "And the Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf that Aaron made"—especially since the point is driven home here by being repeated. For it does not say, "And the Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf that they made," but "that Aaron made." And yet Aaron was not struck. On the contrary, what God had commanded about his priesthood before his sin was carried out. God ordered him and his sons to be washed, and so they were ordained to the priesthood. In this way God knows whom to spare until he changes for the better, and whom to spare for a time even though he foreknows that he will not change for the better, and whom not to spare so that he may change for the better, and whom not to spare without even waiting for him to change. And all this comes back to what the apostle cries out: "How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!"

"Go, go up from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt." God seems to speak in anger when he says "you and your people whom you brought out"; otherwise he would have said, "you and my people whom I brought out of the land of Egypt." But when they demanded the idol, they spoke like this: "As for this man Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him." By placing their deliverance in a man, they had fallen away. That is thrown back at them when it is said, "you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt," which is a charge against them, not against Moses. For Moses wanted nothing else than that they should put their hope not in him but in the Lord, and believe with thanksgiving that they had been freed from that slavery by the Lord's mercy. Yet his merit before God, as a most faithful servant, was so great through God's grace that God said to him: "Let me alone, and in my anger I will crush them." Whether this "Let me alone" is a command or something like a request, either seems absurd. If God was commanding, the servant was disobedient in not complying; and it would not befit God to ask this of a servant as a favor, especially since he could crush them even against Moses' will. So the obvious sense here is that by these words God indicated that it greatly benefited that people in his sight that they were so loved by a man whom the Lord loved so much. In this way we are reminded that when our merits weigh us down so that we are not loved by God, we can be lifted up before him by the merits of those whom he loves. For when the Almighty says to a man, "Let me alone, and I will crush them," what else is he saying than "I would crush them if they were not loved by you"? So "Let me alone" was said as if to say: "Stop loving them, and I will crush them, because your love for them intercedes with me so that I do not do it." Moses would have had to obey the Lord saying "Stop loving them" if he had said it as a command, rather than as a warning and an expression of what was holding him back from punishing them. Yet even with Moses interceding, he did not leave the people without the scourge of discipline. For in some way, in order that Moses himself might love them so much, God was loving them more secretly, even while he openly terrified them with his voice.

Where God says to Moses: "Go, go up from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, saying, 'To your seed I will give it,'" he immediately, as though still speaking to Moses himself, turns by a hidden shift of address, which in Greek is called ἀποστροφή, to speak to the people themselves, saying: "And at the same time I will send my angel before you, and he will drive out the Canaanite and the Amorite and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Girgashite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, and he will bring you into a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people, so that I do not destroy you on the way." Here is a great and wonderful depth of mystery: as though an angel could have more mercy than the Lord, sparing a stiff-necked people whom God himself would not spare if he were with them. And yet he says that even through his angel, while in a certain sense absent from them—he who can never be absent anywhere—he is fulfilling what he swore to their fathers, as if showing here too that he does this because he promised it to those righteous fathers, not because these people were worthy. What, then, did he signify, unless perhaps that he would not be with them because they were stiff-necked, since nothing receives him as gracious and saving except humility and godliness? For God to be with stiff-necked people is nothing other than to be present to punish and chastise them; so when he is not present to the wicked in that way, he does so by sparing them. This is the point of the saying "Turn your face away from my sins," because if he turns away, he overthrows [?]; for as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God.

"And Moses said to the Lord: See, you say to me, 'Lead this people'; but you have not shown me whom you will send with me. Yet you said to me, 'I know you above all, and you have found favor with me.' If, then, I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself; let me see you manifestly, so that I may be one who finds favor before you, and so that I may know that this nation is your people." Where the Greek has γνωστῶς, some Latin translators rendered "manifestly," though Scripture did not say φανερῶς. So perhaps it could more aptly be rendered: "If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself; let me see you knowingly." By these words Moses shows clearly enough that, even in that great intimacy of sight, he did not see God as he longed to see him. For all those visions of God that were offered to the eyes of mortals, and from which came a sound that reached mortal hearing, were presented through something assumed, as God willed and in the form he willed, so that in them the divine nature itself was not perceived by any bodily sense, since it is invisible, wholly present everywhere, and contained by no place. And because the whole law hangs on two commandments, the love of God and of neighbor, Moses showed his longing with respect to both: with respect to the love of God where he says, "If I have found favor in your sight, show me yourself; let me see you manifestly, so that I may be one who finds favor in your sight"; and with respect to the love of neighbor where he says, "and so that I may know that this nation is your people."

What does God mean when he says to Moses, "since I know you above all"? Does God know some things more and some less? Or is it in the sense in which it is said to some in the Gospel, "I do not know you"? According to this kind of knowing, by which God is said to know what pleases him and not to know what displeases him—not because he is ignorant of it but because he does not approve it, just as an art is rightly said not to know faults even though it detects faults—God knew Moses above all, because Moses pleased God above all.

Should we note that Moses himself had first said to God, "You said to me, 'I know you above all'"? We read that God said this to him after Moses had said it to God, but we do not read it before. Does this mean we should understand that not everything God said to him has been written down? But we must look more carefully in the earlier parts of Scripture to see whether this is really so.

When Moses had said to the Lord, "Show me your glory," the Lord answered him, "I will pass before you in my glory, and I will call out the name of the Lord in your sight; and I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I will show compassion." Yet a little earlier he had said, "I myself will go before you and give you rest." Moses seems to have taken this "I will go before you" to mean that God would not be present with him and the people on the journey, and that is why he said, "If you yourself do not come along with us, do not bring me up from here," and so on. God did not refuse him this either, but said, "This word that you have spoken I will also do for you." How is it, then, that when Moses said to him, "Show me your glory," he again seems to speak as one who will go on ahead and not be with them, saying, "I will pass before you"? It can only be that this is something different. For the one understood to be speaking here and saying "I will pass before you" is the one of whom the Gospel says, "When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father"; and this passing over is also said to be what "Passover" means. So this is a very great prophecy indeed. For he passed from this world to the Father ahead of all the saints, to prepare for them the dwelling places of the kingdom of heaven, which he will give them at the resurrection of the dead; for in order to pass over ahead of all, he became the firstborn from the dead.

He strongly commends his grace in this very thing when he says: "And I will call by the name of the Lord in your sight." It is as if he said, "in the sight of the people of Israel," whom Moses represented as a type when he heard these words. For in the sight of that very nation, scattered everywhere, Christ is called Lord among all the nations. He said "I will call," not "I will be called," putting an active verb in place of a passive by an unusual turn of speech, and a great meaning certainly lies hidden in it. Perhaps he wished to show in this way that he himself brings it about, that is, that it happens by his grace, that the Lord is called upon among all the nations.

In what he added, "And I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy," he shows quite plainly the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and glory, not according to our merits but according to his mercy. For since he was promising that he would bring in the Gentiles when he said, "I will call by the name of the Lord in your sight," he made clear that he does this out of mercy, as the apostle says: "For I tell you that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy." This, then, is what was foretold: "And I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy." With these words he forbade anyone to boast as if on the merits of his own virtues, so that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. For he did not say, "I will have mercy on such and such people," but "on whom I have been merciful," in order to show that no one has earned the mercy of so great a calling by good works of his own done beforehand. For Christ died for the ungodly.

But whether he meant to repeat the same thing when he added, "I will show mercy to whom I have shown mercy" (or, as others have translated it, "to whom I have been merciful"), or whether there is some difference, I do not know. What is said in Greek with two verbs, ἐλεήσω and οἰκτειρήσω, which seem to mean one and the same thing, the Latin translator could not render with distinct verbs, and so he repeated the same "mercy" in different forms. If it were said, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have mercy on whom I have mercy," or "I will have mercy on whom I shall have had mercy," it would not seem to be put very well. And yet the meaning there is all the stronger: either God showed by this repetition the steadfastness of his mercy (as in "Amen, amen," as in "So be it, so be it," as in the repetition of Pharaoh's dream, and many similar cases), or in this way God announced beforehand that he would show mercy to both peoples, that is, to the Gentiles and to the Hebrews.
