The apostle puts it like this: "For just as you once did not believe God, but now have received mercy through their unbelief, so they too have now not believed, for the sake of the mercy shown to you, so that they also may receive mercy. For God has shut up all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all."

Then, after this commendation of his mercy, he answered what had been said to him: "Show me your glory," or what Moses had asked earlier when he said, "Show me yourself, let me see you plainly." "You cannot see my face," he said, "for no one shall see my face and live." He was showing that God as he is cannot appear to this life, which is lived in the mortal senses of corruptible flesh. That is, he can be seen as he is in that other life, and in order to live that life one must die to this one.

Again, after a break in which the scripture says, "And the Lord said," there follows, and he speaks: "Behold, there is a place beside me." For what place is not beside God, who is absent nowhere? But in saying, "Behold, there is a place beside me," he signifies the church, commending it as his temple. "And you shall stand," he says, "upon the rock" (for the Lord says, "Upon this rock I will build my church") "as soon as my glory passes by." That is: as soon as my glory passes by, he will stand upon the rock, because after Christ's passing, that is, after the passion and resurrection of Christ, the faithful people stood upon the rock. "And I will put you," he says, "in a cleft of the rock": this signifies a very strong fortress. Others have translated it "in a lookout of the rock," but the Greek has [?]. We more correctly translate this as "hole" or "cleft."

"And I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will take away my hand, and then you will see my back, but my face will not be seen by you." Since he had already said, "You shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by," where we understand that he promised a firm standing on the rock after his passing, how are we to take what he says: "I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will take away my hand, and then you will see my back"? It is as though he covers Moses with his hand when Moses is already set on the rock, and then passes by, whereas Moses cannot be on the rock except after he has passed. But we must understand a recapitulation of something passed over, of the kind scripture often uses in many places. He said afterward what comes first in the order of time. The order is this: "I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and then you will see my back, for my face will not be seen by you; and you shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by, and I will put you in a cleft of the rock." This came about in those whom the person of Moses then signified, that is, the Israelites who afterward believed in the Lord Jesus, as the Acts of the Apostles shows; that is, as soon as his glory had passed by. For after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, and the Holy Spirit was sent from above and the apostles spoke in the tongues of all nations, many of those who had crucified Christ were cut to the heart. That they did not recognize him, and crucified the Lord of glory, was because blindness had come upon part of Israel, just as had been said: "I will cover you with my hand until I pass by." So the psalm says, "For day and night your hand was heavy upon me," calling it day when Christ was working divine miracles, and night when he was dying as a man, when even those who had believed in the day wavered. This, then, is the meaning of "When I have passed by, then you will see my back": when I have passed from this world to the Father, those whose type you bear will believe in me later. For then, cut to the heart, they said, "What shall we do?" And they were told by the apostles to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, so that their sins might be forgiven them. In that psalm, after it has said, "Day and night your hand was heavy upon me" (that is, so that I did not recognize him; for if they had recognized him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory), it continues and adds: "I was turned to misery while the thorn was driven in," that is, when I was cut to the heart. Then it adds: "I acknowledged my sin and did not cover my crime," after they saw how great a crime it was to have crucified Christ. And because they accepted the counsel to repent and receive forgiveness of sins in baptism, it says: "I said, I will declare my offense against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart."

That what the Lord spoke to Moses was a prophecy rather than anything else is shown clearly enough by the facts themselves, since we read of nothing following afterward as a visible act concerning the rock or its cleft, or the laying of his hand over him, or the sight of his back. For immediately, after a break, the scripture adds: "And the Lord said to Moses," though it was of course the Lord himself who was also speaking the words above. And from there it goes on with what the Lord says next: "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first," and so on.
What is meant by what is said of the Lord, "And he will not purify the guilty," if not "he will not declare him innocent"?

When Moses was about to write the two stone tablets again on the mountain, God says to him among other things: "Before all your people I will do glorious things." He does not yet deign to say, "before all my people." Or did he say "your people" in the way it might be said to any man of that same people, that is, "the people you belong to," just as we say "your city," not meaning a city you rule or have founded, but the one of which you are a citizen? For so he also says a little later: "all the people among whom you are." Otherwise, what does it mean but "your people"? That he did not say "in which you are" is simply a habit of speech.

What does it mean when Moses is told, "Take heed to yourself, lest at any time he make a covenant with those who dwell on the land"? For the Greek does not have "lest at any time you make," but "lest at any time he make." Did he perhaps mean to say this to him about the people whose leader he was? But it was not Moses himself who brought the people into that land, where he forbids a covenant to be made with those who lived there. So this is a strange turn of speech, one not met with or noticed before; if, that is, it is a turn of speech and not some meaning.

When God, speaking to Moses, commanded that once the land had been given into their power all idolatry should be overthrown and no foreign gods worshiped, he said: "For the Lord God, jealous is his name; he is a jealous God." That is, the very name by which he is called Lord God is jealous, because he is a jealous God. God, who is always and in every way unchangeable and calm, does not do this out of the fault of a human passion; rather, by this word he shows that his people will not go unpunished for committing fornication with foreign gods. The word is taken by metaphor from a husband's jealousy, by which he guards his wife's chastity, and this benefits us, not God. For who could harm God by that kind of fornication? But one harms oneself greatly, so as to perish. God forbids this with the gravest threat by calling himself jealous; to him it is said in the psalm: "You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication against you; but for me it is good to cling to God." Then it follows: "lest perhaps you make a covenant with those who dwell on the land, and they commit fornication after their gods."

What does he mean by "You shall not be seen in my sight empty-handed"? As the surrounding passage he is speaking about shows, by "in my sight" God meant in his tabernacle. And "you shall not be seen by him empty-handed" means: you shall never enter without some gift. Understood spiritually, this is a great mystery. But these things were said about shadows that signified something else.

Having given his command about the sabbath, what does he mean by adding, "In sowing and harvest you shall rest"? He seems to be saying, "at the time of sowing and harvest." Or did he perhaps command that the sabbath rest be kept in such a way that even those seasons, which are so necessary to farmers for their food and livelihood, should give no excuse? So it was commanded that even at the time of sowing and harvest, when work presses hard, there should be rest on the sabbath. And so, by naming these seasons, which demand the most work, it is signified that one must cease from work on the sabbath at every time of year.

When he says, "No one shall covet anything of your land when you go up to be seen in the sight of the Lord your God three times a year," he means that each person should go up without worry and without being anxious about his land, since God promises to guard it so that no one will covet anything of it, for the sake of the one who goes up, so that he need not fear his absence from it. And here he shows clearly enough what he said above, "You shall not appear in the sight of the Lord your God empty-handed": he said it of the place where God was to have his tabernacle or temple.

What does he mean by "You shall not slaughter the blood of my sacrifices over leaven"? Does he in this passage call "his sacrifices" those that are slain at the Passover, and command that there be no leaven in the house at that time, since those are the days of unleavened bread?

What does he mean by "And the sacrifice of the feast of the Passover shall not sleep until morning," except what he plainly commanded above, that none of the flesh of the animal sacrificed should be left until morning? But the expression has made it obscure, for he said "shall sleep" instead of "shall remain."

"You shall not cook a lamb in its mother's milk." See, he has said again something I do not know how to understand. Yet it is a great prophecy about Christ, even if it can be done literally, and how much more so if it cannot! For in the words of God not everything is to be referred to actual deeds, just as that passage about the rock, its cleft, and the laying on of the hand is not. But this much must certainly be required of the narrator's faithfulness: what he says was done must truly have been done, and what he says was said must truly have been said. This is required of the narrators of the gospel too; for when they relate that Christ said certain things which he spoke in parables, still the statement that he said them is not a parable but historical narrative.

"And Moses was there in the sight of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he did not eat bread and did not drink water." He had said this before too, when Moses received the tablets that he broke, and he repeats it now in the same way, not recapitulating something already done, but making clear that it was done a second time. We have already said what the repetition of the law signifies. When it says, "He did not eat bread and did not drink water," we understand that he fasted, the whole being expressed by a part; that is, by the word "bread" scripture means all food, and by the word "water" all drink.

"And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words." It is said of Moses that he himself wrote them, and a little before God had also said to him, "Write these words for yourself." But when he first received the law, whose tablets he threw down and broke, he was not said to have cut the stone tablets himself, whereas now he is told, "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone"; nor was he told to write, as he is told now; nor is he said to have written them himself, as scripture now says. And it says, "He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words." But at that time it was said: "And as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone written by the finger of God"; and then a little later: "And Moses turned and went down from the mountain, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hands, tablets of stone written on both their sides, written on the one side and on the other; and the tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God engraved on the tablets." So a great question arises: how is it that those tablets, which Moses was going to break, as God certainly foreknew, are said to be not the work of man but of God, and not written by man but with the writing of God, by the finger of God; while the later tablets, which were to last so long and to be kept in the tabernacle and temple of God, were indeed made at God's command, yet were cut by a man and written by a man? Was it perhaps that in those first tablets God's grace was signified, not the work of man, the grace of which they made themselves unworthy by turning back in their hearts to Egypt and making an idol, so that they were deprived of that benefit, and for this reason Moses broke the tablets? And that by these later tablets are signified those who boast of their own works, of whom the apostle says, "Not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God"? And that therefore tablets cut by human work and written by human work were given, to remain with them, to signify those who would boast of their own works and not of the finger of God, that is, of the Spirit of God?

Certainly, then, the repetition of the law signifies the new covenant, while that first giving signified the old, which is why it was broken and abolished. This is especially so because when the law is given the second time, it is given without any terror, unlike the first amid such a din of fire, clouds and trumpets, at which the trembling people said, "Let not God speak to us, lest we die." This signifies that fear belongs to the old covenant and love to the new. How, then, is this question resolved: why were the first tablets the work of God and these the work of man, and why were the first written by the finger of God and these written by a man? Is it perhaps that the old covenant was signified rather in the first tablets because there God commanded but man did not do? For in the old covenant the law was laid down to convict transgressors; it came in so that sin might abound. For it was not being fulfilled through fear, since it is fulfilled only through love. And so it is called the work of God, because God established the law and God wrote it, and it was no work of man, because man did not obey God, and the law instead made him guilty. But with the second tablets man makes and writes the tablets with God's help, because the love of the new covenant fulfills the law. Hence the Lord says, "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it," and the apostle says, "Love is the fulfillment of the law," and "faith working through love." So in the new covenant what was difficult in the old became easy for a man who has faith working through love, while the finger of God, that is, the Spirit of God, writes it within, on the heart, not outside on stone. Hence the apostle says, "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts," because the love of God, by which the commandment is truly fulfilled, has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. This, then, is the meaning: first the law was given, and in it is signified the old covenant, which is solely the work of God and the writing of God's finger. Of this the apostle says, "So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good." The law, then, holy and good, is the work of God, in which man does nothing because he does not obey, but is rather weighed down by guilt as the law threatens and condemns. For sin, he says, "in order to be shown up as sin, worked death in me through what is good." But a man is blessed when this holy, just and good commandment is also his own work, though by the grace of God.

After Moses had come down from the mountain carrying the second tablets of the law, with a veil placed over himself because of the glory of his face, which the children of Israel could not look upon, he said to the children of Israel: These are the words which the Lord has said, to do them. It is left ambiguous whether the Lord himself is to "do them" or the people; yet it is surely clear that the people are meant, since he commanded the things that were to be done. But perhaps it was put this way so that it might be taken in both senses, because the Lord also does them when he helps those who do them, as the Apostle says: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

Everyone who set apart a deduction of silver and bronze brought them, deductions for the Lord. It is as if he said: "Everyone who brought something brought this or that", among the other things he was listing, mentioning both silver and bronze. The Latin translators have rendered as "deduction" what the Greek has as afoapsfta [?] (presumably aphairema). It was called a "deduction" because whoever brought it to the Lord deducted it from himself.

In Moses' account, what God had said to him about Bezalel is repeated in exactly the same words and at the same length: that he had filled him with the divine spirit of wisdom, understanding and knowledge for making the works of the tabernacle, which belong to the craftsmen's arts. We have already said what we thought about this. But I thought it worth mentioning again now, because it is not without purpose that it is repeated in exactly the same words in which the Lord had earlier communicated it to Moses. It is certainly an unusual usage that here the craftsmen's work in gold, silver and every kind of metal is called the architect's art, since "architectural" is usually said of what pertains to the construction of buildings.

And all who of their own accord wished to come to the work, to complete it; and they received from Moses all the deductions. Moses only made known what works the Lord had commanded to be made, namely the tabernacle with everything that was to be in it, and the priestly vestments. He mentioned certain people, of whom he said that a spirit had been given them by God by which they could make these things; and yet we understand that many came of their own accord to the same work, who had neither been commanded nor had their names mentioned in what the Lord said to Moses. So those who are named were not the only ones who had this gift from God, though perhaps they had it especially and in a higher degree. What deserves praise in all of them, however, is a spirit not dragged to the work like a slave's, but freely and willingly devoted.

It should be noted that those who are called wise, the makers of the holy works, were also of such character that, when they received everything the people offered in the belief that it was needed to complete all those things, and saw that more was being offered than was necessary, they told Moses. And he, through a herald, forbade the people to offer any more. Yet they could have carried off a great deal if they had wished; but modesty prevented them, or reverence deterred them.

After Moses came down from the mountain, the works of constructing the tabernacle and the priestly vestments are enjoined; but before he gave any instruction about making them, he spoke to the people about keeping the sabbath. Here it is not without reason that one is puzzled why, having received the ten words of the law a second time on tablets of stone, which he himself cut and himself wrote upon, he admonished the people about the sabbath alone after he came down. For if it was superfluous for the people to hear the ten commandments of the law again, why was it not superfluous for them to hear about the sabbath, since this too is read among those same ten commandments? Or is this too like the veil with which he covered his face, because the children of Israel could not look upon the brightness of his countenance? For of the ten commandments he enjoined on the people only this one, which is stated there figuratively; for we have no doubt at all that the other nine there are to be kept as commandments in the New Testament as well. But that one about the sabbath was so far veiled among the Israelites by the figurative observance of the seventh day, and was commanded in a mystery and figured by a kind of sacrament, that today it is not observed by us; we only look upon what it signified. In that rest, however, where servile works are ordered to cease, lies the great depth of God's grace. For good works are done with rest when faith works through love; but fear has torment, and what rest is there in torment? Hence there is no fear in love; and love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Therefore the sabbath is a holy rest to the Lord, that is, it is to be ascribed to the grace of God, not to ourselves as if it came from ourselves. Otherwise our works will be such that they are merely human, or sins, or done with fear and not with love, and therefore servile and without rest. But the fullness of the sabbath will be in everlasting rest. For it is not for nothing that the sabbath of sabbaths was also instituted.

Earlier, when God first spoke about anointing the tabernacle, he said that all those things would be sanctified by this anointing and become holy of holies. But the altar of burnt offerings, sanctified by the same anointing, he had said would become holy of the holy. And there seemed to be this difference, that he had called none of them holy of holies except what was separated from the holy place by the veil alone, that is, where the ark of the covenant and the altar of incense were. Now, however, in repeating the same things, he said of the anointed tabernacle and the things that were in it that they would be sanctified by this anointing and become holy; whereas that altar of burnt offerings, of which he had said before that it would become holy of the holy, he now said would become holy of holies by the same anointing. From this we are given to understand that what had been called holy of the holy means just as much as what is called holy of holies; and accordingly that all those anointed things, that is, the whole tabernacle and whatever was in it, which he had earlier called holy of holies, mean just as much as what he now calls holy; and that after this anointing each of them is called not only holy of the holy but also holy of holies, like the altar of burnt offerings. So now, as far as this title is concerned, there is no difference between the things that had been inside, within the veil, that is, where the ark of the testimony was, and the rest outside, except that the things inside were called holies of holies, or holy of holies, in such a way that they were so named even before the anointing, whereas the rest were sanctified by the anointing so as to receive this name. What these things signify must be discussed at leisure.

When Scripture tells how Moses set up the tabernacle, it says: And he spread the hangings over the tabernacle, not, of course, as a roof above it, but going around the columns, since it had said of the columns that he set up the tabernacle with them.

When it says: and over the court round about the tabernacle and the altar, it shows that the altar of burnt offerings stood outside, at the entrance of the tabernacle, so that the whole was surrounded by the court, and the altar was within the court, between the gate of the court and the entrance of the tabernacle.

A very remarkable thing should be noted: when the cloud came down and filled the tabernacle—though it is called the glory of the Lord—Moses could not enter the tabernacle, even though on Mount Sinai, when he first received the law, he had entered into the cloud where God was. Without doubt, then, he represented one person then and another now: then those who become partakers of the inmost truth of God, but now the Jews, to whom the glory of the Lord that is in the tabernacle—that is, the grace of Christ—is set before them like a cloud, since they do not understand it. And therefore he does not enter the tabernacle of the testimony. And we should believe that this happened only once, as soon as the tabernacle was set up, for the sake of this meaning or of some other. For the cloud was not always over the tabernacle in such a way that Moses could not enter it, since the cloud was not removed except when it gave them the signal to set out, that is, to break camp from the place where they were and go where the cloud led by day and the flame by night. These two also remained over the tabernacle in turn wherever they had pitched camp: the cloud by day, the flame by night.
QUESTION 177. An explanation of the tabernacle.

The book called Exodus ends with the setting up of the tabernacle, and much is also said about this tabernacle in the earlier parts of the same book. These passages are hard to understand, as any τοπογραφία (topographia), that is, a description of a place, tends to be in any history. So I have decided to discuss the whole tabernacle separately, so that we may understand, if possible, what it was like and what it was. For the present I keep to the literal sense of the narrative and leave the figurative meaning for another time. We must not suppose that anything set up there at God's command was without the sacrament of some great reality, the knowledge of which builds up faith and the pattern of godliness.

God commands Moses to make the tabernacle of ten hangings of twisted fine linen, blue, purple and twisted scarlet, with cherubim, the work of a weaver. What the Greeks call αὐλαίαι (aulaiai), Latin speakers call aulaea, and people commonly call them curtains. So he did not command that ten courts be made, as some have carelessly translated, for he did not say αὐλάς (aulas, courts) but αὐλαίας (aulaias, hangings). He commanded, then, that cherubim be woven into the hangings. He prescribed that each hanging be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide, and that the hangings be fastened and joined to one another, five on one side and five on the other, so that the space they enclosed would be the space of the tabernacle. He prescribed how these groups of five hangings were to be joined to one another, as follows: "And you shall make for them loops of blue on the edge of one hanging, on one side, at the join; and so you shall make them on the edge at the second join." That is, where one hanging is joined to another, namely the third to the second, the second having already been joined to the first, that is, linked and fastened to it, they stand face to face, each opposite the other, since he commanded the hangings to be joined in fives so as to be set opposite one another. Whether the space they enclosed was square or round is not yet clear, but it will become clear when he begins to speak of the columns on which the hangings are stretched. He chose to describe only the joining of three hangings, which takes place at two joins, the second to the first and the third to the second, so that the rest might be joined by this as a sort of rule. He therefore prescribed that fifty loops be made on the first hanging, on the side where the second was to be joined to it, and fifty loops on the third hanging, on the side where it was joined to the second. The second hanging itself, which lies in the middle between the two sets of fifty loops, he wished to have fifty gold rings on one side, by which it would be joined to the fifty loops of the first hanging. It followed that it should have as many rings on the other side, by which it would be joined to the loops of the third hanging. Scripture says this briefly: "And you shall make fifty gold rings and join hanging to hanging with the rings, and it shall be one tabernacle." So the fifty gold rings of the second hanging were inserted into the fifty blue loops of the first hanging, and fifty rings were inserted into the fifty loops of the third hanging. The rest were then joined in the same way until five were completed, and likewise five more on the opposite side.

Next he says: "And you shall make curtains of hair to cover over the tabernacle," that is, curtains that would go over it not by way of a roof but by wrapping around it. For we also speak of something being placed "over" something in this sense: not as the roof is over a house, but as plaster is over a wall, like one band laid over a linen one. "Eleven curtains," he says, "you shall make. The length of one curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the width of one curtain four cubits; the eleven curtains shall have the same measure. And you shall join five curtains together and six curtains together." Just as he wished the hangings to be joined in fives, so these curtains were to be joined in five and six, because there were eleven, not ten. "And you shall double the sixth curtain at the front of the tabernacle," he says, so that it should cause no difficulty that the six and the five did not match each other evenly. Then he also says how these curtains of hair were to be joined to one another. He says the same thing as before, but perhaps more plainly: "And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the one curtain that is against the middle" (that is, against the second, since that will be in the middle between the first and the third) "at the join" (that is, at the joining). "And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is joined to the second curtain" (that is, on the edge of the third curtain, since it is joined to the second). "And you shall make fifty bronze rings and join the rings to the loops; and you shall join the curtains, and it shall be one." So he wanted the rings put on the middle curtain, that is, the second, by which it would be joined to the first and the third through their sets of fifty loops. The only difference here is that he now commanded the rings to be made of bronze, not gold. For the hangings he had said the loops were blue. For the curtains of hair he said nothing about what the loops were made of, so what is more likely than that we should take them to be of hair?

What follows is so hard to understand that I fear I may make it more obscure by explaining it. He says: "And you shall put underneath what is left over in the curtains of the tabernacle: half of the curtain that is left over you shall tuck under; what is left over of the curtains of the tabernacle you shall tuck under behind the tabernacle. A cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, from what is left over of the curtains from the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall cover over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and on that, to cover it." Since he commanded the sixth curtain to be doubled at the front of the tabernacle, who could easily understand what he means by half a curtain being left over in the curtains, or what he means by "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side", when half a curtain is fifteen cubits, since he commanded each curtain to be thirty cubits? Or suppose something is left over from the length of the curtains because he prescribed that the first hangings, of fine linen, scarlet, purple and blue, be twenty-eight cubits long, but wanted these curtains of hair to be thirty cubits. Then each hair curtain exceeds each hanging by two cubits. Added together, leaving out the eleventh, which he commanded to be doubled, these come to an excess of twenty cubits, by which the circuit of the hair curtains exceeds the circuit of the hangings. For the two cubits by which each of the ten curtains was longer make twenty, and of these ten could be left over on one side and ten on the other, not a cubit on this side and a cubit on that, as Scripture says. I think, therefore, that the explanation of this passage should be put off until the tabernacle stands complete on every side with all its columns and with the court placed around it. For perhaps he is saying something in advance about these curtains of hair that bears on things he has not yet spoken of. When he says, "And you shall make curtains of hair to cover over the tabernacle," it is uncertain whether he wants the whole tabernacle covered with these curtains, including the court, of which he speaks afterwards as to be placed around it, or only this inner tabernacle, which he commanded to be made of ten hangings. He goes on to say: "And you shall make a covering for the tabernacle of rams' skins dyed red." Whether he commanded this covering too to be made around the whole tabernacle or only around the inner one is likewise uncertain. But when he adds, "and coverings of blue skins above," this must be understood not as going around but as a roof, like a vault.

"And you shall make columns for the tabernacle of wood that does not rot: one column ten cubits long, and the width of one column a cubit and a half; two small arms on one column, standing opposite each other. So you shall do for all the columns of the tabernacle." Why he commanded these small arms to be made (I have said before what they were) is not very clear to me. If they were made to support the columns, there would be at least four. If they were for the bars to rest on, there would be even more, for he assigns five bars to each column. Unless perhaps these small arms had no practical use but only a meaning, as with the eleventh curtain of hair. For a column stretching out two small arms like arms on either side forms the figure of a cross. Now let us look at the number of the columns, from which the shape of the tabernacle may also be seen: whether it is square, or round, or an oblong rectangle with longer sides and shorter ends, as most basilicas are built. It is this last that is clearly expressed here. For he says: "And you shall make columns for the tabernacle, twenty columns on the side that faces north. And you shall make forty silver bases for the twenty columns, two bases for one column at both its ends. And on the second side, toward the south, twenty columns and their forty silver bases: two bases for one column at both its ends, and two bases for one column at both its ends." The repetition should not trouble us. It is a manner of speaking, so that all the columns he does not mention are understood in the same way. As for the bases, we have already said before why one column has two: because in this passage he also calls the capitals bases.

We see, then, the two sides of the tabernacle, north and south, each extended by twenty columns. Two sides remain, east and west, and if they had had as many columns, the tabernacle would undoubtedly have been square. How many they have is stated for the west side but not for the east. Whether that is because the east side had none, and the hangings alone were stretched there without columns from the end column of one side to the opposite end column of the other, or whether they are left unmentioned for some reason, to be understood even without being mentioned, I do not know. Later, indeed, ten columns are mentioned on the east side, but they belong to the court, of which he speaks afterwards and which he commands to be placed around this tabernacle. Having mentioned the north and south sides of the tabernacle with twenty columns each, he goes on to add: "And at the back of the tabernacle, on the side that faces the sea, you shall make six columns. And you shall make two columns at the corners of the tabernacle at the rear. And they shall be equal from the bottom, and meeting together they shall be equal at the capitals into one join. So you shall do for both of the two corners; let them be equal. And there shall be eight columns, and their silver bases sixteen: two bases for one column and two bases for one column at both its ends." The reasoning and the manner of speaking about the bases are the same as before. So the west side (for this is the side toward the sea) extends across eight columns: six in the middle and two at the corners, which he says must be equal at one join. I believe this is because a corner joins two sides together, and the corner column is common to both sides, the one to the west and north sides, the other to the west and south. When he says they should also be equal "from the bottom," he surely means that they should be plumb, not thicker below than above, as most columns are.

Then he says: "And you shall make bars of wood that does not rot, five for one column on one side of the tabernacle, and five bars for a column on the second side of the tabernacle, and five bars for a column on the rear side of the tabernacle, toward the sea." It would be surprising if anyone could still doubt that the east side of this inner tabernacle, around which the court is afterwards placed, had no columns. So he commands that each column on all three sides have five bars. "And the middle bar," he says, "shall pass through between the middle columns from one side to the other side." He seems to mean that a bar reached from column to column and stretched across the gap between the columns from the side of one to the side of the next. Consequently, of all these columns one was not going to have five bars of its own: to this last one came the five bars from the column next to it. "And you shall overlay the columns with gold, and you shall make bronze rings into which you shall put the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold." So that the columns would not be hollowed out with holes for the bars to go into, he commanded rings to be made, which would hold the ends of the bars on either side. We may therefore understand that these rings hung from small loops fixed in the wood, so that they could receive and hold the ends of the bars.

"And you shall set up the tabernacle according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain. And you shall make a veil of blue, purple, twisted scarlet and spun fine linen; you shall make it woven work with cherubim. And you shall place it on four columns of wood that does not rot, overlaid with gold; and their capitals shall be of gold and their four bases of silver. And you shall put the veil on the columns, and you shall bring the ark of the testimony in there, inside the veil; and the veil shall divide for you between the holy place and the holy of holies. And you shall cover the ark of the testimony with the veil in the holy of holies." All this makes it clear that the ark of the testimony was placed inside, within this veil hung on four columns. He did not command the ark to be covered with the veil in the sense that the veil would lie on top of the ark's lid, but that it would be set up in front of it. Then he says: "And you shall put the table outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table, on the side of the tabernacle that faces south; and you shall put the table on the side of the tabernacle that faces north." This too is plain. Then follows: "And you shall make a screen of blue, purple, twisted scarlet and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer. And you shall make five columns for the veil and overlay them with gold, and their capitals of gold. And you shall cast five bronze bases for them." What purpose this veil stretched on five columns serves will become clear later; here it is not clear. He means it to be the veil of the door of the tabernacle, that is, of this inner tabernacle around which the court is placed. Then he commands that the altar of sacrifices and burnt offerings be made, and he says how it is to be made, but he does not yet say where it is to be placed. This too will become clear later.

From here to the end he speaks of the court, which is to be placed around the tabernacle whose construction he described first. "And you shall make a court," he says. In Greek he says αὐλήν (aulēn), not αὐλαίαν (aulaian). Some of our translators did not distinguish this word from the hangings that the Greeks call αὐλαίαι (aulaiai), not αὐλαί (aulai), and translated both as "courts", saying, "And you shall make the tabernacle of ten courts," where they ought to have said "of ten hangings." Some, far less skilled, translated both αὐλαί and αὐλαίαι as "doors." But just as we find aulaea in Latin for what the Greeks call αὐλαίαι, so our people have called what they call αὐλή an aula. In Latin, however, this word no longer means a court but a royal palace, whereas among the Greeks it means a court. So he says: "And you shall make a court for the tabernacle. On the side that faces south, the hangings of the court shall be of twisted fine linen, a hundred cubits long for one side. Their columns shall be twenty and their bronze bases twenty, and their rings and their arches of silver. So also for the side that faces north, hangings a hundred cubits long; and their columns twenty and their bronze bases twenty, and their rings and the arches of the columns and the bases overlaid with silver. And the width of the court toward the sea shall have hangings of fifty cubits; their columns ten and their bases ten. And the width of the court toward the east shall be fifty cubits; its columns ten and their bases ten."

Here at last we see columns mentioned on the east, when he speaks of the court, ten of them with bronze bases, just as he said of the western ones. This raises a very difficult question. It is easy enough to accept on the east a single row of columns belonging to the court, by which the inner tabernacle is surrounded on all four sides, since the inner tabernacle had no columns on that side. But on the west, where there were already the eight columns of the inner tabernacle, how are we to understand these ten as well, which he mentions as belonging to the outer court? Are there two rows of columns on the west, eight inner and ten outer? If so, the sides of the outer court will also be longer than those of the inner tabernacle, so that there is room for another row of columns to run from end to end without running into the first row, which belongs to the inner tabernacle. And if that is so, it will follow that the twenty columns on each of the two sides of the inner tabernacle, south and north, are set at shorter intervals than the twenty columns the outer court has on the same sides. Scripture says that the outer rows of twenty columns span a hundred cubits each; the inner rows of the same number of columns must span somewhat fewer cubits, how many Scripture has not stated. It will then follow that the eight columns of the inner tabernacle on the west side are spaced more widely than the twenty columns of the same tabernacle on the south and north, so that they can take in enough space for stretching around it the ten hangings of which he said at the start this tabernacle was to be made. For these are twenty-eight cubits each, which together make two hundred and eighty. If a hundred of these were on each of the two sides, south and north, where the rows of twenty columns stand, then forty cubits would of course be stretched across each of the other two sides, east and west. Forty cubits would then correspond to eight columns in the same proportion as a hundred cubits to twenty columns. But then the sides of the outer court would not be longer, since they are fixed at a hundred cubits each, and so there would be no way for that row of ten columns, running from the south corner to the north corner, to enclose the row of eight inner columns. Therefore, for the inner tabernacle to be surrounded on every side by the court, it must also be shorter in length. Thus its twenty columns on the two sides along which it extends lengthwise must necessarily be set more closely than the twenty of the outer court, and the eight columns of the inner tabernacle on the west must be set more widely than the ten of the outer court on the same side. For whatever is lost in the length of hanging stretched along the twenty columns on each of the two sides, south and north, must be made up in the width of the east and west sides, so that the full two hundred and eighty cubits of hangings are used. For he did not command any of these hangings to be doubled, as he did with the curtains of hair, where there was one too many. So if the length of the inner tabernacle is shortened just enough for it to be enclosed by the outer court, so that its twenty columns on each side carry not a hundred cubits of hanging but, say, at least ninety-six, being four cubits shorter on each side, then those four cubits on each side, eight in all, must of course be stretched along the other two sides, east and west. Thus the eight western columns of the inner tabernacle carry not forty cubits but forty-four, and another forty-four are stretched on the east. Since, then, fifty cubits are stretched across the ten columns of the outer court, and forty-four across the eight of the inner tabernacle, the intervals between the eight inner columns are found to be wider than those between the ten outer ones. If they were equal, forty cubits would be stretched across eight columns just as fifty were across ten, since forty stands to fifty in the same proportion as eight to ten. For forty contains the number five eight times, and fifty ten times.

The unequal spacing of the columns would not trouble us — that they were set closer together along the sides of the length, where there are twenty, and farther apart along the side of the breadth, where there are eight — unless something else came up that forced us to change our view. For when he had said that the length of the court toward the sea has hangings of fifty cubits, with ten columns and their ten bases, and that the breadth of the court toward the east is likewise of fifty cubits, with ten columns and ten bases, it seemed that with these words the shape of the tabernacle, with its court surrounding it on every side, was complete. But then he added something else, and where and how it is to be understood is very hard to discover. "And fifteen cubits," he says, "the height of the hangings for one side; their columns three and their bases three. And the second side, fifteen cubits the height of the hangings; their columns three and their bases three. And the covering of the gate of the court, twenty cubits in height, of blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, embroidered in varied needlework; their columns four and their bases four." Where these are to be placed, once that shape of the tabernacle is complete, I do not see; but I clearly see that the number of columns is the same, ten, in three and three and four: three, that is, at the sides and four in the middle. And so those hangings of fifty cubits will not be woven in one piece, or there would be no entrance into the court; rather, the middle twenty cubits will be separated from the fifteen cubits on either side, to form the covering of the gate of the tabernacle, that is, the curtain, which hangs down as ornament and veil and occupies the space of four columns that has been assigned and set apart for the gate of the court. That is why he wanted this curtain, divided and separated from the sides of fifteen cubits, to be distinguished in appearance as well, being varied with those four colors in embroidered work. But if those sides of fifteen cubits, with three columns on either side, are joined in one straight line with the gate of the court, there will be no space between the ten columns of the outer court and the eight of the inner tabernacle where the altar can stand, occupying a space five cubits square; nor space in front of the altar, where service is done at the altar; nor space between the altar and the door of the inner tabernacle where the bronze laver can stand. For it was commanded to be placed there, so that the priests might wash their hands and feet from it when they enter the tabernacle or when they approach to serve at the altar. Unless we understand this to be outside the tabernacle, in the court, how can they first wash their hands and feet and then enter the tabernacle? Yet we cannot set the altar outside the court, because he commanded that both the tabernacle and the altar be surrounded by the court. It remains, therefore, that we understand those sides of fifteen cubits with three columns on either side as side walls, so that they themselves make an interval of that many cubits between the gate of the court and the door of the inner tabernacle: the gate open for twenty cubits across four columns, with a curtain of twenty cubits varied with embroidered work; and the door of the inner tabernacle, where that screen stretched on five columns is to be placed. This screen we ought surely to understand as placed not within that row of eight columns but outside, toward the court. For then it will be the curtain of the door of the tabernacle, a door that opened as if with folding leaves, where the drapes were not joined to one another by rings and loops. Or else, if it was perhaps within that row of eight columns of the inner tabernacle, this screen on five columns was set before the door of the tabernacle so that when the door was opened the interior would not be laid bare to the view of those looking in. Yet whether this screen was placed inside or outside that row of columns — which is not sufficiently clear — it undoubtedly stood at a moderate distance from that row, so that five columns crowded too closely against four would not block the entrance rather than veil it.

According to this arrangement, then, and this shape of the tabernacle, there is no longer any need to set the twenty columns on the south and north sides of the inner tabernacle closer together and to space the eight on the west farther apart. For the ten columns of the outer court on that same western side do not form a long row of columns enclosing the eight inner ones. Instead, with three set on either side and four at the gate, they enclose a space in which there can be the altar of burnt offerings, within the gate of the court and before the door of the tabernacle; the laver, between the door of the tabernacle and the altar; and the interval needed for ministry between the altar and the gate of the court. And so that whole space of the court is enclosed by ten columns, three on the north, three on the south and four on the west, as if you were drawing the Greek letter Π. And this same space was joined to the longer row of columns of the inner tabernacle, as if you were to add to that letter, on the side where it is open, the stroke of the letter called iota, so that the open side is closed by the middle part of the iota, while the remaining parts of the iota stick out on either side. Ten columns, then, could be counted in that long western row of the inner tabernacle, but only if the two that were the last in the rows of the north and south sides of the court were added to those eight. For the ten columns that belonged properly to the court on the western side, from which one entered the tabernacle, also had three on the sides and four at the front, where the gate was, and so they enclosed within the court, in front of the tabernacle, the space needed for the business of the sacrifices. On the three columns at the sides were hangings of fine linen, fifteen cubits each; on the four where the gate was, a curtain of twenty cubits varied with embroidered work.

Nor should anyone be troubled that Scripture says: "fifteen cubits the height of the hangings for one side; their columns three and their bases three. And the second side, fifteen cubits the height of the hangings; their columns three and their bases three. And the covering of the gate of the court, twenty cubits in height." For it calls "height" the very thing that had been the length of the hangings: the dimension that is height when they are woven is length when they are stretched out. Lest we seem to be merely guessing at this, Scripture mentions the same thing in another place and says: "And they made the court that is toward the south; the hangings of the court of twisted fine linen, a hundred by a hundred" — that is, a hundred cubits of hangings along a hundred cubits of the space that twenty columns occupied. Then it goes on: "and their columns twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze. And the side that is toward the north, a hundred by a hundred; and their columns twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze. And the side that is toward the sea, drapes of fifty cubits; their columns ten and their bases ten" — by "drapes" he means the same as "hangings." "The side that is toward the east, hangings of fifty cubits." After this he returns to the rear of the tabernacle, to show how those ten columns enclosed the space of the court he was speaking of. "Fifteen cubits," he says, "which is at the back" — he calls it the back because it was the rear of the tabernacle, that is, on the western side — "and their columns," he says, "three and their bases three. And at the second back, on this side and that, beside the gate of the court, drapes of fifteen cubits; their columns three and their bases three." It is surely clear that here, where everything is related as it was made, the two that are called "backs" are the same as those called "sides" when it was being commanded that they be made: "sides," because they were joined on either side to the western gate of the court and enclosed its space; "backs," because this part of the court lay behind the tabernacle, that is, on the western side. He then goes on to say: "All the drapes of the court of twisted fine linen; and the bases of the columns of bronze, and their hooks of silver, and their capitals overlaid with silver, and the columns overlaid with silver, all the columns of the court." Then he adds what he had not yet mentioned in this passage: "And the curtain of the gate of the court, the work of an embroiderer, of blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, twenty cubits in length and height." See, here it is plain that what was called height above is the same as what had been the length of the drapes when stretched out. Finally he adds: "and a breadth of five cubits." For the hangings of the outer court rose up to that many cubits of breadth, just as those of the inner tabernacle rose four cubits. So too he had said earlier: "The length of the court a hundred by a hundred, and the breadth fifty by fifty, and the height five cubits, of twisted fine linen," calling "height" here what he later called "breadth," since what is the breadth of things lying flat is the height of the same things set upright; just as, as I mentioned a little earlier, what is height when they are woven is length when they are stretched out.

Now let us look at what I had put off: how, from this shape of the whole tabernacle, which I have set before your eyes as best I could, that difficulty about the hair curtains may be resolved. It was perhaps the more obscure because something was said there in anticipation, to serve a part of the work of which he was going to speak later, when he described the court to be set around the tabernacle. So let us now look at the words themselves. "And you shall put underneath," he says, "what is left over in the curtains of the tabernacle; the half curtain that is left over you shall tuck under; what is in excess in the curtains of the tabernacle you shall tuck under behind the tabernacle." All of this has a single sense: "the half curtain that is left over, that is, what is in excess of the curtains of the tabernacle, is to be tucked under behind the tabernacle." How, then, a half curtain is left over — that is, is in excess and remains — we must work out from that series of joined curtains. For he wanted five joined to one another and six joined to one another, as he had said earlier, the sixth curtain to be doubled over at the front of the tabernacle, that is, on the east. He indicated many times that the rear of the tabernacle was on the western side, that is, toward the sea; so what is to be understood as the front of the tabernacle but the part toward the east? The part, then, in which the five curtains were joined has a hundred and fifty cubits, that is, five times thirty — for each was thirty cubits, as God had commanded them to be made — while the part in which not five but six curtains were likewise joined together had a hundred and eighty cubits, that is, six times thirty. Therefore, when one of them was doubled over at the front of the tabernacle, as commanded, fifteen cubits were lost in that doubling, and when these were subtracted a hundred and sixty-five remained. So beyond the hundred and fifty cubits by which this part of six curtains matched the part of five, fifteen cubits were left over and in excess. On the one side, the part of five curtains, there were a hundred and fifty cubits; on the other, the part of six curtains, with one curtain doubled at the front of the tabernacle, there were a hundred and sixty-five. This part therefore had fifteen cubits more. This is what he calls the half curtain, which he orders to be tucked under behind the tabernacle. Since the one at the front was doubled over, this excess half at the rear of the tabernacle was not to be doubled but tucked under; that is, all those fifteen cubits were to be let down underneath and covered, and so they too would be taken off that length, just as the other fifteen had been taken off at the front of the tabernacle by doubling one curtain. In this way the hundred and fifty cubits of the five curtains would be matched on the other side by a hundred and fifty cubits of the six: thirty cubits, that is, being taken from the hundred and eighty, by doubling a curtain at the front of the tabernacle and tucking a half curtain under at the rear.

What follows next is a different matter and raises a different question, and it was chiefly on its account that I thought the explanation of this passage should be put off, so that we might first see both the shape in which the tabernacle was to be set up and what is written about the court to be placed around it. It goes on, then: "A cubit on this side and a cubit on that, from what is left over in the curtains from the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle, to cover it on this side and on that." It is one thing for the one part, of six curtains, to exceed the other part, of five curtains, because of the greater number of curtains, which we have already discussed; it is another thing to speak of what is left over from the length of the curtains, which is what is now being said. For here it is not a matter of comparing part with part and finding that one exceeds the other — the part with six curtains, that is, exceeding the part with five; to make those equal, one curtain was doubled at the front of the tabernacle and a half curtain tucked under at the back. Rather, the hair curtains themselves, compared with the drapes, of which he ordered ten to be made for the inner tabernacle, woven in four colors, are found to be longer by two cubits each. For those drapes were twenty-eight cubits each, these thirty. That is why he does not say here "from what is left over from the curtains," but "from what is left over in the curtains from the length of the curtains." What, then, does "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle" mean, if not that the length by which each hair curtain is longer than each drape is not all to be gathered to one side — so that whatever is in excess is collected at the rear of the tabernacle — but is to be shared out equally, with as much of it given to the front of the tabernacle as to the rear? That is, since two cubits in each curtain make up the excess length, this part takes one cubit of it and that part one cubit; and so from its single cubits this part will have ten cubits and that part, from its single cubits, ten, since ten curtains each two cubits longer make up a length of twenty cubits, by which their series appears to exceed the series of drapes.

Next we must see what space these twenty cubits, left over from the length of the curtains, serve to enclose. For if it is the inner tabernacle that is covered all round with the hair curtains, they are in excess in such a way that there is nothing at all for them to cover. It would follow that these too must be tucked under and removed by tucking — which Scripture does not say. For the ten drapes of twenty-eight cubits each, with which the inner tabernacle is hung, encompass as much space as two hundred and eighty cubits can encompass. Of these cubits the longer sides, south and north, which have twenty columns each, take a hundred cubits each; eighty remain, to be divided forty apiece between the two remaining, shorter sides: the east, which has no row of columns, and the west, where there were eight columns. Accordingly, with the hair curtains, since three hundred cubits remained after thirty were subtracted, if the two hundred and eighty cubits of the drapes are covered with three hundred cubits of hair curtains, twenty will be left over with nothing for them to cover. Therefore the two cubits by which each hair curtain is longer, out of which the total of twenty cubits is made up, are to be distributed thus: "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that"; that is, they are not all to be gathered to one part, so that they may serve to cover the sides of the tabernacle — but the sides of the outer court; that is, so that all those three hundred cubits of hair curtains may enclose the tabernacle on the outside. For when the sides of the outer court, a hundred cubits each, are added — that is, the south and the north — there remain fifty cubits each for the east and west, and all of these together make three hundred, and the three hundred cubits of the hair curtains are enough to cover them. This is what he means by "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that": the distribution of the two cubits by which each hair curtain is longer. This is what "from what is left over in the curtains from the length of the curtains shall be a covering over the sides of the tabernacle" means — over the outer sides, that is, which belong to the court — "to cover it on this side and on that." It does not mean those sides of the court itself which stretch a hundred cubits along twenty columns, for these were made no longer than those of the inner tabernacle, which are hung with ten drapes and likewise have twenty columns each. Just as the two sides of the inner tabernacle on the north and south extend a hundred cubits each, so too do those of the outer court. So the length by which the hair curtains exceed the length of the drapes does not serve to cover those outer sides with the same number of columns; for they give the outer sides as much as they would have given the inner ones, that is, a hundred cubits each, which makes two hundred. But forty cubits apiece would have been enough for the east and west sides if only the inner tabernacle were enclosed with the hair curtains; once the sides of the court were added, however, the breadth of the tabernacle grew, so that to cover the east and west sides not forty but fifty cubits apiece are now needed. To cover these, the extra length of the hair curtains over the drapes could be put to use, so that the two cubits by which each is longer were not both spent on one part, but "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that"; and so out of that very surplus the east side would have ten cubits and the west another ten. For twenty is ten times two, since the thirty cubits of the eleventh curtain are taken off this circuit by the doubling and the tucking under.

Now the passage rendered in Latin as "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, from what is in excess in the curtains, of the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, will be covering over the sides of the tabernacle" has in the Greek the word plagia [πλάγια], which some Latin translators have rendered not as "sides" but as "oblique parts." This rightly gives us pause. Admittedly nothing here seems oblique, since all the angles of the four sides are right angles. Still, the sides that cannot be called plagia are the two of which one is at the front and the other at the back, that is, the eastern and the western; the sides that can be called plagia are those on the right and the left, that is, the northern and the southern. So the sides of fifty cubits each, which we said the surplus length of the hair curtains could have served to cover, are not plagia. How then will it be true that "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, from what is in excess in the curtains, of the length of the curtains of the tabernacle, will be covering over the sides of the tabernacle"? No doubt he is speaking of covering those sides which he also calls "backs," of fifteen cubits and three pillars each. Together with the gate of the court, which had twenty cubits and four pillars, they make up fifty cubits and ten pillars. At one end these sides had the gate of the court between them, and at the other end the door of the tabernacle. Between the gate of the court and the door of the tabernacle lies a space as large as those cubits enclose, twenty at the gate and fifteen on the right and on the left. In that space, inside the gate of the court and in front of the door of the tabernacle, is the altar of burnt offerings; and between the altar and the door of the tabernacle is the bronze basin, where the priests washed their hands and feet. If the measurements are carefully examined, perhaps some obliqueness is actually found in these sides of three pillars, which in Greek are called plagia, so that some of our translators were not wrong to render as "oblique" what they found in the Greek as plagia. For the hair curtains could not cover the fifteen cubits of hangings on those sides with their own fifteen cubits unless they spent no more than ten cubits on the back parts of the tabernacle before turning onto those sides. Consider the straight line at the back of the tabernacle, that is, on the west side. This line had eight pillars belonging to the inner tabernacle, and came to have ten when the sides of the outer court were added; and where it had had forty cubits belonging to the eight pillars, it came to have fifty with ten pillars. When ten cubits coming from each corner of this line have been covered by the hair curtains, thirty cubits will remain in the middle, covered not by the hair curtains but only by the tapestries; and in the middle of those thirty cubits, however many cubits it extended, was the door of the tabernacle. Now those sides of three pillars and fifteen cubits were twenty cubits apart at the end where they joined the gate of the court, because that was the width of the gate that separated them; but at the other end, where they joined that back line of the tabernacle we have spoken of, they were thirty cubits apart. So they were undoubtedly oblique, since they lay farther apart at the end where there were thirty cubits between them than at the end where there were twenty. Thus the ten cubits of the hair curtains that served the back part of the tabernacle, that is, the western part (half of the surplus length, just as the other ten served the front part, that is, the eastern), completed the covering of those sides called plagia in Greek with five cubits each, five on one side and five on the other. Had these been lacking, ten cubits of those sides would have been covered and five left bare. So, as far as I can see, it is better to understand that the words "a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, from what is in excess in the curtains, of the length of the curtains of the tabernacle" were said not because there was a single cubit on each side, since there were five on each side, but because these cubits came from the surplus length by which the hair curtains were two cubits longer than the tapestries. Of those two cubits of each curtain, one went to the eastern part, and the other was of course left for the western part, so that a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side would be covering over the plagia of the tabernacle. Hence it is said, "to cover it on this side and on that," because it would not have covered the whole if those same five cubits had been lacking.

Now that there has been enough discussion of how we are to understand everything in the construction of the tabernacle that seemed obscure, let us try, if we can, to show briefly what that discussion has established. The entrance, then, was from the west, and the first gate one came to was the gate of the court. It was twenty cubits wide and had four pillars, from which hung a curtain twenty cubits long and five cubits high, worked in needlework of the four colors so often mentioned. Entering by this gate, one found oneself in a court whose sides on the right and left ran inward for fifteen cubits each, with three pillars each. Where they ended, they had the door of the inner tabernacle in the middle between them, just as where they began they had the gate of the court in the middle between them. This court was therefore wider than it was long. Its length, from its gate to the door of the inner tabernacle, was about fifteen cubits, while its width was twenty cubits at the gate and thirty cubits at the door. From this we understand that the sides on the right and left, with their three pillars and fifteen cubits each, were oblique. In this court was the altar of sacrifices, which was square, five cubits long and as many wide. Between the gate and the altar was a space where those who placed the sacrifices on the altar moved about. Farther in, between the altar and the door of the tabernacle, was the place for the ashes in front of the altar, and then the bronze basin, where the priests washed their hands and feet whether they were about to serve at the altar in the court or to enter the inner tabernacle. The hangings of this court on the sides with three pillars were of fine linen, fifteen cubits long and five cubits high.

From this court, then, after passing the altar and the bronze basin, one entered the door of the tabernacle. One entered by parting the tapestries, ten in number, five on one side and five on the other, set facing each other, which enclosed the whole inner tabernacle. On entering this door one met the curtain that had been placed at the door, stretched on five pillars and made of those four colors. When he commanded this curtain to be made, he called it a draw-curtain, I suppose because it ran back and forth as it was drawn and drawn back to close and open the entrance. Past this curtain one came into the middle part of the tabernacle, between this curtain and the other, inner one, which had been hung on four pillars, was made of those four colors, and divided the holy place outside from the holy of holies within. In this middle space between the two curtains stood the golden table, which held the bread of the Presence, on the north side, and opposite it, on the south side, the golden lampstand with seven lamps. Priests of the second rank were permitted to enter this far.

Farther in, that is, in the holy of holies beyond the curtain of four pillars, was the gilded ark of the testimony. In it were the stone tablets of the law, Aaron's rod, and the golden jar with the manna. Above it was the golden mercy seat, on which stood two cherubim, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings and facing each other and the mercy seat. In front of the ark, that is, between the ark and the curtain, was placed the altar of incense, which Scripture sometimes calls golden and sometimes gilded; it calls it golden, of course, because it was overlaid with gold. Only the high priest was permitted to enter this holy of holies: daily, to bring in the incense, and once a year with blood to purify the altar, and also whenever need required it on account of a sin of the priest or of the whole congregation, as is written in Leviticus. In this way the tabernacle was entered from the west, that is, from the gate of the court inward to the eastern side, where the ark of the testimony was.

This inner tabernacle began not at the gate of the court but at the door that was called the door of the tabernacle, and in length it ended at the eastern side, where the ark of the testimony was. It was enclosed by ten tapestries of twenty-eight cubits each, five on one side and five on the other, joined to one another by loops and rings and set facing each other. It had twenty pillars on each of the longer sides, north and south, and eight pillars on the western side; on the eastern side it had no pillars, only the tapestries. These ten tapestries rose four cubits high and stretched around the whole circuit for two hundred and eighty cubits. A hundred cubits of these were on each of the longer sides, south and north, along twenty pillars, and forty cubits on each of the two remaining, shorter sides: on the western side along eight pillars, and on the eastern side, where there were no pillars, the tapestries alone were stretched from the two corner pillars, with none in between. These ten tapestries were woven of the four colors. This inner tabernacle, then, was surrounded by the court, with twenty pillars on the south and twenty on the north. These two sides of the court were equal in length to the sides of the inner tabernacle, since they too stretched along twenty pillars for as many cubits, that is, a hundred cubits each. On the eastern side the court was enclosed by ten pillars and fifty cubits. This row of pillars was straight and ran into the two corner pillars of the inner tabernacle, the only ones the eastern side had; so together with them it made up ten. On the western side the court did have ten pillars, but not in a straight row; rather, as we have already shown, they formed a kind of three-sided portico, with four at the gate and three on each side.

The whole court around the tabernacle was enclosed by hangings of fine linen, five cubits high. Over these came the eleven hair curtains, five joined together on one side and six on the other. In the five joined curtains there were a hundred and fifty cubits, and on the other side, in the six joined curtains, a hundred and eighty, since each curtain was thirty cubits long. But to make one side equal to the other, one curtain was doubled over at the front of the tabernacle, that is, on the east, and half a curtain was tucked under at the back, that is, on the west. In this way thirty cubits, the length of one curtain, were taken away, and a hundred and fifty remained, as many as on the other side. So the circuit of hair curtains enclosing the court of the tabernacle stretched for three hundred cubits, just as the circuit of the ten tapestries of the inner tabernacle stretched for two hundred and eighty cubits; for each tapestry was twenty-eight cubits long, while the hair curtains were thirty cubits long. Accordingly, of the circuit of tapestries of the inner tabernacle, which measured two hundred and eighty cubits, a hundred cubits were on each of the longer sides, south and north, and forty on each of the two shorter sides, east and west. Of the circuit of hair curtains covering the outer court, which measured three hundred cubits, a hundred were on each of the longer sides, south and north, since these were equal to the sides of the inner tabernacle, and fifty on each of the two remaining sides, east and west. Hence the two cubits by which a hair curtain was longer than a tapestry served not the southern and northern sides, which were equal for the outer court and the inner tabernacle, but the eastern and western sides; for it was on those sides that the width of the tabernacle had grown when the court was placed around it on the outside. Now the fifty cubits of hair curtains on the eastern side stretched along the straight row of ten pillars, and they were served by one of the two cubits by which those curtains were longer. The other fifty cubits, which belonged to the western side and were served by the other of the two cubits, did not stretch along a straight row of pillars. For there stood that kind of three-sided portico, with four pillars at the gate and three on each side, enclosing the space of the court where the altar of sacrifices stood. For this reason those fifty cubits could not also go around the gate; they stretched only far enough to cover the oblique sides of three pillars and fifteen cubits each. The hair curtains rose four cubits high, and they covered the linen hangings of the court, which were five cubits high.

The rams' skins dyed red came over the hair curtains. On top, that is, at the roof in place of a vault, the tabernacle was covered with hyacinth-blue skins. Whether the court was covered along with that inner space is not clear; but it is more credible that the spaces of the court between the outer and inner pillars were open to the sky, especially the western one, where the altar of sacrifices stood.
BOOK THREE. QUESTIONS ON LEVITICUS.

QUESTION 1. "If a soul sins, and hears the voice of an oath, and is himself a witness, or has seen it or been privy to it, if he does not report it. And he will bear sin." That is: if he does not report it, he will bear sin. The added "and" is an idiom common in the Scriptures. But since the sense here is obscure, it seems to need explaining. It seems to be saying that a person sins when someone swears falsely in his hearing, and he knows that the man is swearing falsely, and he keeps silent. He knows it if he was a witness to the matter sworn about, or saw it, or was privy to it. That is, he learned of it in some way: either he saw it with his own eyes, or the man who swears told him himself, for in that way he could have been privy to it. But between the fear of this sin and the fear of betraying people there often arises no small temptation. If someone is ready to perjure himself, we can call him back from so grave a sin by warning him or forbidding him. But if he will not listen and swears falsely in our presence about a matter we know, then whether he ought to be betrayed, when betrayal might even put him in danger of death, is a most difficult question. Since the text does not state here to whom this should be reported, whether to the person to whom the oath is sworn, or to the priest, or to someone who not only cannot pursue him by inflicting punishment but can even pray for him, it seems to me that a person frees himself from the bond of sin if he reports it to those who can do the perjurer more good than harm, whether by correcting him or by appeasing God on his behalf, provided that the perjurer also applies the medicine of confession.

After this kind of sin, which he mentioned in connection with someone's perjury left unreported, he ordered no sacrifice to be offered for it. Instead he went on to add: "Any soul that touches any unclean thing, whether a carcass, or something unclean caught by a wild beast, or any of the carcasses of unclean abominations, the carcass of unclean beasts, or touches any of a person's uncleanness, any uncleanness of his by touching which he will be defiled, and it was hidden from him, but afterward he comes to know it and has transgressed." Here too he did not mention any sacrifice to be offered for this kind of sin.
