He added still more and said: "Any soul that swears, distinguishing with his lips to do evil or to do good, in all things whatsoever that a person distinguishes with an oath, and it was hidden from him, and he comes to know it, and he sins in one of these, and confesses the sin for which he sinned, against it." Having joined all these together and set them out without any sacrifice in between, he goes on to say: "And he shall offer to the Lord for the things in which he transgressed, for the sin which he sinned, a female from the sheep, a ewe-lamb, or a she-goat from the goats, for sin; and the priest shall make entreaty for him for the sin, and the sin shall be forgiven him." Why is it, then, that he mentioned no sacrifice for someone's perjury passed over in silence, or for touching a carcass or something unclean, but for the sin in which someone swears falsely without knowing it he said that a ewe-lamb or a she-goat should be offered? Or should this sacrifice be understood as covering all the cases mentioned above? Perhaps he wanted to list them all first and only then state by what sacrifice they could be expiated. But among all these kinds of sin mentioned above, some are put somewhat obscurely because of the idioms used, such as when he says "the carcass of beasts." What the Greeks call ktēnē most of our translators have rendered as "iumenta." In Latin usage that name belongs to the animals whose labor helps us most in carrying loads, such as horses, asses, mules, camels and the like. But what the Greeks call ktēnē is understood so broadly that all, or nearly all, livestock is included under that name. That is why, by an unusual idiom, as a kind of pleonasm, the Greek added "unclean" when it said "of beasts," since there are also clean animals that are called ktēnē. But the animals that Latin usage calls iumenta are, by the distinctions of the law, all unclean.

Again, where he says, "Any soul that swears, distinguishing to do evil or to do good," one may ask what he meant by "distinguishing." Scripture uses this word constantly. From it comes this too: "I will pay my vows, which my lips distinguished." Again, it is said to Ezekiel: "When I say to the wicked man, 'You shall surely die,' and you did not distinguish it or speak." And again it is written: "If a woman living in her father's house vows a vow, distinguishing with her lips against her own soul." This distinguishing, then, seems to be a kind of defining, by which something is set apart from other things that are not bound by what is said alone. So let the passage be taken as though it said: "Any soul that swears, defining with his lips to do evil or to do good, in all things whatsoever that a person defines with an oath, and it was hidden from him" (that is, he swore to do something without knowing whether it should be done or not) "and he comes to know it, and he sins in one of these" (either because he swore before he understood, or because he did what he swore to do and learned afterward that it should not have been done or sworn) "and confesses the sin for which he sinned," that is, the sin that he sinned, for this is an idiom. When he adds "against it," what is meant except that he confessed against the sin itself, that is, accused the sin by confessing it? "And he shall offer to the Lord for the things in which he transgressed, for the sin which he sinned, a female from the sheep, a ewe-lamb." By a customary idiom he speaks of a "female" ewe-lamb, as if a ewe-lamb could be anything but female, "or a she-goat from the goats," as he said a ewe-lamb "from the sheep," as if a ewe-lamb could come from anything but sheep or a she-goat from anything but goats. There is, however, a real question, and not a small one, about why he constantly says, "but afterward he comes to know it and has transgressed," as though the transgression happens only when it becomes known. Or is it rather because satisfaction cannot be made except for what is known? But he does not say, "but afterward he comes to know it and repents." What, then, does "afterward he comes to know it and has transgressed" mean? Does it mean if he transgresses after coming to know it, so that he does knowingly what ought not to be done, and only then is purification owed for the transgression? But that is not what he said beforehand, for he seems to be dealing with sins committed by people who do not know, and therefore by people who do not will them. Perhaps, then, by some idiom "has transgressed" was said for "has learned that it was a transgression." Or was it rather said in reversed order, since Scripture has idioms of that kind too, while in other similar places it was said in the proper order? For elsewhere it is written so often, "and he has transgressed, and it has become known to him," whereas only here, in reversed order as I said, "he comes to know it" is said first and then "and has transgressed." In its proper order it could be put like this: "Any soul that touches any unclean thing, whether a carcass, or something unclean caught by a wild beast, or any of the carcasses of unclean abominations, the carcass of unclean beasts, or touches any of a person's uncleanness, any uncleanness of his by touching which he would be defiled, and it was hidden from him and he has transgressed, but afterward he comes to know it."

"But if his hand is not able to provide enough for a sheep, he shall offer to the Lord for the sin which he sinned two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and one for a burnt offering." Here he clearly resolves the question we were unsure about when he was speaking above. He seems to say "one for sin, the other for a burnt offering" because a sacrifice for sin was never offered except together with a burnt offering. Indeed, when he spoke earlier about burnt offerings on their own, he mentioned a turtledove and did not say two. Now he says two, because the sacrifice for sin was not offered without a burnt offering. So where he said above, "and he shall place it on the burnt offering," there is no doubt that the burnt offering came first and the other was then placed on top of it. But now he speaks differently about the birds: one bird is offered first for sin, and then the other for a burnt offering.

Where he says, "A soul, if it was hidden from him through forgetfulness," this means: if it happened through forgetfulness that it was hidden from him, or from it, if you refer it to the soul. By saying "him" he referred it to the person, for here he uses "souls" to mean people.

"And sins unwillingly in the holy things of the Lord." This kind of sin seems to be stated obscurely, but it is made clear in what follows, where he says, after the sacrifice of the ram has been offered: "He shall restore it and add a fifth." From this we understand that to sin through forgetfulness in the holy things means to appropriate through forgetfulness something that is owed to the holy things, whether to the priests or to the offerings, whether of firstfruits or anything of that kind.

"And any soul that sins and does one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done, and did not know it, and has transgressed, and bears his sin, he shall also bring to the priest a ram without blemish from the sheep, at a price in silver, for the transgression; and the priest shall make entreaty for him on account of his ignorance, in which he was ignorant and did not know, and it shall be forgiven him. For he has transgressed a transgression before the Lord." Leaving aside the unusual crowding of idioms, which by now should be very familiar from constant repetition, the whole sense here is obscure. The question is how this kind of transgression is to be distinguished from those he covered above in general terms. Reason seems to require that particular kinds of sacrifices be applied to particular kinds of sins to expiate them. But what I have just quoted does not name a specific sin. It seems to move within the same generality as the earlier passage, where he laid down as the sacrifice a calf for the priest, likewise a calf for the whole congregation, a he-goat for a ruler, and for any soul, that is, any person, a she-goat or, if he wished, a sheep, but in any case a female animal. Then he began to make exceptions of certain kinds of sins and to state by name what should be offered for them. For instance, for someone's perjury heard and kept silent, for touching a carcass or something unclean, and for a false oath sworn in ignorance: a ewe-lamb from the sheep or a she-goat from the goats, or a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, or a tenth of an ephah of fine flour. And for someone who sins by appropriating through forgetfulness something belonging to the holy things: a ram, together with restitution of that thing with a fifth added. But now, without naming a particular kind of sin, he adds in general terms: "Any soul that transgresses and does one of all the commandments of the Lord which ought not to be done" (just as in that general passage he said, "one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done") "and did not know it, and has transgressed," that is, has sinned unwillingly through ignorance, and he orders a ram to be offered, not a she-goat or a female from the sheep, as he had laid down above for this same general class of sins. What, then, does this mixing up mean? Unless perhaps, when he says here, "For he has transgressed a transgression before the Lord," by "before the Lord" he meant us to understand transgression in the things done before the Lord, that is, in the service rendered to the Lord in the tabernacle. He had said something about this a little earlier, when he said, "He sinned in the holy things," and we understood "he appropriated something belonging to the holy things," since he had also ordered restitution. Accordingly, one can sin in these matters not only by appropriating something from them through forgetfulness, but a person can also transgress through ignorance in many other ways in what is rendered in the service of the Lord. It was this kind of transgression that he afterward chose to mention in general terms, and that is why in both places he ordered a ram to be offered. The Scriptures are full of instances where "before the Lord" is said and nothing is meant except what is rendered to the Lord, such as a sacrifice, or firstfruits, or some service in sacred rites.

It is also asked whether the statement that, if his hand is not able to provide enough for a sheep, he should offer a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, and, if he cannot manage even that, a set quantity of fine flour, is to be applied everywhere. If it is understood to be allowed everywhere, it still cannot be said that the priest, or the whole congregation, does not have a calf, or that a ruler does not have a he-goat or a sheep. And if that is so, why did he need to say afterward that someone's perjury passed over in silence, or touching something unclean, or perjury committed in ignorance, is purified by the sacrifice of a ewe-lamb or a she-goat? The same sacrifices were already prescribed for that general class of sin, to which these cases could also have belonged. But suppose these cases are distinguished from it by this: that for them it was permitted to offer turtledoves and pigeons, or, failing these, fine flour, while where this was not said it was not permitted. Then the poor do not seem to have been provided for. There could be many transgressions not specifically named that would fall under that general class, and the needy would be burdened if only a she-goat or a ewe-lamb from the sheep were allowed there, and not those little birds and the fine flour. Unless perhaps someone says that these excepted sins, named individually, are distinguished from those mentioned in general terms by the fact that here he said "ewe-lamb" and there "sheep," so that the age of the animals makes some difference. Even so, we should understand that the poor were provided for equally in both cases: if they had no four-footed animals at all, they could offer the birds mentioned or the fine flour for their sins of ignorance. But one may be troubled by this: he had included all sins of ignorance in general terms and distinguished the sacrifices not by differences among the sins, which he had not made, but by differences among the persons. Why did he afterward choose to distinguish the sins as well and prescribe different sacrifices for their different kinds, as though they did not all belong to that general class? The later exception should be understood in this way: whatever remains, once the cases he mentioned by name and individually have been excepted, we should take as covered by that general statement. This manner of speaking is not to be found elsewhere, but in the holy Scriptures there is a similar case where the apostle says, "Every sin that a man commits is outside the body." Here he seems to have left out no sin, since he says, "Every sin that a man commits." Yet afterward he excepted fornication when he added, "But he who commits fornication sins against his own body." In our customary way of speaking this would be put: "Every sin that a man commits, except fornication, is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body." So here too: he first said in general terms that all sins of ignorance were to be expiated by the sacrifices he mentioned. Afterward, however, he excepted certain sins, which he set out explicitly and separately and to which he applied a specific sacrificial purification, so that, with these excepted, whatever remained would belong to that general class.

"He shall offer a ram from the sheep without blemish, at a price, for that in which he transgressed." This should not be punctuated as if "at a price for that in which he transgressed" meant the price for which he transgressed. Rather: "if he offers a ram, he shall offer it at a price," that is, bought. Even this seems intended to belong to the mystery of some meaning, since he did not fix the price itself. Had he fixed it, he might have seemed to be commanding only that a cheap animal not be offered, so that even if the offerer did not buy it, he would still offer one worth that much. But he added not only "at a price," so that the ram offered would be bought, but also "of shekels, by the holy shekel." For this is how he puts it: "at a price in silver of shekels, by the holy shekel." So he wanted the ram to be bought for several shekels, not for one. What "the holy shekel" means we have already discussed where it seemed fitting. As for his saying, "And for his transgression he shall offer to the Lord a ram from the sheep without blemish, at a price," and then adding, "for that in which he transgressed," this should be understood as: "he shall offer it for that in which he transgressed," that is, for that matter, on account of that matter. "And he shall take away from the altar the holocarpoma which the fire has consumed, that holocaustosis." What will he take away, if it has been consumed? For he ordered the priest, after the fire had burned all night, to take away the holocarpoma, that is, the burnt offering that the fire has consumed. Or what is meant by his further addition, "that holocaustosis," since holocarpoma is understood to mean the same as holocaustosis? Unless perhaps the true reading is the one we found in a certain Greek copy. It does not say "he shall take away the holocarposis" but "he shall take away the catacarposis," that is, the remains of the burnt offering that the fire has consumed. And these remains, such as ash and charcoal, he called "that holocaustosis" by the name of the thing that was consumed, calling the remains of the consuming by the name of the consuming itself.

Above he said, "This is the law of the burnt offering," and then, explaining what that law is, he says, "This burnt offering shall be on its burning on the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn on it; it shall not be put out." In our customary way of speaking it would be clearer without the "and." Remove that conjunction and the sense runs together like this: "This burnt offering shall be on its burning on the altar all night; until morning the fire of the altar shall burn on it," that is, on the altar. Then, to give the statement full emphasis, he added, "it shall not be put out"; for this had already been said by "all night."

"And he shall put on another robe and cast the holocarpoma outside the camp into a clean place." Here he calls "holocarpoma" what has already been burned up; in that Greek copy the word read here is katakarpōsis. Some Latin translators added "which has been burned up" and rendered it thus: "and he shall cast the holocarpoma, which has been burned up, outside the camp into a clean place."

"And the fire on the altar shall burn from it and shall not be put out"; that is, from the fire in which the burnt offering burned until morning. For he does not want the fire ever to be put out entirely. When the burnt offering has burned until morning and the remains of the burning have been taken away, even then the fire is not to be put out, but renewed from there, so that the other things placed on it may burn.

Then follows: "And the priest shall burn wood on it morning, morning, and shall heap the burnt offering upon it, and shall place on top of it the fat of the peace offering; and the fire shall always burn on the altar; it shall not be put out." We must consider whether by "morning, morning" he meant every day, so that no day was to pass without a burnt offering and the fat of the peace offering being found there, or whether "morning, morning" means that on whatever day it was placed there, it was placed only in the morning. If we take it as every day, what if no one brought anything? But if the priests provided daily burnt offerings, at public expense as it were or at their own, then the offerings brought by the people for sins, which he ordered to be placed on burnt offerings, were placed on these. In that case someone offering a sacrifice for sin did not also need to offer a burnt offering on which to place it, except when a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons was offered. In that case he lays down quite definitely that one must be offered for sin and the other for a burnt offering, first the one for sin and then the burnt offering. A further question can be asked: did the burnt offering that he ordered to be placed there "morning, morning" also burn through the whole night until the next morning? Or was the burnt offering that he says must burn all night the evening one, so that, in beginning to speak of the law of the burnt offering, he started from the evening burnt offering? Yet it would be strange if he were silent about this and gave no instruction that such offerings should be made in the evening.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the gift of Aaron and his sons which they offer to the Lord on whatever day you anoint him." The sacrifices he recorded in Exodus, by which the priests are sanctified over seven days so that they may begin to exercise their priesthood, are one thing. What he now records is another: what the high priest offers when he is installed, that is, when he is anointed. For this is what follows, when he says, "on whatever day you anoint him." He did not say "anoint them," although he orders the priests of the second rank to be anointed as well. Then he names the sacrifice itself: "a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual sacrifice." The question is how it can be perpetual if it is offered on the day the high priest is anointed, by the one who has been anointed. Perhaps it means that this is always to be offered on the day a high priest is anointed, that is, through the succession of priests. It could, however, also be understood as perpetual in this sense: not the thing itself, but what it signifies.

"Half of it," he says, "in the morning and half of it in the afternoon," where the Greek has deilinon. "In a pan," he says, "it shall be made with oil; he shall offer it moistened, crushed"; "it" means the fine flour. Then he says "crushed," if this has been rightly translated from what the Greek has, erikta [?], and he put this in the neuter plural. For he did not say "crushed" in the feminine, as referring to the same fine flour that he had called "moistened." He says that these crushed things are a sacrifice made of broken pieces. So it is not clear whether by "crushed things" he means the broken pieces themselves, that is, things broken small, or whether he called the finest particles of the flour "crushed things."

Then he says: "a sacrifice for an odor of sweetness to the Lord. The anointed priest from among his sons who takes his place shall make it." Perhaps this is why he had said "perpetual": every high priest, when he succeeds one who has died, is to do this on the day he is anointed. For he added, "an eternal law," though "eternal" can also be understood in terms of what it signifies.

Then follows: "The whole shall be consummated," where the Greek has epitelesthēsetai, and some translators said, "the whole shall be placed on." By this he wants it understood to be a burnt offering, since nothing is left of it. Then he adds, "And every sacrifice of a priest shall be a burnt offering and shall not be eaten." This, then, is what he had meant by "the whole shall be consummated."

Speaking of the sacrifice for sin, he says: The priest who offers it shall eat it. He will not eat what he offers, since that will be consumed by fire, but what is left over from it; for it is not a whole burnt offering, which burns entirely on the altar. Later, however, he says: All the sin offerings from which some of their blood has been brought into the tabernacle of witness to make atonement in the holy place shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. How, then, do the remains of the sacrifices for sins belong to the priests to be eaten? We must understand that the exceptions are those with whose blood the altar of incense in the tabernacle of witness is touched. For he commanded this earlier about the calf that the priest was to offer for his own sin, and about the calf offered for the sin of the whole congregation: the flesh that remained was to be burned outside, beyond the camp. He has now briefly called this to mind again.
And this is the law of the ram that is for trespass: they are most holy; that is, they belong to the priests to be eaten.

What does it mean that, after speaking of the ram for trespass and setting out the law of its sacrifice, he says: As that which is for sin, so also that which is for trespass; there is one law for them? The question is what difference there is between sin and trespass, since, if there were none, it would by no means be said: As that which is for sin, so also that which is for trespass. For although there is no difference in the law and its sacrifice, because there is one law for them, they are nevertheless two things with one sacrifice. That is, if sin and trespass did not differ from each other at all and were two names for one thing, Scripture would not take such care to point out that both have one sacrifice.

Perhaps, then, a sin is the doing of evil, and a trespass the abandoning of good. In a praiseworthy life, turning away from evil is one thing and doing good is another, as Scripture reminds us when it says, “Turn away from evil and do good.” In the same way, in a life deserving condemnation, turning away from good may be one thing and doing evil another, so that the first is a trespass and the second a sin. Indeed, if we examine the word itself, what does delictum (trespass) suggest but derelictum (abandoned)? And what does the one who trespasses (delinquit) abandon (derelinquit) but the good? The Greeks too have given this plague two customary names, for among them a trespass is called both paraptōma and plēmmeleia. In this very passage of Leviticus the word is plēmmeleia. But where the Apostle says, “If a man is overtaken in some trespass,” the Greek has paraptōmati. If we examine the origin of these words, paraptōma suggests that the one who trespasses falls away, as it were. Hence a corpse, which Latin speakers called cadaver from cadere, “to fall,” is called ptōma in Greek, apo tou piptein, that is, from falling. So the one who does evil by sinning has first fallen from the good by trespassing. Plēmmeleia, for its part, is a word akin to negligence. In Greek negligence is called ameleia, because what is neglected is not cared for; for a Greek says “I do not care” as ou melei moi. The particle that is added to make plēmmeleia, namely plēn, means “beyond.” So ameleia, which we call negligence, seems to mean “without care,” and plēmmeleia “beyond care,” which comes to almost the same thing. This is why some of our translators preferred to render plēmmeleia not as “trespass” but as “negligence.” In Latin, moreover, what is neglected (neglegitur) except what is not chosen (non legitur, that is, non eligitur)? This is also why Latin authors said that lex, law, is named from legere, that is, from eligere, “to choose.” From these traces, so to speak, we may gather that the one who trespasses is the one who abandons the good and, by abandoning it, falls from the good, because he neglects it, that is, does not choose it. But where the word peccatum (sin), in Greek hamartia, comes from does not occur to me for the present in either language.

It may also seem that a trespass is what is committed imprudently, that is, in ignorance, and a sin what is committed knowingly. These divine testimonies seem to agree with this distinction: “Who understands trespasses?” and also, “For you have known my folly.” For he goes straight on to add, “and my trespasses are not hidden from you,” as though repeating the same thought in another way. Nor does the Apostle’s saying that I mentioned a little earlier disagree with this reasoning: “If a man is overtaken in some trespass.” By saying “overtaken” he indicates that the man slipped through imprudence. That sin, on the other hand, belongs to the one who knows, the apostle James states as though defining it: “So for one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin.” But whether it is this distinction or that one or some other between sin and trespass, if there were none at all, Scripture would not speak as it does when it says, “As with the offering for sin, so with the offering for trespass: there is one law for them.”

For the most part, however, the two words are used without distinction, so that a sin is called by the name of trespass and a trespass by the name of sin. When we say that the remission of sins takes place in baptism, it is not as though trespasses were not also remitted; yet both are not mentioned, because both are understood under that one name. So too the Lord says that his blood is poured out for many for the remission of sins. Just because he did not add “and of trespasses,” will anyone dare to say that in his blood there is no remission of trespasses? Likewise, in what is written in the Apostle, “For the judgment following one led to condemnation, but the grace following many trespasses leads to justification,” what else is meant but that sins too are included under the name of trespasses?

Even in this very passage of Leviticus, which compels us either to find or to believe that there is some difference between trespass and sin, we read as follows, where God is speaking about the very sacrifices that were commanded to be offered for sins: “But if,” he says, “the whole congregation of the children of Israel is ignorant, and the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do one thing out of all the commandments of the Lord that is not to be done, and they trespass, and the sin that they sinned in it becomes known to them…” See: where he said, “and they trespass,” he immediately added, “the sin that they sinned,” meaning of course the very thing in which they trespassed. And a little later he says: “But if a ruler sins and does unwillingly one thing out of all the precepts of the Lord his God that is not to be done, and trespasses…” Likewise in what follows: “But if one soul of the people of the land sins unwillingly, in doing one thing out of all the precepts of the Lord that is not to be done, and trespasses, and the sin that he sinned in it becomes known to him…” Likewise elsewhere: “Any soul that swears, pronouncing with its lips to do evil or to do good, in all things whatsoever that a man may pronounce with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and then he comes to know it and sins in one of these things, and he confesses the sin by which he sinned against it, he shall also offer to the Lord, for what he trespassed, for the sin that he sinned…” And a little later: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a soul is unaware through forgetfulness, and sins unwillingly in the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer for his trespass to the Lord a ram without blemish from the flock, valued in silver by shekels according to the holy shekel, for that in which he trespassed. And he shall make restitution for that in which he sinned in the holy things, and shall add a fifth to it, and shall give it to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him with the ram of the trespass, and he shall be forgiven.” It goes on still and says: “And any soul that sins and does one thing out of all the precepts of the Lord that ought not to be done, and does not know it, and trespasses, and bears his sin, shall offer a ram without blemish from the flock, at its value in silver, for a trespass offering to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him for the ignorance in which he was ignorant and did not himself know, and he shall be forgiven. For he has trespassed with a trespass [?] before the Lord.” And further it says this: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Any soul that sins, and despises with contempt the precepts of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor about something entrusted to him or about a partnership or about robbery, or does his neighbor some wrong, or finds something lost and lies about it, and swears falsely about any one of all the things a man may do so as to sin in them, then it shall be, when he has sinned and trespassed, that he shall give back what he took by robbery, or the wrong by which he did harm, or what was entrusted and deposited with him, or the lost thing that he found, of anything about which he swore falsely; and he shall restore the principal itself and add a fifth of it to it, and give it back to the one to whom it belongs on the day he is convicted. And he shall offer to the Lord for his trespass a ram from the flock without blemish, at the value for that in which he trespassed; and the priest shall make entreaty for him before the Lord, and he shall be forgiven for any one of all the things he did and trespassed in.” So in almost all the acts that he calls sins, he also calls the same acts trespasses. Hence it is clear that in many passages of Scripture they are used without distinction, and yet Scripture testifies that there is some difference between them when it says, “As with the offering for sin, so with the offering for trespass.”

“You shall not eat any fat of oxen or of sheep or of goats. The fat of animals that die of themselves and of those taken by wild beasts may be put to any use, but it shall not be eaten as food. Whoever eats the fat of the cattle from which you offer a sacrifice to the Lord, that soul shall perish from his people.” Earlier he had said of fat, “All fat is the Lord’s,” and we had asked whether this meant all fat of any animal at all, of clean animals at least (for about the unclean there is no question), and what was to be done with fat, since he forbade it to be used as food. Now, however, he has said what was to be done with the fat of an animal that died of itself or was taken by a wild beast, namely, that it may be put to any use; “any use,” that is, any work for which something of the kind is needed. So the question remains what is to be done with the fat of the other animals that are clean for eating. But since he says that anyone who eats the fat of the cattle from which an offering is made to the Lord shall perish from his people, he seems to have specified that only the fat of clean cattle from which sacrifice is made is forbidden as food. Yet we have heard that the Jews take no fat whatever as food. But what we must look for is what Scripture intended, not what they have supposed. In the end they do not find any proper use for the fat from which they abstain, nor a way of disposing of it, since it was said, “All fat is the Lord’s,” if they want this to be understood not only of the fat of the sacrifices but also of the fat of animals from which no sacrifice is made, even unclean ones.

What does it mean that he again gives instructions about sacrifices of salvation and says that the one who offers the gift of his sacrifice of salvation must give the breast and the shoulder to the priests, but in such a way that the fat of the breast is offered to the Lord along with the lobe of the liver? For earlier, speaking of the sacrifices of salvation, he commanded that the lobe of the liver be offered to the Lord with the fat of the belly and of the kidneys and of the loins, but said nothing about the fat of the breast. Is he mentioning here what he left out there? Why, then, does he mention the lobe of the liver both there and here? Or does it perhaps make some difference that earlier he gives instructions about the sacrifice “of salvation,” while here he adds “his,” as though a sacrifice of salvation were one thing and a sacrifice of one’s own salvation another?

When he first mentioned the sacrifices for sins, he said that a calf was to be offered for the sin of the priest who had caused the people to sin. Later too, when Scripture related how what the Lord commanded was carried out regarding Aaron and his sons, a calf is said to have been offered for sin. But earlier he commanded that the horns of the altar of incense be touched with the calf’s blood, that some of that same blood also be sprinkled toward the holy veil, and that the rest of the blood be poured out at the base of the altar of burnt offerings. Later, however, when Aaron is consecrated, nothing is said about sprinkling blood toward the veil. The horns of the altar are mentioned, but “of incense” is not added; and it is added that the blood was poured out “at the base of the altar.” He did not say “at its base,” as though we had to take it as the same altar whose horns he had touched with the blood. So although it is stated ambiguously, we are free to understand that it was done as had earlier been commanded concerning the calf for sin: that is, we need not take it that the horns touched belonged to the altar at whose base the blood was poured, but that the horns of the altar of incense were touched, while the blood was poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifices.

Earlier, because he was giving a general rule, he commanded that if the priest sinned, the anointed and consecrated priest himself, by whom he means the high priest, should offer these sacrifices. But now, when Aaron is being consecrated, Moses offers them and himself receives the breast of the laying-on, which he had earlier said was to be given to the priest. I think it is called the breast of the laying-on because the fat was laid on it, as he mentioned earlier regarding the sacrifice of salvation. Since, then, the high priesthood seems to have begun with Aaron, what are we to think Moses was? If he was not a priest, how were all those things carried out through him? But if he was, how can we maintain that the high priesthood began with his brother? And yet that psalm where it says, “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” removes any doubt that Moses too was a priest. Still, it is Aaron and his successors, the high priests, who are commanded to put on that priestly vestment which contains a great mystery. In Exodus, before anything at all is commanded about consecrating and, in a sense, ordaining the priests, when Moses goes up the mountain the priests are ordered not to go up. We cannot understand these to be any others than the sons of Aaron, and Scripture already called them priests at that time not because they already were, but because they were going to be, by anticipation, as in very many expressions of this kind. For the son of Nun too is called Joshua, though Scripture relates that this name was given to him much later. So were Moses and Aaron both high priests at that time? Or rather Moses, with Aaron under him? Or was Aaron high priest by reason of the pontifical vestment, and Moses by reason of his more exalted ministry? For from the beginning it is said to him: “He shall speak for you in what concerns the people, and you for him in what concerns God.”

One may also ask: after the death of Moses, who anointed the high priest’s successor, who certainly could not succeed until his predecessor had died? Or, since he had already been anointed among the priests of the second rank (for it was the same oil with which both the high priest and those of the second rank were anointed), did that pontiff simply put on the vestment by which his supreme rank was made evident? And if so, did he put it on himself, or did another clothe him, as Moses clothed his brother’s son after his brother’s death? If he was clothed by another, could the high priest be clothed by one of the second rank? Especially since the vestment was such that it had to be put on him by another. Or was he clothed the first time in the same way as afterward? For once he had put it on, he did not keep it on without ever taking it off, nor, having taken it off, did he never put it on again. So perhaps it could happen that priests of the second rank clothed the first as an act of service, not of superiority. But how was it made known which of the sons ought to succeed the high priest? For Scripture did not specify the firstborn or the eldest. Unless we are to understand that it was usually done by some divine sign, whether through a prophet or by any other means by which God is accustomed to be consulted. And yet it seems that the matter came to be settled by contention, so that later on there were for this reason several high priests: when the more eminent men contended, the honor itself was granted to several in order to end the dispute.

What does Moses mean when he says to Aaron and his sons, as they are being consecrated to enter the priesthood: “You shall sit at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony for seven days, day and night, so that you do not die”? Is it credible that they were commanded to sit bodily in one place for seven days, day and night, without moving at all? Yet we are not compelled to take this as something meant allegorically, which was not to be done but only understood. Rather, we should recognize here an idiom of the Scriptures, which uses sitting to mean dwelling and staying. For when it is said of Shimei that he sat in Jerusalem for three years, we are not to suppose that during that whole time he sat in a chair and never got up. This is also why we speak of “seats” for the places where those whose seats they are have their abode; for dwelling took on this name.

“And it came to pass on the eighth day that Moses called Aaron and his sons and the senate of Israel.” Some of our translators have rendered this as “sedatum” [?]; the Greek has gerousia. The translator followed this, because senatus too seems to be named from senium, old age. But in Latin it would not sound right to say “he called the old age of Israel” instead of “the old men” or “the elders,” although it would be the same idiom if one said “he called the youth of Israel” instead of “the young men.” But that is customary in Latin, while the other is not. For it would be the literal rendering if one said, “he called the old age of Israel.” Hence some, thinking it unusual even to say “senate,” translated it as “the order of elders.” Yet it would perhaps be better to say it briefly: “he called the elders of Israel.”

Moses says to Aaron: “And speak to the senate of Israel, saying: Take one he-goat from the goats for sin, and a ram and a calf and a yearling lamb for a whole-burnt offering, without blemish, and a calf from the herd and a ram for a sacrifice of salvation before the Lord, and fine flour mixed with oil, for today the Lord will appear among you.” Earlier he set out four kinds of animal sacrifices: the burnt offering, the offering for sin, the offering of salvation, and the offering of completion. But the offering of completion belongs to the consecration of the priest. So the three remaining kinds are commanded to be offered here, and this is said to the elders of Israel so that it may concern the whole people. In this passage, however, the sacrifice for sin includes three animals, the he-goat, the ram, and the calf; the lamb belongs to the burnt offering, and the calf and the ram to the sacrifice of salvation. Therefore the passage should not be divided so that only the he-goat is understood as being for sin and the other three, the ram, the calf, and the lamb, as being for the burnt offering. Rather, the first three are for sin. That is, in the words “Take one he-goat from the goats for sin, and a ram and a calf,” we should understand “for sin” as applying to all three, and the lamb alone remains for the holocarposis, that is, the burnt offering. We had to point this out because the passage could also be divided so that, after the words “Take one he-goat from the goats for sin,” the rest would be said to belong to the holocarposis. The addition “without blemish” can be referred to all of them. Since it is ambiguous, then, how the passage is better divided, the following consideration leads us to understand the first three as being for sin. Earlier he commanded a he-goat to be offered for the sin of a ruler; for the individual sin of any person, when he sins before the Lord by doing one of the things that ought not to be done, he prescribed a ram; and for the sin of the whole congregation a calf. So when he was telling the senate what the whole people ought to offer, it was fitting that a he-goat be commanded on account of the rulers, a ram on account of each person’s own sin, and a calf on account of the sin of the whole congregation. For it is one thing when each person among the people has his own sin, and all can have sins of their own; it is another when the sin is common, done with one mind, when something is committed by one will once a multitude has been brought together.

As for his commanding a calf and a ram for the sacrifices of salvation, he commands these because they are the choicest, since the occasion concerns the whole people. When he gave instructions earlier about sacrifices of salvation, he ordered that they be offered from any animal, male or female, provided they were offered only from oxen, sheep, and goats. But if one asks why he prescribed two, a calf and a ram, it is hard to find the answer. Unless perhaps he intended the calf as the sacrifice of salvation of the whole people, and the ram as being for each person, for every individual, so to speak. For earlier too he seems to have prescribed, as it were, two kinds of sacrifice of salvation. The one, which was as it were for everyone together, he called the sacrifice of salvation; the other he described when he said, “If anyone offers the sacrifice of his salvation.” There too we found a difference: in the one he called “of salvation” he did not mention that the fat of the breast was to be offered to the Lord and the breast itself and the right shoulder given to the priest; but he commanded this to be done in the one he afterward calls “the sacrifice of his salvation,” which is perhaps to be understood as the private sacrifice of each individual, not the public sacrifice of all together. Moses, too, offered sacrifices of salvation, and it is not said there “of his salvation”; I believe this is because he offered them for the whole people. Where all are, there each one is as well; but where each one is, it does not follow that all are there. For individual things can exist without the whole, but the whole cannot consist of anything but individual members. For the individuals, gathered together or counted up in a total, make up the whole.

It should certainly be noted that when sacrifices are offered for the people, the sacrifices commanded are the offering for sin, the burnt offering, and the sacrifices of salvation. For the priest, however, the offerings made were for sin, the burnt offering, and the offering of completion, but not that of salvation. But the offering of completion was made at the time when the priests were consecrated to exercise the priesthood, and Moses offered these for Aaron and his sons. Afterward Aaron himself, now consecrated and exercising the priesthood, was commanded to offer for himself a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering. He was not, however, commanded to offer the offering of completion for himself, because it had been offered on that earlier occasion so that he might be completed by consecration and be able to exercise the priesthood. Since he was now exercising it, there was no need for him to be completed again.

"And Moses said to Aaron: Approach the altar and make your sin offering and your whole burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself and for your house." It is strange that he says the sin offering is to be made first and then the burnt offering, since earlier he commands that sacrifices for sins be placed on top of burnt offerings, except in what he prescribed about birds. Or perhaps here he mentioned last the thing that was done first, namely the burnt offering? For he did not say, as he did about the birds, "Do this first and afterward that," but "Do this and that." What is to be done first is shown by the instruction set out earlier, where he says that the sacrifice for sins is placed on top of the burnt offering. And yet it is very troubling that Scripture also tells how Aaron did what he had heard in such a way that it mentions first his making the sin offering and then the burnt offering. Whether he himself also did this first, or whether Scripture told first what was done later, as it often does in many places, would remain uncertain, were it not for the passage I mentioned above, where it dealt with the sacrifice for sin. For there we read: "And the priest shall place it on the altar, on top of the whole burnt offering of the Lord; and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has sinned, and it shall be forgiven him." How then could this be placed on top of the burnt offering unless the burnt offering had been placed there first? He also commanded this about the sacrifice of salvation, that it be placed on top of the burnt offering. But because he does not say this everywhere, not for all sacrifices of salvation nor for all sacrifices for sin, it can perhaps be said that this was not commanded as a general rule. Rather, it was said that it should be done only in those cases where it is stated: in the sacrifice of salvation when it is made from cattle, for there he commanded it, and in the sacrifice for sin when it is made from a female of the sheep. The others, whether sacrifices of salvation or for sin, need not be placed on top of burnt offerings.

It is also troubling that when Aaron was making the people's gifts that Scripture mentioned above, not all the animals that had been specified beforehand are said to have been sacrificed, but only the he-goat for sin and the burnt offering, and even there it did not specify that lamb. The two others, which we said belong to the sacrifice for sin rather than to the burnt offering, namely the ram and the calf, it passed over in silence. Unless perhaps it wanted the whole to be understood from the part, so that from the mention of the goat alone we would understand that the others followed as well.

When Scripture was telling how Aaron made the people's sacrifices of salvation, it says of the calf and the ram: "And he slaughtered the calf and the ram of the people's sacrifice of salvation; and the sons of Aaron brought the blood to him, and he poured it out against the altar all around; and the fat that was from the calf and from the ram, the loin and the fat covering the belly and the two kidneys and the fat that is on them and the lobe that is on the liver; and he placed the fats on the breasts, and he laid the fats on the altar; and the breast and the right shoulder Aaron took away as a portion removed before the Lord, as the Lord commanded Moses." Now it speaks in the singular, now in the plural, although it is speaking of two animals, the calf and the ram. So when it says "two kidneys," this must be understood of each animal, and so they make four; and likewise with the rest. But when it says "and he placed the fats on the breasts," although he did not place the breasts themselves on the altar, since they were due to the priest along with the right shoulders, what does it mean? Should it be understood as "and he placed the fats that are on the breasts"? For those were the fats he placed, taken from the breasts, which he was to lay on the altar; that is what had been commanded earlier as well. Then it continues: "and he laid the fats on the altar, and the breast and the right shoulder Aaron took away as a portion removed before the Lord," now putting "breast" in the singular, though it certainly means both of them, one from each animal, which it had called "breasts."

What does it mean when it says: "And when Aaron had lifted up his hands over the people, he blessed them and came down, after he had made the sin offering and the whole burnt offerings and those of salvation"? Where did he do these things if not on the altar, that is, standing at the altar and serving it? So he came down from the place where he had been standing. Indeed, this testimony seems to help solve the question we raised in Exodus: how service could be performed at the altar, which was three cubits high. We could not understand there to have been a step, because God had forbidden it, so that the private parts of the man ministering would not be exposed above the altar. That would certainly happen if the step were part of the altar, that is, if it were built into it and fixed to it. In fact he forbade this where he was speaking of a built altar, for the altar would be one with the step, and the step would be part of it; that is why it was forbidden. Here, however, the altar was so high that the priest could not minister properly unless he stood on something. So it must be understood that whatever it was, it was set in place for the time of ministering and then taken away, and was not part of the altar; therefore it did not go against the precept forbidding the altar to have a step. Scripture said nothing about this thing, whatever it was, and that is why the question arose. But now, when Scripture says that the priest came down after he had made the sacrifices, that is, after he had placed the slaughtered victims on the altar, it plainly shows that he had stood somewhere from which he could come down. And because he had stood there, he was able to serve the three-cubit altar in his ministry.

"And all the people saw and were beside themselves." Other translators rendered this "were terrified," trying to translate the word used in the Greek. From that word also comes ekstasis, which in the Latin Scriptures is often rendered "excess of mind."

"And fire came out from the Lord and consumed what was on the altar, the whole burnt offerings and the fats." One may ask what it meant by "from the Lord": whether the fire came because it was done at the Lord's command and will, or whether it came out from the place where the ark of the testimony was. For the Lord is not in any place in such a way that he is not elsewhere.

The sons of Aaron had dared to put strange fire in their censers and lay incense on it before the Lord. This was not permitted, because everything that had to be kindled in the tabernacle was to be kindled from the fire that had come down from God onto the altar and was then kept burning. They were burned up by fire coming out from the Lord, and after they had died Moses said: "This is what the Lord said: In those who draw near to me I will be sanctified, and in all the congregation I will be glorified." By those who draw near to the Lord he wished to be understood those who performed the office of priest in the tabernacle; and the Lord is sanctified in them even by punishing them, as happened here. Is the point that we should learn from this how much less he spares others if he does not spare them, in the sense in which it is said, "If the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?" Or is it rather in line with the saying, "To whom more is given, more is required of him"? And with this one: "The servant who did not know his master's will and does things deserving blows will be beaten with few; but the servant who knew his master's will and does things deserving blows will be beaten with many"? And this one: "For to the lowly mercy will be granted, but the mighty will suffer mightier torments"? But where the Lord said what Moses reports him as saying is not found in the preceding Scripture. This case, then, is like the one in Exodus, where Moses says to the Lord, "You said: I know you above all," which the Lord is indeed found to have said to him, but only later. Since Moses would never have said this falsely, we understand that the Lord had also said it to him before, although it was not written down; and so too here. From this it is clear that not everything God spoke to those through whom his holy Scripture has been delivered to us was written down.

Why does Moses, when he forbids Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn the death of those two, say, "You shall not uncover your head of the turban," which certainly shows that turbans were head coverings? It must be because mourners did things contrary to their customary adornment. In our custom the head is usually left uncovered, so it is covered in mourning; in the same way, because they adorned themselves with a covering on the head, mourners had to bare it. He forbids them to mourn those in whose punishment the Lord was sanctified, that is, in whose punishment the fear of him was impressed on all. This was not because the dead were not to be mourned, for he allows others to mourn them. It was because Aaron and his sons ought not to mourn at that time, while the days of their consecration were being kept and the seven days had not yet been completed, during which he commanded them not to leave the tabernacle. And yet, because they had been consecrated with that oil, it could seem that this was said to mean that they should never mourn anyone. For he says: "But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, shall weep for the burning with which they were burned by the Lord. And you shall not go out from the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, lest you die; for the oil of anointing that is from the Lord is upon you."

"And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You shall not drink wine or strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter the tabernacle of the testimony or when you approach the altar, and you shall not die." When, then, were they permitted to drink, since they had to enter the tabernacle and approach the altar every day because of the continual service? If someone says that sacrifices were not usually offered every day, what does he say about entering the tabernacle? That happened daily, because of the lampstand and the loaves of presentation to be set on the table. If the answer is that "the tabernacle of the testimony," as he now says, must be understood as the place where the ark of the testimony was, the high priest still had to enter there because of the continual incense. For he did not enter only once a year: he entered once a year with the blood of purification, but daily because of the incense. Or should we understand that God commanded them not to drink wine at all? Then why did he not rather command it briefly, saying, "You shall not drink wine," instead of adding, "when you enter the tabernacle or when you approach the altar"? Was it because the reason for not drinking was not to be left unsaid? This would be especially so because God foreknew that later there would be many priests, even high priests, at the same time, that is, not one succeeding another, who would serve the tabernacle, the sacrifices, the incense and that whole ministry in turns. Those whose turn it was to serve would then not drink, while the others would drink. Or is something else to be understood in this place? For after forbidding the priests to drink wine and strong drink, he went on to say: "an everlasting statute for your generations." It is ambiguous whether this is connected to the preceding sense, so that it refers to not drinking wine, or to what follows: "to distinguish between the holy and the defiled and between the clean and the unclean, and to instruct the sons of Israel in all the statutes that the Lord spoke to them by the hand of Moses." In that case this would be an everlasting statute for the priests' office throughout their generations. We have often explained already in what sense he says "everlasting." This too is put ambiguously: "to distinguish between the holy and the defiled and between the clean and the unclean." Does it refer to things that are holy and clean or defiled and unclean, or to persons who are holy and clean or defiled and unclean? That is, did he want the priests to distinguish among the sacred rites themselves, whether they were performed properly or not, or among people, approving some and rejecting others? Or should it rather be referred to both, people and rites alike?

"The breast of separation and the shoulder of removal you shall eat in a holy place." Although each is given its own name, either could certainly be called "of separation," because both are set apart for the priest. Both could also be called "of removal" or "of taking away," in Greek aphairema, because both are taken away from those on whose behalf they are offered and given to the priest. Earlier, indeed, we read "the breast of placing" and "the shoulder of removal," because nothing from the shoulder was placed on the altar, whereas the fat from the breast was.

What does it mean when it says "from the sacrifices of saving things" (salutarium)? It is speaking of what it elsewhere called "sacrifices of salvation" (salutaris), and it also said this in the singular, "sacrifice of salvation," when speaking of the same thing. Or perhaps here, where it says "from the sacrifices of saving things," it should have said "of healings" (sanitatum)? For in the psalm where it says, "Hear us, O God of our healings," the Greek has the same word as here, namely sōtēriōn. In Greek this genitive plural is ambiguous: the noun could be declined from "salvation" or from "saving thing." Sōtēria means salvation or health, and its genitive plural is tōn sōtēriōn; but a saving thing is called sōtērion, and its genitive plural is exactly the same. Salvation is given by the saving thing, and the saving thing is that from which salvation is received. So if a sacrifice of salvation (salus) can rightly be understood as the same as a sacrifice of the saving thing (salutare), then where it says "from the sacrifices of saving things" we need not understand sacrifices of many saving things. We may perhaps understand them as sacrifices of many healings, which are nevertheless received from one saving thing. And what the saving thing (salutare) of God is, the Christian faith knows: it is the one of whom it is said, "I will take the cup of salvation," and of whom Simeon says in the Gospel, "For my eyes have seen your salvation." It would certainly not be absurd to understand or call them "saving sacrifices" as well, since they are sacrifices of the saving thing.

"And it shall be for you and your sons and your daughters an everlasting statute." "Daughters" is not added without reason, since he forbids women to receive certain things belonging to the priests' food and commands that only males receive them.

Moses looked for the goat offered for the sins of the people and did not find it, because it had been burned up. He was angry, because the Lord had appointed that what the people offered for sin should be eaten by the priests once its fats and kidneys had been offered. He was angry not with his brother but with his brother's sons, I believe because it was their task to remind him. Aaron answered him and said: "If today they have offered what is for their sin and their burnt offerings before the Lord, and such things have happened to me, and I eat what is for sin today, will it be pleasing to the Lord?" And Moses heard, and it pleased him. Aaron seems to have meant this: on that very day, when the sons of Israel first offered for their sin, the offering ought not to be eaten by the priests but burned whole. He was not making this a rule for other occasions, for afterward the priests did eat the sacrifices for sins. But because this was the first such sacrifice, offered for the first time on that very first day, we must believe that Aaron the priest said this by divine inspiration. In this way what the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the priests would be observed from then on, and Moses would approve what Aaron said as something spoken by God. What, then, of the other sacrifices of that same day, the ram and the calf, which we said must also be understood as offered for sin? Is there no question about the calf? Its offering had to be done as commanded, with some of its blood brought inside, by which the horns of the altar of incense would also be touched, and it followed that the whole calf was to be burned. What then of the ram? Since Moses asked first about the goat, should what was answered about the goat be understood of the ram as well? He would have asked about the ram next if the priest's answer had not satisfied him. As for the calf, what would he have asked? It could have been dealt with under the law that God had laid down for the calf offered for the sin of the whole congregation, as for the calf offered for the sin of the priest, namely that it be burned whole outside the camp. For these are the words of Moses, angry with his brother's sons when he looked for the goat offered for sin and did not find it because it had been burned whole: "Why did you not eat what was for sin in the holy place? For since these are holy of holies, he gave you this to eat, so that you might take away the sin of the congregation and make atonement for it before the Lord. For none of its blood was brought into the sanctuary, before the presence within. You shall eat it in the holy place, as the Lord appointed me." When he says, "For none of its blood was brought into the sanctuary, before the presence within," he undoubtedly distinguishes the offering made in that way for the sin of the priest or for the sin of the whole congregation, which was not a goat, from the goat. No order had been given to bring the goat's blood inside to touch the horns of the altar of incense, and so the goat should not have been burned whole but eaten by the priests. As for why this was done, that is, why the goat too was burned whole, Aaron gave his answer, and it pleased Moses.

Six animals had been commanded to the elders of the people to be offered for the people. He mentioned four of these first: the he-goat, the ram, the calf and the yearling lamb. Of these, it is clear that the goat was for sin, and clear too that the yearling lamb was for a burnt offering. But we had seen that the two in the middle, the ram and the calf, were placed ambiguously: did they belong to the sacrifice for sin and go with the goat, or rather with the lamb, to be offered as a burnt offering? We have explained our view on this in its place. Afterward, to make up the six animals, he mentioned a calf and a ram for the sacrifice of salvation. Yet in what follows, when the animals are sacrificed and listed again, there is no mention of the ram and calf that he had placed between the goat and the lamb. Only the calf and the ram that he had ordered to be offered as a sacrifice of salvation are mentioned, so that there appear to have been not six animals but four. Perhaps it can be understood that he named again the two he had earlier placed between the goat and the lamb, and that the calf and ram for the sacrifice of salvation are not a different calf and ram. On this reading, he had said "a goat for sin, and a ram and a calf" without saying what they were for, but "a yearling lamb for a burnt offering." Afterward he wanted to say what was to be done with the calf and the ram: they were to be brought neither for sin like the goat, nor as a burnt offering like the lamb, but as a sacrifice of salvation. But if we understand it this way, a question will remain. Why was a goat offered for the sin of the congregation? When the Lord spoke at the beginning about the sacrifices to be offered for sins, he commanded that a calf, not a goat, be offered for the sin of the congregation, just as for the sin of the priest. He also commanded that the blood of this calf be brought inside to touch the horns of the altar of incense, as for the sin of the priest. And why, when Moses offered a calf for Aaron's sin, and Aaron himself offered another calf as God had commanded for the sin of the priest, was a goat offered instead for the sin of the people, rather than a calf as had been commanded? Because this troubled us, we concluded, as we said above, that not only a goat but also a ram and a calf were ordered to be offered for the sin of the people, so that "for sin" is to be understood with all three. There were rulers among the people, for whom the goat was to be offered. Each individual could have his own sins, and for these the ram was offered. All of them together could share some one sin, and for this the calf was offered, just as it had been commanded at the beginning that a calf should be offered for the sin of the whole congregation. Only the goat is named when they are sacrificed so that the others might be understood though not mentioned, by the figure of speech that names the part for the whole, since all had been offered for sins.

When he was dealing with the carcasses of unclean animals, he said: "And every earthen vessel into which any of them falls, whatever is inside it shall be unclean, and it shall be broken," that is, the vessel itself. "And all food that is eaten, on which water from it comes, shall be unclean to you." This is not to be understood of any water at all, as though any water coming upon food made it unclean, but of water from that vessel which has been made unclean by the unclean carcasses, if that vessel happened to hold water.

"To instruct the children of Israel between the life-giving creatures that are eaten and the life-giving creatures that are not eaten." Where the Greek has ζωογονοῦντα, some of our translators preferred to render it "life-giving" (vivificantia), since our usage has in some fashion accepted this word, rather than to coin something new and unfamiliar, as it would be if one could say "live-bearing" (vivigignentia). For the creatures called ζωογονοῦντα are not those that give life, that is, make alive, but those that give birth to living young, that is, not to eggs but to offspring.

What does he mean when he says of a woman who has given birth: "She shall not touch anything holy, and she shall not enter the sanctuary"? What sanctuary does he mean us to understand, since we read that only the priests were accustomed to enter the tabernacle, and only as far as the second, inner veil, while beyond that veil, where the ark was, only the one high priest might go? Or could the area in front of the tabernacle, where the altar of sacrifices stood, also be called the sanctuary? For the court itself is often called a holy place, as when it is said: "They shall eat them in a holy place." Perhaps women used to enter there when they brought their gifts to be placed on the altar.

What does he mean when he says: "If a woman gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean seven days; according to the days of her separation she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. And for thirty-three days she shall remain in her clean blood; she shall not touch anything that is holy, and she shall not enter the sanctuary"? What difference is there between those seven days, during which he calls her unclean, and the thirty-three during which she will remain in her clean blood? For if she is no longer unclean during the thirty-three days, why may she not touch what is holy? Or is the difference still this, that she is in blood, even if clean blood? So that the distinction is this: while she is unclean, she makes unclean wherever she sits; but when she is already remaining in clean blood, she is only not permitted to touch what is holy and to enter the sanctuary? For this is what he means by "according to the days of the separation of her purification," since he says in another place that the uncleanness of a woman being purged by her menstrual flow lasts seven days, during which everything on which she sits shall be unclean. He says "separation" because she withdrew somewhat, so as not to defile everything, while she completed those days. If she bore a female, the law doubled these days of her uncleanness and made them fourteen; and it had ordered that the remaining days, during which she remained in her clean blood, should also be observed doubled, that is, sixty-six, so that the total for the birth of a male would be forty and for a female eighty. Some Greek manuscripts, however, do not have "in her clean blood" but "in her unclean blood."

"And when the days of her purification are fulfilled, for a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, to the priest. And he shall offer it before the Lord, and the priest shall make entreaty for her and shall purify her from the source of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a male or a female. But if her hand does not find what is sufficient for a lamb, and she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for sin; and the priest shall make entreaty for her, and she shall be purified." It is right, then, that the earlier passage should not be read: "she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering [?] and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin," as some manuscripts have it, but as it was stated: "and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin," since he says afterwards: "If her hand does not find what is sufficient for a lamb, and she shall take two turtledoves." Here the "and" seems superfluous; for with that conjunction removed, the sentence runs on complete: "she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons," that is, one bird as a burnt offering and the other for sin.

But for what sin? Is it a sin to have given birth? Or is that descent from Adam being shown here, of which the apostle says, "From one to condemnation," and, "Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed through to all men"? Here too it becomes quite clear in what sense it was said: "For I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb." Why, then, does Scripture say that it is not the one who was born who is purified by this sacrifice, but the woman herself who gave birth? Was the purification referred to her, from whom that origin was drawn, because of the source of blood, while it could nevertheless not take place without the purification of the offspring itself, which arose from that very blood? For what is the point of what he says above, "for a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin," if nothing was done by this sacrifice on behalf of those who were born?

Suppose someone tries to divide the sentence so as to say that "for a son or for a daughter she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering and a young pigeon for sin" should not be joined together, but that it should rather be read thus: "And when the days of her purification are fulfilled for a son or for a daughter"—that is, when the days of purification have been fulfilled for him or for her, namely the son or the daughter—so that what follows begins a new sense: "she shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering and a young pigeon for sin," that is, for her own sin, when the days of her purification have been completed for a son or for a daughter. Whoever thinks the sentence should be divided in this way will be refuted by the Gospel. There, when they did something of this kind for the Lord born of the virgin, more because of the custom of the law than because there was any need to expiate and cleanse sin in him, we read: "And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law." It does not say "for his mother" but "for him," even though what was done was what is prescribed in this place concerning two turtledoves or two young pigeons. In the same way he also deigned to be baptized with the baptism of John, which was a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, although he had no sin. With good reason, then, some of our translators have rendered this passage in Leviticus too so as to say, not "over a son or over a daughter," but "for a son or for a daughter." For they understood this to be the force of the preposition in this place, where the Greek says ἐφ' υἱῷ ἢ ἐπὶ θυγατρί. We should certainly take note of how poor the Lord chose to be born: no lamb and young pigeon or turtledove was offered for him, but a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, as we read in the Gospel—the offering that the scripture of Leviticus ordered to be made when the hand of the one offering did not have what was sufficient for a lamb.

"If in the skin of any man's body there appears a shining scar of a sign, and there is in the skin of his complexion a touch of leprosy." He said the latter by way of explanation, so that what he had said first might be understood. For he had said, "If in the skin of any man's body there appears a shining scar"; and so that we should not understand "scar" in the usual sense of the mark left by a healed wound, he made clear that he was speaking of color when he added, "and there is in the skin of his complexion a touch of leprosy." Whatever it is, then, that he calls by the name of scar, it is a defect of color. When he says "touch of leprosy," it is not that a color is perceived by touch; rather he speaks of a touch of leprosy as though the man himself, or his body, had been touched by leprosy, that is, stained and blemished, just as people commonly say, "A fever has touched him," or "has not touched him." Indeed he calls the spot itself a "touch" and always refers to it by that name. Hence some of our translators have rendered it not "touch" but "spot." That word does seem to convey the meaning of the text more plainly; but the Greek too could have said, not ἁφή, that is, "touch," but μῶμος, that is, "blemish," from which comes ἄμωμος, "unblemished." Yet Scripture usually calls ἄμωμος what is free not only from what affects the color but from every defect, so that it means by the word not a spot of color but the mark of any defect whatever. For what pertains to color alone, then, it could have said σπίλος, the word the apostle used when he said of the church, "having no spot or wrinkle." But it said neither σπίλος nor [μῶμος], but ἁφή, that is, "touch," which even in the Greek language is an unusual thing to say of colors; and yet the Seventy translators were not ashamed to say it in Greek. Why, then, should the Latins be ashamed of it? As for the expression "scar of a sign," it is used either because it signifies something or, more likely, because it marks the man himself off from others with a kind of sign, that is, makes him conspicuous.

What does he mean by "And the priest shall see, and shall defile him," when the man comes to him to be cleansed? "Shall defile" is said for "shall declare defiled," if he sees in him the things that Scripture describes concerning the spot of leprosy.

"But if it is shining white in the skin of his complexion, and its appearance is not lower than the skin." With "shining white" we are to supply "touch," that is, that spot of color, not the hair. Afterwards he says, "But if the signification in the skin is changed and altered": by "signification" he means what above is read in Latin as "sign." For the Greek both there and here used one and the same word, saying σημασία.

"And the priest shall set him apart for seven days a second time; and the priest shall see him on the seventh day the second time, and behold, the touch is dark, the touch has not changed in the skin; and the priest shall cleanse him, for it is a sign": that is, he shall declare him cleansed, for it is not leprosy but a sign.

"But if the signification in the skin is changed and altered after the priest has seen him in order to cleanse him, and he is seen again by the priest, and the priest sees him, and behold, the signification in the skin is changed, and the priest shall defile him; it is leprosy." Here too he said "shall defile" for "shall declare defiled"; the "and" is superfluous, after the usual idiom of Scripture. So he seems to have given this instruction: when only a white and shining color is seen, differing from the healthy color, it should be further examined by the priest, so that if he also sees the hair turned to a white color and the place where the white color is become lower than the skin, he should then declare it leprosy, that is, defile the man by declaring him leprous. "But if," he says, "it is shining white in the skin of his complexion"—that is, if that touch is shining white, the name he gives to the same spot—"and its appearance is not lower than the skin, and the hair has not turned white, but it is dark"—that is, the hair itself, because it is not white—"and the priest shall set apart the touch for seven days. And the priest shall see the touch on the seventh day"—that is, that spot—"and behold, the touch remains before him, the touch has not changed in the skin"—that is, it has not been found differing in color and unlike the skin. So what was defective has been healed. But he orders that this same soundness be tested for another seven days, and so he goes on to say: "and the priest shall set him apart seven days a second time"—that is, another seven days—"and the priest shall see him on the seventh day the second time, and behold, the touch is dark"—that is, because it is not white and shining and is therefore of the same color as the healthy color—"the touch has not changed in the skin"—as he said a little earlier, that is, it is not unlike the rest of the skin—"and the priest shall cleanse him," that is, he shall declare him cleared of the suspicion of leprosy.
