This is not because he had leprosy which he no longer has, but because it was not leprosy: when, in that shining and white color of the touch, that is, of the spot that had appeared, it was awaited whether the place would become lower and the hair there turn white, this did not happen; rather that touch, which had earlier been shining and white, was found to be dark, that is, like the rest of the color, not shining. So it was not leprosy; for what appeared in this way is a sign, not leprosy. Yet even on this account, though cleared of the suspicion of leprosy, "he shall wash his garments"—because even in that sign there was something on account of which his garments had to be washed—"and he shall be clean."

Then follows: "But if the signification in the skin is changed and altered after the priest has seen him in order to cleanse him"—that is, after the priest had first seen him sound on the seventh day so as to cleanse him, that signification, that is, that sign in the skin, has changed—"and he is seen by the priest a second time"—that is, after another seven days—"and the priest sees him, and behold, the signification in the skin is changed"—that is, it has not remained in the soundness in which he had seen him after the first seven days—"and the priest shall defile him; it is leprosy." Here, since what had appeared sound after the first seven days did not stay as it was but changed back to its former defect, it is declared leprosy, without waiting for the place to become lower or the hair to turn white. For since leprosy is nothing other than a conspicuous and defective variegation, this very change from a defective color back to a healthy one and from a healthy one back to a defective one is so conspicuous that there was no need to wait for what he had prescribed to be awaited in the first case, namely the lower place and the whiteness of the hair; but now, by this very variegation, it is leprosy beyond doubt.

Then follows: "And if a touch of leprosy is on a man, he shall come to the priest; and the priest shall see, and behold, a white scar in the skin, and it has changed the hair to white, and from the healthy part of the living flesh in the scar." If we remove the "and" here—for it is put in according to the idiom of the Scriptures—the sense will be this: "and the priest shall see, and behold, a white scar in the skin, and it has changed the hair to white from the healthy part of the living flesh in the scar." The order is: it has changed the hair in the scar to white, unlike the healthy part of the living flesh; that is, while the living and healthy flesh has dark or black hair, this scar has white. "It is an old leprosy in the skin of his complexion; and the priest shall defile him"—that is, shall declare him defiled—"he shall not set him apart, for he is unclean." He seems to be saying that when hair is found turned white, matching the white defect of the skin, the man is no longer set apart to be tested, nor is it awaited whether the place will also become lower; but solely from the fact that the skin is white, differing from the rest, and has white hair, differing from the other hairs on the living and healthy flesh, it is declared an old leprosy—"old" because it no longer needs to be tested over those twice seven days. "But if the healthy color is restored and turned white": [this is said] because he had said that when the whole had become white over all the skin, by that very fact it was now clean, since there would no longer be any variegation there. Then he says: "And on whatever day living color appears in him, he shall be defiled"—by which he shows clearly enough that it is variegation that is condemned. And so, in what he has just said, "But if the healthy color is restored and turned white, and he comes to the priest, and the priest sees, and behold, the touch has turned white, and the priest shall cleanse the touch; he is clean," we should not take "the healthy color restored" to mean that the color became healthy; for that color was already present, and yet through it he was made unclean because of the variegation. He said, then, that the healthy color was restored in the sense that it became what it had been, that is, white, with the healthy color disappearing. For then he will be clean again, when he is entirely white, because there will be no variegation there. But to take "restored" in the sense of "disappearing" is a very unusual expression; he would seem rather to have needed to say, "But if the white color is restored." As it is, he says, "if the healthy color is restored and turned white," as if to say: if the healthy color is restored into white.

Why is it that, when he was speaking of leprosy of the head, he also called it a "shaking," although it consists only in the color of the skin or the hair, and in its appearing lower than the rest of the skin, yet without pain and without any affliction? Did he mean to call what is unclean a "shaking" in the sense of a blow, as though a man had been struck by this uncleanness?

What does it mean that, when he was speaking of leprosy in garments and in other things belonging to people's use, he says: [?] "in a woolen garment or in a garment of flax, or in the warp, or in wool, or in linen things, or in woolen things," when he had already said above, "in a woolen garment or in a garment of flax"? For flax is of course linen. Did he mean garments to be understood there, but here anything woolen and anything linen? For saddle-cloths for beasts of burden are not garments, though they are woolen, nor are nets garments, though they are linen. So he wished to speak first specifically of garments, and then generally of all woolen and linen things.

The question is asked what he meant by "in every working hide," which some have translated "in every finished hide." But the Greek does not say εἰργασμένῳ δέρματι; it says ἐργασίμῳ, a word that is also used in the book of Kingdoms where Jonathan says to David, "Be in the field on the working day," that is, on the day on which work is done. Therefore here too we should take a "working hide" to be one with which work is done, that is, one suited to some work. For there are hides that are kept only for ornament, not for work.

What does he mean by "in every working vessel of hide," if not something made of hide, that is, in every leather vessel? In this place he calls a "vessel" what the Greeks call σκεῦος, for this is a general name for all utensils. But what is called ἀγγεῖον is something else, for Latin also calls this a "vessel." But ἀγγεῖον is understood rather as a vessel that holds liquid.

What does he mean by "And whomever one who suffers a discharge of seed touches without having washed his hands in water, he shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water and be unclean until evening"? The phrase "without having washed his hands in water" is ambiguous, as though it meant after he has touched. But it is to be understood thus: whomever he touches with unwashed hands, the one he has touched shall wash his garments, and so on.

What does it mean that, when he was prescribing how the high priest should enter the holy place that is within the veil, he says among other things: "And he shall make entreaty for the holy from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and from their injustices concerning all their sins"? How is it for the holy, if it is from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and from their injustices concerning all their sins? Since he does not say "for the uncleannesses" of the children of Israel but "from the uncleannesses," should "he shall make entreaty for the holy from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel" be understood thus: that is, for those who are holy, free from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, not consenting to their uncleannesses? Not that entreaty was to be made for them alone, but that it was to be made for them too, so that no one would think they were so holy that there was nothing for which entreaty needed to be made on their behalf, even though they had no part in the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and their injustices. "Concerning all their sins": that is, the injustices that came from all their sins.

The phrase "he shall make entreaty for the holy ones from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel" could also mean that the entreaty is made for them so that they may be kept safe from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel. But "he shall make entreaty" can only be taken to mean what is expressed by another word, "he shall propitiate." That is why it is also called the propitiatory, which others have translated "place of entreaty"; in Greek it is called hilastērion. And where the Latin says in this passage "he shall make entreaty for the holy ones," the Greek has exilasetai, which can only be understood as referring to sins. Hence it is written in the psalm: "who is propitious to all your iniquities." So the more fitting sense here is that the priest propitiates God even for those who are holy, kept apart from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel. For although they are holy in the sense that they do not consent to the uncleannesses and wrongdoings of the children of Israel, they still have something for which they need God's propitiation.

In one Greek manuscript, in fact, we found: "and he shall make entreaty to the holy," not "for the holy ones," and "holy" there is in the neuter gender, that is, to hagion. Now it could have been understood as "he shall make entreaty to the holy God," and there would be no problem. But how "he shall make entreaty to this holy thing" can be understood is hard to say, unless perhaps "the holy" is whatever God is, since the Holy Spirit too, who is certainly God, is called in Greek by a neuter, to pneuma to hagion. And perhaps that is the meaning, if indeed that manuscript, which seemed the more correct one, is the more accurate: exilasetai to hagion, that is, to pneuma to hagion, which cannot be expressed in the neuter in Latin. Yet in three other manuscripts, one Greek and two Latin, we found only what we cited above: "he shall make entreaty for the holy ones." This can also be taken to refer not to holy people but to the things that are holy, that is, the tabernacle itself and whatever things in it were consecrated to the Lord. Then "he shall make entreaty for the holy things from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel" would mean: he shall propitiate God for the things consecrated to the Lord, on account of the uncleannesses of the children of Israel, since the tabernacle stood in their midst. For that is what follows. Having said, "he shall make entreaty for the holy things from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and from their wrongdoings, concerning all their sins," he immediately added, "and so he shall do for the tabernacle of testimony, which was set up among them in the midst of their uncleanness." So that propitiation for the holy things, that is, for the tabernacle and all the things in it that are called holy, appears to be needed for this reason. Indeed, shortly afterward he says the same about the altar: that the priest should cleanse it by sprinkling blood and sanctify it from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel.

"And he shall complete, making entreaty to the holy." Does it mean "he shall complete the holy"? Or "making entreaty to the holy," in the sense we discussed above? For here too the Greek has the neuter, to hagion. So does it mean that by entreating the Lord he shall complete the holy, that is, perfectly sanctify what he sanctifies? Or does "he shall complete" govern what he says next, "making entreaty to the holy," that is, to the holy one who is to pneuma to hagion?

Concerning the two goats, one to be sacrificed and the other to be sent away into the wilderness, which they call the apopompaios, there is usually some debate. Some take the one to be sacrificed in a good sense and the one to be sent away in a bad sense. But this interpretation should not be accepted on the ground that the man by whose hand the goat is sent into the wilderness is ordered, when he returns, to wash his clothes and his body with water and only then to enter the camp, as though this were a sign that the goat must be taken in a bad sense, since the man has to be washed of contact with it. For he says that the man who takes the flesh of the other goat and of the calf and burns it outside the camp must also wash. He commands this to be done in the case of that goat and the calf too, whose blood is sprinkled after they are sacrificed and which are offered for sins. For this reason the distinction between these two goats must be treated with care in its allegorical meaning. Again, after appointing the tenth day of the seventh month as a sabbath of sabbaths, on which the cleansing described above was to be performed by the one priest who succeeds his father, he says of that same priest: "he shall make entreaty to the holy of the holy." I do not know whether this is to be understood otherwise than as "he shall make entreaty in the holy of the holy," by a certain idiom; that is, in that holy place which the high priest alone entered, which is within the veil, where the ark of the testimony and the altar of incense stood. For he will not make entreaty to the place itself as if it were God; but because he will make entreaty to God there, it is put this way: "he shall make entreaty to the holy of the holy." For this too is put in the neuter in the Greek: to pneuma to hagion. Or does it perhaps mean the Holy Spirit of the holy God, that is, to hagion pneuma tou hagiou theou? Or is "he shall make entreaty" rather used to mean "by entreating he shall cleanse"? For the words run as follows: "and he shall make entreaty to the holy of the holy, and he shall make entreaty to the tabernacle of testimony and the altar, and he shall make entreaty for the priests and for the whole congregation." How, then, can he make entreaty to the tabernacle and the altar, unless, as was said, we understand "by entreating he shall cleanse"?

Where he says, "Whoever slaughters a calf or a sheep or a goat in the camp, and whoever slaughters it outside the camp and does not bring it to the door of the tabernacle of testimony," and counts this as a sin and threatens the one who does it, he is not speaking of animals slaughtered for food or for any other use, but of sacrifices. He forbade private sacrifices, so that no one would dare to act as his own priest, as it were, but would bring his offering to the place where it would be offered to God through the priest. In this way they would not sacrifice to idols either; for he had warned them in advance to guard against this in that custom too. Since, then, it was not lawful to offer sacrifices except in the tabernacle, which the temple later replaced (which is why Jeroboam, king of Israel, dared to make calves for the people to sacrifice to, so that those under his rule would not be drawn away from him by the obligation of this law as they went to Jerusalem to offer their sacrifices in the temple of God, an act for which the Lord condemned him), it is rightly asked how Elijah lawfully sacrificed outside the temple of God, when he called down fire from heaven and defeated the prophets of the demons. To me it seems that this can be defended on no other ground than the one on which Abraham's act is defended, when at God's command he was willing to sacrifice his son. When the one who established the law commands something to be done that he prohibited in the law, the command itself takes the place of law, since it comes from the author of the law. There could have been other miracles besides a sacrifice by which the prophets of the groves might be overcome and refuted; but the Spirit of God, who was in Elijah in whatever he did in this matter, cannot act against the law, since he is the giver of the law.

What does he mean when, forbidding the eating of blood, he says, "The soul of all flesh is its blood"? He sets out the whole passage this way: "And any man of the children of Israel, or of the proselytes who have been added among you, who eats any blood, I will set my face against the soul that eats blood and will destroy it from among its people. For the soul of all flesh is its blood, and I have given it to you to make entreaty for your souls; for its blood shall make entreaty for the soul. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood, and the proselyte who has been added among you shall not eat blood." Surely, if we say that the soul of a beast is blood, are we also to think that the soul of a human being is blood? Far from it. Why, then, does he not say, "The soul of all the flesh of beasts is its blood," but says, "The soul of all flesh is its blood"? Human flesh is certainly counted as part of "all flesh." Or, since there is something life-giving in the blood, because it is chiefly by blood, spread through the veins into every part of the body, that life is sustained in this flesh, did he call the very life of the body "soul"? Not the life that departs from the body, but the life that ends at death? It is in this way of speaking that we say this life is temporal, not eternal, mortal, not immortal, although the nature of the soul is immortal: the soul that was carried by angels into Abraham's bosom, the soul to which it was said, "Today you will be with me in paradise," and the soul that burned in the torments of hell. It is in this sense, then, in which this temporal life too is called "soul," that the apostle Paul said, "For I do not count my soul precious to myself," where he wished to show that he was ready even to die for the gospel. For in the sense in which "soul" means what departs from the body, he was all the more making it precious, since he was gaining for it so great a reward. There are other expressions of this kind as well. So this temporal life is held in the body chiefly by the blood. But what does he mean by saying, "I have given it to you at the altar of God, that it may make entreaty for your soul"? As though a soul were making entreaty for a soul. Is it blood for blood, as if we were anxious about our blood when we want entreaty made for our soul? That is absurd.

But it is far more absurd that the blood of a beast should make entreaty for the soul of a human being, which cannot die, since Scripture plainly testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the blood of those victims was of no use in entreating God for people's sins, but signified something that would be of use. "For it is impossible," it says, "for the blood of goats and bulls to take away sins." It remains, then, since it is that Mediator who makes entreaty for our soul, the one prefigured by all those sacrifices offered for sins, that the thing which signifies the soul is here called "soul."

A thing that signifies is often called by the name of the thing it signifies. Thus it is written, "The seven ears of grain are seven years"; he did not say "signify seven years." And: "The seven cows are seven years," and many things of this kind. Hence the saying, "The rock was Christ"; he did not say "the rock signified Christ," but spoke as if it were so, although it was certainly not so in substance, only in signification. So too blood, since by reason of a certain life-bearing bodily quality it signifies the soul, has been called "soul" in the sacred rites. But if anyone thinks that the soul of a beast is blood, we need not labor over that question. We must only take great care that the human soul, which gives life to human flesh and is rational, is not thought to be blood, and this error must be refuted by every means. We should also look for expressions in which what contains is used to signify what is contained. Since the soul is held in the body by the blood (for if the blood is poured out, the soul departs), the soul would more fittingly be signified by it, and the blood would have taken its name. In the same way the place where the church gathers is called a church; for the church is people, of whom it is said, "that he might present to himself a glorious church." Yet the same apostle bears witness that the house of prayer itself is also called by this name, where he says, "Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God?" And everyday usage has established that one is said to go out into the church or to take refuge in the church only when one goes to or takes refuge in the place itself and the walls within which the congregation of the church is held. It is also written: "And he who defrauds a hired worker of his wages sheds blood." He called wages blood, because by them is sustained the life that is called by the name of blood.

But since the Lord says, "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in you," what does it mean that the people were so strictly forbidden the blood of the sacrifices offered for sins, if those sacrifices signified this one sacrifice in which the true forgiveness of sins takes place? Yet not only is no one forbidden to take the blood of this sacrifice as food; rather, all who wish to have life are urged to drink it. We must therefore ask what it signifies that in the law a person is forbidden to eat blood and is commanded to pour it out to God. As for the nature of the soul, and why it was signified by blood, we have said as much as seemed sufficient for the present.

"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother; for it is their nakedness." He forbids lying with one's mother, for in that case it is the nakedness of both father and mother. Afterwards he also forbids it with a stepmother, where he says: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; for it is your father's nakedness." Here he has explained how, in the case of a mother, the nakedness belongs to both, that is, to the father and to the mother, while in the case of a stepmother it belongs to the father alone.

"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, whether by your father or by your mother, whether born at home or born outside; you shall not uncover their nakedness." "Born at home" is understood as by the father; "born outside" is understood as by the mother, in case the mother had conceived her by a former husband and had come with her into the house when she married the father of the man whom Scripture warns not to uncover his sister's nakedness. Here he seems not to have forbidden, and as it were to have passed over, intercourse with a sister born of both parents. For he does not say, "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister by your father and by your mother," but "by your father or by your mother." But who does not see that this too is forbidden, and far more so? For if it is not lawful to uncover the nakedness of a sister born of either parent, how much less one born of both! But why is it that, after inserting a prohibition of intercourse with one's granddaughters, whether by a son or by a daughter, he goes on to say: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of the daughter of your father's wife"? If he had stopped there, we would understand that intercourse was forbidden even with the stepmother's daughter, whom the stepmother had borne to a former husband, and who would not be the sister of the man addressed by the prohibition, whether by father or by mother. But when he adds, "She is your sister by the same father; you shall not uncover her nakedness," he makes it clear that this prohibition concerns a sister by the father and the stepmother, of whom he had already spoken above. Or did he wish to forbid this again more plainly because the earlier statement had been somewhat obscure? Scripture often does this.

"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother, and you shall not go in to his wife." He has explained what he meant by "You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's brother," that is, of your paternal uncle: it means "you shall not go in to his wife." For he wished the nakedness of the uncle to be understood in the uncle's wife, just as the father's nakedness is understood in the father's wife.

"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness." The question is whether this is forbidden while the brother is alive or after he has died, and it is no small question. If we say that Scripture is speaking of the wife of a living brother, this is certainly already contained in the one general commandment that forbids a man to approach another man's wife. Why, then, does it so carefully single out these persons, whom it calls members of the household, from all others with prohibitions of their own? For the prohibition concerning the father's wife, that is, the stepmother, is surely not to be taken as applying while the father is alive rather than after his death. Who does not see that it is forbidden far more while the father is alive, if the wife of any other man whatever is forbidden to be defiled by adultery? He seems, then, to be speaking of persons who, having no husbands, could enter into marriage if the law did not forbid it, as is said to be the custom of the Persians. But again, if we understand that marrying a brother's wife is forbidden after the brother's death, we are met by the fact that Scripture commands it to be done in order to raise up offspring, if the brother has died without children. Therefore, when this prohibition is set beside that command, so that they do not contradict each other, an exception must be understood: namely, that no one may marry the wife of a dead brother if the dead man has left descendants. Or else what is forbidden is marrying a brother's wife even when she has left the living brother by divorce. For at that time, as the Lord says, Moses had permitted a certificate of divorce to be given because of the hardness of the Jews' hearts, and through such a dismissal someone might have thought it lawful to take his brother's wife for himself, since he need not fear adultery, she having departed by divorce.

"You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and of her daughter": that is, let no one think it lawful for him to marry the daughter of his wife. For it is not lawful to uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter together, that is, to have relations with both, mother and daughter.

"You shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter." He has forbidden marrying even the wife's granddaughter, whether by a son or by a daughter. "You shall not take a wife in addition to her sister, as a rival." Here he did not forbid taking an additional wife, which was lawful for the ancients for the sake of increasing offspring; but he did not want a sister to be taken in addition to her sister. Jacob seems to have done this, either because it had not yet been forbidden by the law, or because he was deceived by the substitution of the other sister, and the one he took afterward was the one he had actually agreed to marry; but it would have been unjust to send away the first and so make her commit adultery. As for the words "as a rival," were they added so that there would be no rivalry between sisters, whereas rivalry between women who were not sisters was not to be regarded? Or rather, so that it should not be done for this purpose, that is, with the intention that a sister be brought in as a rival to her sister?

"And you shall not approach a woman in the separation of her uncleanness to uncover her nakedness": that is, you shall not approach a menstruating woman, for according to the law she was set apart because of her uncleanness. Since he had already forbidden this quite sufficiently above, why did he want to add it here as well, among these same precepts? Was it perhaps because, having been said among the earlier precepts, it might be thought to be meant figuratively, and so it is placed here too, where those things are forbidden that, even in the time of the New Testament, once the observance of the ancient shadows has been removed, must undoubtedly still be kept? This seems to be indicated also through the prophet Ezekiel, who, among those sins that are not figurative but manifest iniquity, mentions this too, if someone approaches a menstruating woman, and counts it among the merits of righteousness if he does not. In this matter it is not nature that is condemned; rather, it is said to be harmful to the conceiving of offspring.

"And you shall not give your seed in intercourse with your neighbor's wife, to be defiled with her." Here again he forbids adultery committed with another man's wife, which is also forbidden in the Decalogue. From this it appears that those women whose nakedness he forbids to be uncovered were forbidden in such a way that they may not be married even after their husbands have died.

"And you shall not give any of your offspring to serve a prince." Here I do not see what can be meant except a prince who is worshiped in place of God. For in the Greek he does not say douleuein but latreuein, which a Latin translator usually renders only by "serve"; yet there is a great difference. Scripture does not forbid serving human beings as slaves serve, which is not latreuein but douleuein; but service in the sense of latreuein is not commanded toward human beings, only toward the one true God, as it is written: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." He indicates clearly enough which prince he means, namely one to whom worship is offered as to a god, not only by this word latreuein, but also by what he adds: "and you shall not profane the holy name" — whether the name of God, from whose people someone is given to serve a prince in that way, or the holy name of the people of Israel itself, on account of which it is said: "You shall be holy, for I too am holy." Most fittingly he also adds here: "I am the Lord," reminding them, surely, that latreia, that is, the kind of service by which God is served, is owed to him alone.

As for the words "And the land abhorred those who dwell on it," because of their evil deeds which he mentioned above, we must not suppose this was said because the land has some sense by which it perceives and abhors these things. Rather, by the name of the land he means the people who are on the land. So when people do these evil things, they defile the land, because those who imitate them are defiled; and the land abhors them, because those who neither do nor imitate such things abhor them.

"You shall not steal, nor lie, nor shall anyone falsely accuse his neighbor." The commandment about theft is set down in the Decalogue. But as for the words "nor lie, nor shall anyone falsely accuse his neighbor," it would be surprising if they were not contained in the commandment given there: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor," since false accusation cannot be made without a lie, and this is included under the general heading of false witness. But whether these things may be admitted when there is some compensating good is a great question. Concerning lying, nearly everyone holds that where no one is harmed, one should lie for the sake of someone's safety. Is the same true of theft, then? Or can there be no theft where no one is harmed? On the contrary, it can happen even when the interest of the person stolen from is being served, as if someone were to steal a sword from a man who wanted to kill himself. As for false accusation, I do not know whether it can ever be made against anyone for his own benefit — unless perhaps in the case of Joseph, who falsely accused his brothers about the cup, having also charged them with the false crime of spying, which was done to bring about a greater joy that they would afterward enjoy. Yet if we try to settle these matters by definitions, perhaps it is not theft except when a neighbor is harmed by having his property secretly taken away, and not false accusation except when a neighbor is harmed by the charge of a false crime. But we cannot say that a lie exists only when a neighbor is harmed; for when something false is said knowingly, it is without doubt a lie, whether anyone is harmed or no one. Accordingly, the great question about lying, whether a lie can ever be just, might perhaps be easily resolved if we looked only at the commandments and not also at the examples. For what is more absolute than this commandment: "You shall not lie"? It is said in the same way as "You shall not make yourself an idol" — and making one can never be just; and as "You shall not commit adultery" — for who would say that adultery can ever be just?; and "You shall not steal" — and by that definition of theft, theft can never be just; and "You shall not kill," since when a man is justly killed, it is the law that kills him, not you. Can it be said likewise that when a man lies justly, it is the law that lies? But the examples make it a very difficult question. The Egyptian midwives lied, and God rewarded them with good things; Rahab lied on behalf of the spies of the land, and for that reason she was spared. Or are we to understand that from the time it was said in the law, "You shall not lie," a lie is not lawful even in a case such as the one in which Rahab is read to have lied? But it is more credible that lying was forbidden because it was unjust, not that it became unjust because it was forbidden. Perhaps, then, as we said of the midwives, what was rewarded in them was not that they lied but that they saved the Hebrew infants, so that on account of this mercy that sin was made pardonable, though it should not be thought not to have been a sin. So too in the case of Rahab we should understand that what was rewarded in her was her rescue of the spies, so that on account of that rescue pardon was granted to the lie. And where pardon is granted, it is plain that there is sin. But one must beware lest anyone suppose that pardon can likewise be granted for other sins too, if they are committed to save people. For many intolerable and utterly detestable evils follow from that error.

"You shall not harm your neighbor." If it were clear to people what harming and not harming are, this general commandment would perhaps be enough for preserving innocence. For everything that is forbidden to be done against one's neighbor must be referred to this one saying: "You shall not harm your neighbor." As for what follows, "You shall not seize by force," unless it is referred to this, namely that no harm be done by seizing, it sometimes happens that a person does harm by not seizing. For a sword must be snatched from a madman, and if someone fails to do so when he ought, he will rather do harm.

Why is it that, after saying above, "You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and you shall not incur sin on his account," he went on to add, "and your hand is not avenged"? Does it mean "is not punished"? For you act with a good intention when you impose discipline on a neighbor who sins, so that you do not incur his sin by neglecting him. This is what he had said before: "You shall not hate your neighbor in your heart." For it may seem to the one being rebuked that you hate him, though that is not in your heart. Or does "your hand is not avenged" rather warn you not to seek to have your hand avenged, nor to be carried away by the lust for revenge? For what else is wanting to be avenged but to rejoice or take comfort in another's misfortune? And therefore it is said: "You shall not be angry with the children of your people." For anger is rightly defined as the lust for revenge. Some manuscripts, however, read: "and your hand will not be avenged"; that is, you should not wish to avenge yourself by rebuking, but rather to look to the good of the one you rebuke.

"And you shall not make cuts in your body for a soul." By "for a soul" he meant "for the funeral of a dead person"; for the grief is over the soul that has departed. To this grief belongs mourning, and in mourning some nations have the custom of cutting their bodies. God forbids this to be done.

"So that they commit fornication with princes from among their people." It is not that the princes are from among their people, but that they commit fornication from among their people. For here he wants us to understand those princes who were worshiped as gods, as the apostle says, "according to the prince of the power of the air," and the Lord in the Gospel: "Now the prince of this world has been cast out," and: "Behold, the prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me."

"Any man whatever who commits adultery with the wife of a man, or whoever commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, let them be put to death." He said "let them be put to death" in the plural, meaning the man who committed adultery and the woman with whom it was committed. Here he wanted to make some distinction between any man whatever and a neighbor, although in many places he uses "neighbor" for every human being. But what kind of expression is this, that having already spoken of a man, he repeated the same thing about a neighbor? For it follows that if one must keep away from the wife of any man whatever, one must keep away all the more from a neighbor's wife. If he had spoken first of the neighbor, he would have had to add something about any man whatever, lest it be thought lawful to commit adultery with the wife of someone who is not a neighbor. But as it is, if the lesser thing is not lawful, how much less is what is a greater evil! For if it is not lawful to commit adultery with the wife of any man whatever, how much more is it unlawful with a neighbor's! Or perhaps this repetition serves as an explanation of what was said first, so that a man may understand how great an evil it is to commit adultery with another man's wife: if he does this, he commits adultery with his neighbor's wife. For every human being is a neighbor to every other.

"And a woman who approaches any beast to be mounted by it, you shall kill the woman and the beast. Let them be put to death; they are guilty." The question is how a beast can be guilty, since it is irrational and in no way capable of law. Perhaps, just as words are transferred by the figure of speech called metaphora in Greek from what is animate to what is inanimate — as when we speak of a wicked wind or an angry sea — so here the word has been transferred from the rational to the irrational? For we should believe that the beasts were ordered to be killed because, having been polluted by such a crime, they revive the shameful memory of the deed.

"Whoever takes his sister, his father's daughter or his mother's daughter, and sees her nakedness, and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace; they shall be cut off in the sight of their kindred; he has uncovered his sister's nakedness; they shall bear their sin." What does he mean here by "sees" except that he has known her by lying with her? Just as the law says, "he knew his wife," meaning that he had intercourse with her. And why does he say "they shall bear their sin" when he is speaking of their punishment, unless he wanted the very punishment of sin to be called sin?

"Whoever sleeps with his kinswoman has uncovered the nakedness of his kindred; they shall die childless." The question is how far this kinship is to be understood, since it is certainly permitted, and has always been permitted, to take a wife from a distant degree. But it must be understood that it is unlawful within the degrees he has forbidden, and that "whoever sleeps with his kinswoman" was said with reference to them. There he left some cases unmentioned, to be understood, such as a sister by both parents, or the wife of the mother's brother, that is, the maternal uncle. For he did first forbid the wife of the paternal uncle, although this is said to be not kinship by blood but kinship by marriage. But what does "they shall die childless" mean, since children have been born from unions of this kind in the past and are still born today? Are we to understand that it was established by the law of God that whoever were born of them should not be reckoned as children, that is, should have no right to succeed their parents, even while they live?

"And you shall not make yourselves abominable through beasts and birds and all the creeping things of the earth which I have set apart for you as unclean." Here he seems to indicate that these things are unclean not by nature but as a sign of some sacred mystery, since he says, "which I have set apart for you as unclean," as though they would not be unclean for them if they had not been set apart for them.

"And a man or a woman, if there is perhaps a ventriloquist or an enchanter in them, let both die the death. You shall stone them with stones; they are guilty." Does "both" mean the man and the woman, or the man and the ventriloquist, or the woman and the ventriloquist or enchanter? Rather, it means this: both the one who has and the one whom he has.

"They shall not take a woman who is a harlot and profane, nor a woman cast out by her husband, for he is holy to the Lord his God." Earlier he had said "they shall not take," but now he says "for he is holy," not "for they are holy." He was speaking of the several men who are priests at one time, and of each of them he said "for he is holy," using a turn of phrase that Scripture often uses. For he mentions that one supreme priest, who used to enter the holy of holies, only afterward. Indeed, he also concluded in the plural, saying: "And you shall sanctify him: he offers the gifts of the Lord your God; he is holy, for I the Lord who sanctify them am holy." As for the gifts, since he said, "he offers the gifts of the Lord your God," it was not only the high priest who offered them but also the priests of the second rank. And so, when he says, "They shall not take a woman who is a harlot and profane and cast out by her husband," the priests of the second rank too were forbidden this. For he speaks afterward of the high priest, who was further commanded to take no one but a virgin.

"And the priest who is great among his brothers": that is, the one who is great among his brothers, namely that one great priest, "on whose head some of the christ oil was poured": Scripture calls the oil itself "christ."
"And whose hands were consecrated to put on the vestments": those, of course, which are described with such painstaking detail in the account of the priestly dress.

"He shall not uncover his head of the turban, nor tear his garments, and he shall not go in to any dead soul." This is understood to mean that he is forbidden to do the things just mentioned when in mourning, that is, to bare his head of the turban and to tear his garments. For tearing one's garments was what mourners did in ancient times, as is written of Job when news was brought to him that his sons had been crushed by a collapsing house. Baring the head of the turban, for its part, could be a sign of mourning because it is a removal of adornment. But when he says, "he shall not go in to any dead soul," it is hard to understand how he can call a dead body a dead soul; yet this is an expression common in the Scriptures, though most uncommon to us. The body, then, even when bereft of the soul, takes the name of its ruler, because it is to be restored to it in the resurrection; just as the building called a church is still called a church even when the church, which is the people, has gone out of it. But since the body does not take the name of soul while the person is alive, it is strange that it should be called a soul when it lacks a soul. Again, suppose we take "dead soul" to mean the soul separated from the body, so that he seems to have called the separation itself death; that is, the soul would be dead in the sense of being severed from the body, not in the sense of having lost its own nature. For when we are said to be dead to sin, our nature is not said to have perished, but only that we no longer make use of sin; so in the same way the soul would be understood as dead, that is, dead to the body, because it has ceased to use it, while living on in its own nature. But in that case, how can anyone go in to a dead soul, as this priest is forbidden to do, since whoever goes in goes in to a dead body, not to a soul that has departed from the body? Or did he use the word "soul" for temporal life itself, which is certainly dead in the lifeless body once that soul which cannot die has gone out of it? Not that this life was itself the soul, but that it received the soul's name through the presence of the soul by which it subsisted, as we explained when we were speaking about blood and why it was said, "The soul of all flesh is its blood." For the blood too is dead in a dead man's body; it did not depart when the soul departed. So Scripture forbade the high priest to go in even to the funeral of his father or mother, which it did not forbid the second priest. For it goes on: "He shall not be defiled for his father and for his mother"; the order of the words is: he shall not be defiled for his father, nor for his mother.

"And he shall not go out of the holy places." This doubtless refers to the time when the funerals of his kin were being held, just as he was forbidden to go out of the holy places during the seven days of his sanctification, but not at all times. Indeed, if the high priests of that time were not forbidden to marry or to beget children, a great question arises. The law declares a person unclean even from marital intercourse until evening, even after he has washed his body with water; and the high priest is commanded, because of the perpetual incense, to go inside the veil, where the altar of incense was, twice every day; and no unclean person was permitted to approach the holy things. How, then, did the high priest fulfil this duty every day if he begot children? If someone asks who would have acted in his place had he fallen ill, one can answer that by the grace of God he did not fall ill. But can the same answer be given about the begetting of children? It follows, then, that either he was continent, or the incense was left off on some days, or else, if it could not be left off, since it had to be offered by the high priest and no one else, he did not become unclean through marital intercourse by virtue of his special sanctification. Or, if what Scripture says further on about all the sons of Aaron also applies to him, that none of them is to approach the holy things if any uncleanness has befallen him, then the only remaining conclusion is that on some days the incense was not offered.

As for the high priest being forbidden to go in to his father's funeral, one may ask how he could already be high priest while his father was not yet dead, since the law commands them to succeed their fathers. The answer is that it was necessary for a priest to be substituted at once, before the high priest was even buried, because of the perpetual incense, which had to be offered every day by the high priest. Yet that question about the high priest's illness still remains, if even one who was about to die must have been ill for some days; unless perhaps this too is resolved by saying that high priests did not usually die except suddenly, without any illness beforehand, as Scripture testifies of Aaron himself.

We should note how often, speaking of the priest, he says, "I am the Lord who sanctifies him," although he also said to Moses, "And you shall sanctify him." How, then, do both Moses and the Lord sanctify? Not that Moses does so in place of the Lord: Moses sanctifies through his ministry by visible sacraments, while the Lord sanctifies by invisible grace through the Holy Spirit, and in this lies the whole fruit even of the visible sacraments. For without this sanctification by invisible grace, what use are visible sacraments? But it is fair to ask whether this invisible sanctification is likewise of no use without the visible sacraments by which a person is visibly sanctified, which would certainly be absurd. For it would be more tolerable to say that the one does not exist without the others than to say that, if it does exist, it is of no use, since all the usefulness of the visible sacraments lies in it. But even the claim that it cannot exist without them needs to be examined to see in what sense it can rightly be made. Visible baptism was of no use to Simon Magus, who lacked invisible sanctification; but those who had this invisible sanctification, and were helped by it, had likewise received the visible sacraments, having been baptized too. Yet Moses, who visibly sanctified the priests, is nowhere shown to have himself been sanctified by those sacrifices or by the oil; but who would dare deny that he was invisibly sanctified, when his grace was so preeminent? The same can be said of John the Baptist, for he appeared as a baptizer before he appeared as one baptized. So we cannot possibly deny that he was sanctified, yet we do not find that this was done in him visibly before he came to the ministry of baptizing. The same is true of the thief to whom the Lord, crucified with him, said, "Today you will be with me in paradise." For he was not granted such great happiness without invisible sanctification. We therefore conclude that invisible sanctification has been present in some people, and has benefited them, without the visible sacraments, which have changed according to the difference of times, so that some were in force then and others are now; whereas visible sanctification, brought about through visible sacraments, can be present without the invisible kind but cannot be of use without it. Yet the visible sacrament is not on that account to be despised, for whoever despises it can in no way be sanctified invisibly. That is why Cornelius and those who were with him were nevertheless baptized, even though they had already plainly been sanctified by the invisible outpouring of the Holy Spirit; nor was the visible sanctification judged superfluous, though the invisible had already gone before it.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, and let them keep away from the holy things of the children of Israel, and they shall not profane my holy name in whatever they themselves sanctify to me; I am the Lord. And you shall say to them: Throughout your generations, any man at all of all your offspring who approaches whatever holy things the children of Israel sanctify to the Lord while his uncleanness is upon him, that soul shall be cut off from me: I am the Lord your God." This removes all doubt that no priest, whether high priest or of the second rank, was to approach the holy things if his uncleanness was upon him. It followed, then, that the priest had to be continent, so that the perpetual incense, which only the high priests used to offer twice a day, morning and evening, would not be left off on some days because of the begetting of children; for after marital intercourse the one who had to offer it was unclean until evening, even after washing his body. As for the words "which the children of Israel sanctify," they are to be understood as meaning that they sanctify things by offering them to the priests to be offered through them to the Lord. And we should note this kind of sanctification, which comes about through the vow and devotion of the one making the offering. But whether, just as the things people offer are sanctified in this way, people themselves are also said to sanctify themselves in the same way when they vow themselves in some matter, is something to watch for in the Scriptures.
"And whoever touches any uncleanness of a soul": that is, any carcass, the touching of which defiles according to the law.

"A man, a man, if he curses his God, shall bear his sin; but whoever names the name of the Lord, let him die the death." It is as though cursing one's God were one thing and naming the name of the Lord another, and the former were a sin, while the latter were so great an outrage as to deserve even death. In this passage, however, the words "the name of the Lord" must be understood as being spoken with a curse, that is, as naming it in cursing. What difference, then, is there between that sin and this crime of such great wickedness? Or perhaps by repeating the same thing he showed that the sin was not a light one but so great a crime as to be punishable by death? But because he introduced it with a contrast, saying not "for whoever names" but "but whoever names," the passage has become somewhat obscure. And so, if this is rightly understood, we should also take note of this manner of expression.

"And the man who strikes [any] soul of a man, and he dies, let him die the death." He does not say, "whoever strikes a man and he dies," but "the soul of a man," although it is rather the man's body that is struck by the assailant, as the Lord too says: "Do not fear those who kill the body." In its usual manner, Scripture calls the life of the body itself, which comes about through the soul, a soul; and in this way it wanted to describe a murderer as one who strikes a man's soul, that is, who deprives a man of life by striking him. Why, then, did he add "and he dies," if he had already indicated murder by saying that he struck the man's soul, that is, that the man was deprived of life by his assailant? Or did he want to explain how his phrase "the man's soul was struck" is to be understood, and so said "and he dies," as if to say, "that is, he dies"? For that is what it means for a man's soul to have been struck.

"When you enter the land that I am giving you, and the land that I am giving you rests, the sabbaths of the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be sabbaths, a rest for the land, sabbaths for the Lord." How are we to understand "When you enter the land that I am giving you, and the land rests, for six years you shall sow your field," and so on? It is as if the command were to be carried out when the land rests, whereas the land rests precisely because this command is carried out. For by the land's rest he clearly means the seventh year, in which he commanded that no one should do any farm work on it. But no doubt a long hyperbaton makes this meaning obscure. The order of the words, then, seems to be this: "When you enter the land that I am giving you, and the land that I am giving you rests, the sabbaths of the Lord: what springs up of itself from your field you shall not reap, and the grapes of your consecration you shall not gather. It shall be a year of rest for the land. And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you and for your manservant and your maidservant and your hired worker and the sojourner who has attached himself to you. And for your livestock and the beasts that are in your land, all that grows from it shall be for food." But in between he inserted an explanation of how the land is to rest, saying: "For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vine and gather its fruit; but in the seventh year there shall be sabbaths, a rest for the land, sabbaths of the Lord. You shall not sow your field and you shall not prune your vineyard." And by saying "you shall not prune," we should understand that all cultivation is forbidden in that year. For if it is not to be pruned, neither is it to be ploughed, or propped up on supports, or given any other treatment that belongs to its cultivation; rather, just as the whole is often understood from a part, so all cultivation is signified by pruning. And by the field and the vineyard, when he forbade the one to be sown and the other to be pruned, every kind of land is to be understood. For no work is to be done in an olive grove either, or in land of any other kind, about which he said nothing. As for his saying, "And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you and for your manservant and your maidservant," and so on, he made it quite clear that the owner of the land was not forbidden to eat what grew of its own accord that year without cultivation, but was forbidden to gather in the produce. So he was permitted to take some of it as food only in the way a passer-by would, taking just what he would consume at once by eating it, not what he might store away for later use.

"And the land shall not be sold for profanation." Other manuscripts have "for confirmation." I think this error first arose in one or the other set of Greek manuscripts because of the similar sound of the words: for βεβήλωσις means profanation, and βεβαίωσις confirmation. The first sense is plain: "And the land shall not be sold for profanation," that is, no one was to dare to sell the land he had received from God to profane people who would use it for impiety and for the worship of foreign and false gods. But the other reading is somewhat obscure: "the land shall not be sold for confirmation." I think this is to be understood only in the sense that the sale is not to be confirmed in such a way that the seller does not get the land back at the time of release, as was commanded. What follows, however, can fit either sense, whether one reads "And the land shall not be sold for profanation" or "for confirmation." For he went on to add: "For the land is mine, because you are proselytes and sojourners before me."

"And throughout all the land of your possession you shall pay the land a rent." Other manuscripts, however, have "you shall pay the land a redemption." The sense, then, is this: the land shall not be sold "for profanation," that is, to people who would use it to insult the Creator; or "for confirmation," that is, so that the buyer would possess it in perpetuity and not restore it to the seller after the fixed interval of years in accordance with God's command. "For the land is mine," he says; and so you ought to use it according to my command. And to show that it was his and not theirs, he went on to add what they themselves were in it, saying: "because you are proselytes and sojourners before me"; that is: although you have proselytes, that is, newcomers, who join your nation from among foreigners, and sojourners, that is, people who are not living in their own land, yet you all are newcomers and sojourners before me. God says this either to the Israelites, because he gave them the land of other nations which he drove out, or to every human being, because before God, who abides forever and, as it is written, fills heaven and earth with his presence, every human being is a newcomer by being born and a sojourner by living, since he is compelled to move on by dying.

Then he adds: "And throughout all the land of your possession you shall pay the land a rent," as tenants, "or a redemption." Unless I am mistaken, he wants us to understand what they paid back from it, so to speak, through the fallow seasons of every seventh year and of the fiftieth year, which he calls the year of release, so that the land's very rest was a kind of rent for their dwelling, or a redemption from him whose land it is, that is, from God, its Creator.

"And I will set my tabernacle among you, and my soul shall not abhor you." God calls his will his soul. For he is not a living creature having a body and a soul; nor is his substance of the same kind as that creature of his which is called the soul, which he made, as he himself testifies through Isaiah, saying, "And I made every breath"; the context makes it clear that he is speaking of the human soul. So just as, when he speaks of "his eyes" and "his lips" and uses the other words for bodily members, we certainly do not take him to be bounded by the shape of a body, and we understand all those names of members to mean nothing but the effects of his works and powers, so too when he says "my soul" we ought to take it to mean his will. For that perfect and simple nature which is called God is not made up of body and spirit, nor is it changeable in its spirit as the soul is; rather, God is spirit and is always the same, he in whom there is no change. But from this the Apollinarians took occasion to say that the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, did not have a soul but was only Word and flesh, although he said, "My soul is sorrowful even to death." But in his very conduct, which is made known to us through the gospel narrative, the functions of a human soul are so plainly evident that only a madman could doubt it.

Why is it that when God threatened punishments for disobedience, he said among other things, "And the sword shall go through and consume you"? Then he says: "And your land shall be deserted, and your cities shall be deserted. Then the land shall fully enjoy its sabbaths all the days of its desolation, and you shall be in the land of your enemies." How, then, will the sword consume them, if they are to be in the land of their enemies? Or will it consume them in that land itself, since once they have been slaughtered they will no longer be there? Or did he say "it shall consume you" as if he were saying "it shall kill you," so that this consuming applies to those who will fall by the sword, not to all of them, since a little later he says, "And on those of you who are left I will bring fear into their hearts"? Or is "it shall consume you" said by hyperbole, the manner of speaking in which their multitude was said to be like the sand of the sea? What follows next is also said in this manner: "And the sound of a flying leaf shall pursue them," that is, their fear will be so great that they will dread even the slightest things.
BOOK FOUR. QUESTIONS ON NUMBERS.

Question 1. Why does he order that leaders be chosen, one from each tribe, and call them chiliarchs? Some Latin translators have called them "tribunes", but chiliarchs seem to take their name from "a thousand". Now when Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, gave his son-in-law advice about organizing the people under leaders, so that the cases of everyone would not burden Moses beyond his strength (advice that God also approved), he called those to be set over thousands chiliarchs, those over hundreds hecatontarchs, those over fifties pentecontarchs and those over tens decadarchs, each named from the number he was to be in charge of. Are the chiliarchs here, then, to be understood in the same way, as each being over a thousand? Certainly not. The whole people of Israel did not then number only twelve thousand men. He chose one from each tribe, and these twelve tribes without doubt contained not a thousand men each but many thousands. So the name is shared with those who are called chiliarchs in Exodus, because each of them was the leader of a thousand men; but each of these is the leader of thousands. Whether it comes from "a thousand" or from "thousands", the compound name sounds the same, so that they are called chiliarchs.

It is rightly asked what is meant by the fact that, throughout all the tribes, where the sons of Israel of military age are counted tribe by tribe, it says: according to their kinships, according to their peoples, according to the houses of their families, according to the number of their names, according to their head. These five are repeated in exactly the same way until all the tribes have been completed, as if "according to their kinships" were one thing, "according to their peoples" another, "according to the houses of their families" another, "according to the number of their names" another, and "according to their head" another, when all of these seem rather to signify the same thing in different words. Yet it catches the attention that the same things are repeated so carefully through all the tribes, so that anyone would judge it is not done for nothing, even if he does not understand it. No doubt, then, the number itself hints at some mystery, since the same thing is repeated five times in different ways. For this number, five, is especially commended in the Old Testament, as in the five books of Moses themselves. The four items joined next, namely every male from twenty years old and upward, everyone who goes forth in strength, their review, are also repeated in exactly the same way through all the tribes, but they have a necessary distinction among them. Since the question was the number of the whole multitude belonging to one tribe, the sex had to be distinguished; so it says: every male. So that little children would not be counted as well, it adds: from twenty years old and upward. Again, so that the unwarlike age of old men would not be counted, it adds: everyone who goes forth in strength. And everything is concluded with the word for the work that was being done, so that it says: their review. For a review was being held so that these thousands of men could be counted. So those five, "kinships, peoples, houses of families, number of names, and head", and then these four, "sex, age, strength, review", perhaps hint at something by their very number. For if one of these two numbers, five and four, is multiplied by the other, that is, five times four or four times five, they make twenty. This number also marks that age of young men. The number is mentioned again when the land of promise is entered, and that age of twenty years is spoken of which had not turned aside to the right or to the left. There, it seems to me, the holy faithful of both testaments who hold the true faith are signified. For the Old Testament is preeminent above all in the five books of Moses, and the New in the four Gospels.

He speaks of taking down, lifting and setting up the tabernacle, and says: and the foreigner who approaches shall die. Here "foreigner" is to be understood even of those sons of Israel who were not of the tribe he commanded to serve the tabernacle, that is, of anyone who was not of the tribe of Levi. But it is strange that "foreigner" is used loosely here, since it rather signifies a man of another race, that is, allogenēs, and the word used is not allophylos, which signifies a man of another tribe. Scripture uses that word more for men of other nations, so that they are called, as it were, men of other tribes.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the tribe of Levi and set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall minister to him; and they shall keep his guards and the guards of the sons of Israel before the tabernacle of testimony. What the Greek called phylakas, some of our translators rendered "guards" and others "sentry-posts". But it would be surprising if they were not better called "watches", which in camps usually consist of keeping guard for three hours at a time. Hence it is written: In the fourth watch of the night he came to them walking on the sea, that is, after the ninth hour of the night, after three watches, that is. And in many places of Scripture our translators have rendered as "watches" what the Greeks call phylakai. There is no doubt that periods of the night are meant there, and I think it should be taken that way here too. For how are the Levites commanded to keep the watches (phylakas) of Aaron and the watches of the sons of Israel? Perhaps it was said so that they would not think that the honour of serving the tabernacle ought to exempt them from keeping the watches normally kept in camps. They too had to take their turn in keeping watches for the sake of the work of the tabernacle, no less than the watches kept in the rest of the camp of the sons of Israel round about.

The foreigner who touches it shall die. We must ask how he could say in Leviticus: whoever touches the tabernacle shall be sanctified, when here he says: the foreigner who touches it shall die, meaning those who were not of the tribe of Levi. Or perhaps here he used "touches" of the work of service, which he commanded that the Levites alone owed to the tabernacle? For that was what he was speaking about.

Why does God claim the Levites for himself in place of the firstborn of the sons of Israel? When the firstborn of the people were counted, they were found to be more numerous than the Levites, and so the extra ones were redeemed with silver, five shekels being paid for each. This was not done for the cattle, although he willed the cattle of the Levites to be his in place of the firstborn of the cattle of Israel. How, then, did their firstborn, both of humans and of cattle, belong to God from then on, when he commanded that the unclean and the human firstborn be exchanged for sheep? And why were the sons of the Levites not also counted in place of these later firstborn? For the same tribe remained in their descendants, and it could have been counted in place of the later firstborn. Surely it was because it was just that God should now have as his own, as his from his own, those who were born of men who already belonged to the Lord's portion, which had been given in place of the firstborn who came out of Egypt. So they could not justly be counted in place of the firstborn who were owed to God from then on. For a portion was given to God from the whole people and from all the people's cattle in place of the firstborn, and this portion was the Levites and their cattle. Whatever they begot after that was already God's. It could not be given as though it came from the people, since it no longer belonged to them. So the firstborn had to be rendered to God as a debt from then on, and the descendants of the Levites and of their cattle could not be counted in their place.

When he gave instructions about taking up the table, he ordered the loaves to be taken up with it, saying: and the loaves that shall always be on it. Of course those very loaves would not always be on it, but others like them, because those were removed and fresh ones were set out every day, so long as the table was never left without loaves. That is why he said: that shall always be on it. There are always loaves, though not always the same ones.

And over the golden altar they shall cover a blue garment, and they shall cover it with a covering of blue skin. Latin translators were unwilling to render this expression, it seems, as if it were absurd and incomplete: and over the golden altar they shall cover a blue garment. They took it as though it should have said: and they shall cover the golden altar with a blue garment. For "they shall cover a blue garment" seems to mean that the garment itself was covered with something else, not that the altar was covered with the garment. But to me this seems to be not so much an idiom as a rather obscure meaning. For it can be understood this way: and over the golden altar they shall cover a blue garment. That is, he commanded that the blue garment, which was already on the altar, should itself be covered with something else, and so he briefly included both points: that the altar was to be covered with the blue garment, and that the blue garment was to be covered with another covering. Then he added what he wanted the blue garment covered with: and they shall cover it with a covering of blue skin.

Any man or woman who commits any of all the human sins, and despising despises and transgresses, that soul shall declare the sin which it has sinned and shall restore the trespass, the principal, and shall add its fifths to it and shall give it to him against whom he trespassed. But if the man has no next of kin, so that he may render the trespass to him, the trespass that is rendered to the Lord shall belong to the priest, apart from the ram of propitiation, by which he shall make atonement in it for him. The sins to be understood here are those committed in matters that can be restored with money. He would not say how they are to be restored unless they were financial losses. For he commands the principal and the fifths to be restored, that is, the whole of whatever it was and a fifth part of it besides, apart from the ram that had to be offered in sacrifice to expiate the trespass. And he commands that what is restored, that is, the principal and the fifth, shall belong to the priest if the one wronged has no next of kin. Clearly this means that what goes to the priest is to be rendered to the Lord only when neither the man who suffered the loss is still alive nor his next of kin, by whom I think he meant his heir. Scripture said nothing about the man himself. But when it says, "if he has no next of kin", it briefly hints that his next of kin is to be sought when he himself is no longer living. And if there is no next of kin either, it shall be restored to the Lord, so that the wrong done does not go unpunished. Yet it is not used for the sacrifice but belongs to the priest. The words of Scripture are certainly to be punctuated thus: But if the man has no next of kin, so that he may render the trespass to him. The added "to him" is an idiom, or perhaps he said "to him" meaning what belongs to him, that is, what he would possess. Then follows: the trespass that is rendered to the Lord shall belong to the priest. He calls it the "trespass" when the thing taken away by the trespass is rendered.

But it may be asked how it can be said in Exodus that if someone steals a calf or a sheep, he must restore five calves or four sheep if he has killed or sold it, but double if what he took is found safe in his possession, when here the command is to restore the principal and a fifth. That falls far short even of double, and much further short of fourfold or fivefold. Perhaps the explanation is that, because he says here: any man or woman who commits any of all the human sins, he meant "human sins" to be understood as sins of ignorance. For it can happen that a person, through negligence and lack of attention, transfers someone else's property into his own. This is a sin because it would not have been committed if he had paid careful attention. And he willed that such sins be restored with the principal and a fifth, not penalized like thefts. But suppose we understand thefts and frauds here, committed not through negligent ignorance but with the intent to steal and defraud, and called "human" because they are done against humans. Then, unless I am mistaken, the solution to this question is that the person who did it does not pay even double because he has not been caught or convicted. Rather, while people do not know who did it, or whether it was done at all, he himself declares his trespass. For when Scripture had said: any man or woman who commits any of all the human sins and despising despises and transgresses, that is, commits these things out of contempt, it went on to say: that soul shall declare the sin which it has sinned and shall restore the trespass, the principal, and its fifths. Perhaps, then, he pays only this much because he declared it himself, and so was not to be punished with the penalty that a thief who was caught or convicted ought to suffer.

Scripture says the priest is to speak these words to the woman when her husband brings her on suspicion of adultery: May the Lord make you a curse and an execration. For "execration" the Greek has ἐνόρκιον [?]. This word seems to mean "an oath by execration", as when someone says, "So may this or that not happen to me", or at any rate swears like this: "May this or that happen to me if I do, or do not do, such a thing." So the words May the Lord make you a curse and an execration are said as if to mean: may those who swear with an execration swear by you, saying, "So may it not happen to them," or "May this happen to them, unless they have done that."

And he shall offer his gift to the Lord: a year-old male lamb without blemish as a holocaust, and one year-old ewe-lamb without blemish as a sin. Some of our translators were unwilling to render this literally, avoiding what they took for an unusual expression, and said "for sin" rather than "as a sin". Yet the expression contains a meaning that should not have been disturbed. It says "as a sin" because the very thing offered for sin was called "sin". Hence the Apostle says of the Lord Christ: Him who knew no sin he made sin for us. God the Father, that is, made God the Son sin for us, meaning a sacrifice for sin. So just as the male lamb is offered as a holocaust, so that the animal itself is a holocaust, the ewe-lamb is offered as a sin, so that the animal itself is sin, that is, becomes a sacrifice for sin. In the same way, in what follows, he says of the ram "as a salvation", as though it were itself salvation, since it is a sacrifice of salvation. He makes this clear later by repeating it, for he says "for sin" of what he had earlier called "as a sin", and "sacrifice of salvation" of what he had earlier called "as a salvation".

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is concerning the Levites. Others have translated this as: This is the law concerning the Levites. But the words as written, This is concerning the Levites, are understood to mean: This I establish concerning the Levites.

Then follows: From the twenty-fifth year and upward they shall go in to minister the ministry in the works in the tabernacle of testimony; and from the fiftieth year he shall withdraw from the service and shall work no more, and his brother shall minister, in the tabernacle of testimony to keep the watches, but the works he shall not work. A hyperbaton [?] makes this sense obscure. The words are so jumbled that "to keep the watches" seems to be said of the brother. In fact it is said of the man who withdraws from the works; it remains for him to keep the watches in the tabernacle of testimony, but he will not work the works. His brother will work them, that is, the one who has not yet reached the age of fifty and begins to work at twenty-five. So it is to be punctuated thus: and from the fiftieth year he shall withdraw from the service and shall work no more, and his brother shall minister. Then he returns to the fifty-year-old he was speaking of and explains the rest about him, saying: in the tabernacle of testimony to keep the watches, but the works he shall not work. With the words "to keep", "he shall begin" is understood, as though he were saying in one word, "he shall keep the watches". For even in Latin idiom the infinitive is commonly used in place of a finite verb.

At the time of Passover, some people who had become unclean through the soul of a man, that is, through a dead body, asked how they should keep the Passover, since the law required them to be purified from their uncleanness for seven days. Moses consulted the Lord and received the answer "that anyone to whom such a thing had happened, or who was on so distant a journey that he could not arrive in time, should keep the Passover in another month, on the fourteenth day of the month", for there the count of the moon was observed. But if it is asked what they would do if the same kind of uncleanness happened to them in the second month as well, I think that what was said about the second month was to be kept as a general rule, so that they would observe it in the third month. Or at any rate, failing to keep the Passover under such necessity would not be counted as a fault.

And on the day the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony; and in the evening there was over the tabernacle something like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night. And when the cloud went up from the tabernacle, and afterwards the sons of Israel moved on; and in whatever place the cloud had stopped, there the sons of Israel pitched camp.
