At the command of the Lord the sons of Israel shall pitch camp, and at the command of the Lord they shall move on. All the days on which the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the sons of Israel shall stay in camp. And when the cloud lingers over the tabernacle many days, and the sons of Israel shall keep the watch of God and shall not move on. And it shall be, when the cloud covers the tabernacle for a number of days, at the voice of the Lord they shall stay in camp, and at the command of the Lord they shall move on. And it shall be, when the cloud is there from evening until morning, and the cloud goes up in the morning, and they shall move on by day; or by night, and if the cloud goes up, they shall move on; for a day or a month of days, while the cloud abounds, overshadowing it, the sons of Israel shall stay in camp and shall not move on, because at the command of the Lord they shall move on. They kept the watch of the Lord at the command of the Lord by the hand of Moses. This whole passage needs careful explanation, since unusual kinds of expression make it obscure. And on the day, it says, the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony. He called the same tabernacle the house of testimony. And in the evening there was over the tabernacle something like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was always. Then he carefully spells out what always happened. The cloud, he says, covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night. And when the cloud went up from the tabernacle, and afterwards the sons of Israel moved on. This sentence is obscure only because of the idiom that adds "and". The word order stays complete even without that conjunction, so that it would read: And when the cloud went up from the tabernacle, afterwards the sons of Israel moved on. Indeed, even without the word "afterwards" the sentence could be complete. Then he goes on to say: and in whatever place the cloud had stopped, there the sons of Israel pitched camp.

Scripture then refers everything they did to the Lord's command and sums it up like this: "At the command of the Lord the children of Israel shall pitch camp, and at the command of the Lord they shall set out." By "the command of the Lord" it means the sign itself that was given in the cloud: whether it stood still overshadowing the tabernacle, so that the camp also stayed where it was, or rose and moved on, so that they broke camp and followed it. In this sentence it has plainly changed its narrative mode and, as if foretelling and announcing something, has begun to use verbs in the future tense. For it does not say, "At the command of the Lord the children of Israel used to pitch camp," but "shall pitch camp"; nor does it say, "At the command of the Lord they used to set out," but "they shall set out." It keeps to this mode in what follows as well, and this mode is extremely unusual in the Scriptures. We know that future things are often foretold in verbs of the past tense, as in "They pierced my hands and feet," and "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter," and countless other such passages. But it is very hard to find a place in the Scriptures where someone narrating past events uses verbs of the future tense, as happens here.

So after it has spoken of day and night, and of the sign by which the people set out or stayed, it goes on to add something, so that no one would think they travelled by night and usually encamped by day, and did this every day. It says: "All the days on which the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the children of Israel will remain in camp. And when the cloud lingers over the tabernacle for many days." Then, to point out that this happened not because of their own needs but because of God's will, it says: "the children of Israel will keep the charge of God," that is, the charge that God commanded, "and will not set out." And as if someone were asking, "When, then, will they set out?" it says: "And it shall be, when the cloud covers the tabernacle for a number of days"—that is, for a fixed number of days, a number which was certainly what pleased God—"at the voice of the Lord they will remain in camp, and at the command of the Lord they will set out." By "the voice of the Lord" it seems to mean the sign the Lord gave by the cloud's standing still or moving, since a speaker's voice is undoubtedly a sign of his will. So when it says "and at the command," I think the same sign is to be understood. Admittedly, "the voice" and "the command of the Lord" could also be taken to refer to the fact that he "spoke to Moses," as he usually did, and "commanded this to be done." For they would not have known that they were to set out when the cloud moved on and stay when the cloud stood still unless they had been commanded this beforehand.

In what has been said so far, however, it has not yet become clear whether they travelled only by day or also by night, following the sign the cloud gave by its movement. For although they might remain in camp for many days while the cloud did not move on, it could perhaps still have been thought that the cloud did not usually rise from the camp and give the signal for a march except by day. So it goes on to say: "And it shall be, when the cloud has stayed from evening until morning and the cloud goes up in the morning, and they will set out by day." Here the copulative conjunction "and" is placed in the manner of Scripture, for if it is removed, the sense is complete, like this: "And it shall be, when the cloud has stayed from evening until morning and the cloud goes up in the morning, they will set out by day." Then, because they also set out by night if the cloud went up, and made a night march if they received that sign, it adds: "or by night and if the cloud goes up, they will set out." But this expression is rather unusual. It is not only that "and" has been inserted; it has been inserted in a way it normally is not. So it seems to me that the word order has been inverted, as often happens in Latin expressions too; this kind of figure is called antistrophe. Accordingly, if it is put like this: "or even by night, if the cloud goes up, they will set out," or certainly like this: "if the cloud goes up even by night, they will set out," the sense is perfectly clear.

A further question, however, would occur to someone thinking it over. We have learned that, at the sign of the cloud, they used to travel by day and by night, or to remain in camp by day and by night. He might want to know whether, in the same way, they also used to stay put by day only, on days whose nights they spent travelling. I think Scripture indicated this in what follows, when it says: "By day, or for a month of daytime, while the cloud abundantly overshadows it, the children of Israel will remain in camp and will not set out." Since it had said, "or by night and if the cloud goes up, they will set out," it still remained, so to speak, for it to say: "But by day, if it does not go up, they will not move," at a time when it looked as though they ought to set out. But because this could also go on for many days, so that they travelled by night when the cloud moved on and did not travel by day while it stayed, it put "by day, or for a month of daytime." It did not say "a month," or the nights of that same month would also have been included, but "a month of daytime," that is, a month with respect to the part that was day for them, not the part that was night. "By day," then, "or for a month of daytime, while the cloud abundantly overshadows"—that is, overshadows abundantly, or more abundantly—"it"—namely, the tabernacle—"the children of Israel will remain in camp and will not set out." Finally, it repeated that this was done by divine authority, which certainly ought not to be resisted, adding: "for at the command of the Lord they will set out. They kept the charge of the Lord at the command of the Lord by the hand of Moses." It went back to a verb in the past tense, so as to say "they kept." As for what it put at the end, "by the hand of Moses," this is a very common expression in the Scriptures, because God gave these commands through Moses.

"And when you assemble the congregation, you shall blow the trumpet, but not as a signal." He does not, then, command the trumpet to be blown so that the congregation may be assembled, since that would be a signal. Rather, he commands it to be blown when the congregation has already assembled, as if it now belonged to music, not to giving a signal that tells people to do something. So when someone of the New Testament gives a spiritual interpretation of the fact that they blew trumpets after the congregation had already assembled, it is a sign for the one who understands why it is done. It was not a sign for those who did not understand, except when it was done to announce some task.

"And I will take some of the spirit that is in you and place it upon them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, and you shall not carry them alone." Most Latin translators have not rendered this as it is in the Greek. They have said, "I will take some of your spirit which is in you and place it upon them," or "place it in them," and so have made the meaning hard to understand. For it could be thought to refer to the man's own spirit. This spirit, joined to a body, makes up human nature, which consists of body and spirit, and is also called the soul. Of this spirit the apostle says: "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." And when he adds, "But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is from God," he certainly shows that the Spirit of God is different, and that the human spirit comes to share in it by the grace of God. Even so, as others have translated it, the phrase "of your spirit which is in you" could also be understood of the Spirit of God. It would be called "yours" because the Spirit that is God's also becomes ours when we receive it, just as it was said of John: "in the spirit and power of Elijah." For the soul of Elijah had not been transferred into him. And if some hold that it was, out of heretical perversity, what will they say about what is written, "The spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha"? Elisha certainly already had his own soul. Surely this was said of the Spirit of God, meaning that the Spirit would also work through Elisha the kinds of things it worked through Elijah. It did not withdraw from Elijah in order to fill Elisha, nor was it divided, becoming less in Elijah so that some part of it could also be in Elisha. For God is able to be present in his fullness in all those in whom he has willed to be present by that grace. But now, since it is written this way, "And I will take some of the spirit that is upon you," and not "of your spirit," the question is more easily resolved. We understand that God meant nothing else than this: those men too would receive help from the same Spirit of grace from whom Moses received it, so that they would have as much as God willed, without Moses therefore having any less.

"And Moses said: Six hundred thousand foot soldiers, and I am among them, and you have said, 'I will give them meat, and they shall eat for a month of days.' Shall sheep and oxen be slaughtered for them, and will that be enough for them? Or shall all the fish be gathered for them, and will that be enough for them?" The usual question is whether Moses said this out of distrust or out of inquiry. If we suppose that he said it out of distrust, the question arises why the Lord did not rebuke him for it, as he rebuked him when Moses seems to have doubted the Lord's power at the rock from which water flowed. But if we say that he said this asking how it would be done, the Lord's own reply, in which he said to him, "Is the hand of the Lord not sufficient?", seems like the reply of someone reproving him for not believing it. I think it is better to understand that the Lord answered in this way because he did not wish to state how the future deed would come about, as Moses was asking, but preferred to demonstrate his power by the deed itself. For Mary too said, "How shall this be, since I do not know a man?" Slanderers could have objected that she lacked faith, when in fact she was asking about the manner and not doubting the power of God. And the answer given to her, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you," could just as well have been given as it is here: "Is anything impossible for the Holy Spirit, who will come upon you?" The meaning would have been the same. Zechariah, on the other hand, is charged with unbelief for saying something of this kind and is punished by being struck dumb. Why? Only because God judges not by words but by hearts. Otherwise the words of Moses at the rock from which water flowed could also have been excused, were it not for God's plain judgment against him that he had said such things out of distrust. For his words run like this: "Hear me, you unbelievers: shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" Then follows: "And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock twice with the rod, and much water came out, and the congregation drank, and their cattle." Certainly this was why he assembled the people, why he took that rod with which he had worked such great miracles, and why he struck the rock with it, and from it he obtained the usual effect of that power. So the words in which he says, "Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" could be taken as if he meant: "Of course, according to your unbelief, water cannot be brought out of this rock." Then by striking it he would show that God could do what they in their faithlessness did not believe, especially since he had said, "Hear me, you unbelievers." These words could indeed be understood this way, were it not that God, who sees into the heart, revealed in what spirit they were spoken. For Scripture goes on to say: "And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Because you did not believe so as to sanctify me in the sight of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this congregation into the land that I have given them." From this it is understood that Moses spoke those words as one who struck the rock without knowing what would happen. If no result had followed, he would be thought to have predicted this when he said, "Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?" This would have stayed completely hidden in his mind had it not been exposed by God's judgment. In this passage, then, by contrast, we should understand that Moses' words about the promised meat came from one asking how it would happen rather than from one who distrusted. For no judgment of the Lord followed that punished him, only one that taught him.

About the Ethiopian wife of Moses, people often ask whether she is the daughter of Jethro, or whether he married another woman, or took a second wife in addition. But it is credible that she was the same woman. For she was one of the Midianites, and in Chronicles they are found to be called Ethiopians, when Jehoshaphat fought against them. For there it is said that the people of Israel pursued them into the regions where the Midianites live, who are now called Saracens. But hardly anyone now calls them Ethiopians, just as the names of places and peoples commonly change over time.

"And he said to them: Go up by this wilderness, and you shall go up into the mountain and see what the land is like, and the people who dwell in it, whether it is strong or weak, whether they are few or many." We understand that he has explained what he meant by "whether it is powerful or weak": that is, "whether they are few or many." For how could men looking out from a mountain judge the strength of human forces? There may also be another meaning, much more consistent with the truth. When he says, "you shall go up into the mountain," he means the land itself which they wished to explore. For the spies could not easily be recognized as spies there, since they were looking into everything as though they were travelers. For if we suppose that they looked at the land and explored it from the top of a mountain, how could they look into all the things Moses told them to examine? How could they enter the cities that Scripture says they entered? How could they take the cluster of grapes from that valley, from which the place also got its name, so that it was called the Valley of the Cluster? So the land was explored on the mountain itself, because the mountain was the very land that was to be explored. And there was a lower-lying place there, from which valley the cluster was taken.

"And they brought out the terror of the land which they had explored." He said "the terror of the land," not meaning a terror felt by the land itself, but the terror they had conceived from that land.

Caleb and Joshua the son of Nun, speaking to the people of Israel so that they would not be afraid to enter the land of promise, said among other things: "But do not fear the people of the land, for they are food for us. For their time has departed from them, but the Lord is among us; do not fear them." By saying, "they are food for us," they meant, "we will consume them." What they added, "For their time has departed from them, but the Lord is among us," they said with great care. They did not say, "The Lord has departed from them," for those people had been ungodly from of old. But since even the ungodly are given a time to flourish and to reign, by the hidden dispensation of divine providence, they say, "their time has departed from them, but the Lord is among us." They did not say, "their time has departed from them and ours has taken its place," but "the Lord is among us," not a time. For those people had a time; these had the Lord God, who creates and orders times and allots them to each as he pleases.

Since instructions are given for how sins committed involuntarily are to be expiated, it is right to ask what these sins of the unwilling are. Are they sins committed by those who do not know? Or can a sin also rightly be called the sin of an unwilling person when he is compelled to do it? For this too is commonly said to be done against one's will. Yet he certainly wills that for the sake of which he acts. Suppose someone does not want to perjure himself, yet does so because he wants to live, since someone threatens him with death if he does not. He wills to do it, then, because he wills to live. So he does not seek to swear falsely for its own sake, but swears falsely in order to live. If this is so, I do not know whether such acts can be called sins of the unwilling, of the kind said here to need expiation. For if the matter is carefully considered, perhaps no one wills sinning itself; it is done for the sake of something else that the sinner wants. For all people who knowingly do what is not permitted would wish it were permitted. So true is it that no one seeks sinning for its own sake, but for what follows from it. If this is how things are, then the sins of the unwilling are only the sins of those who do not know, and they are distinguished from the sins of the willing.

"And any soul that sins with a hand of pride, whether native-born or proselyte, provokes God, and that soul shall be cut off from its people, because it has despised the word of the Lord and scattered his commandments; that soul shall be crushed with crushing; its sin is upon it." Scripture itself explains clearly enough in what follows what the sins are that are done "with a hand of pride," that is, committed through pride, when it says: "because it has despised the word of the Lord." It is one thing, then, to despise the commandments. It is another to value them highly yet act against them, either out of ignorance or because one is overcome. These two perhaps belong to the sins committed by the unwilling. Earlier he explained how these were to be expiated when God had been appeased, and then he added the sins of pride, when someone does wrong out of pride, that is, by despising a commandment. He did not say that this kind of sin should be cleansed by any kind of sacrifice. He judged it incurable, at least by that remedy which was carried out through sacrifices of the kind this Scripture commands. Considered in themselves, these sacrifices cannot heal any sin. But if we look for the realities of which they are sacraments, the cleansing of sins can be found in those. So the one meant by the text "When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises" is the one whom Scripture here says offends "with a hand of pride." This sin, therefore, cannot be wiped away without the punishment of the one who commits it. For that reason it cannot go unpunished, even when it is healed by repentance. For the affliction of the penitent is itself a punishment for sin, though a medicinal and healing one. It is rightly judged a great sin when pride despises a commandment. But on the other hand, so that it can be healed, God does not spurn a contrite and humbled heart. Yet because this does not happen without punishment, such things are said here. "It provokes God," he says, because God resists the proud. "And that soul shall be cut off from its people," since such a soul is not at all counted among those who belong to God, "because it has despised the word of the Lord and scattered his commandments; that soul shall be crushed with crushing." And he goes on to say why it will be crushed with crushing: "its sin is upon it." And so, if by repenting the soul applies to itself the contrition owed for such a sin, God, as has been said, does not spurn a contrite heart. In the Greek, however, this passage does not say "shall be crushed with crushing" but "that soul shall be ground out with grinding out." This could be taken to mean that it is entirely ground away until it is extinguished and ceases to exist. But first, the immortal nature of the soul rules out this interpretation. Second, if whatever is ground out were made to cease existing altogether, it would not say of the wise man: "And let your foot wear out the steps of his doors." But we need to consider more and more carefully the distinction of whether no one sins except out of ignorance, or because he is overcome, or out of contempt. It would take too long to discuss that now.

What does it mean that Dathan and Abiram, when they had risen in sedition and were summoned by Moses, answered proudly and insultingly: "Is it a small thing that you have brought us out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness, because you rule over us, you are a prince? And have you brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey and given us an inheritance of fields and vineyards?" After this they added: "You would have cut out the eyes of those men; we will not come up." Whose eyes did they mean by "the eyes of those men"? Was it the people of Israel's, as if they were saying, "If you had provided these things, you would have cut out the eyes of those men," that is, they would have loved you so much that they would tear out their own eyes and give them to you? The apostle too speaks of this as a great sign of love: "for if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me." Then they added outright defiance: "we will not come up," that is, "we will not come," since he had summoned them. Or does "the eyes of those men" rather mean the enemies, who had been reported as exceedingly fierce and terrible? As if they were saying, "Even if you had done this, we would not obey you." The only difference is that one mood of the verb is used for another, so that they did not say "we would not come up" but "we will not come up," by a certain figure of speech.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation." Note that the Lord orders a bodily separation to be made at the moment when punishment is already about to fall on the wicked. So Noah with his household is separated from the rest who were to perish in the flood. So Lot with his family is separated from the people of Sodom, who were to be consumed by fire from heaven. So the people itself is separated from the Egyptians, who were to be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea. And so these now are separated from the congregation of Korah, Abiram and Dathan, who had first sought to break away through sedition. Yet the saints had previously lived and dwelt among these men, and among the others whom God condemns in the rebukes he speaks against them, and they could not be defiled by them in the least. Nor were they ordered to separate themselves when the Lord either delayed punishment, or inflicted a kind that could not endanger or harm the innocent. Such were the bites of serpents, or the slaughter by deaths in which God struck whom he wished, as he wished, leaving another untouched. It was not like the water of the flood, or the rain of fire, or the water of the sea, or the opening of the earth, which could sweep away all alike when they were mingled together. This was not because God could not have preserved his own even there. But what need was there to put a miracle to the test when a separation could be made, so that the water or fire or opening of the earth would carry off whomever it found? So too at the end the wheat will be separated from the weeds, so that while flames burn the wicked, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

When Moses says of Korah, Abiram and Dathan, "The Lord will show it in a vision, and the earth will open its mouth and swallow them," some have translated, "The Lord will show it in a chasm." I think they supposed that the word was chasmati [?], whereas the Greek reads phasmati [?]. This is used as though it said "in a manifestation," meaning what will openly appear to the eyes. For "in a vision" is not said here in the way visions are usually spoken of, whether in dreams or in any images seen in ecstasy, but, as I said, in the sense of a manifestation. Some, however, thinking otherwise, chose to translate "in a phantasm." This is so far from the usage of our language that "phantasm" is hardly ever said except where our senses are deceived by false appearances. Admittedly this word too comes from seeing. But, as I said, the usage of speech has settled it otherwise.

"And they and all that belonged to them went down alive into the underworld." Note that the underworld here means a place in the earth, that is, the lower parts of the earth. In the Scriptures, the word "underworld" is used in various ways and with many meanings, as the sense of the matters under discussion requires, and it is most often understood in reference to the dead. But since these men are said to have gone down alive into the underworld, and the narrative itself makes clear enough what happened, it is evident, as I said, that the lower parts of the earth are called by the name "underworld" in comparison with this upper earth on whose surface we live. In the same way, Scripture says that the angels who sinned were thrust down into the darkness of this air, in comparison with the higher heaven where the holy angels dwell, and are being kept for punishment as if in the prisons of the underworld. For it says: "If God did not spare the angels who sinned, but thrust them down into the prisons of the darkness of the underworld and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment." And the apostle Paul calls the devil the prince of the power of the air, who works in the children of unbelief.

"And the Lord said to Moses and to Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron: Take the bronze censers from among those who were burned, and sow this strange fire there, for they have sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls. And make them into hammered plates as a covering for the altar, because they were offered before the Lord and have been sanctified and have become a sign among the children of Israel." Why in this passage did the Lord speak not to Moses and Aaron, as in the earlier ones, but to Moses and Eleazar the son of Aaron? For the moment the following reason occurs to me. The question at issue was the line of the priests, that is, what family they ought to come from. That was why those men from another family perished by so horrible and astonishing a punishment, because they dared to usurp the priesthood. So God chose to speak not to Aaron, who was already high priest, but to Eleazar, who was to succeed him and already held the priesthood of the second rank. In this way he commended the order of descent that ought to hold in the succession of the priests. Hence in what follows it also says: "And Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, took the bronze censers, as many as those who were burned had offered, and added them as a covering for the altar, a memorial for the children of Israel, so that no outsider who is not of the seed of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the Lord. And he shall not be like Korah and like his conspiracy, as the Lord spoke by the hand of Moses." In this way, then, God chose through Eleazar to commend not the priesthood, which was already in Aaron, but the line of priestly succession. When he says, "and sow this strange fire there," "scatter" is to be understood. And in what he added, "for they have sanctified the censers of these sinners in their souls," the thought is expressed in an unusual idiom. But note that the punishment of those who had committed this sin is said, in a new way, to have been sanctified, because through them an example was given to the rest that they should fear. And he went on to say why he wanted a covering for the altar made from the censers: "because they were offered before the Lord and have been sanctified and have become a sign among the children of Israel." So he did not want them rejected because they had been offered by such men. Rather, he wanted people to think about and attend to the one before whom they had been offered, that is, before the Lord. In this way the name of the Lord, before whom they were offered, would count for more in them than the utter wickedness of those by whom they were offered. Scripture had already mentioned this in Exodus, where it speaks of the altar being made. From this it is understood that the kinds of events are distributed among the books, and the order of time is not kept in sequence. For Scripture also narrated in this book how the matter of Aaron's rod came about: by flowering and budding it divinely showed that he had been chosen for the priesthood. And yet in Exodus it is said of this same rod that it was to be placed with the manna in the ark in the Holy of Holies, when instructions are given for building the tabernacle. That was certainly commanded long before the tabernacle itself was built, completed and set up. It was set up in the first month of the second year after they came out of Egypt, and this book begins on the first day of the second month of that same second year. So if we consider the order of the books, it is clear that these things are mentioned by recapitulation, that is, by recalling past events. Those who pay less careful attention think they happened in the same order in which they are told.

And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You and your sons and your father's house with you shall bear the sins of the holy things; and you and your sons shall bear the sins of your priesthood. These are the sins that are called sacrifices for sins. So "the sins of the holy things" does not mean sins that holy people commit; "of the holy things" is said because these are holy things. Because they are offered in the holy place, and the "sacrifices for sins" are called sins, they have been called the sins of the holy things. And the sins of your priesthood are the very same things that are offered for sins, as Scripture also makes clear in Leviticus, where it says that they are to belong to the priest.

All the first-born things that are in their land, as many as they bring to the Lord, shall be yours. Here "first-born" does not mean the first offspring of livestock. In Greek those are called πρωτότοκα, but these are πρωτογενήματα. In Latin, however, no two separate names have been found for these two things. That is why some have translated these πρωτογενήματα as "first-fruits"; but it is something else that is called first-fruits. These three are therefore distinguished as follows: ἀπαρχαί are the first offspring of animals, including those of human beings; πρωτογενήματα are the first produce taken from the land, or from a tree, or from a vine; first-fruits, on the other hand, are taken from the produce too, but from produce already brought in from the field, as from the heap of grain, the winepress, the jar or the cask, from which they used to be taken first.

On the red heifer, whose ashes the law commanded to be used for the water of sprinkling and for the cleansing of those who had touched a dead body: we are not allowed to pass over it in silence, for a most evident sign of the New Testament is prefigured in it; yet, hurrying on as we are, we cannot speak worthily enough of so great a mystery. To begin with, who would not be struck by the very way Scripture opens its account of this matter, and be roused to give the closest attention to the depth of the mystery? And the Lord spoke, it says, to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatever the Lord has established. Without doubt there can be no distinction except between two or more things; a single thing calls for no distinction. Nor did it speak of the distinction of just anything; it added: of the law. And not of just any law. Scripture constantly says of each particular matter on which a legal command is given: This is the law of this or that thing, and not the universal law that contains everything commanded by law. But here, having said: This is the distinction of the law, it went on to add: whatever the Lord has established, that is, by commanding, of course, not by creating. Indeed, some translators have rendered it "whatever the Lord has commanded." If, then, this is the distinction of the law, whatever the Lord has commanded, this distinction is without doubt a great one, and it is rightly understood as distinguishing the two testaments. For the same things are in the Old and the New: there overshadowed, here revealed; there prefigured, here made manifest. For not only the sacraments differ, but the promises as well. There temporal things seem to be held out, by which a spiritual reward is secretly signified; here spiritual and eternal things are promised quite openly. And what clearer and surer distinction is there between temporal and carnal goods and spiritual and eternal ones than the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? His death made it plain enough that this earthly and passing happiness is not to be hoped for and desired from the Lord God as some great gift, since in his only-begotten Son, whom he willed to suffer such great things, he declared by the clearest distinction that something far different must be sought and awaited from him. This passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, then, as the distinction between the two testaments, is fittingly enough prefigured by what is told of the slaughter of the red heifer.

<And> the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatever the Lord has established. And then he begins to give commands, adding these words: Speak to the children of Israel. The passage can also be divided like this: And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: This is the distinction of the law, whatever the Lord has established by speaking. That is, not whatever the Lord established by creating, such as heaven and earth and everything in them, but whatever the Lord established by speaking, namely in the two testaments. Then follows: Speak to the children of Israel, and let them bring you a red heifer without blemish. The red heifer signifies the flesh of Christ. It is female because of the weakness of the flesh; it is red because of the bloody passion itself. When he says, Let them bring you, he shows in Moses himself a figure of the law, since they thought they were killing Christ in accordance with the law, because by their reckoning he was breaking the sabbath and, as they supposed, profaning the observances of the law. It is no wonder, then, that this heifer is said to be without blemish, for the other sacrificial victims also prefigured this flesh, where animals are likewise ordered to be sacrificed without blemish. That flesh was indeed in the likeness of sinful flesh, but it was not sinful flesh. Here, however, where God wished to set forth the distinction of the law more plainly, it was not enough to say without blemish; he also had to say which has no blemish in it. Even if this was said simply as a repetition, perhaps it is not pointless, since the repetition itself has commended the matter more firmly. Yet it is also not far from the truth to understand that "which has no blemish in it" was added, after he had already said a heifer without blemish, because the flesh of Christ had no blemish in itself, though it did have blemish in others, who are his members. For what flesh in this life is without sin except that one alone which has no blemish in it? And no yoke has been laid upon it. For it was not subjugated to iniquity; rather, finding others subjugated to it, he set them free and broke their bonds, so that it may be said to him: You have broken my bonds; to you I will offer a sacrifice of praise. No yoke, indeed, was laid upon the flesh of him who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again.

And you shall give it, he says, to Eleazar the priest. Why not to Aaron? Perhaps it was prefigured in this way because the Lord's passion would come not in the time that then was, but in the time of the descendants of this priesthood. And they shall take it outside the camp: so too the Lord was taken outside the city when he was about to suffer. When he says, to a clean place, this signifies that he had no evil cause against him. And they shall slaughter it in his sight: just as the flesh of Christ was slain in the sight of those who were to be the Lord's priests in the new testament.

And Eleazar shall take some of its blood and sprinkle some of its blood toward the front of the tabernacle of the testimony seven times. This is a testimony that Christ, according to the Scriptures, shed his blood for the remission of sins. It is "toward the front of the tabernacle of the testimony" because it was made known in no other way than it had been foretold by divine testimony; and it is "seven times" because that number pertains to spiritual cleansing.

And they shall burn it in his sight. I think that the burning pertains to a sign of the resurrection. For it is the nature of fire to move upward, and what is burned is turned into fire. Indeed, the very word cremare ("to burn") was taken from Greek into Latin from the idea of suspension. The addition in his sight, that is, in the sight of the priest, seems to me to suggest that the resurrection of Christ appeared to those who were to be a royal priesthood. What follows—and its skin and its flesh and its blood, with its dung, shall be burned—explains how it will be burned. It signifies that not only the substance of Christ's mortal body, indicated by the mention of skin, flesh and blood, but also the insult and contempt of the people, which I think is signified by the word "dung," would be turned into glory, which the flame of burning signifies.

And the priest shall take cedar wood and hyssop and scarlet and throw them into the midst of the burning heifer. The cedar wood is hope, which ought to dwell firmly in the things above; the hyssop is faith, which, though a lowly plant, clings by its roots to the rock; the scarlet is charity, which bears witness to the fervor of the spirit by its fiery color. These three we ought to cast into the resurrection of Christ, as into the midst of that burning, so that our life may be hidden with him, as the apostle says: And your life is hidden with Christ in God.

And the priest shall wash his clothes and wash his body in water, and afterward he shall come into the camp; and the priest shall be unclean until evening. What is the washing of the clothes and of the body but the cleansing of the outer and the inner man? That is what concerns the priest. Then follows: And the one who burns it shall wash his clothes and wash his body in water and shall be unclean until evening. In the one who burns it I think are figured those who buried the flesh of Christ, committing it to the resurrection as if to the flames.

And a clean man shall gather up the ashes of the heifer and lay them outside the camp in a clean place. What do we say the ashes of the heifer are—the remains, that is, of that slaying and burning—but the report that followed the passion and resurrection of Christ? For there are remains for the peaceable man. It was ash, because he was despised by unbelievers as one who was dead; and yet it cleansed, because believers also held that he had risen. And because this report shone out most of all among those who were in the other nations and did not belong to the fellowship of the Jews, I think that is why it was said: And a clean man shall gather up the ashes of the heifer—clean, that is, of the killing of Christ, which had made the Jews guilty. And he shall lay them in a clean place, that is, he will treat them with honor—yet "outside the camp," because the honor of the gospel shone out beyond the celebration of Jewish custom. And it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel; the water of sprinkling is a purification. Afterward he explains more fully how the water of sprinkling was made from these ashes, by which people were cleansed from contact with the dead; this certainly signifies cleansing from the iniquity of this dying, or rather dead, life.

But what follows is remarkable: And the one who gathers the ashes of the heifer, he says, shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. How could someone who had come clean become unclean by this, unless it is because even those who seem clean to themselves in the Christian faith recognize that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely through his blood? Yet he says that this man washes his clothes, not his body as well. I believe this is because, by gathering those ashes and laying them in a clean place, if these things are understood spiritually, he wants us to understand that the man had already been cleansed within. So Cornelius, hearing and believing what Peter had preached, was so cleansed that he received the gift of the Holy Spirit, together with his household who were present, before visible baptism. Yet even so the visible sacrament could not be despised, so that, being washed outwardly too, he might in a certain way wash his clothes. And it shall be, he says, for the children of Israel and for the proselytes who are added a perpetual statute. What does this show but that the baptism of Christ, which the water of sprinkling signified, would benefit both Jews and Gentiles—that is, the children of Israel and the proselytes, as the natural branches and the wild olive grafted into the richness of the root? And who would not be struck by the fact that, after the washing, it is said of each of them: and he shall be unclean until evening? This is said not only here but in all, or nearly all, such cleansings. I do not know whether anything else can be understood here except that every person, even after the fullest remission of sins, by remaining in this life contracts something that makes him unclean until the end of that same life, when his day, so to speak, is brought to a close, which is what evening signifies.

Then the Scripture begins to tell, and sets out in order, how people who have become unclean are to be purified by that water of sprinkling. Whoever touches a dead body, it says, every human soul, shall be unclean seven days; he shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh day and shall be clean. Here too I see nothing else to be understood but that contact with a dead body is a person's iniquity. The uncleanness of seven days, I think, is spoken of on account of soul and body: the soul in the number three, the body in the number four. Why this is so would take a long time to discuss. In keeping with this, I think, it was said through the prophet: For three ungodly deeds and for four I will not turn away. He then adds: But if he is not purified on the third day and on the seventh day, he shall not be clean. Everyone who touches a dead body, of any human soul, if he dies and has not been purified—that is, if, having touched a dead body, he dies before he has been purified—defiles the tabernacle of the Lord: that soul shall be cut off from Israel. It should be noted that it is very hard to find anything in these books written more plainly about the life of the soul after death. Here, then, when he says that "if he dies before purification, uncleanness remains in him and that soul is cut off from Israel," that is, from the fellowship of the people of God, what else does he want us to understand but that punishment remains for the soul even after death, if while it lives it has not been cleansed by this sacrament, which prefigures the baptism of Christ? Because the water of sprinkling, he says, was not sprinkled around upon him, he is unclean; his uncleanness is still in him. "Still" means even after death. As for what he said above, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord, he certainly said it with respect to what lies in the man's own power, just as the apostle says: Do not quench the Spirit, although the Spirit cannot be quenched. For if he had meant us to understand that the tabernacle was actually made unclean by this, he would surely have commanded that it be cleansed.

Afterward he commands that those who have become unclean from the dead—that is, from dead works, which are all iniquities—be cleansed in this way. And for the unclean person, he says, they shall take some of the ashes of that burnt purification and pour living water over it—that is, over those ashes—in a vessel; and a clean man, taking hyssop and dipping it in the water, shall sprinkle it around upon the house and upon the vessels and upon the persons, as many as are there, and upon the one who touched a human bone or someone slain or a dead body or a tomb; and the clean man shall sprinkle the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day, and he shall be purified on the seventh day and shall wash his clothes and wash himself in water and shall be unclean until evening. The water of sprinkling is one thing, and the water in which he will wash his clothes is certainly another. And he shall wash himself in water: this water, I think, is to be understood as spiritual by way of signification, not literally. For without doubt it was visible, like all those shadows of things to come. Accordingly, whoever is rightly washed in the sacrament of baptism, which that water of sprinkling prefigured, is also cleansed spiritually, that is, invisibly, both in flesh and in soul, so that he may be clean in both body and spirit. As for his saying that the water of sprinkling is sprinkled with hyssop, the plant we said above signifies faith, what else comes to mind but what is written: cleansing their hearts by faith? For baptism is of no benefit if faith is lacking. He said that this is done by a clean man, which signifies the ministers who act in the person of their Lord, who is truly the clean man. For of these ministers he says in what follows: And the one who sprinkles the water of sprinkling shall wash his clothes—that is, he will observe this in body as well—and the one who touches the water of sprinkling shall be unclean until evening. And whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean; and the soul that touches it shall be unclean until evening. I have already said above what "until evening" seems to me to signify.

"Whoever in the open field touches one wounded or dead, or a human bone, or a tomb." One may ask what is meant by "wounded or dead". If Scripture meant "wounded" to be understood as one thing and "dead" as another, we must take care not to suppose that even someone who touched a wounded man who was still alive would be unclean, which is plainly absurd. But since the dead can also have been wounded, it is understood to have distinguished between the dead themselves, so that we take "wounded" to mean wounded and dead, that is, killed by a wound, and "dead" to mean dead without a wound.

The apostle Paul explained what it meant that water was drawn out of the rock, where he says: "And all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." So what is signified is the spiritual grace flowing from Christ, by which inner thirst would be watered. And the fact that the rock is struck with a rod prefigures the cross of Christ: it was when the wood came to the rock that this grace flowed out. And that it is struck twice signifies the cross more clearly still, for the cross is two pieces of wood.

Of the water that flowed from the rock it is said: "This is the water of contradiction, because the children of Israel railed before the Lord, and he was sanctified among them." First they railed, when they spoke against the Lord's kindness in bringing them out of Egypt; and afterwards he was sanctified among them, when his holiness was declared by that miracle of the flowing water. Or perhaps it pointed to two kinds of people, those who speak against the grace of Christ and those who receive the grace of Christ, so that for the former it is water of contradiction and for the latter water of sanctification? For of the Lord himself we read in the Gospel: "and for a sign that will be spoken against."

Among the messages Moses sends to the king of Edom he says, among other things: "Nor will we drink water from your cistern." This is to be understood as "for free", that is, "we will not drink without paying". He makes this clear afterwards when he says: "But if I and my livestock drink of your water, I will give you the price."
"We will not turn aside to the right hand or to the left": it is said in the plural, meaning into the parts that are on the right or the parts that are on the left.

"You shall not enter the land that I have given the children of Israel as a possession, because you provoked me at the water of reviling." The water he called above the water of contradiction he here calls the water of reviling: for the Greek does not say antilogia (contradiction) but loidoria (reviling).

"And Israel vowed a vow to the Lord and said: If you deliver this people into my hands subdued"—that is, if by delivering them to me you subdue them—"I will anathematize them and their cities." Here we must consider how "I will anathematize" is used: it is something vowed, and yet it stands for a curse, as it is said of this people. Hence the saying: "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be anathema." From this comes the common use of the word "devoting"; for hardly anyone speaks of devoting someone except when cursing.

"And he anathematized them and their cities, and the name of that place was called Anathema." From this it has come about that an anathema is taken to be something detestable and abominable. For when the victor carried off nothing from there for his own use, but vowed the whole of it to pay the penalty, that was to anathematize, which is commonly called "devoting". But the origin of this word is in the Greek language, from those things which, having been vowed and paid, that is, promised and rendered, were set up on high in temples: apo tou ano tithenai, that is, "to set up on high", whether by fixing or by hanging.

In the account of the journey of the children of Israel, as they moved and pitched their camp, it is written among other things: "And from there they encamped beyond the Arnon, in Ermon, which projects from the borders of the Amorites. For the Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorite. That is why it is said in the book: The war of the Lord set Zoob ablaze, and the torrents of the Arnon; and he appointed the torrents to inhabit Er." In what book this was written it does not mention, nor is there any such among those books of divine Scripture that we call canonical. From things like this, those who try to slip apocryphal books into the ears of the unwary and the curious find their openings, in order to win people over to fabulous impieties. But here it says "written in the book"; it does not say in the holy book of which prophet or patriarch. Nor should it be denied that there were already books, whether of the Chaldeans, from whom Abraham came out, or of the Egyptians, among whom Moses had learned all their wisdom, or of any other nation, in one of which this could have been written; yet that book is not for that reason to be taken up among the Scriptures commended by divine authority. Neither is that Cretan prophet whom the apostle mentions, nor the Greek writers, whether philosophers or poets, whom the same apostle, speaking to the Athenians, affirms to have said something truly great and truthfully expressed: "For in him we live and move and have our being." For divine authority may take testimony to whatever truth it finds from wherever it wishes; but it does not for that reason confirm that everything written there is to be accepted. Why this was mentioned in this place, however, is not plainly evident; unless perhaps the boundaries there between the two nations were established by a war, and the people of that region, because of its greatness, called the war "the war of the Lord", so that it was written in some book of theirs: "The war of the Lord set Zoob ablaze", either because that city was burned in that same war or because it was set ablaze, that is, roused, to fight; or else something else lies hidden in the obscurity of this passage.

"This is the well of which the Lord said to Moses: Gather the people, and I will give them water to drink." This is recorded as though we read somewhere above that the Lord said this to Moses; but since it is found nowhere, we must understand here that the people, who were complaining of the drought, drank there too.

"And Israel struck him with the edge of the sword, and they took possession of his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, as far as the children of Ammon, for Jazer is the border of the children of Ammon. And Israel took all these cities, and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon." Here, certainly, Israel took possession of the cities of the Amorites that it had overcome in war, because it did not anathematize them; for if it had anathematized them, it would not have been permitted to possess them or to appropriate any of the spoil from them for its own use. It should indeed be noted how just wars were waged. A harmless passage was being refused, which by the most equitable law of human society ought to have been open. But now, so that God might fulfil his promises, he helped the Israelites here, to whom the land of the Amorites was to be given. For when Edom likewise denied them passage, the Israelites did not fight with that nation, that is, the sons of Jacob with the sons of Esau, two brothers and twins, because he had not promised that land to the Israelites; instead they turned aside from them.

"Therefore the riddlers will say: Come to Heshbon," and so on. Who these riddlers (aenigmatistae) are is not apparent, because the word is not in the usage of our literature, and in the divine Scriptures themselves this name is found hardly anywhere else. But since they seem to be reciting a kind of song, in which they sang of the war waged between the Amorites and the Moabites, in which Sihon king of the Amorites defeated the Moabites, it is not implausibly thought that those whom we call poets were then called riddlers, because it is the custom and licence of poets to mix into their songs riddles of fables, by which they are understood to signify something. For they would not be riddles unless there were figurative speech in them, which when unravelled would lead to the meaning hidden in the riddle.

Scripture says that after Israel defeated the Amorites and took possession of all their cities, Balak king of the Moabites sent envoys to hire Balaam, so that Israel might be cursed by him. This shows clearly enough that not all the Moabites came under the rule of Sihon king of the Amorites when he defeated them in war, since the nation of the Moabites remained until the time when Balak reigned as king of Moab. As for Moab saying to the elders of Midian, that is, the Moabites to the elders of the Midianites, "Now this assembly will lick up all who are around us," they were not one nation; rather, neighbours said to neighbours that they had equally to be on their guard. For Moab was the son of Lot by one of his daughters, whereas Midian was the son of Abraham by Keturah. So they were not one nation but two, neighbouring and bordering on each other.

What does it mean that it is written, "and divinations in their hands," when it was speaking of those whom Balak had sent to hire Balaam to curse Israel? Were they themselves practising divination? Or were they bringing something that Balaam could use in order to divine, such as things to be burned in sacrifices or expended in some other way, and so they are called divinations because by means of them he could divine? Or does it mean something else? For it is obscurely expressed. It should certainly be noted that "God came to Balaam and said to him: Who are these men with you?" and so on. Nor is it said whether this happened in a dream, though it is clear enough that it happened during the night, since Scripture then says: "And Balaam rose in the morning." For one may be troubled as to how God spoke with a thoroughly wicked man; and even if it were certain that this happened in a dream, the question would not on that account vanish, because of the very unworthiness of it. So too the Lord Jesus Christ says of that rich man who was planning to tear down his old storehouses and fill larger new ones: "God said to him: Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" So let no one boast that God speaks to him in the way he knows such people must be spoken to, since this can happen even to the reprobate; for even when he speaks through an angel, it is he himself who speaks.

When the more honourable messengers were sent to him a second time, Balaam said: "If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not transgress the word of the Lord God to do it, small or great, in my mind." In this there is no sin whatever; but what follows is not without grave sin. For having once heard what the Lord had told him—"You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people, for they are blessed"—he ought already to have stood firm, and not given them any hope that the Lord, as if he were Balaam himself, swayed by gifts and honours, could change his decision against his own people, whom he had said were blessed. But he showed himself overcome by greed when he wanted the Lord to speak to him again about a matter on which he already knew his will. For what need was there to add what follows: "And now, you too stay here this night, and I will know what more the Lord will say to me"? Accordingly the Lord, seeing his greed captured and conquered by gifts, allowed him to go, so that he might check his avarice by means of the beast he rode, confounding that madness by the very fact that the ass did not dare to transgress the Lord's prohibition given through the angel, which he, out of greed, was trying to transgress, though he kept that same greed down through fear. For "God came to Balaam by night and said to him: If the men have come to call you, rise and follow them; but whatever word I speak to you, that you shall do. And Balaam rose in the morning, saddled his ass, and went off with the princes of Moab." Why did he not consult God again after this permission, when after that prohibition he thought he should consult him again, unless because his malignant greed was showing, even though it was held down by fear of the Lord? Then Scripture goes on: "And God was angry with indignation because he went; and the angel of God rose up so as not to let him go on the way," and the rest that follows, until the ass spoke. Nothing here seems more astonishing than that he was not terrified when the ass spoke, but, as if accustomed to such prodigies, answered it besides with his anger unabated. After that the angel too speaks to him, rebuking him and condemning his journey; and at the sight of him he was indeed terrified and bowed down. Then he was allowed to go, so that a most glorious prophecy might now be uttered through him. For he was not at all allowed to say what he wanted, but what he was compelled to say by the power of the Spirit. And he himself remained reprobate; for holy Scripture later spoke of him in such a way that certain blameworthy and reprobate people were said to have followed his way: "Following," it says, "the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of iniquity."

Of the angel who spoke to Balaam on the way, at the sight of whom his ass did not dare to go on, Scripture speaks thus: "And God was angry with indignation because he went; and the angel of God rose up to differre him on the way." Here it should first be noted how, because God was angry, it said, "and the angel of God rose up". It did not insert that the angry God sent an angel, but signified, as it were, the angry God in the angel, since the truth and justice of God made the angel angry. For the words "rose up" are surely to be understood of agitation. Next, where it says "to differre him on the way", the Greek has diabalein, and the angel himself says the same in what follows: "And behold, I came out for your dilatio," where the Greek has diabolen. There perhaps "accusation" is the more fitting meaning, so that here "to differre him on the way" may be taken as "to accuse him". Hence too the devil is believed to have been so named, as though in Latin he should be called "accuser"; not because no one can also accuse well and rightly, but because the devil loves to accuse, driven of course by the goads of envy, as testimony is borne of him in the Apocalypse. This word is also used in comedy, which leaves no doubt that it is Latin, with the same meaning or at least a close one, where it is said of a father angry with his son: "He hopes he has found a speech with which to differre you." Here "differat" is usually understood as "carry you this way and that in a storm of words", as if to say "tear you apart and scatter you": which is precisely what he seemed about to do by accusing. But even if we understand "to differre him on the way" to mean that the angel delayed his haste by holding him back, so as both to show him and to tell him what was needed, the use of this word in that sense too is not absurd.

"And when the ass saw the angel of God standing against her in the way, with his sword drawn in his hand, the ass turned aside from the way and went into the field." This field was still outside the walls of the vineyards. "And he struck the ass with his rod to set her right on the way. And the angel of God stood in the furrows of the vineyards, with a wall on this side and a wall on that." It is rightly asked, if the walls on either side had the road between them, as usually happens, how the angel standing there is said to have stood in the furrows of the vineyards; for there could not have been furrows of vineyards in the road between the walls. But the order of the words is: "to set her right on the way, with a wall on this side and a wall on that." So it was on this road that Balaam wanted to set the ass right, so that she would walk between the walls. Inserted in between is: "And the angel of God stood in the furrows of the vineyards," that is, in one of the vineyards that had the road between them. "And when the ass saw the angel of God, she pressed herself against the wall," that is, against the wall of the vineyard in which the angel was not, since he was on the other side in the furrows of the vineyards. "And she crushed Balaam's foot against the wall, and he went on beating her. And the angel of God went further and stood in a narrow place"—no longer in the furrows of the vineyards but between the walls themselves, that is, on the road—"where there was no turning aside to the right or to the left. And when the ass saw the angel of God, she lay down under Balaam." For though beaten, she would not go back, and she did not press against the wall, since she was not frightened from the other side, but the angel was in the middle of the road in the narrow place; so it remained for her to lie down. "And Balaam was angry and struck the ass with his rod. And God opened the mouth of the ass, and she said to Balaam: What have I done to you, that you have struck me this third time? And Balaam said to the ass: Because you have mocked me; and if I had a sword in my hand, I would already have run you through." Clearly this man was carried away by such greed that he was not frightened even by the miracle of so great a prodigy, and answered as if speaking to a human being, when God had certainly not changed the ass's soul into a rational nature, but had made what pleased him sound from her in order to restrain the man's madness; perhaps prefiguring that God would choose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, for the sake of that spiritual and true Israel, that is, the children of the promise.

"And the Spirit of God was made upon him," that is, upon Balaam. The Spirit of God was not made, as though the Spirit of God were something made; but "was made upon him" means it came about that he was upon him. So too: "He who comes after me was made before me," that is, it came about that he was before me, that he was preferred to me, "for he was," it says, "before me." Likewise: "The Lord was made my helper"; for the Lord is not something made, but it came about that he helped me. And: "The Lord was made a refuge for the poor," that is, it came about that the poor took refuge in him. And: "The hand of the Lord was made upon me," that is, it came about that it was upon me. And many such expressions are found in the Scriptures.

"And the Lord said to Moses: Take the leaders of the people and display them to the Lord against the sun, and the anger of the Lord's indignation will be turned away from Israel." God, angered by Israel's fornications, both carnal and spiritual—for they had both lain shamelessly with the daughters of Moab and been consecrated to idols—said this to Moses: that he should display the leaders of the people to the Lord against the sun. By this phrase they are understood to have been ordered to be crucified, so that "display them to the Lord against the sun" means openly, in full view of this daylight. For the Greek says paradeigmatison, which could be rendered "make examples of them", since paradeigma means an example. Besides the Seventy translators, Aquila is reported to have said "fasten", or rather "fasten up high", that is, anapexon, while Symmachus used the plainer word "hang". It is surely remarkable that Scripture failed to relate whether this was carried out according to the Lord's command. I do not see how it could have been disregarded, or, if it was disregarded, disregarded with impunity. But if it was done and passed over in silence, why does Scripture testify that the Lord was appeased, and the plague ceased, because Phinehas son of Eleazar ran the adulterers through? As if, once the leaders had been crucified as the Lord had commanded, his indignation still persisted and seemed to need appeasing in another way, when undoubtedly what the Lord had foretold and promised could not be false, saying: "Take the leaders of the people and display them to the Lord against the sun, and the anger of the Lord's indignation will be turned away from Israel." So if it had been done, who would doubt that the Lord's anger had been turned away from Israel? What need was there, then, for Phinehas still to punish the adulterers in this way to appease God, and for Scripture to testify of him that by this means he appeased the Lord? Unless perhaps we understand that while Moses was arranging to carry out what he had commanded about the leaders of the people, he also wanted to punish such crimes and sacrilegious audacity according to the law, by ordering each man to kill his neighbour who had been wickedly consecrated to foreign gods; and that meanwhile Phinehas also did that deed, and so, the Lord's anger now being appeased, there was no need for the leaders of the people to be crucified. This severity, suited to that time, shows clearly enough to the faith of the wise how great an evil fornication and idolatry are.

The Lord gives the same cause for the death of Moses as for that of his brother. For he had earlier foretold this to both of them: that they would not enter the land of promise with the people of God, because they did not sanctify him before the people at the water of contradiction; that is, because they doubted his gift, that water could flow from the rock, as we explained at that very passage of Scripture. The mystery of this matter is given us to understand: that neither the priesthood that was instituted first, whose person Aaron bore, nor the law itself, whose person Moses bore, leads the people of God into the land of the eternal inheritance, but Jesus, that is, Joshua, in whom there was a type of the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, grace through faith. And Aaron indeed died before Israel entered any part of the land of promise; but while Moses was still alive the land of the Amorites was taken and possessed, though he was not allowed to cross the Jordan with them. For in some part the law is observed in the Christian faith: there are in it precepts that we Christians are commanded to observe even today. But that priesthood and its sacrifices hold no part in the Christian faith today, except that they were performed and completed as shadows of things to come. But when it is said to both brothers, that is, Aaron and Moses, that they are to be gathered to their people, it is clear that the wrath of God that separates people from the peace of the holy eternal fellowship was not upon them. From this it is evident that not only their offices but their deaths too were signs of things to come, not punishments of God's indignation.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take to yourself Joshua the son of Nun, a man who has the Spirit in himself, and lay your hands upon him; and you shall set him before Eleazar the priest, and you shall give him his charge in the sight of the whole congregation, and so on. It should be noted that although Joshua the son of Nun already had the Spirit in himself, as Scripture testifies (and what are we to understand here but the Holy Spirit? For Scripture would not say this of the human spirit, since there was no one who did not have that), Moses was nevertheless commanded to lay his hands on him. This was so that no one, however outstanding in grace, should dare to refuse the sacraments of consecration.

What does it mean that when God was giving Moses instructions about Joshua the son of Nun, he said among other things: And you shall give of your glory upon him? The Greek idiom has τῆς δόξης, which amounts to saying "of the glory," that is, τῆς δόξης. Some Latin translators, however, have rendered it: you shall give your glory, not: of your glory. But even if the text did say "your glory," that would not mean Moses was no longer going to have it; nor, because it says "of the glory," is what he had thereby diminished. It should be understood as though it said: You shall make him a sharer in your glory. Things of this kind are not diminished as if divided into portions; they belong wholly to all, and wholly to each one who shares in them.

Any man who vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath, or makes a binding pledge concerning his soul, shall not profane his word: whatever comes out of his mouth he shall do. This does not apply to every oath, but to the case where someone vows concerning his soul to abstain from some thing which the law permitted him to use, but which he makes unlawful for himself by his vow.

But if a woman vows a vow to the Lord or makes a binding pledge in her father's house in her youth, and her father hears her vows and the pledges she has made against her soul, and her father keeps silent, then all her vows shall stand, and all the pledges she has made against her soul shall remain binding on her. But if her father firmly refuses them on whatever day he hears all her vows and the pledges she has made against her soul, they shall not stand; and the Lord will cleanse her, because her father refused. Since the passage speaks of a woman who is still in her youth in her father's house, it is right to ask here about the vow of virginity as well; for it is very well known that in Scripture even virgins are commonly called women. And the apostle too seems to be speaking of a father when he says: let him keep his virgin, and: let him give his virgin in marriage, and so on. Some have understood "his virgin" there to mean "his virginity"; yet they cannot show any similar expression in the Scriptures, since it is a most unusual one. As for the words against her soul, they should not be taken to mean that such vows harm the soul; rather, "against the soul" means against the pleasures of the animal life, just as, in giving the command about fasting earlier, it says: and you shall afflict your souls.

As for the words: and the Lord will cleanse her, because her father refused, by "will cleanse" it means "will absolve her of the guilt of an unfulfilled vow." So too in many places it says: and the priest shall cleanse him, that is, he shall regard him as clean, he shall judge him clean; and likewise the saying: you shall not cleanse the guilty with a cleansing, that is: you shall not declare clean one who is unclean.

But if she becomes a man's wife, and her vows are upon her according to the utterance of her lips, all that she has pledged against her soul, and her husband hears and keeps silent toward her on whatever day he hears, then all her vows shall stand, and her pledges that she has made against her soul shall stand. But if her husband firmly refuses them on whatever day he hears, none of her vows and pledges that she has made against her soul shall remain, since her husband has refused them on her behalf, and the Lord will cleanse her. The law did not want a woman, whether under her father before she marries or under her husband once married, to vow anything to God against her soul (that is, by abstaining from things that are lawful and permitted) in such a way that the woman's authority should prevail in those vows; rather, the man's authority prevails. So if her father had already allowed her to fulfill her vows while she was still unmarried, but she married before fulfilling them, and her husband, on learning of this, did not approve, she should not fulfill them and is entirely without sin, because the Lord will cleanse her, as it says, that is, he will judge her clean. Nor should this be thought to be done against God, since God himself commanded it and willed it.

Next he deals with widows and women cast off by their husbands, that is, women not placed under the authority of a husband or of a father, and he says that they are free to fulfil their vows, in this way: "And the vow," he says, "of a widow and of a woman put away, whatever she has vowed against her soul, shall stand for her." Then he speaks of a married woman, if she makes some such vow when already settled in her husband's house. For earlier he had spoken of the woman who had vowed in her father's house and had married before she fulfilled the vow. Of this woman, then, who made her vow in her husband's house, he speaks as follows: "But if in her husband's house there is her vow, or a binding pledge against her soul with an oath, and her husband has heard it and kept silent toward her and has not refused her, then all her vows shall stand, and all her pledges by which she has bound herself against her soul shall stand against her. But if her husband utterly annuls them on whatever day he hears them, then whatever has gone out of her lips concerning her vows and concerning the pledges against her soul shall not stand for her; her husband has annulled them, and the Lord will cleanse her. Every vow and every oath of a bond to afflict the soul, her husband shall confirm for her, and her husband shall annul. But if he keeps utterly silent toward her from day to day, then he confirms for her all her vows, and the pledges upon her he confirms for her, because he kept silent toward her on the day he heard. But if her husband utterly annuls them after the day on which he heard, then he shall bear his sin."

It is plain that the law wanted the woman to be under her husband in such a way that none of the vows she made for the sake of abstinence should be fulfilled by her unless her husband authorized them by giving permission. For although the law wished it to count as the husband's sin if he first permitted and afterward forbade, even here it did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed on the ground that her husband had first permitted her. It said the sin was the husband's, because he refused what he had earlier granted; yet not even on this ground did it give the woman leave to disregard her husband if, having first granted it, he afterward forbade it.

It is rightly asked whether these provisions also apply to vows of continence and of abstinence from intercourse, or whether perhaps only things concerning food and drink are to be understood as vowed "against the soul." This seems also to be indicated where the Lord says, "Is not the soul more than food?" And when fasting is commanded, it is commanded thus: "You shall afflict your souls." I do not know whether anywhere one can read that a vow concerning abstinence from intercourse is called a vow "against the soul"—especially since here the law gives authority to the husband, not to the wife who is subject to the husband, so that a wife's vows are to be fulfilled if the husband approves, but are not owed if he refuses. Yet the apostle, when he spoke of intercourse between married people, did not there give the husband greater authority than the wife, but said: "Let the husband render to his wife what is due, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does." Since, then, he wished the authority of both to be equal in this matter, I think he is suggesting to us that this rule about having or not having intercourse does not belong among those vows in which husband and wife do not have equal authority, but in which the husband's authority is greater and almost his alone.
