For the law does not say that a husband ought not to fulfil his vows if his wife forbids, but that the wife ought not, if her husband forbids. Hence it does not seem to me that, among vows, pledges and obligations of this kind made "against the soul," we ought also to include the agreements that husband and wife have made between themselves about having intercourse or abstaining from it.

Next, since these too are called "ordinances," and we remember that in the other ordinances recorded under that name in Exodus many things are commanded that cannot be taken literally and are not observed in the New Testament—such as piercing a slave's ear, and anything of that kind—it is not absurd to understand that something is said figuratively here as well. Since there are many ceremonial abstinences that are irrational and sometimes even hostile to the truth, perhaps he wished it to be understood here that they are valid only when they are rational, that is, when reason approves them—reason, which, standing in the husband's place, ought to govern every movement of the soul, whether in desiring or in abstaining. Thus if a thing is decided by mind and reason, it should be done; but if it is disapproved by the counsel of reason, it should not be done. And if reason afterward disapproves what it had earlier rightly decided should be done, let that be a sin of its counsel; yet even so, that movement should consent to nothing but reason.

What does this mean: "And Moses sent them, a thousand from a tribe and a thousand from a tribe, with their strength"? Does he want "their strength" to be understood as "their leaders"? Or as strength given them by the Lord, or obtained through Moses himself? Or rather does he call "their strength" the things by which their strength was to be sustained?

A question may be raised as to how, when the Israelites defeated the Midianites, Scripture says that Balaam was killed—Balaam, who had been hired to curse the people of Israel. For earlier, when he was compelled to bless, Scripture had concluded that same episode by saying: "And Balaam rose and went away and returned to his place; and Balak went away to himself." If, then, Balaam had returned to his place, how was he killed here, since he had come from so far away, that is, from Mesopotamia? Perhaps he went back to Balak, and Scripture did not say so? Yet he can also be understood to have returned to his place in the sense that, from the place where he was offering sacrifices, he returned to the place from which he had gone out there, that is, where he had lodging as a stranger. For it does not say "to his house" or "to his country," but "to his place." And every stranger, too, has his place where he lives for a time. But of Balak himself, who had hired him, it does not say "to his place," but "to himself," that is, to where he lived as ruler. So "to his place" could be said both of a ruler and of a stranger; but I do not see how "to himself" could be said of a stranger when he had come back to his lodging.

"And they took as plunder the women of Midian and their goods and their cattle and all that they possessed, and they plundered their strength." Having already mentioned the women, the goods, the cattle and all that they possessed, why did he then add, "and they plundered their strength"? This must surely be understood as the same strength of which it was said above that he sent a thousand from each tribe "with their strength." Perhaps the food by which they were sustained was called their strength, since when it is supplied strength is at hand, and when it is withdrawn strength fails? Hence God, threatening through the prophet, says: "I will take away the strength of bread and the strength of water." So Moses had sent those thousands with provisions, which is what "with their strength" means; and these men, having conquered the Midianites, had also plundered this from them among their other possessions.

"Why have you kept every female alive? For these were, according to the word of Balaam, the means of making the children of Israel fall away and despise the word of the Lord on account of Peor." Scripture did not say when Balaam gave this wicked counsel—that women should be set before them as an enticement, through whom they would commit fornication not only bodily but also spiritually, by worshipping an idol—and yet it is evident that it happened, since it is mentioned here. In the same way, then, Balaam himself, who had already gone to his place, could also have come back, so that we need not understand his place to be a stranger's lodging, even though Scripture is silent about this.

What does this mean: "And the cities shall be refuges for you from the avenger of blood, and the one who has killed shall not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment"? He is speaking of those who killed unintentionally, and elsewhere he says that each person who takes refuge in such a case goes out free from the city to which he had fled when the high priest has died. How then does he say here, "and the one who has killed shall not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment," unless it is because he is judged precisely so that he may then be permitted to stay in the city of refuge, if it has been made clear in the judgment that he killed unintentionally?

What does this mean: "The avenger of blood shall himself kill the murderer; when he meets him, he shall kill him"? To those who misunderstand it, it sounds as if the avenger of his kinsman's death had been given license to kill the killer anywhere and without trial. But he wanted it understood thus: according to what was said above, the one who has killed should flee to one of the cities of refuge until he stands trial, so that he is not found and killed by the kinsman beforehand; because, even if he killed unintentionally, if he is found outside those cities he is killed. But when he has stood trial in one of those cities and has been judged a murderer, he is not permitted to stay in any of the cities to which flight is allowed; then at last, once he has been judged, the kinsman may kill him wherever he is found. For there is no need for him to be brought to trial, since he has already been judged a murderer and for that reason has been expelled from those cities.
BOOK FIVE. QUESTIONS ON DEUTERONOMY.

QUESTION 1. Moses recalls that, when the people feared the enemies inhabiting the land into which they were to be brought, he said to them: "Do not be alarmed or afraid of them; the Lord your God, who goes before your face, will himself fight them together with you." This shows clearly enough that God is a helper in such a way that human beings also do something.

"And Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through his land, because the Lord our God had hardened his spirit and strengthened his heart, so that he might be delivered into your hands, as on this day." In saying this as he addresses the people, Moses recalls something like what was said in Exodus, "I have hardened Pharaoh's heart," and what we read in the Psalms: "He turned their heart to hate his people." Nor is the reason for this hardening left unstated here, for it says, "so that he might be delivered into your hands, as on this day," that is, so that he might be conquered by you. That would not have happened unless he resisted; and he would not have resisted except with a hardened heart. If we ask about the justice of this, the judgments of God are unsearchable; but there is no injustice with God. It should certainly be noted that a heart can be said to be "strengthened" in evil as well.

"But Og king of Bashan was left over from the Rephaim." Those who know Hebrew say that this name, Rephaim, signifies giants in the Hebrew language. Hence what most manuscripts render as "was left behind by the Rephaim" is certainly put more plainly as "was left over," so that he is understood to have survived from among them; and accordingly the length and breadth of his iron bed is then mentioned, to emphasize his size.

"Do not act wickedly and make for yourselves a carved likeness, any image." People often ask what the difference is between a likeness and an image. But here I do not see what difference he intended, unless either he meant one thing by these two words, or he called something a likeness if, for example, a statue or figure is made having a human form but not reproducing the features of any particular person, as painters or sculptors do when they look at those whom they paint or model—for no one would doubt that this latter is called an image. On this distinction every image is also a likeness, but not every likeness is also an image. So if twins resemble each other, either can be called a likeness of the other, but not an image. But if a son resembles his father, he is rightly called an image too, so that the father is the prototype from which that image appears to be copied. Some images are of the same substance, as a son is; others are not of the same substance, as a painting is. Hence what is written in Genesis, "God made man in the image of God," is clearly said in such a way that the image that was made is not of the same substance. For if it were of the same substance, it would be said to be not made but begotten. But because he did not add "and likeness," though it had been said above, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," some have thought that likeness is something more than image, reserved for man later, to be restored through the grace of Christ. I wonder, however, whether he did not mention only the image later for this reason: that where there is an image, there is at once a likeness as well. So here too Moses forbids making a likeness and an image, perhaps according to the reasoning we have given. In the Decalogue, however, it is said in general that no likeness should be made, and image is not mentioned. For when no likeness is made, without doubt no image is made either, since if there is an image there is certainly also a likeness; but if a likeness is made, an image is not at once made too. Still, if there is no likeness, it follows that there is no image. Finally, where he forbade both likeness and image, he meant a human figure to be understood, for in that case one can make both a likeness—not of this or that man, but of any man—and an image, that is, of this or that particular man; but when he spoke of cattle and irrational animals, he said only likeness. For who can be found who sets one particular dog, or something of the kind, before himself and paints or models its image while looking at it? Yet with human beings this is extremely common.

And what does it mean when he says, "the likeness of any fish, whatever are in the waters beneath the earth"? Did he want water too to be understood as earth because of its tangible bodily nature, so that accordingly, in what is written, "God made heaven and earth," we should take the waters to be included as well? For Scripture constantly names these two parts in order to mean the whole world, as in "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth," and countless passages of this kind. Or is it said "beneath the earth" because the earth, unless it were above the waters, could certainly not be inhabited by human beings or contain land animals?

"And lest, looking up to heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars and all the adornment of heaven, you go astray and worship them and serve them, which the Lord your God has distributed to all the nations that are under heaven." This is not said as though God had commanded that they be worshipped by the nations and not worshipped only by his own people. Rather, either it is said because God foreknew that the nations would offer worship to these heavenly bodies and yet, foreknowing this, created them, while foreknowing that his own people would be one that did not worship them; or else "distributed" is said so that their use may be understood, the use commended in Genesis, "let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years"—a use which the people of God has in common with all the nations, but not the worship which the other nations give them.

"Do not forget the covenant of the Lord your God, which he made with you, and make for yourselves a carved likeness of anything that the Lord your God has appointed for you." Here certainly, speaking in general terms, he put "likeness" and said nothing of "image," since if no likeness is made, surely no image is made either; for where there is an image there is at once a likeness, though where there is a likeness there is not at once an image.

We must ask how this is meant: "Ask about the former days that were before you, from the day when God created man upon the earth, and from the height of heaven to the height of heaven"—for "ask" is understood. It seems to signify the whole world. But why he says "from the height of heaven to the height of heaven," and not "from the height of the earth to the height of the earth," is not easy to discern. For there is a similar expression in the Gospel too, when the Lord says that his elect will be gathered from the heights of the heavens to their ends. Unless perhaps he wants it understood here that what he commends as unique, done among this people, had never been heard of either among men or among angels; for this is what follows: "whether anything has been done like this great word, whether anything such has been heard; whether a nation has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard and lived." But if it is so, that he is saying this had not been heard of either among men or among angels, what then is that passage in the Gospel, "from the heights of the heavens to their ends," since without doubt the Lord said this when speaking of the final gathering of his elect?

What does this mean: "The Lord your God made a covenant with you at Horeb; not with your fathers did the Lord make this covenant, but with you, all of you who are alive here today. Face to face the Lord spoke with you on the mountain, out of the midst of the fire"? Is it because those who do not enter the land of promise—for they have all died—do not belong to this covenant, namely those whose census was taken then, when men from twenty years of age and upward to fifty, fit for war, were counted? How then did the Lord speak to those who are alive today? Is it because there could have been many then, from twenty years and under, who remembered this well and were exempt from the penalty God laid on those who were counted then, that they should not enter the land of promise? These are surely the ones he addresses: though they were not twenty years old and over when God spoke on the mountain, so as to be counted then, they could nevertheless have been nineteen and under, down to a boyhood age capable of seeing and hearing what was done and said and of retaining it in memory.

But what does it mean when he says, "Face to face the Lord spoke with you," to those whom he had taken particular care to warn just before that they saw no likeness but only heard a voice from the midst of the fire? Did he use these words because of the evidentness of the events and the presence, as it were, of the manifested Godhead, about which no one could have any doubt? If so, what prevents us from understanding in the same way what is said of Moses himself, that the Lord spoke with him face to face, so that he too saw nothing with his eyes except fire? Or is he understood to have seen something more, since it is written that he entered the cloud or thick darkness where God was? But even if he saw something more than they did, it cannot be understood that he saw the substance of God with mortal eyes, as is clear from his own words to God: "If I have found favour before you, show me yourself, that I may see you knowingly." Nor should we suppose that this people to whom Moses was speaking saw God face to face then, when he spoke on the mountain from the midst of the fire, in the way the apostle says we shall see him at the end, where he says: "We see now through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face." And what this is, and how great, he went on to disclose, saying: "Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I have been known." This too must be taken with caution, lest it be thought that man will have as great a knowledge of God as God now has of man. Rather, man's knowledge will be perfect in its own measure, so that nothing further remains to be added to it: just as God now knows man perfectly, but as God knows man, so then man will know God perfectly, but as man knows God. For neither, because it is said, "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect," ought we on that account to hope for equality with the Father, which the only-begotten Word possesses—though there have been some who thought that even this would come to pass, unless perhaps we do not properly understand what they mean.

What does this mean: "And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord," as if the Lord were in a place, namely on the mountain from which they heard the voices? This must be taken in such a way that we do not suspect from it that the substance of God is in any bodily place, since he is wholly everywhere and neither draws near nor withdraws across intervals of space; rather, his manifestations are presented to human senses in no other way than in the creature, which is not what he himself is. Hence the Lord, wishing to draw our minds away from suspicions of this kind, in which God is thought to be contained in some place, said: "The hour will come when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." So Moses said that he stood in between, not between the substance of God and the people by some interval of space, but because it pleased the people to hear the rest of God's words through him, after they had been terribly frightened on hearing, from the midst of the fire, the voice of the Lord speaking the Ten Commandments of the law.

But it is rightly asked how we are to take these words of Deuteronomy, where Moses says: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you were afraid of the fire and did not go up the mountain, saying: I am the Lord your God,” and so on. What follows are now the words of God, those contained in the Decalogue. What, then, is meant by the added word “saying”? If we suppose a hyperbaton, so that the order of the words is “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time to announce to you the words of the Lord, saying: I am the Lord your God,” the statement will not be true. The people did not hear these words through Moses but from the midst of the fire. Because they could not bear this, once they had heard the Decalogue they asked to hear the rest through Moses. It remains, then, that we understand “saying” as standing for “when he said,” so that the sense is: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time to announce to you the words of the Lord, because you were afraid of the fire and did not go up the mountain, when he said: I am the Lord your God.” Here “when the Lord, of course, said” is understood. For it was while the Lord was speaking these words, all of which Moses then goes on to recount from the Decalogue, that the people were afraid of the fire, did not go up the mountain, and asked to hear the words of the Lord through Moses instead.

In Deuteronomy Moses recalls words spoken to him by the people when they no longer wished to hear the voice of God but asked that what God was saying be told to them through him: “Behold, the Lord our God has shown us his glory, and we have heard his voice from the midst of the fire,” and so on. These words are not found in exactly the same form in Exodus, where the events now being repeated were first narrated. From this we should understand, as I have already pointed out several times, that it is not to be counted as a falsehood if the same intention is expressed in other words. This also applies to the words of the evangelists, which the ignorant and the slanderous criticize as contradictory. It would have been no great matter for Moses to look at what he had written in Exodus and repeat it in exactly the same words. He did not, because it was the concern of our holy teachers to impress this very point on learners: that in the words of those who speak they should look for nothing but the intention that the words were framed to express.

What does it mean when Moses says that the Lord said to him about the Hebrew people: “Who will grant that their heart be such in them that they fear me and keep my commandments?” Does he already want it understood here that this benefit is granted by his grace, so that the righteousness of God may be in human beings by faith, and not as if it were their own, coming from the law? He signifies this through the prophet as well, saying: “I will take from them the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh.” This is said with reference to feeling, which flesh has and stone does not, and the word is of course used figuratively. He says the same thing elsewhere: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will accomplish for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a new covenant, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. For this is the covenant that I will make with them: after those days I will put my laws into their heart and write them on their mind, and I will remember their iniquities and their sins no more.” Here he distinguished the new covenant from the old. In the old the law was given on tablets of stone, but in the new it is given on hearts, and this comes about through grace. That is why the apostle too says: “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,” and in another place: “He has made us competent ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit.”

When he says of the Lord, “And you shall swear by his name,” this should not be taken as a command, as though he ordered people to swear. Rather, he forbade swearing by the name of any other god. It is better, however, if in keeping with the gospel you do not swear at all. This is not because a true oath is evil, but so that a readiness to swear does not lead to perjury. Whoever swears can swear falsely as well as truly, but whoever does not swear at all keeps far away from perjury.

“And you shall remember all the way by which the Lord your God led you in the desert, to afflict you and test you and make known what is in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” This states more plainly what is obscured elsewhere by a turn of phrase, where we read: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.” There “to know” is understood to stand for “to make known.” That has now been said clearly: “to test you and make known what is in your heart.” For he does not say “and to know,” though if he had, it would have had to be understood as “make known.”

“And you shall know today that it is not because of your righteous deeds that the Lord your God is giving you this good land to inherit, for you are a stiff-necked people.” Surely these are the people who were spared from perishing in the desert because they knew neither right nor left. And now they are called stiff-necked! So we must recognize that the earlier statement was said as a mystery, not to commend their merits. And in case anyone thinks that these people, who had earlier been deservedly praised, had suddenly become blameworthy, a little later it is said to them: “Remember, do not forget how greatly you provoked the Lord your God in the desert. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you persisted in unbelief toward the Lord.” Some of them may have been like this while others were faithful and good. Even so, the land of promise is not given to those who know neither right nor left in a sense that would mean they had not offended God. Their fathers too, who died and were not allowed to enter that land, are found to have included some good people. That is why the apostle, when he recounts their sins, says not that all of them but that some of them gave offense. This passage of Deuteronomy shows quite clearly that these people were like their parents, by what it goes on to add: “And at Horeb you provoked the Lord.” Surely those who provoked him there were the very ones who, because of the same evil deeds, were not brought into the land of promise.

“At that time the Lord said to me: Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first ones and come up to me on the mountain, and make yourself an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke, and you shall put them in the ark. So I made an ark of wood that does not decay, cut two tablets of stone like the first ones, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my two hands. And he wrote on the tablets, as in the first writing, the ten words which the Lord spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire, and the Lord gave them to me.” It is reasonable to ask how these things can be said in Deuteronomy, where Moses recalls and repeats what happened. In Exodus, where these words and deeds are first narrated, it is written: “And the Lord said to Moses: Write these words for yourself, for in these words I have established a covenant with you and with Israel. And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water, and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.” Since Exodus says that Moses himself wrote the ten words of the law on the tablets, how is it recalled here in Deuteronomy that God wrote those same words on the tablets?

Earlier, when we dealt with that passage of Exodus in passing, we wrote down our view of this difference. The question was why the first tablets, which were broken, are reported to have been written by the finger of God, while the second, which were to remain so long in the ark and the tabernacle, are said to have been written by Moses himself. We said that the two covenants were signified by this difference. In the old covenant the law was presented as the work of God, in which man did nothing, because the law could not be fulfilled through fear. When the work of the law is truly done, it is done out of love, not fear, and this love is the grace of the new covenant. Therefore a man is said to have written the words of God on the second tablets, because a man can do the work of the law through love of righteousness, which he cannot do through fear of punishment.

Now, however, we read in Deuteronomy about the second tablets: “And I cut two tablets of stone like the first ones and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my two hands. And he wrote on the tablets, as in the first writing, the ten words.” He does not say “and I wrote” but “he wrote,” meaning God. This matches the words of God that Moses had reported a little earlier: “Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first ones and come up to me on the mountain, and make yourself an ark of wood. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets.” So a question arises that needs to be examined, since here both sets of tablets, the first and the second, are said to have been written by God, not by man. Yet when we read God's words in Exodus itself, where he commands Moses to cut those same second tablets, we find only that God himself promised to write on them. It is written: “And the Lord said to Moses: Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first ones and come up to me on the mountain. And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.” So, leaving the book of Deuteronomy aside, the book of Exodus by itself raises this question. How could God have said, “And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets,” when a little later we read: “Write these words for yourself, for in these words I have established a covenant with you and with Israel. And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water, and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words”? The first part, “Write these words for yourself, for in these words I have established a covenant with you and with Israel,” may refer back to the earlier matters God was commanding, so that they were to be written not on the two stone tablets but in the book of the law where many things were recorded. Even so, what follows certainly shows clearly enough that Moses himself, not God, wrote these ten words on the tablets: “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water, and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.” The only alternative is that we are compelled, forcibly but by sheer necessity, to take the subject of “And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words” as the Lord rather than Moses, since just before it says: “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord.” Then these ten words would be understood to have been written on the tablets by the Lord, in whose presence Moses spent forty days and forty nights eating no bread and drinking no water, just as he had promised earlier.

If that is so, the difference between the two covenants that we proposed cannot be supported from these words, since both the first and the second tablets were written by God and not by man. Yet one distinction is beyond doubt: God both made the first tablets and wrote on them. At that time Moses was not told, “Cut for yourself two tablets.” Instead we read: “And Moses turned and went down from the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hands. They were tablets of stone written on both their sides, written on this side and on that. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.” Earlier he had already said that those tablets were written by the finger of God: “And as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone written by the finger of God.” In that case, then, the tablets were the work of God and their writing was done by the finger of God. But Moses himself is commanded to cut the second tablets, so that they at least are understood to have been cut by human labor, although God himself wrote on them, as he had promised when he ordered them cut. If we look more carefully, we see that both things are said of the second tablets because God, through his grace, does the work of the law in a person, and that person, receiving by faith the grace of God that belongs to the new covenant, works together with God who helps him. With the first tablets only the work of God is mentioned, because the law is spiritual, and the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good. No human work is mentioned there, because unbelievers do not cooperate with the help of grace. Ignorant of God's righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. So for them the law serves only to condemn, and this is what the breaking of the tablets signifies. Seen this way, we are surely not compelled to adopt a forced interpretation and understand God as the one who wrote where Scripture says: “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights. He ate no bread and drank no water, and he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant.” That passage strongly suggests that Moses was the writer. Rather, God promised earlier that he would write, and Deuteronomy says not only that he promised this but also that he wrote himself, in order to signify what the apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” That is, he works in those who receive grace by faith and do not wish to establish their own righteousness but submit to the righteousness of God, so that they themselves may become the righteousness of God in Christ. In that passage the apostle says both things, that God works and that they themselves work. If they were not working themselves, how could he say to them: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling”? So he works, and we work with him. He does not take away the free choice of a good will but helps it.

At that time the Lord set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, to stand before the Lord, to minister and to pray in his name, to this day. For this reason the Levites have no portion and inheritance with their brothers; the Lord himself is their portion, as he told them. If this tribe did not signify the whole royal priesthood that belongs to the new covenant, a man who was not from that tribe would never have dared to say, "The Lord is my portion," and in another psalm, "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance."

What does Moses mean when, commending the words of the Lord, he commands, "And you shall write them on the thresholds of your houses and of your gates"? No Israelite is recorded or read to have done this literally, nor could anyone do it, unless perhaps he divided the words among many parts of his house. Or is this an exaggerated way of commending them, as many things are said?

We must ask how he can command that the tithes of all produce and the firstlings of the flocks be eaten only in the city where the temple will be, when he has commanded in the law that they be given to the Levites.

"But if a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder he spoke of to you comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us go and serve other gods, whom you do not know,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or the dream of that dreamer, for the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul." Some Latin translators did not render this "to know whether you love" but "so that he may know whether you love." Although the meaning seems the same, the phrase "to know" can more easily be referred to the people themselves, so that we take "he tests you to know" as if it said, "by testing you he makes you know." Here he clearly meant us to understand that even when things foretold by diviners who do not speak according to God come to pass, this is no reason for doing what they command or worshiping what they worship. God does not show that these things happen outside his power; rather, as though someone were asking why he permits them, he explains the reason for the test: to bring to light their love, whether they have it toward their God. And it is to be brought to light for them rather than for him, who knows all things before they happen.

"After three years you shall bring out the whole tithe of your produce; in that year you shall lay it up in your cities, and the Levite shall come, because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the stranger and the orphan and the widow who are in your cities, and they shall eat and be filled, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works that you do." He did not say that the giver himself should eat of this tithe with his household; and so he commanded it to be spent on the Levites, strangers, orphans and widows. But the point is stated obscurely, since this tithe is not distinguished from the one he wished to be eaten with the Levites in the place the Lord would choose for his temple. In the translation made from the Hebrew, however, we find this distinguished more plainly. It says: "In the third year you shall set aside another tithe of everything that grows for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates; and the Levite, who has no other portion or possession with you, shall come, and the foreigner and the orphan and the widow who are within your gates, and they shall eat and be filled, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do." First, the very words "in the third year" are plainer, for they are understood to mean "with one year intervening." In the Septuagint, however, since it says "after three years," it is uncertain whether he meant three years to intervene, so that it would happen every fifth year. Next, when it says, "you shall set aside another tithe," it shows clearly that the tithe he wanted the offerer himself to eat with his household and the Levites in the place the Lord would choose is a separate one. For he commanded him to lay up this other tithe within his own gates, not to bring it to the place where the Lord willed to be called upon. "And the Levite shall come," it says, "who has no portion or possession with you, and the foreigner and the orphan and the widow who are within your gates, and they shall eat." From this it is certainly and plainly true that God did not wish this tithe to be shared between the offerer and those on whom it was to be spent; he commanded that it be paid out only to those who had nothing else, and among them he put the Levite first. "After seven years you shall make a release." This certainly makes clear how he also said above, "after three years." For here too he did not mean seven years to intervene; he commanded the release to take place in the seventh year, as a kind of sabbath of years.

"Take heed to yourself, lest a hidden word, an iniquity, arise in your heart, saying, 'The seventh year, the year of release, is approaching,' and your eye be evil toward your needy brother and you give him nothing; and he will cry out against you to the Lord, and it will be a great sin in you." He splendidly called this a hidden word, because no one who could think it would dare say it aloud: that one should not lend to a person in need because the year of release is approaching. For God out of mercy commanded both things: that a loan be made whenever anyone is in need, and that it be remitted in the year of release. How then will someone mercifully remit in the year when remission is due, if he cruelly thinks he should not give at the time when giving is due?

"If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh you shall let him go free from you." He did not mean these purchased slaves to be released in the year of release, which everyone was to observe every seventh year, but in the seventh year after their purchase, in whatever year of the general cycle that seventh year happened to fall.

"Every firstborn male that is born among your cattle and among your sheep you shall sanctify to the Lord your God." We must ask whether the animals that in Greek are called prōtotoka, which could not be expressed in Latin except as primogenita ("first-begotten"), are to be understood only in relation to their mothers, from whom they are born; for strictly speaking they are borne rather than begotten. To bear is tiktein [?], which comes from the female, and from it prōtotokos is formed; to beget, however, is tiktein [?], from which the Latin primogenitus is properly said. The firstlings given were reckoned from the females, that is, those born first, not those first begotten by the males, in case they happened to be begotten from widowed females that had already borne young. Otherwise they would not be the ones that opened the womb, which the law meant to be the distinctive mark of the firstborn owed to the Lord. If, then, there is a definite distinction in these words, it is not for nothing that the Lord is not called monotokos in relation to the Father, but monogenēs, that is, "only-begotten," meaning unique. Yet in relation to the dead he is indeed called in Latin primogenitus, because a Latin word could not be formed otherwise according to the usage of the language; in Greek, however, he is called prōtotokos, not prōtogenēs, as though the Father begot him equal to himself, while the creation bore him. For the phrase "the firstborn of all creation," where the Greek also reads prōtotokos, can be understood with reference to the new creation, of which the apostle says, "If anyone, then, is in Christ, he is a new creation." Of this he is the firstfruits, because he was the first to rise in such a way that he will never die again and death will no longer have dominion over him, which is promised at the end to the new creation that is in him. But this distinction should not be asserted rashly; it must be examined more carefully in the Scriptures. For it is puzzling how it could be said in Proverbs, "Firstborn, I say to you, my son"; that is, in whose person we are to understand it spoken. If it is spoken in the person of God the Father to Christ (and whether what follows agrees with that interpretation is hard to affirm), then he calls the same one firstborn and only-begotten: firstborn, because we too are sons of God; only-begotten, because he alone is of the substance of the Father, equal to the Father and coeternal with him. But it is a remarkable question whether sacred Scripture distinguishes between bearing and begetting by the clearest proofs.

"And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen." What does he mean by adding "oxen," when he prescribed the Passover sacrifice from a sheep only, which he commanded to be taken from the sheep and the kids, or from the goats? This is taken mystically to refer to Christ, whose fleshly origin comes from both the righteous and sinners. For he did not say "from the sheep or from the goats," although strictly a sheep cannot be understood as coming from goats; but so that the Jews might not say that a goat was meant if it had said "or from the goats," it said "from the sheep and the goats." What then are the oxen doing here? Are they mentioned because of the other sacrifices that were to be offered during the days of unleavened bread?

We must ask how he intended to be observed what he says: "You shall count for yourself seven full weeks; from when you begin to put the sickle to the harvest you shall begin to count seven weeks. And you shall keep the feast of weeks to the Lord your God, as far as your hand is able, whatever the Lord has given you, according as the Lord your God blesses you; and you shall feast before the Lord your God." If the whole people was commanded to observe this Pentecost, are we to believe that everyone was told to put the sickle to the harvest on the same day? But if each person observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day he puts in the sickle, then it is not one for the whole people. Yet that Pentecost is one which is reckoned from the sacrifice of the Passover to the day the law was given on Sinai.

"When you have entered the land that the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance, and have possessed it and live in it, and you say, 'I will set rulers over me like the other nations around me,' you shall surely set over you as ruler the one whom the Lord your God chooses; from among your brothers you shall set a ruler over you; you cannot set a foreigner over you, because he is not your brother." It may be asked why the people displeased God when they asked for a king, since here this is found to be permitted. But rather we should understand from this that it was rightly not according to God's will, since he did not command it to be done but allowed it to those who wanted it. He did, however, command that the king should not be a foreigner but a brother, that is, a native of the same people, not a man of another race. And when he says "you cannot," it is to be understood as "you must not."

Speaking of the king, he says: "And he shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away; nor shall he greatly multiply silver and gold for himself." So it is asked whether David did not act against this commandment, since he did not have just one wife. As for Solomon, it is evident that he transgressed this commandment both in women and in gold and silver. But we should rather understand from this that kings were permitted to have more than one wife; what they were forbidden was to multiply them. This prohibition is not transgressed if the wives are few, as David's were, but not many, as Solomon's were. However, when he added "lest his heart turn away," he seems rather to have commanded that the king not, by multiplying wives, come to take foreign women, through whom it came about in Solomon's case that his heart turned away from God. Still, multiplying wives is forbidden in general, so that even if he had multiplied them from among Hebrew women alone, he could rightly be charged with acting against this commandment.

"If a Levite comes from one of your cities out of all the sons of Israel, where he lives, as his soul desires, to the place the Lord will choose" (that is, if he wishes to go to the place where the Lord is called upon) "and ministers to the name of the Lord his God, like all his brothers the Levites who stand there before the Lord, he shall eat an allotted portion, apart from the sale which is according to family." What he means by "sale" is obscure; unless perhaps it is because he commanded that tithes and firstlings be sold by those who lived far away, so that they would not be forced to carry much to the place where the Lord was called upon or to drive cattle there, and that they should buy them back there with the same money; and he had ordered that the Levite who lived in the city from which those tithes and firstlings were owed should have a share there. And he said that this was owed to the Levite "according to family" because, by the succession by which he succeeds his parents, what was rendered to his parents ought to be kept for him.

Since he forbids there to be observers of portents among the people of God, we must ask how the portents that are forbidden to be observed are to be distinguished from those given by God in such a way that what they signify ought to be explained. Such are all the miracles found in the Scriptures that signify something belonging to the rule of faith, as when we explain what was signified by the fleece that was dry when the threshing floor was wet, or wet when the floor was dry, or by the rod of Aaron that blossomed and bore nuts, and other things of this kind. Just as the divinations that he goes on to forbid are distinguished from the predictions or proclamations of the prophets, so those observations of omens must be distinguished from the meanings of divine miracles.

"For the Lord your God, who goes before you, will fight your enemies together with you and will save you." See how in spiritual conflicts too we must hope for and ask God's help, not so that we may do nothing, but so that, being helped, we may work together with him. For he says "he will fight with you" to show that they too would do what needed to be done.

"And the scribes shall speak to the people, saying: 'Who is the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man dedicate it. And who is the man who has planted a vineyard and has not feasted from it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man feast from it. And who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man take her.'" These things may raise a question, as if those who have already dedicated their buildings, already enjoyed their young vines and already married their betrothed die in battle under a better condition than those who have not yet done so. But since human affection is held by such things and people value them highly, we should understand that these words were spoken to those going out to war so that anyone whose mind was held by them might be revealed when he turned back, lest he fight less bravely because he feared dying before he had dedicated his house, drunk from his new vineyard or married his betrothed. For certainly, as far as the woman is concerned, it is better for her to marry another man untouched than as a widow. But these rules, as I said, were laid down to test the spirit of the men.
"A man's gear shall not be upon a woman": he means the gear of war, that is, weapons. Indeed, some have even translated it that way.

"If a man takes a wife and lives with her, and hates her, and lays pretexts of speech against her, and brings an evil name upon her, and says, 'I took this woman, and when I came to her I did not find the tokens of her virginity,' then the girl's father and mother shall take the tokens of the girl's virginity and bring them out to the elders at the gate, and the girl's father shall say to the elders, 'I gave my daughter to this man as his wife, and hating her he now lays pretexts of speech against her, saying, "I did not find in your daughter the tokens of virginity"; and here are the tokens of my daughter's virginity.' And they shall spread out the cloak before the elders of that city, and the elders of that city shall take that man and punish him and fine him a hundred shekels and give them to the girl's father, because he brought an evil name upon a virgin of Israel; and she shall be his wife, and he may not send her away for all time. But if the charge proves true and the tokens of the girl's virginity are not found, they shall bring the girl out to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones and she shall die, because she has committed folly among the sons of Israel by playing the harlot in her father's house; and you shall remove the evil from among you." From this it is quite clear how subject to their husbands, almost as servants, the law meant wives to be. For when a husband gives testimony against his wife by which she would be stoned if it were shown to be true, he is not stoned in turn if it is established to be false, but is only punished and fined and ordered to cleave for ever to the woman he had wanted to be rid of. In other cases, however, the law orders that anyone who has harmed another by false testimony be punished with the same penalty that the accused would have suffered had the charge been true, if the death penalty was what he had sought.

"If someone finds a girl who is a virgin and not betrothed, and forcing her lies with her, and he is found out, the man who lay with her shall give the girl's father fifty didrachmas of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; he may not send her away for all time." It is rightly asked whether this is a penalty, that he may never send away the woman whom he violated in a disorderly and unlawful way. For if we want to understand that she cannot, that is, must not, be sent away for all time because she has become his wife, we run up against the fact that Moses permitted a man to give a certificate of divorce and send his wife away. But he would not allow this to those who defile a woman unlawfully, lest they seem to have done it for sport and to have pretended to marry her rather than truly and willingly to have married her. The same was commanded concerning the woman whose husband had falsely accused her of not being found a virgin.

"An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord; even to the tenth generation he shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, and for ever." The question is how Ruth, who was a Moabite, entered, from whom even the Lord's flesh traces its descent. Unless perhaps he prophesied mystically that she would enter, in saying "even to the tenth generation." For the generations are counted from Abraham, in whose time Lot also lived, who fathered the Moabites and Ammonites by his daughters; and counting Abraham himself, ten generations are found to be completed down to Salmon, who fathered Boaz, Ruth's second husband. These are they: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon. Salmon fathered Boaz, who married the widow Ruth; and so after the tenth generation she seems to have produced offspring in the assembly of the Lord by bearing sons to Boaz. But why "and for ever" was added is still rightly asked. Is it because from then on no soul from the Ammonites and Moabites entered that assembly of the Hebrew people, after this prophecy was fulfilled in the tenth generation? Or rather was "even to the tenth generation" said in such a way that he meant it to be understood as "always," by a kind of totality expressed in the number ten, so that he explained this, as it were, by adding "and for ever"? If so, Ruth seems to have been admitted against the commandment that forbade it. Or did he forbid Ammonite men to be admitted, but not Ammonite women, that is, the men from that people, not the women? Especially since, when the Israelites overthrew that nation, they were ordered to kill all the men, but not the women, except those who had known a man, because these were the ones who had seduced the people into fornication; but they willed the virgins to be spared, not charging them with the guilt for which that nation deserved to be overthrown. He mentions this guilt here too, as if someone were asking why he would not let Moabites and Ammonites be admitted into the assembly of the Lord. For he adds: "because they did not meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia to curse you." Even then, when that nation was conquered, they did not charge these faults to the women, whom they chose to preserve alive.

"You shall not hand over to his master a servant who has been joined to you from his master." It does not mean that his master placed him with you, that is, entrusted him to you (for then he would rather have said "deposited"); it says "joined to you from his master," that is, attached to this man after he had left the other. So he did not forbid fugitives to be received, but rather forbade them to be given back. One might indeed take it that way, unless we understand that these words are addressed to a nation and people, not to a single individual. So he forbade that a man fleeing from another nation to this nation he was addressing be returned to his master, that is, to his king. Even a foreigner observed this: Amman [?], king of Gath, when David fled to him from the face of his lord, that is, King Saul. And he explains this very plainly when he says of the fugitive himself: "He shall live among you in any place he pleases."

"There shall be no harlot among the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no fornicator among the sons of Israel." Here he clearly forbade both men and women to commit fornication, showing that it is a sin to have intercourse with those who are not one's spouse, even when they are not other people's spouses, since he forbids both being harlots and going to harlots, whose shame is publicly for sale. In the Decalogue, however, he does not seem to have forbidden this openly under the name of moechia, since moechia is usually understood only as adultery. What we thought about this we discussed there.

You shall not bring the wages of a harlot or the exchange for a dog into the house of the Lord your God for any vow, since both are an abomination to the Lord your God. This is to be understood as: "since this is an abomination to the Lord your God, and not just one of these, but both." For he forbids the firstborn to be exchanged for a dog, though he orders such an exchange to be made with other unclean animals, that is, horses and asses and any others of those that help (adiuuant) human beings, and which in Latin are called iumenta, beasts of burden, from iuuare, "to help." But he did not want it done with a dog. Whether he also did not want it with a pig, and why he did not want it, must be investigated; and if he did not want it with any such animals, why he singled out the dog alone in this passage. As for his speaking of the wages of a harlot, the reason seems to be that he had forbidden just above that there be a harlot among the daughters of Israel, or that any of the sons of Israel make use of a harlot. And so that the thought might not creep in that this sin could be expiated if something from those earnings were offered in the temple, it had to be said that this is an abomination to the Lord.

That thief shall die (that is, the one who has stolen a person), and you shall remove the wicked one from among yourselves. Scripture says this constantly when it orders the wicked to be put to death. The apostle too used this expression when he said: For what have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge? Remove the evil one from among yourselves. For the Greek has τὸν πονηρόν, which is also what is written here; and this is usually rendered "wicked" rather than "evil." Nor does it say τὸ πονηρόν, that is, "this wicked thing," but τὸν πονηρόν, which is "this wicked man." From this it is clear that he wanted us to understand the one who had committed something of such a kind that he deserves excommunication. For excommunication now does in the church what execution did then. The apostle's words could, however, also be understood differently, as meaning that each person is commanded to remove evil or wickedness from himself. That sense would be more acceptable if the Greek had "this evil thing" or "this wicked thing" rather than "this wicked man"; as it is, it is more credible that it was said of a person than of a vice. Yet it could also be nicely understood that a person removes the wicked man from himself, in the way it was said: Strip off the old man, which he explains by saying: Let the one who used to steal steal no longer.
According to all the law that the Levitical priests may [?] to you. Here it is evident that every priest was a Levite, although not every Levite was a priest.

If your neighbor owes you a debt, any debt whatever, you shall not go into his house to take a pledge. You shall stand outside, and the man who owes you shall bring the pledge out to you. But if the man is poor, you shall not go to sleep with his pledge; you shall be sure to return his garment to him around sunset, and he will sleep in his garment and bless you, and it will be counted to you as mercy before the Lord your God. It seems, not without reason, to belong to the work of mercy that the one taking the pledge should not enter the house, so that the debtor may not be put into confusion; but by this he also instructs the debtor himself to bring the pledge out to the creditor. But his command that a pledge taken from a poor man be returned the same day, so that the man who has nowhere else to sleep may sleep in it, rightly gives us pause. One may ask why he did not rather instruct the creditor not to take away a pledge that he has to return the same day. And if he wanted this done to put pressure on the debtor, how would the debtor press himself to pay when he knows he will get the pledge back the same day? Or perhaps he wanted it done as a reminder, so that the debtor would not forget to pay, and would then fail to pay only if he truly did not have the means? Especially since he is won over by the mercy of his creditor, to whom he must not be ungrateful if he has received back the pledge to sleep in. At the same time, when the debtor has not paid, the creditor ought to believe that he does not have the means, since he is in need even of this mercy, that the pledge be returned to him because he has nothing else to sleep in.

Fathers shall not die for their sons, and sons shall not die for their fathers; each shall die in his own sin. See: not only did the prophets say this, but the law too says that each person is to be put to death for his own guilt, not for that of his father or his son. What, then, of the saying elsewhere: God, who repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation? Is that to be understood of sons not yet born, on account of original sin, which the human race has also drawn from Adam, whereas here the distinction is made concerning sons already born, so that each dies in his own sin? For one who was already born when his father sinned draws nothing from his father. But since it says there too: to those who hate me, it is plain that even that condition can be changed if the sons have not imitated the deeds of their parents. For what comes from Adam, too, is repaid in time, since all die on account of it, but not for eternity to those who have been spiritually reborn through grace and have remained in it to the end. Still, one may rightly ask: if the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons of those who hate God, why to the third and fourth generation, either passing over the first and second, or not extending to the rest as well, if ungodliness and the imitation of wicked parents persist? Was it through this number, since seven is understood, that he wished to signify totality? And did he therefore not rather put seven itself, saying "to the seventh generation," so that every generation might be understood, because in this way he better conveyed the reason for this number's perfection? For it is held to be perfect because it is made up of these two: three, the first whole odd number, and four, the first whole even number. So I think this is also the sense of the prophetic saying that is so often repeated: For three and four ungodly deeds I will not turn away; by which he meant us to understand all ungodly deeds rather than three or four.

You shall not pervert the judgment of the stranger and the orphan and the widow; you shall not take the widow's garment in pledge. Why does he not say, "and you shall not take their garment in pledge"? For what reason is there for forbidding the perversion of judgment for all three, yet forbidding the garment to be taken in pledge from the widow alone, and not from the others too? Surely because he commended justice to all of them for this reason, that they have no one to defend them: the stranger, because he is in a foreign land; the orphan, that is, the ward, because he lacks parents; the widow, because she has no husband. But when he forbids a widow's garment to be taken in pledge, I think he is quite neatly reminding us that those women are truly to be called widows who are also poor. The apostle too clearly shows this where he says: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household piously and to make a return to her parents; for this is acceptable before the Lord. But she who is truly a widow and left alone has set her hope on the Lord and continues in prayers night and day. He called her truly a widow who has no one to support her, because she is bereft not only of a husband but also of descendants and of all help; for he would not call a rich woman "left alone." So a garment is not to be taken in pledge from a poor woman; and indeed, by the very fact that he forbids a garment to be taken, he shows she is poor. For a creditor would surely rather take silver, or anything else, than a garment. Further, if it occurs to someone to ask: what if she has many garments, not necessary but superfluous, how then is she understood to be truly a widow, that is, not only left alone but also not living in luxury? He spoke of such a one next, saying: But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives. For he set her in contrast to the true widow, as if such a woman is not a true widow. But in the case of any rich women who have refused to try another marriage, it is their continence that is praised, not their being left alone that is commended. For they have been widowed only of their husbands, not of other things.

As for his instruction that no one should gather a sheaf forgotten at harvest, and that no one should go back over olives or grapes left behind to gather carefully what was overlooked, and his saying that these are to be left for the needy, the thought may occur: what if it is not the needy but the shameless who gather what the owners of the fields leave behind? But it must be considered, first, that the one who leaves it with the intention that the needy should have what is left is doing a work of mercy. Second, when these things are commanded to the people, those who are not in need are at the same time warned not to go after them. And if they do go after them, what else are they to be judged but invaders of what belongs to others, and, what is more serious, of what belongs to the poor? So both are addressed by these precepts: those whose fields they are, that they leave these things out of mercy, and those who are not in need, that they keep away from them; since both are stated, both by whom these things are to be left and for whom they are to be left.

But if there is a dispute between men and they come to judgment, and they judge and justify the just. We are to understand that it is the judges who judge, not those who were said to have the dispute. Then follows: and they condemn the ungodly, then if the one who acts ungodly deserves blows, you shall set him in the sight of the judges and they shall flog him before them according to his ungodliness. They shall flog him forty times, and shall not add more; but if they add to flogging him more blows beyond these, your brother will be disfigured before you. This must be carefully noted. Although he prescribed that those sins should be corrected with blows which do not deserve to be punished with death, and with so few blows at that, he nevertheless called the one who is beaten ungodly, or one who acts ungodly, so that we may know that the Scriptures did not speak the way most people speak. We read them too carelessly when we think that adultery is not ungodliness, because the one who has done it seems to have sinned against a human being, although the law orders that sin to be punished with death; and when we say that ungodly deeds are graver than these sins, although there are some of them that are punished with forty strokes of the lash. So there is a light ungodliness that deserves a beating, and a grave one that deserves death. Likewise, of those sins too that seem to be committed not against God but against a human being, some deserve death, others rebuke, or a beating, or a readier pardon. For it is clear that the Seventy translators spoke in such a way that they called even the offense of one who deserves blows ungodliness.

But if brothers live together and one of them dies and has no offspring, the wife of the dead man shall not marry outside to one who is not near of kin; her husband's brother shall go in to her and take her as his wife and live with her. And the child who is born shall be established from the name of the dead man, and his name shall not be blotted out of Israel. The law seems to have commanded the marrying of a brother's wife for no other reason than to raise up offspring for the brother who died without children. As for his saying: shall be established from the name of the dead man, and his name shall not be blotted out of Israel, that is, the name of the dead man, it seems to have been said so that the one who is born should be called by the name by which the dead man was called, whose line is in a certain way continued through him. That is why we thought it better to resolve the question in the Gospel about the two fathers of Joseph, one of whom Matthew mentions, namely the one who begot Joseph, and the other Luke, the one whose son Joseph was, according to the custom of adoption, since Joseph took the name of neither of them. Unless perhaps "shall be established from the name of the dead man" was said not to mean that he takes his name, but that from his name, that is, as the son not of the man from whose seed he was begotten but of the dead man for whom offspring was raised up, he is established as heir. For the added words, and his name shall not be blotted out of Israel, can be understood not as meaning that the boy accordingly takes his name, but that the man will be seen not to have died without posterity; and so his name, that is, his memory, endures. For even if he had begotten a son himself, he would not have given him his own name so that his name might not be blotted out of Israel; rather, it would not be blotted out simply because he did not depart this life without children. And his brother is commanded to accomplish through his wife what he himself could not. For even if there was no brother, a near kinsman would marry the wife of one who had died without sons, to raise up offspring for his brother, as Boaz did by marrying Ruth, to raise up offspring for his kinsman, whose wife she had been without bearing him a child. And yet the one born of her was established from the name of the dead man, since he was called his son (and so it came about that the dead man's name was not blotted out of Israel), and yet he was not called by his name.

Since this is so, the question about the Gospels can be answered more fully in two ways. The first is that one of the two men whom Matthew and Luke name as different fathers was related to the other closely enough to marry his wife, yet distantly enough that each could have had different parents and ancestors further back. If they had been the sons of brothers, they would have had one grandfather. That is not the case. According to Matthew, Joseph's grandfather is Matthan; according to Luke, he is not Matthan but Matthat. Someone may think the names are so alike that the scribes have made a mistake in a single letter, producing a difference so small as to be almost none. But what will he say about the fathers of these two? According to Luke, Matthat was the son of Levi, while according to Matthew, Matthan is found to have been begotten by Eleazar. From there upward the fathers, grandfathers and earlier ancestors are all different, as far as Zerubbabel, who is about the twentieth generation back from Joseph in Luke but the eleventh in Matthew. He is believed to be the same man because in both evangelists his father is found to be Shealtiel; yet there could have been another man of the same name whose father bore the same name as the first man's father. For from there upward they differ again: in Luke Zerubbabel has one grandfather, Neri, and in Matthew another, Jechoniah. Above that point there is no agreement anywhere until we come to David, by way of Solomon in Matthew and by way of Nathan in Luke. It seems very hard to believe, however, that there was no nearer relative to marry his brother's wife than one who was related only by descent from David, at so distant a degree and with no closer kinship further down, since in Luke David is almost the fortieth generation from Joseph, and in Matthew about the twenty-seventh. Or, if men related through the female line were also sought out as kinsmen to marry the widows of the dead, it could have happened that someone related in that way begot Joseph by the wife of his kinsman who had died without children. Joseph would then have had one father by nature and another by law. No kinship would appear among their fathers, grandfathers and earlier ancestors because they were related not through men but through women. Yet if that were so, they would never meet in David as a single father either. Or, if someone insists that this could have been the case, what do we make of the fact that it is not the custom of Scripture to put women in a genealogy in place of men, just as no evangelist inserted them? Where mothers are mentioned, they are given only alongside the fathers. Therefore either there was no nearer kinsman to take the dead man's wife, so that the origin of their kinship had to be traced back to David, or else adoption gave Joseph a second father whom he could have.

Among the things that Scripture tells a man to say once he has fulfilled every command about giving tithes and whatever else he was ordered to give or spend, why is he also told to say this, to his own praise and credit: "I have not given any of it to the dead"? Does it thereby forbid the offerings to the dead that the Gentiles are accustomed to observe?

"You shall not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left, to go after other gods to serve them." One may ask how a person who goes after foreign gods to serve them can be understood to go to the right, since the right is used in a sense of praise, and that act can never be praiseworthy. Even when someone who turns aside to the right from the way of life is rebuked, what is rebuked there is not the things on the right, but the person who turns aside to them, that is, the one who claims for himself what belongs to God. That is why it is said in Proverbs: "Do not turn aside to the right or to the left; for the Lord knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left are perverse." So the right-hand ways, which the Lord knows, are good; for "the Lord knows the ways of the righteous," as we read in the psalm. Why, then, was it said, "Do not turn aside to the right"? The text goes on to show the reason by adding, "For he himself will make your paths straight." Far be it from us to deny that the right-hand ways which the Lord knows are straight; but, as I said, to turn aside to them is to want to attribute what is right not to his grace but to oneself. And so, as I said, it goes on to add: "For he himself will make your paths straight, and will lead all your journeys forward in peace."

Accordingly, what is said in this passage of Deuteronomy that we are discussing, "You shall not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left, to go after other gods to serve them," was not said because other gods can also be taken to be on the right. Either geographical places are meant, since the people had nations worshiping other gods both on their right and on their left; or else the part about other gods must be read separately, so that there are two statements. One is: "You shall not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left," in the sense I explained above. The other is: "to go after other gods to serve them," where we are to supply here too, "You shall not turn aside from any of the words that I command you today." If we wanted to state this whole meaning in full, we would repeat the earlier words that are common to both statements. Just as it is said there, "You shall not turn aside from any of the things that I command you today, to the right or to the left," so here it would be repeated: "You shall not turn aside from any of the things that I command you today, to go after other gods to serve them." For turning aside from the words that have been commanded also leads a person to go after other gods. Not going after other gods is not the only thing God commanded, nor is it the only command he does not want transgressed; he wants none of his commands transgressed. Yet this one matters so especially that, after the general precept warning them not to turn aside from any of the words of his commandments, he wished to urge this one on them separately as well.

The words "to the right or to the left" can also be understood this way: God commanded them not to go after other gods, either for the sake of the things that are sought because they bring good fortune, or for the sake of the things that are shunned because they bring misfortune. That is, they must not ask other gods for help, either to gain what they love or against what they hate; or at any rate they must not seek to win them over so that they will help, or to appease them so that they will not harm. For of certain people it is written in the psalm: "Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity." This is because they suppose that a person is made happy by things that both good and bad people can possess, and so it is a right hand of iniquity, because those who think it the right hand are wicked. It is not the true right hand, but the right hand of those whose mouth has spoken vanity: "they called the people happy who have these things," when instead, as the psalm soon adds and teaches, "happy is the people whose God is the Lord." This is the true right hand, a right hand of justice, not of iniquity. One must not, then, go after foreign gods either to the right, as though a person thought they could make him happy, or to the left, worshiping them to avert their hostility because he thinks they could make him miserable if they opposed him. Or at any rate, if we take the right to mean eternal goods and the left temporal goods, then Holy Scripture should be understood to have warned in this passage that those gods are not to be worshiped for the sake of either.

"These are the words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to establish with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he made with them at Horeb." This shows why the book is called Deuteronomy, as if "second law": in it there is more repetition of that law than anything else, for there are few things in it that were not in what was given first. Yet these are not called two covenants, even though these words seem to say so; both together are one covenant, the one the Church calls the old. For if these words meant we had to speak of two covenants, there would already be not two but several, apart from the new. Scripture speaks of a covenant in many places, such as the one made with Abraham concerning circumcision, or the earlier one with Noah.

"You have seen all that the Lord your God did before you in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh and to all his servants and to all his land: the great trials which your eyes saw, those great signs and wonders, and the mighty hand. Yet the Lord God has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this very day." How then can he say above, "You have seen the great trials which your eyes saw," if the Lord did not give them eyes to see and ears to hear? Only because they saw with the body and did not see with the heart, since the heart too is said to have eyes. That is why he began with, "Yet the Lord God has not given you a heart to know." The two phrases that follow belong to this: "and eyes to see and ears to hear," that is, to understand and to obey. As for his saying, "the Lord God has not given you," he would certainly not say it as a rebuke and a reproach unless he wanted it understood that the fault was also theirs, so that no one should think himself excused by this. He shows at once both that without the help of the Lord God they cannot understand and obey with the eyes and ears of the heart, and yet that if God's help is lacking, human fault is not therefore excusable, since God's judgments, though hidden, are just.

"And he led you forty years in the wilderness; your clothes did not wear out, and your sandals were not worn off your feet; you did not eat bread, and you did not drink wine or strong drink, so that you might know that he is the Lord your God."
