From this it appears that when the Israelites came out of Egypt they could carry in their baggage only as much wine as they could quickly use up. For if they had brought none at all with them, where did that come from of which it is said, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play"? This would not have been said of water, since Moses' own words state quite plainly that the sound was not the beginning of war but the beginning of wine.

"Is there perhaps among you a man or woman, or family or tribe, whose mind has turned away from the Lord your God to go and serve the gods of those nations? Is there among you any root springing up with gall and bitterness? And it will happen that when he hears the words of this curse, he will think in his heart, saying, 'Let things be holy for me, for I walk in the error of my heart,' so that the sinner may not destroy together with himself the one who is without sin. God will not be willing to be merciful to him, but then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will blaze against that man, and all the curses of this covenant which are written in the book of this law will cling to him." It is phrased, "Is there perhaps among you?" so that we may take it as inquiring, lest perhaps there be such a one. But if there were anyone, he struck strong fear into him, so that no one, on hearing those curses, should say in his heart, "Let things be holy for me, for I walk in the error of my heart"; that is: far be it that these things should happen to me; may these be not evils for me but holy, that is, favourable and harmless, though I walk in the error of my heart, by going after the gods of the nations, of course, and serving them as though with impunity. It will not be so, he says. "So that the sinner may not destroy together with himself the one who is without sin": as if he were saying, take care that the one who thinks such things does not persuade any of you of them. "God will not be willing to be merciful to him," whether to the one who thinks such things or to the one who has been persuaded of them, as he imagined when he said, "Let things be holy for me," thinking in this way to turn the force of that curse away from himself. "But then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will blaze against that man," at the very moment when he thinks he is turning it away by saying these things in his heart. "And all the curses of this covenant which are written in the book of this law will cling to him." Of course they cannot all happen to one man; he cannot die as many times as there are kinds of death mentioned here. But he said "all" meaning "any of them," so that the man to whom some of them happen, and by which he perishes, is not exempt from all. As for the words, "so that the sinner may not destroy together with himself the one who is without sin," where the Greek has anamartēton, this is not to be taken as though he called someone anamartēton, that is, "without sin," in the sense of being entirely pure and free from every sin, but as meaning one who was without the particular sin he was speaking about. So the Lord says in the Gospel, "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin"; not, of course, all sin, but this sin, that they did not believe in him. God also says to Abimelech concerning Sarah, Abraham's wife, "I know that you did this with a pure heart"; he certainly did not mean that man's heart to be understood as pure in such a way that he was like those of whom it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," but that his heart was pure of the sin in question, since as far as he himself was concerned he had not desired another man's wife.

"And the Lord will cleanse your heart all around, and the heart of your offspring, to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live." A clear promise of grace: God promises that he himself will do what he usually commands to be done.

"For this commandment which I command you today is not beyond measure, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, saying" (that is, so that you should say), "'Who will go up to heaven for us and get it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?' Nor is it beyond the sea, saying" (that is, so that you should say), "'Who will cross over the sea for us and get it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?' The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart and in your hands, to do it." The apostle says that this is the word of faith, which belongs to the new covenant. But it may be asked why he called these things the commandments "written in the book of this law" above, unless it is because all these signify spiritual things belonging to the new covenant, if they are rightly understood. It may also be asked why, in place of what is written here, "Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, 'Who will cross over the sea for us and get it for us?'", the apostle said, "Or who will go down into the abyss?", and, explaining it, added, "that is, to bring Christ up from the dead." It must be that he called the sea this whole life in the present age, which is crossed over by death, so that in a certain sense the sea comes to an end and death itself is called "beyond the sea," as being beyond this life, which is signified by the word "sea." Next, where "and in your hands" is added here, the apostle says only, "in your mouth and in your heart," and he followed this through to the end, saying, "For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Rightly so, for the translation from the Hebrew, as far as we have been able to examine it, does not have "in your hands." Yet I do not think the Seventy translators added it for nothing; they must have wanted it understood that the hands themselves, which signify works, ought to be taken as being in the heart, where faith is, the faith that works through love. For if what God commands is done outwardly with the hands and not done in the heart, no one is so foolish as to think the commandments are fulfilled. On the other hand, if love, which is the fulfilment of the law, dwells in the heart, then even if someone cannot work with the hands of the body, he certainly has peace, among people of good will.

"They have sinned, not to him, blameworthy children." Where the Greek has tekna mōmēta, some have translated it as here, "blameworthy children," some "stained children," some "faulty children." There is no great question about that; indeed there is none at all. But there is good reason to inquire into this: if it is said in general, "They have sinned, not to him" (since one who sins does not sin to God, that is, does not harm God, but himself), how are we to understand what we read in the psalm, "To you alone have I sinned," and in Jeremiah, "To you have we sinned, O patience of Israel, O Lord," and again in the psalm, "Heal my soul, for I have sinned to you"? And is "sinning to God" the same as "sinning against God"? For Eli the priest says, "If someone sins against God, who will pray for him?" I will say for the time being what seems right to me at present. Perhaps those who understand these things better will understand something better, or we ourselves may at another time, as far as the Lord helps us. "To sin against God" is to sin in matters that belong to the worship of God. The passage I mentioned indicates nothing else; that is how the sons of Eli were sinning, to whom their father said this. In the same way we should consider that one also sins against people who belong to God; for we read that God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, "That is why I spared you, so that you would not sin against me." But "to sin to the Lord," or rather "to have sinned to the Lord" (unless perhaps something is found written somewhere that opposes this sense), seems to me to be said, not without reason, of those who do devout penance for their sin, so that the Lord may be glorified in forgiving. For when David gives the reason why he said, "To you alone have I sinned, and done evil in your sight," he goes on to say, "so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged." This may refer to God's saying, "Judge between me and my vineyard"; or it may be understood of the Lord Jesus Christ, who alone could say with perfect truth, "For the ruler of the world is coming, and he has nothing in me" (that is, nothing of sin that deserves death), "but so that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father has commanded me, so I do. Rise, let us go from here"; as if he were saying: even if the ruler of the world pursues the slightest sins with the penalty of death, he has nothing in me; but rise, let us go from here, that is, so that I may suffer, because in what I suffer I am fulfilling my Father's will, not paying the penalty for my own sin. And when Jeremiah says, "To you have we sinned, O patience of Israel," this is surely said to the Lord as a plea in penitence, with hope of salvation through pardon. And in the words, "Heal my soul, for I have sinned to you," the same thing is going on: that God may be glorified by forgiving, since great is his mercy towards those who confess to him and return to him, he who says that he does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn back and live. Hence David himself too, not only in the psalm but also when God rebuked him through the prophet, answered, not without hope of the Lord's mercy, "I have sinned to the Lord." For in a way he seems like a wounded man who submits himself to the physician's hands in order to be healed, so that the work of medicine may be accomplished in him. But in this song the prophet foresaw that there would be some who would sin by offending God with their great iniquities in such a way that they would not be willing to do penance and return to God to be healed. Of them it is also said elsewhere, "For they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return." It can also be understood like this: "They have sinned, not to him," in the sense that by their sin they harmed not him but themselves.

"And this is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before he died. And he said: The Lord came from Sinai and shone forth upon us from Seir; and he hastened from Mount Paran with many thousands of Kadesh, angels with him at his right hand. And he spared his people; and all the sanctified are under your hands, and these are under you. And it received from his words the law which Moses commanded us, an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob. And there will be a ruler in the beloved, when the rulers of the peoples are gathered together with the tribes of Israel." This prophecy must not be passed over carelessly. It plainly appears that this blessing concerns the new people whom the Lord Christ has sanctified, and that these words are spoken by Moses in Christ's person, not in Moses' own person, as clearly appears from what follows. For if "The Lord came from Sinai" is said because the law was given on Mount Sinai, what is meant by what follows, "and shone forth upon us from Seir," since Seir is a mountain of Idumea, where Esau reigned? Then, since Moses is blessing the children of Israel with these words, as Scripture said beforehand, how can the same man say, "And it received from his words the law which Moses commanded us"? Clearly, then, it is a prophecy, as we have said, foretelling the new people sanctified by the grace of Christ, and it does so under the name of the children of Israel because they are the seed of Abraham, that is, they are the children of the promise, and the meaning of Israel is "seeing God." So the Lord who came from Sinai is to be understood as Christ, since Sinai means "temptation." He came, then, from the trial of his passion, the cross, and death. "And shone forth from Seir." Seir means "hairy," which signifies the sinner; for Esau, who was hated, was born so. But since "for those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death a light has dawned," therefore "he shone forth from Seir." At the same time it may also reasonably be understood as foretelling that the grace of Christ would come to the people of Israel from the Gentiles, who are signified by the name Seir, since it is a mountain belonging to Esau. That is why the apostle says, "So they too have now not believed, in the mercy shown to you, so that they too may obtain mercy." It is they, then, who say, "He shone forth upon us from Seir." "And he hastened from Mount Paran" (that is, from the fruitful mountain, for that is what Paran means, and it signifies the Church) "with many thousands of Kadesh." Kadesh means "changed" and "holiness." So the many thousands have been changed and sanctified through grace, the thousands with whom Christ comes afterwards to gather in the Israelites. It goes on to say, "angels with him at his right hand"; this needs no explanation. "And he spared his people," it says, by granting forgiveness of sins. So it turns to address him directly and says, "And all the sanctified are under your hands, and these are under you": not, of course, those who are proud and want to establish their own righteousness, but those who acknowledge grace, so as to submit to the righteousness of God. "And it received from his words the law," it says, meaning the people of whom it says, "And he spared his people." So it received from his words the law "which Moses commanded us," it says; that is, his people received the law from his words, because through his teaching it understood that very law which Moses commanded us. For he himself says in the Gospel, "If you believed Moses, you would believe me too; for he wrote about me." That people did not receive the law that it did not understand; it received it when it understood it from his words, turned to the Lord and freed from the old veil. This he calls "an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob," an inheritance to be understood not as earthly but as heavenly, not temporal but eternal. "And there will be a ruler in the beloved," it says: the Lord Jesus himself will be ruler among the beloved people, "when the rulers of the peoples," that is, of the Gentiles, "are gathered together with the tribes of Israel," so that what was said above may be fulfilled: "Rejoice, you nations, together with his people"; for blindness has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel would be saved.

When he was blessing Joseph, he said among other things, "The firstborn of a bull, his beauty." This is not to be read as though he had said "the firstborn of a bull," but rather: since he is the firstborn, his beauty is that of a bull. Because of the horns of the cross it is understood as a figure of the Lord.
BOOK SIX. QUESTIONS ON JOSHUA SON OF NUN.

QUESTION 1. The Lord says to Joshua son of Nun: "And as I was with Moses, so I will be with you also." Not only this testimony but also many proofs in Deuteronomy show that Moses died as a servant of God and pleasing to God, even though the punishment was carried out on him that he should not enter the land of promise. From this we are given to understand that the Lord, when he is angry with his good servants in some matter, punishes them in this life, and yet counts them among those vessels in his house that are for honour and useful to the Lord, to whom he will give what was promised to the saints.

The question is how, after the Lord had spoken to Joshua son of Nun, exhorting and strengthening him and promising that he would be with him, this same Joshua ordered the people through the scribes to prepare provisions, because they would cross the Jordan in three days, when in fact they are found to have crossed the Jordan many days later. For after he had given the people these orders, he sent spies into Jericho, since that was the nearest city once the Jordan was crossed. They turned aside to Rahab, a harlot; she hid them, and the king searched for them but did not find them; she let them down through a window and advised them to hide in the hill country for three days. Thus four days appear to have been used up. Then, after they reported what had happened to them, Joshua set out at dawn with all the people from the place where he was. When he came to the Jordan, he turned aside and stayed there; then the people were again instructed to prepare themselves to cross the Jordan after three days, with the ark of the Lord going before them. From this, then, we understand that it was a human arrangement which he had announced to the people, that they should prepare provisions as though they would cross that river after three days; for as a man he could hope this might be done if the spies returned quickly. Since they were delayed, we understand, although Scripture is silent about it, that the rest was accomplished by divine arrangement, so that Joshua might now begin to be glorified among the people and it might be shown that the Lord was with him as he had been with Moses. For this too is said to him when he is about to cross the river, as it is written: "And the Lord said to Joshua: This day I will begin to exalt you before all the children of Israel, so that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I will be with you also." Nor should it seem incredible that even those with whom God spoke wished to do something according to a human arrangement, in which they nevertheless trusted God to be their guide, and that their plans were changed by the providence of him by whom they were guided. For Moses himself had certainly thought, as a man, that he ought to hear the people's cases in such a way that, by taking on a burden unbearable both to himself and to them, he could not be of benefit; and his arrangement was changed by God's doing, through the suggestion and advice of his father-in-law, which advice God approved.

The scribes say to the people: "When you see the ark of the testimony of the Lord our God, and our priests and the Levites carrying it, set out from your places and go after it. But let there be a long interval between you and it; you shall stand about two thousand cubits away. Do not come near it, so that you may know the way by which you are to go; for you have not gone this way before, yesterday or the day before." The ark was ordered to go far ahead so that it could be seen by the people. For so great a host, if it followed close behind, would not see it going before them nor know where to follow. From this fact we must understand that the pillar of cloud, which used to give the signal for breaking camp and to show the way, had now withdrawn and no longer appeared to them; this is why even those three days were announced according to a human arrangement. Now, therefore, with Joshua as their leader, they follow the ark of the Lord, the cloud having been withdrawn as if a veil had been taken away. "Now the Jordan was full along its whole bank, as in the days of the wheat harvest." This seems incredible in our regions. But there, as those who know report, the wheat harvest is at the beginning of spring, and at that time the river rises higher than in winter.

"And these stones shall be a memorial for you, for the children of Israel, forever." How "forever," when heaven and earth will pass away? Is it because these stones signify something eternal, although they themselves cannot be eternal? However, what is in the Greek, ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος, can also be rendered in Latin "to the age," which does not necessarily mean eternity.

"And the Lord spoke to Joshua, saying: Command the priests who carry the ark of the covenant of the testimony." It is usually called the ark of the covenant or the ark of the testimony; here it is called the ark of the covenant of the testimony, so that not only the ark but the covenant itself might be called the covenant of the testimony. For this is why the apostle says: "But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been made manifest, being witnessed by the law and the prophets." For what is called the old covenant had been given as a testimony to something else that was to come.

The Lord said to Joshua: "Make for yourself sharp knives of stone" — or, as the Greek has it, "of sharp stone" — "and sit down and circumcise the children of Israel again." In this command it is asked why he said "again"; for no one man was to be circumcised twice. But because a single people was circumcised in some of its members and uncircumcised in others, it was said "again," so that what was circumcised again was not a man but a people; and what follows shows this. For Scripture says: "And Joshua made himself sharp knives of stone and circumcised the children of Israel at the place called the Hill of the Foreskins. And this is how Joshua purified the children of Israel: those who had at one time been on the way, and those who had at one time been uncircumcised among those who had come out of Egypt — all these Joshua circumcised. For Israel had lived forty-two years in the desert of Mabdaritis [?]. Therefore most of those fighting men who had come out of the land of Egypt were uncircumcised, who had been disobedient to the commands of God, concerning whom the Lord had also decreed that they should not see the land which the Lord had sworn to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey. In their place he put their sons, whom Joshua circumcised, because they had been uncircumcised on the journey." It is clear, then, that not all had been uncircumcised, but some. For some of the sons of those who came out of Egypt were uncircumcised among that people, and these Joshua could circumcise: namely, the sons of those who begot them in the desert and neglected to circumcise them because they were disobedient to the law of God. There is therefore no reason why those who think that people who have the sacrament of Christian baptism should be rebaptized should suppose that they are supported by this testimony of the law, since no single man was circumcised twice; rather, it was a people that had already been circumcised in some of its members but was still uncircumcised in others. And even if it were somehow possible for God to command a man to be circumcised twice, could they claim that it was commanded because those men had been circumcised by Egyptians, or by some heretics cut off from the fellowship of the Israelites? Since it is quite evident why God said this, people can find here no defence for their error.

When Joshua saw a man standing opposite him with a drawn sword, and the man answered that he was the commander of the army of the power of the Lord, Joshua fell prostrate on the ground and said: "What do you command your servant?" It may be asked whether he prostrated himself before an angel and called him lord, or rather, understanding by whom he had been sent, called the Lord himself lord and prostrated himself before him. Now Joshua was, as we read, "in Jericho" — not, of course, in the city itself, whose walls had not yet fallen (which was soon to happen so that they could enter it), but in the territory belonging to it; for the translation made from the Hebrew has it this way.

Concerning what happened when Achan of the tribe of Judah stole from the devoted things of the city of Jericho against the command of the Lord: because of his sin the three thousand who had been sent against Ai turned their backs to the enemy and thirty-six men of them were killed; and when the people were gravely terrified, Joshua prostrated himself with the elders before the Lord, and the answer given him was that this had happened because the people had sinned; God even threatened that he would not be with them unless they removed the devoted thing from among themselves; and the one who had done it was revealed and was killed, not alone, but with all his household. It is commonly asked how it can be just for others to be punished for another's sins, especially since the Lord said in the law that neither fathers should be punished for the sins of their sons nor sons for the sins of their fathers. Is it that this command was given to men when they judge, that they should not punish anyone in place of another, whereas the judgments of God are not of this kind, since he knows by his deep and invisible counsel how far to extend even the temporal punishment of men and a wholesome fear? For nothing dreadful, as far as the governance of the whole world is concerned, befalls mortals when they die, since they must die at some time anyway. And yet among those who fear such things discipline is established, so that each person among the people cares not only for himself, but they exercise mutual diligence for one another, and, as members of one body and one man, some members are anxious for others. Yet we must not believe that even in the punishments inflicted after death one person can be condemned for another; rather, this sort of penalty is inflicted only in those matters which were going to come to an end anyway, even if they did not end in that way. At the same time it is also shown how closely bound together the whole community of a people is, so that individuals are assessed not merely in themselves but also as parts in a whole. Through the sin of one and the death of a few, therefore, the whole people was warned to search out what had been committed, as in one whole body. At the same time it was also signified how great an evil it would be if that whole congregation had sinned, when not even one man could be judged in such a way that the rest could be safe from him. But if Achan had been discovered and seized by someone, and brought to Joshua's judgment as guilty of that crime, it is in no way to be thought that a human judge would have punished anyone else, either in his place or with him, who was in no way implicated in his deed. For he was not permitted to go beyond the command of the law given to men, that in their judgment — that which has been commanded or permitted to man concerning man — no one should think one person ought to be punished for another's sin. But God judges by a far more hidden justice, since he has the power even after death, which man does not have, either to deliver or to destroy. Visible afflictions or deaths of men, then, since they can both harm and benefit those on whom they are inflicted, the Lord knows in the secret of his providence how to dispense justly to each, even when he seems to punish the sins of some in others. But invisible punishments, which can only harm and cannot benefit, no one pays for another's sins when God is judge, just as, when man is judge, no one ought to pay these visible penalties except for his own fault. For this is what God has commanded the human judge in punishing those matters that belong to human judgment; what he does in his own judgment he does himself, where human power does not reach.

It is rightly asked why, when the Lord, regarding the one who had stolen from the devoted things, commanded that whoever was revealed should be burned with fire, Joshua instead had him stoned by the people once he was revealed. Was it that he ought to die in the way that Joshua, who followed the Lord more closely, was able to understand the words of the Lord who gave the command? For no one else could easily have done so. Hence we should rather ask why the Lord called stoning "fire" than believe that Joshua did something other than what the Lord had commanded. For no one could have been wiser in understanding the words of the Lord, nor anyone more obedient in carrying them out. Moreover, Scripture bears witness in Deuteronomy that punishment could be signified by the word "fire," where it is said to the children of Israel: "And he brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt," where he certainly meant harsh affliction to be understood.

Two reasons occur to me — not that both apply, but one or the other — why he and all his household were not burned with visible fire. If the Lord judged his sin to be such that, once expiated by that punishment, he would not punish it eternally, then because of this very expiation and purification that penalty fittingly received the name of fire. And no one would be prompted to reach this understanding if visible fire had literally burned him up; instead everyone would rest in what he plainly saw fulfilled and would look for nothing further. But now, since because of God's words and the act of Joshua, who could not have transgressed those words, it is quite rightly said that even the stoning was fire, it is elegantly recognized that the man was purified by that punishment, so that he would not perish hereafter for that sin. This is also signified by the vessels in Leviticus which are commanded to be purified by fire. If, however, that sin was such that Gehenna would receive him even after this life, then Joshua wished him to be stoned so that what the Lord said, "he shall be burned with fire," might prompt us to understand it as what the Lord would do, not what they themselves were to do. For if the Lord had said, "You shall burn him and all that is his with fire," there would be no room for this sense. But since it was put in such a way that God seems rather to have foretold what would happen to him than to have commanded what ought to be done to him by men, Joshua — who understood the divine words as so great a prophet, and who also did this very thing prophetically — could not have done better than to put him to death with stones rather than flames, lest the words of the Lord seem to be fulfilled in those fires, when he wished them to be understood as spoken with another meaning.

Nor should it trouble us that God foretold that not only he himself but also all that was his would be burned with fire. For he says: "He shall be burned with fire, and all that is his." For "all that is his" can be understood as his works, which he said were to be burned up together with him — not as the apostle says of certain works consumed by fire, "but he himself will be saved" — if this man's sin is to be understood as being punished even with eternal fire. So the people, when punishing him, overwhelmed with stones his sons and daughters along with his cattle and all that he had. Yet Joshua did this not by human judgment but by a prophetic spirit: either understanding "all that is his" in such a way that he did not consider even the sons exempt, inflicting the penalty of stoning in place of fire; or signifying, not only through the other things that belonged to him but also through his sons, the works of his that God was going to burn in him after death.

Nor, certainly, should we believe on this account that they, who were innocent of their father's sin, were burned with the punishment of hell-fire after death for it. For this death which awaits all, although it comes from the first sin, is nevertheless beneficial to some when it is hastened, since we are born in such a condition that we must necessarily die. Hence we read of someone: "He was taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding." By what judgment or mercy of God, then, it was inflicted either on this man's children or on those thirty-six men, since all were strangers to his sin, lies hidden with him in whom there is no unrighteousness. But this much is plain: the people had to search out with fear what had been committed, and the rest dreaded imitating his deed all the more vehemently, the more human weakness shudders both at being delivered over to so great and so just a hatred of the people, and at dying together with one's descendants — those whom one thought to leave behind in hope of continuing one's line — consumed along with oneself through one's own sin.

God, speaking to Joshua, commands him to set an ambush behind the city, that is, warriors lying in wait to ambush the enemy. From this we are reminded that those who wage a just war do nothing unjust by such means. In these matters a just man ought to think chiefly of one thing: that he undertake a just war, and that he be one who has the right to wage war, for not everyone has that right. Once he has undertaken a just war, it makes no difference to justice whether he wins by open battle or by ambush. Just wars are usually defined as those that avenge wrongs: when a nation or city against which war is to be made has either neglected to punish what its own people have wickedly done, or to restore what was taken through wrongdoing. But this kind of war is also undoubtedly just: the war that God commands, in whom there is no injustice and who knows what ought to be done to each. In such a war the leader of the army, or the people themselves, should be judged not so much the author of the war as its servant.

Joshua, sending thirty thousand warriors to subdue Ai, said to them: "You shall lie in ambush behind the city. You shall not be far from the city, and you shall all be ready. I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when those who live in Ai come out against us, as they did before, we will flee before them. And when they come out after us, we will draw them away from the city, and they will say, 'These men are fleeing before us, as they did before.' Then you shall rise up from the ambush and go into the city. You shall act according to this word. See, I have commanded you." We must ask whether every intention to deceive is to be counted as a lie, and, if so, whether a lie can be just when it deceives someone who deserves to be deceived. And if not even this lie is found to be just, it remains that what was done concerning the ambush must be referred to the truth by way of some figurative meaning.

The Gibeonites came to Joshua with stale bread and old sacks, so that they might be thought, as they had pretended, to have come from a distant land, and so be spared; for the Lord had ordained that none of the inhabitants of the land they were entering should be spared. Concerning this, some manuscripts, both Greek and Latin, read: "and taking old sacks upon their shoulders"; but others, which seem more accurate, do not have "upon their shoulders" but "upon their asses." For the likeness of the words in Greek made an error easy, and so the Latin copies also vary: ōmōn and onōn [?] do not sound very different from each other, the first being the word for shoulders and the second for asses. The reading about asses is more credible, because they said they had been sent from their own distant nation; hence it appears that they were envoys, and so could carry their necessities on asses rather than on their shoulders. For there could not have been many of them, and Scripture records that they carried not only sacks but also wineskins.

It may be asked how the Hebrews came to believe that they must keep the oath they had sworn to the Gibeonites as men coming from a distant land, just as the Gibeonites had falsely claimed. For the Gibeonites knew that they would be destroyed if the Hebrews learned that they lived in the land which the Hebrews were to hold as promised to them after killing its inhabitants. So when they lied that they had come to them from a distant land, the Israelites swore an oath to them. But afterward they learned that they lived in the very place where, according to God's command, they were to destroy everyone they found. Yet they would not break the oath, and although they had learned that the Gibeonites had lied, they preferred to spare them for the oath's sake. They could certainly have said that they had sworn to them as to the people they had believed them to be, that is, men coming from far away, and that, once they learned otherwise, the Lord's command concerning them had to be fulfilled, so that they would be conquered like the rest. But God approved of this and was not angry with those who spared them, even though they had not asked him who these people were, and that is why the Gibeonites had been able to deceive them. Hence it is certainly not unreasonable to believe that, although they were willing to deceive men to save themselves, they nevertheless feared God, without deceit, in his people. For this reason the Lord was not angry with those who swore the oath or spared them; so much so that he later avenged these same Gibeonites on the house of Saul, as though they were men of his own people, as the history of the Kingdoms shows. And because the oath was kept in such a way, even toward men who had lied, that the sentence was turned toward mercy, it did not displease God. For if, on the contrary, they had sworn to kill certain people whom they thought to be Gibeonites living in the land of promise, and had afterward learned that these were strangers to that land who had come to them from far away, we must by no means suppose that they would have destroyed them in order to fulfill the oath. For holy David, for the sake of this very mercy of sparing, even after the words in which he had sworn that he would kill Nabal, and though he certainly knew whom he was about to kill, chose to spare him. He did not fulfill his oath in so harsh a matter, judging that he would please God more by not doing what he had sworn in the disturbance of anger to do as harm than by carrying it out.

When the Gibeonites, besieged by the kings of the Amorites, had sent to Joshua for help, Scripture continues and says: "And Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the warrior people with him, all mighty in strength. And the Lord said to Joshua: Do not fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands; not one of them shall stand before you." Here the Lord was not even consulted as to whether they should go to them; but of his own accord he foretold the coming victory to those who rightly wished to help their own. In the same way, then, though not consulted about the Gibeonites themselves, he could have warned who they were when they were lying that they came from far away, had he not been pleased with that oath, which compelled them to spare those who had submitted. For the Gibeonites had believed in God, whom they had heard had promised his people that he would overthrow those nations and that they would take possession of their land; and he rewarded this faith of theirs, in a way, by not betraying them.

It is asked how Adonibezek, king of the city of Jerusalem, and the four others with whom he besieged the Gibeonites, are, according to the Seventy translators, first called kings of the Jebusites when they gathered to besiege them, but afterward called kings of the Amorites by the Gibeonites themselves when they sent messengers to Joshua to deliver them from the siege. Yet, as far as we have been able to examine the translation made from the Hebrew, in both places they are called kings of the Amorites. It is certain, however, that the king of the city of Jerusalem was king of the Jebusites, since that city was called Jebus as being the chief city of that nation; and Scripture very often mentions seven nations which God promised he would wipe out before the face of his people, of which one is said to be that of the Amorites. Perhaps, then, this name was a general one for them all, or rather for the greater part, so that not one but several of the seven were included under this name; although there was also one of the seven that was properly called the Amorites. In the same way there is a certain region properly called Libya, although this name applies to the whole of Africa; and a certain region properly called Asia, although some have taken Asia to be half the world and others a third of it. For it is well known that the Canaanites too are mentioned as one nation among those seven, and yet that whole land was originally called Canaan.

"Joshua left nothing that breathed in it. As the Lord had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did; he did not transgress anything of all that the Lord had commanded Moses." For this reason it must by no means be thought cruelty that Joshua left no one alive in the cities delivered to him, for God had commanded it. Those who suppose from this that God himself was cruel, and therefore refuse to believe that the true God was the author of the Old Testament, judge the works of God as perversely as they judge the sins of men. They do not know what each person deserves to suffer, and they think it a great evil when things that are bound to fall are thrown down and mortals die.

"And there was no city that was not delivered to the children of Israel." It is asked how this can be true, since neither later, in the times of the judges, nor in the times of the kings, were the Hebrews able to capture absolutely all the cities of those seven nations. But either it must be understood to mean that Joshua approached no city in war that he did not capture; or certainly that no city was left uncaptured among those that were in the regions mentioned above. For the regions are listed in which lay the cities about which this conclusion is drawn: "and he took them all in battle."

"For it was brought about by the Lord that their heart was strengthened, so that they went out to battle against Israel, in order that they might be destroyed, so that no mercy should be shown them, but that they should be destroyed, as the Lord said to Moses." The phrase "it was brought about by the Lord that their heart was strengthened" means that their heart was hardened, as was said of Pharaoh. We must not doubt in the least that this is done justly by a high divine judgment, when God abandons and the enemy takes possession; and it is to be understood here just as it is there. But something else raises a question here: how it can be said that their heart was strengthened for this purpose, that they would rise up to war against Israel and that for this reason the Israelites would not show them mercy, as though mercy were to be shown them if they did not fight, when God had commanded that none of them be spared, and when the Israelites spared the Gibeonites for this reason only, that by pretending to have come from a distant land they had obtained their oath. But since the Israelites did of their own accord show mercy to some, even against God's command, we must understand this to be said in order to show that these nations fought in such a way that they would not be spared, and that the Israelites themselves would not be moved by them to mercy in neglect of God's command. Under the leadership of Joshua, who carefully kept all the divine commands, we must not believe this could have happened. Nevertheless, even he would not have destroyed them so quickly had they not come against him in a close alliance; and thus it could have happened that, if they had not been subdued by him, who was careful to fulfill God's commands, they would have survived until a time when, after Joshua's death, they could be spared by those who did not carry out the Lord's commands with such care. For even while he was still living the Israelites spared some, merely bringing them under their rule; and some they could not conquer at all. But these things were not done under his leadership. They were done when, already old, he had retired from war and was only dividing the land among them, so that, without his fighting, they might hold the lands allotted to them, some already empty of enemies, others to be taken by fighting. And that their inability to conquer certain peoples was part of a fitting divine providence will be made clear in certain passages of the Scriptures.

"And Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanite who lived in Gezer; and the Canaanite lived in Ephraim to this day, until Pharaoh king of Egypt came up and took the city and burned it with fire, and pierced through the Canaanites and the Perizzites and those who lived in Gezer; and Pharaoh gave it as a dowry to his daughter." I wonder whether we ought to understand what is said about King Pharaoh as spoken prophetically, since this history is believed to have been written at a time when those events were recent. And what great thing could have been chosen to be spoken prophetically, when past things are narrated and greater and most necessary future things are passed over in silence? It is rather to be supposed that the Seventy translators, who are said to have translated with prophetic authority, as their wonderful agreement shows, added these words, not as foretelling future events, but because they themselves lived at a time when they remembered that these things had happened and had read of them in the books of Kingdoms; for it happened in the times of the kings. This seemed all the more credible to us because we examined the translation made from the Hebrew and did not find this passage there; just as we did not find there what is said about Jericho, that Hoza, who rebuilt it, incurred the curse that Joshua had pronounced. For it is written thus: "And Joshua swore an oath on that day: Cursed be the man who will raise up and build that city; on his firstborn he shall lay its foundation, and on his youngest he shall set up its gates." This much is found in the translation from the Hebrew; but what follows, "And so did Hoza, the man from Bethel: on Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and on his youngest, who survived, he set up its gates," is not read there. Hence it appears that it was inserted by the Seventy, who knew that it had happened.

"And the Amorite remained to live in Elom and in Salamin; and the hand of Ephraim was heavy upon them, and they became tributaries to them." This was already being done against the Lord's command, and Joshua was still alive; but on account of his old age he was no longer their leader in those battles. That is why it was said to have been brought about by the Lord that the heart of those who conspired together to go to war against Joshua was strengthened: so that this mercy would not be shown to them even against God's command, as might have happened if they had remained unconquered and, when Joshua grew old or died, had been left to be conquered by the children of Israel, who could spare them against the Lord's command, which he would not have done.

It is rightly asked, since Israel did not uproot the nations that held the land of promise, not only up to the day of Joshua's death but even afterward, although they partly subdued them and settled in that same promised inheritance, how we are to understand what is said: "And the Lord gave Israel all the land that he had sworn to give to their fathers; and they inherited it and lived in it. And the Lord gave them rest round about, as he had sworn to their fathers; not one of all their enemies stood before their face; the Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands. Not one of all the good words that the Lord spoke to the children of Israel failed; all came to pass."

Everything, then, must be considered carefully. And first we must see the land of how many nations was promised to the Israelites. Seven nations, indeed, are mentioned again and again, as we read in Exodus: And the Lord said to Moses: Go, go up from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, saying: To your offspring I will give it. And at the same time I will send my angel before your face, and he will drive out the Amorite and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Girgashite and the Hivite and the Jebusite and the Canaanite. So it seems that God promised the fathers the land of these seven nations. It is also written in Deuteronomy, much more explicitly: But if you approach a city to attack it and call on them to make peace, and if they give you a peaceful answer and open to you, all the people who are found in the city shall be your tributaries and subject to you; but if they do not submit to you and make war against you, you shall besiege it, and the Lord your God will deliver it into your hands, and you shall kill every male in it with the edge of the sword, except the women and the household goods; and all the cattle and everything that is in the city and all its goods you shall take as plunder for yourself; and you shall eat all the plunder of your enemies whom the Lord your God gives you. So you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not among the cities of these nations. But of these cities, whose land the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall not keep alive anything that lives, but you shall utterly devote them to destruction: the Hittite and the Amorite and the Canaanite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite and the Girgashite, as the Lord your God has commanded you. Here too it is plain that the land of these seven nations was promised as an inheritance, which the Israelites were to possess once those same nations had been fought down to the point of annihilation. As for the others, found farther away beyond these nations, he wished them to become their tributaries if they did not resist; but if they resisted, he wished them too to be killed and given over to destruction, except for the cattle and whatever could be taken as plunder. Again, in another place in Deuteronomy we read: And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to inherit it, and removes great and numerous nations from before you, the Hittite and the Girgashite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Canaanite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations great and numerous and stronger than you, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands and you strike them, you shall utterly exterminate them. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor have mercy on them, nor be joined with them in marriage; you shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, and so on.

Accordingly, in these and other passages of scripture it is often shown that the children of Israel received the lands of these seven nations as an inheritance in such a way that they were to live there not alongside those who held those lands, but in their place. In Genesis, however, not only these seven nations but eleven are promised to the offspring of Abraham. For so we read: On that day the Lord God made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates: the Kenites and the Kenizzites and the Kadmonites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Rephaim and the Amorites and the Canaanites and the Hivites and the Girgashites and the Jebusites. This question is solved if we understand that this was a prophecy given in advance, because Solomon was to extend and enlarge his kingdom to those borders. Of him it is written: And all the plan of Solomon, which he had resolved to build in Jerusalem and in Lebanon and in all the land of his dominion: all the people that was left of the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, who were not of Israel, of their children who remained with them in the land, whom the children of Israel had not finished off — Solomon subjected them to tribute to this day. See: Solomon subjected to tribute the remnants of the peoples who were to be conquered and, by God's command, utterly destroyed; he certainly ought to have destroyed them according to God's command, but nevertheless they were subjugated and held as tributaries. A little later we read: And he ruled over all the kings from the River as far as the land of the Philistines and as far as the borders of Egypt. See where what God had foretold when speaking to Abraham and making his promise in Genesis was fulfilled. For 'from the River' here is understood as from the Euphrates; in those regions 'the great river' can be understood even without its proper name being added. Nor can it be taken to mean the Jordan, since the Israelites had already held lands both on this side of the Jordan and beyond the Jordan even before the reign of Solomon. So the book of Kings said that Solomon's kingdom extended from the river Euphrates in the east to the borders of Egypt, which for them was the west. At that time, then, more was subjugated than those seven nations held, and thus not seven but eleven nations were then reduced to servitude. For what is written in the books of Kings, 'from the River to the borders of Egypt,' where scripture wished to show how far the kingdom extended from east to west, is the same as what was said in Genesis, where the bounds were set from west to east: 'from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates.' For the river of Egypt, the boundary that separates the kingdom of Israel from Egypt, is not the Nile but another, not large, stream that flows past the city of Rhinocorura; from there, going eastward, the land of promise begins. So it had been laid down for the children of Israel that they themselves would inhabit the lands of the seven nations once those nations had been exterminated and destroyed, and would rule over the others, as subjects and tributaries, as far as the river Euphrates. And although they did not obey God in this, since they made some even of those whom they ought to have exterminated their subjects, God nevertheless kept faith with his promise in the time of Solomon.

Now, then, in the book of Joshua son of Nun, which we have undertaken to examine, how will this be true: And the Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give to their fathers; and they inherited it? How did he give them all the land while Joshua was still alive, when they had not yet overcome even the remnants of those seven nations? For what follows, 'and they inherited it,' is true, because they were there and had settled there. Then what it adds, 'And the Lord gave them rest round about, as he had sworn to their fathers,' is true, because while Joshua was still alive the remnants of those nations did not indeed yield to them, yet none of them dared to provoke them to war in the lands where they had settled. That is why the next words were also said: Not one of all their enemies withstood them. And what follows, 'But the Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands,' means that we are to understand as enemies those who dared to come out against them in war. Then what it says, 'Not one of all the good words that the Lord spoke to the children of Israel failed; all came to pass,' is meant to be understood thus: although they had already acted against the Lord's command by sparing some of those seven nations and making them their subjects, they were nevertheless still safe among them. That is why, having said 'of all the words,' it added 'good,' because the curses laid down for those who despise and transgress had not yet come. It remains, then, that the words 'the Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give to their fathers' be understood in this sense: even though there were still remnants of those nations to be crushed and exterminated, or of others as far as the river Euphrates to be either subjugated, if they did not resist, or destroyed, if they resisted, still they were left for Israel's benefit, as a means of training them, so that, being weak in their carnal affections and desires, they would not be unable to bear such great and sudden temporal prosperity with moderation and to their good, but grow proud and perish all the sooner — as will be shown at a suitable point elsewhere. So all the land was given to them, because even the part that had not yet been given into their possession had already been given for a kind of useful training.

As for the words 'Not one of all their enemies withstood them,' one may ask how this is true, since it was written above about the tribe of Dan that their enemies did not allow them to come down into the valley and prevailed against them in the mountains. But what we said when scripture recorded that the twelve sons of Jacob were born in Mesopotamia, where Benjamin had not been born, must be understood here as well: the eleven tribes are reckoned as standing for the whole people, according to the rule that has become well enough known to us from other passages of scripture. But if one asks the reason why this tribe did not obtain sufficient land in the lot that fell to it, and was hard pressed by those who held it, we must believe that it lies in God's secret counsel. Yet when Jacob blessed his sons, he said such things about this Dan that it is thought that the Antichrist will arise from that very tribe. On this we have not undertaken to say more now. This question can also be solved in this way: not one of all their enemies withstood them while they were waging war together under the command of a single leader, before the territories to be defended were divided among the individual tribes.

And in the sacrifices of our saving offerings. Because 'sacrifices' is said in the plural, 'saving offerings' is also in the plural. Here we must note more carefully how one usually speaks of the 'sacrifice of the saving one'; for if we take this to mean Christ, since he himself is called the salvation of God, it is not clear how this word can be understood in the plural: for there is one Lord Jesus Christ. Although people are called christs, that is, anointed ones, through his grace, as we read in the psalm: Do not touch my anointed ones; yet whether they could be called 'saving ones' or 'salvations' is not something one should readily dare to say; for he alone is the savior of the body.

As for what Joshua says about his approaching death, 'But I am running back along the way, as all who are on the earth also do,' in the translation made from the Hebrew we find: 'I am entering upon the way.' So what the Seventy said, 'I am running back,' is to be taken in the sense in which it was said to man, 'until you return to the earth from which you were taken,' so that it is understood as said with respect to the body. But if we wish to take it with respect to the soul, in the way it is put in Ecclesiastes, 'and the spirit will return to God who gave it,' I do not think it can be said of everyone, but only of those who have lived in such a way that they deserve to return to God as to the author by whom they were created. For this cannot rightly be understood of those of whom it is said: a spirit that goes and does not return. Now if this holy man Joshua son of Nun had not added 'as all who are on the earth also do,' there would be no question; for we would believe nothing else of him than what we read that he was worthy of. But since 'as all who are on the earth also do' was added, it is surprising if what the Latin translator rendered 'I am running back' should not rather have been rendered 'I am running through' or 'I am running out,' if that can be said for what the Greek has, apotrecho [?]. For all run through, or run out, the way of this life when they reach its end. But because this word was used where Rebecca's family say to Abraham's servant, 'Here is Rebecca; take her and run back, and let her be the wife of your master's son,' it was translated in the same way here too.

Where the Seventy translators have, 'And I took your father Abraham from beyond the river and led him into all the land,' the translation made from the Hebrew has, 'and I brought him into the land of Canaan.' It is surprising, then, that the Seventy chose to put 'all the land' in place of 'the land of Canaan,' unless they were looking to the prophecy, so that what was foretold as most certainly to come in Christ and in the Church should rather be taken, on the strength of God's promise, as already done; and this is the true offspring of Abraham, not in the children of the flesh but in the children of the promise.

And those who lived in Jericho made war against you. One may ask how this is true, since with their gates shut they only defended themselves within the circuit of their walls. But it is rightly said, because shutting one's gates against an enemy is also part of war. For they did not send envoys to ask for peace. Hence, if it had been said, 'they fought against you,' it would have been false. For war does not involve continuous fighting; sometimes the battles are frequent, sometimes rare, sometimes there are none at all. Yet it is war when there is, in some way, an armed conflict.

What does it mean that, among the other things Joshua son of Nun recalls that the Lord had done for the Israelites, he says: He sent hornets before you and drove them out from before you? This is also read in the book of Wisdom, and yet it is nowhere found to have happened in the record of what was done. Perhaps by the figurative word 'hornets' he meant us to understand the sharpest stings of fear, by which they were pricked, as it were, by flying rumors so that they fled; or hidden spirits of the air, as the psalm says: through evil angels? Unless perhaps someone says that not everything that was done has been written down, and that this too was done visibly, so that he means us to understand real hornets.

What does it mean that Joshua said to the people: You will not be able to serve the Lord, because God is holy? Is it because it is impossible for human frailty to match, as it were, his holiness with perfect service? On hearing this, they ought not only to have chosen his service but also to have placed their confidence in his help and mercy — the mercy understood by the one who says in the psalm: Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified in your sight. But they chose instead to rely on themselves, supposing that they could serve God without any offense; so that already then there began what the apostle described concerning them: For, being ignorant of God's righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. Thus the law was already coming in for them, so that sin might abound, and afterward grace might superabound through Christ the Lord, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

What does it mean that the same Joshua, speaking to the people, says: And now put away the foreign gods that are among you, and direct your hearts to the Lord God of Israel? For we must not believe that they still kept any images of the Gentiles' gods among them, since he had earlier praised their obedience; or indeed, if they had kept them, would such prosperity have followed them after all the threats of the law, when punishment fell on them so severely because one of them had stolen from what was devoted to destruction? Jacob, to be sure, said this to those who had come out with him from Mesopotamia, where idols were worshiped so much that even Rachel stole her father's; but after Jacob's admonition they handed over what they had, which made it clear that he said this to them because he who spoke knew that they had them. Now, however, after this admonition of Joshua son of Nun, no one brought out anything of the kind. Yet we must not think that he gave this command for nothing; for he did not say, 'And now put away the foreign gods, if there are any among you,' but, quite as if he knew they were there, he said, 'that are among you.' The holy prophet, then, perceived that there were in their hearts thoughts about God that were foreign to God, and it was these he urged them to put away. For whoever thinks of God as being such as God is not certainly carries in his thought a foreign and false god. And who is there who thinks of God as he really is? Hence it remains for the faithful, as long as they are away from the Lord, to put away from their hearts the empty phantoms that rush in and thrust themselves upon those who think, as if God were like this or that, which he certainly is not; and to direct their hearts faithfully to him, so that he himself, in the way and to the extent he knows is good for us, may make himself known through his Spirit, until all falsehood is done away with — whence it was said, Every man is a liar — and, when not only ungodly falsehood but even the mirror and the riddle itself have passed away, we may know face to face, even as we are known, as the apostle says: Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known.

And Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day and gave them law and judgment in Shiloh before the tabernacle of the Lord God of Israel. And he wrote these words in the book of the laws of God; and Joshua took a great stone and set it up beneath the terebinth before the Lord. And Joshua said to the people: See, this stone shall be a witness for us, because it has heard all the things that were spoken by the Lord, whatever he has said to you today; and it shall be a witness for you in the last days, when you have lied to the Lord your God. Those who hear these words not only on the surface but examine them somewhat more deeply must by no means think that so great a man was so foolish as to believe that a lifeless stone had heard the words of God that he spoke to the people. Even if it had been shaped by a craftsman into the likeness of a man, it would certainly be counted among those of which the psalm sings: They have ears and will not hear. For it is not that the idols of the nations do not hear only when they are gold and silver, and do hear if they are of stone. Rather, by this stone he surely signified him who was a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the unbelieving Jews, who, though rejected by the builders, became the head of the corner. He was also prefigured by that rock which, struck with a rod of wood, poured out drink for the thirsting people, of which the apostle says: For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. That is also why this outstanding leader circumcised the people with knives of stone; and those stone knives were even buried with him, to point out to later generations a deep mystery that would be of benefit to them. So this stone too, though visibly set up, we ought to understand spiritually as a future witness against the unbelieving Jews, that is, those who lie, of whom the psalm says: The enemies of the Lord have lied to him. For it is not for nothing that, although God's servant Moses — or rather God through him — had already made a covenant with the people, the covenant that was in the ark called the ark of the covenant and written down in the books of the law with such a multitude of sacraments and precepts, it was nevertheless said here too: Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day. For the repetition of the covenant signifies the new covenant; this is also signified by Deuteronomy, which means 'second law,' and by the tablets renewed after the first ones were broken. For what was to be fulfilled in one way had to be signified in many ways. Further, the fact that the stone was set up beneath the terebinth signifies the same as the rod applied to the rock so that water might flow out: here too the stone was not set up without wood. And it was 'beneath' because he would not have been exalted on the cross had he not been brought low in humility; or else because at the time when Joshua son of Nun did this, the mystery still had to be kept in shadow. The wood of the terebinth also exudes a medicinal resin, like a tear; this is the tree the Seventy translators put in this passage, although in other translators we read 'oak.'

It is truly surprising that, at least in his last words addressed to the people, Joshua the man of God did not rebuke them at all for having spared those nations which the Lord had commanded to be utterly destroyed under the ban. For it is written: And it came to pass, after the children of Israel had grown strong, that they made the Canaanites subject to them, but did not utterly exterminate them. At first, as scripture testified, they were not able to do so; but now, after they had prevailed so far as to make them subject, their failure also to exterminate them was certainly done against the Lord's command — something that no one did while Joshua was leading the army. Why, then, did he not rebuke them in his last address for having neglected the Lord's commands in this? Perhaps, since scripture said earlier that they had not been able to — before they prevailed, of course — we should believe that even after they had prevailed they were afraid that, if they refused to spare people who were ready to submit, they would drive them out of sheer desperation to fight against them more fiercely, and then would be unable to overcome them? This human fear, then, the Lord did not wish to hold against them, even though a certain falling short of faith appears in it: had their faith been strong, what attended Joshua himself when he made war would have attended them. But because there was not such great faith in them, even when they had prevailed over their adversaries they did not dare, out of fear, to fight them to the point of destroying them. This fear, as I said, since it arose not from malice or pride or contempt for the Lord's command but from weakness of spirit, the Lord did not wish to hold against them when he spoke to them through the last words of the laws [?]. So also the apostle says: Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. But of those who had deserted him in his danger not out of malice but out of fear, he spoke thus: At my first defense no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be held against them.
BOOK SEVEN. QUESTIONS ON JUDGES.

QUESTION 1. At the end of the book of Joshua son of Nun the narrator briefly carried the history forward to the point where the children of Israel turned aside to worship foreign gods. In this book, however, he returns to the proper order and tells what happened next after the death of Joshua son of Nun. So the book does not begin from the time when the people fell away into the worship of idols, but from the earlier, intervening times in which the events took place that led up to it.

"And it came to pass after Joshua had died that the children of Israel inquired of the Lord, saying: Who will go up with us as leader against the Canaanite, to fight against him? And the Lord said: Judah will go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand." Here the question is whether some man was called Judah, or whether Scripture, as it usually does, gave this name to the tribe itself. Those who had inquired of the Lord were looking for a leader after the death of Joshua son of Nun, and so it is thought that the name of a single man is meant. But Scripture does not usually name leaders when they are appointed without also mentioning the line of their fathers, and it is certain that after Joshua the people of Israel had leaders, the first of whom was Othniel son of Kenaz. So it is more correct to understand that the name Judah signified the tribe of Judah. For the Lord wished the crushing of the Canaanites to begin with that tribe. And since the people had asked about a leader, the Lord's answer served to let them know that God did not want the whole people to make war against the Canaanites. So he said: "Judah will go up." And Scripture goes on to tell: "And Judah said to Simeon his brother" — that is, tribe to tribe. For the sons of Jacob who were called Judah and Simeon, named by their own names among their other brothers, were no longer alive; rather the tribe of Judah said to the tribe of Simeon: "Go up with me into my lot and let us fight against the Canaanite, and I too will go with you into your lot." It is plain that the tribe of Judah asked for the help of another tribe, help it would repay when that tribe in turn came to need it in its own lot.
"And Caleb said: Whoever strikes the City of Letters and takes it first, to him I will give my daughter Achsah as wife." This has already been mentioned in the book of Joshua

son of Nun; but it is fair to ask whether it happened while Joshua was alive and is now repeated by way of recapitulation, or whether it happened after his death, after it was said, "Judah will go up," and Judah began to defeat the Canaanites, the war in which all these things are reported to have been done. It is more credible that it happened after the death of Joshua, and that it was mentioned there by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, like other things too. For here, while the deeds of the tribe of Judah against the Canaanites are being set out, the order of the narrative places it among the other warlike deeds of Judah, of whom the Lord had said after the death of Joshua: "Judah will go up." "And afterward the children of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanite who dwelt in the hill country and the south and the plain. And Judah went against the Canaanite who dwelt in Hebron, and Hebron came out to meet him — now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba-sepher — and he struck Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the sons of Anak. And they went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir was formerly City of Letters. And Caleb said: Whoever strikes the City of Letters and takes it first, to him I will give my daughter Achsah as wife." From this sequence of events, then, so clear as it is, it is certain that this was done after the death of Joshua. But at that earlier point, when the cities given to Caleb himself were being recorded, the narrator took the occasion to go ahead and anticipate what happened later. Yet I do not think it was for nothing that Scripture chose to record twice this account of Caleb's daughter being given as the victor's prize.

Another question arises about Caleb's daughter. In the book of Joshua it is said of her: "And it came to pass when she was going in, she took counsel with him, saying: I will ask my father for a field; and she cried out from her donkey," and so on, where she asks her father for a field and it is granted. But here it says: "And it came to pass when he was going in, Othniel urged her to ask her father for a field." Now there is no contradiction between what is said there, "when she was going in," and what is said here, "when he was going in"; for they were making the journey together. As for what is said there, "she took counsel with him" — that is, with her husband — "saying: I will ask my father for a field; and she cried out from her donkey," and she asked: in that taking of counsel she was urged to ask. One part of this is said there, the other here. Both together would run like this: "And she took counsel with him, saying: I will ask my father for a field; and he urged her. And she cried out from her donkey." Furthermore, there she is reported to have asked for a field, and the name of the field itself is not left unmentioned; but here, though she had been urged by her husband to ask for a field, she is not said to have asked for a field when "crying out from her beast of burden" — what is called "from her donkey" there — but for the redemption of water, because she had been given away into a land of the south. And Scripture adds: "And Caleb gave her, according to her heart, the redemption of the heights and the redemption of the lowlands." What this means is obscure, unless perhaps the field itself was requested so that from its produce she would have the means to buy water, which was scarce in the regions to which she was being led as a bride. But in "Caleb gave her the redemption of the heights and the redemption of the lowlands," I do not see what we are to understand as implied except "of streams": of the heights, that is, in the hill country, and of the lowlands in the plains or the valleys.

"And Judah did not inherit Gaza and its territory, and Ashkelon and its territory, and Ekron and its territory, and Ashdod and the lands adjoining it. And the Lord was with Judah. And he inherited the hill country, because he could not inherit the inhabitants of the valley, since Rechab stood against them, and he had chariots of iron." When I was dealing with the passage in the book of Joshua where it is written, "And the Lord gave Israel all the land," although they did not yet possess many parts of it, I said that it could be understood that all the land was given in this sense: the land that was not given as a possession was given for a certain useful purpose of training. This appears much more plainly here, since the cities that Judah did not inherit are listed, and it is said: "And the Lord was with Judah. And he inherited the hill country, because they could not inherit the inhabitants of the valley." For who would not understand that this very thing too belonged to the fact that the Lord was with Judah, so that he should not be puffed up by gaining everything at once? As for the addition, "since Rechab stood against them, and he had chariots of iron," it is said that those chariots were feared not by the Lord, who was in Judah, but by Judah himself. And if it is asked why Judah, with whom the Lord was, was afraid, this is what we must wisely understand: God in his favor checks, even in the hearts of his own people, the excesses of too great prosperity, so that he turns enemies to their benefit not only when the enemies are conquered but also when they are feared — the one to commend his generosity, the other to curb their pride. For surely the angel of Satan is an enemy of the saints, yet the apostle says that it was given to him to buffet him, so that he would not be puffed up by the greatness of the revelations.

"And they gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said; and he inherited from there the three cities of the sons of Anak, and he drove out from there the three sons of Anak." This was already said in the book of Joshua, since it was done while he was alive; but here it is recorded again by way of recapitulation, since Scripture was speaking of the tribe of Judah, to which Caleb belonged.

It is asked how it can be said: "And the children of Benjamin did not inherit the Jebusite who dwelt in Jerusalem; and the Jebusite has dwelt with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day," when we read above that this same city was captured and burned by Judah, and the Jebusites in it killed. But we should recognize that two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, held this city in common, as is shown by the very division of the land made by Joshua son of Nun. For Jebus is the same as Jerusalem. That is why these two tribes remained with the temple of the Lord when the others — apart from Levi, which was the priestly tribe and received no land in the division — separated themselves from the kingdom of Judah under Jeroboam. We must understand, then, that the city was indeed captured and burned by Judah and those found there were killed, but that not all the Jebusites were wiped out, either because they were outside the city or because they were able to flee; and that these remaining Jebusites were allowed by the children of Benjamin, with whom, together with Judah, the city was held in common, to live in it alongside them. So when it is said, "The children of Benjamin did not inherit the Jebusite," it is to be understood that they either could not or would not even make them tributaries. Or at any rate, "he did not inherit the Jebusite" was said because he did not hold the land that the Jebusite possessed without the Jebusite still being there.

"And Manasseh did not inherit Beth-shan, which is a city of the Scythians." Today it is said to be called Scythopolis. Someone may be puzzled how there could be a city of the Scythians in those parts, so far removed from Scythia.
