But one could equally be puzzled how Alexander the Macedonian founded the city of Alexandria so far from Macedonia — which of course he did by waging war far and wide. In the same way, when the Scythians at one time advanced into distant lands by waging war, they could have founded this city. For we read in the history of the nations that the Scythians once held almost the whole of Asia, when they went out to meet the king of the Egyptians who had unprovoked declared war on them, and he, terrified at their approach, withdrew into his own kingdom.
"And Manasseh did not inherit Beth-shan, which is a city of the Scythians, nor its daughters." By "its daughters" he means the towns which it had founded, as a kind of mother city.

"And it came to pass when Israel grew strong, that he put the Canaanite to tribute, and did not utterly drive him out." Something of this kind was already said in the book of Joshua, in almost the same words. So either it is said here by anacephalaeosis or it was said there by prolepsis, that is, either here by recapitulation or there by anticipation.

"And the Amorite pressed hard on the children of Dan in the hill country, for he did not allow them to come down into the valley." This too, likewise, was either recorded in the book of Joshua by anticipation or is recorded here by recapitulation.

"And the angel of the Lord went up to Klauthmon." The writer of the book called the place by this name because he wrote later; for when the angel of the Lord went up to it, it was not yet so called. It took its name, of course, from weeping, because in Greek weeping is called klauthmos [?]. For there the people wept when they heard from this angel the words of the Lord punishing them for having been disobedient, because they did not exterminate, according to his command, the peoples over whom they had prevailed, choosing to make them tributaries rather than to kill and destroy them as the Lord had ordered. Whether they did this out of contempt for God's command or out of fear — lest they force their enemies to fight against them more fiercely to save their lives than they would to avoid paying tribute — they undoubtedly sinned, either by scorning what was commanded by God or by not trusting that he who had given the command could help them. He did not wish to say this to them through Joshua — if indeed he had already commanded it to be done while Joshua was still alive, and it was not rather recorded by anticipation, something that began to be done after his death — because he wished to reproach all of them for it through the angel; and while Joshua was alive not all had yet done it, even if some had perhaps already begun. It is more credible, however, that nothing of the kind began to be done while Joshua son of Nun was alive, and that under him the children of Israel held only as much land as was enough for them to settle in, although they had within their lots the means by which, as they grew and gained strength, they might go on to exterminate their adversaries. Accordingly, after the death of Joshua, once they had grown strong enough to be able to do this, they preferred to keep them as tributaries according to their own will rather than to kill and destroy them according to the will of God; and for this reason the angel was sent to rebuke them. As for its being recorded in the book of Joshua, I rather think it was recorded by anticipation: either Joshua himself already knew by the prophetic Spirit that it would happen after his death, if the book called Joshua son of Nun was written by him; or, if it was written by someone else, that writer knew that it had already happened after Joshua's death, and recorded it in that book by anticipation.

What does the angel of the Lord mean when, among the other things God threatens, he says: "I will not again remove the people whom I said I would drive out [I will not take them away] from before you; and they will be a distress to you, and their gods will be a stumbling block to you" — unless we are to understand that some sins also come from the wrath of God? For God, in his indignation, threatened this: that the gods of the nations among whom the Israelites chose to live, without having exterminated them, would be a stumbling block to them — that is, would make them stumble with regard to the Lord their God and live in a way that offended him. And this is certainly a great sin, as is plain.

"And Joshua dismissed the people; and the children of Israel went away, each to his own house and each to his own inheritance, to inherit the land." There is no doubt that this is repeated by way of recapitulation. For the death of Joshua son of Nun himself is also recorded in this book, so that everything may be briefly set out, as it were from the beginning, from the time the Lord gave them the land, as well as how they lived under the judges themselves and what they suffered; and then the narrative returns again to the sequence of the judges themselves, starting from the one who was appointed first.

"And another generation rose up after them, who did not know the Lord and his works which he did for Israel." He has explained in what sense he said "they did not know the Lord": namely, in those glorious and wonderful works through which it had come about, before their time, that Israel knew the Lord.

"And they served Baal and the Astartes." It is commonly said that among the peoples of those parts Baal is a name for Jupiter and Astarte for Juno, and the Punic language is thought to show this. For the Carthaginians appear to use Baal to mean "lord": thus by Baalsamen they are understood to mean, as it were, "lord of heaven," since among them the heavens are called samen. And Juno is undoubtedly called Astarte by them. Since these languages do not differ much from one another, it is rightly believed that Scripture is saying here that the children of Israel served Baal and the Astartes, meaning Jupiter and the Junos. Nor should it trouble us that it did not say "Astarte," that is, Juno, but put the name in the plural, as though there were many Junos. It wanted the meaning to refer to the multitude of idols, since each idol of Juno was called Juno; and thus it wanted us to understand as many Junos as there were idols. I think it chose to mention Jupiter in the singular and the Junos in the plural for the sake of variety; for by the same reasoning, because of the many idols, one could also speak of Jupiters in the plural. This plural form, "Junos," we find in the Greek texts according to the Septuagint, while in the Latin it was in the singular. Among these, in the one that did not have the Septuagint translation but was made from the Hebrew, we read "Astaroth," and not "Baal" but "Baalim." But if perhaps these names mean something else in the Hebrew or Syriac language, it is still certain that these were other and false gods, whom Israel ought not to have served.

"And he sold them into the hand of their enemies round about." People often ask why he said "sold," as though some price were to be understood as having been paid. But we also read in the psalm: "You sold your people for no price," and in the prophet: "You were sold for nothing, and you will not be redeemed with silver." Why then "sold," if it was "for nothing" and "for no price," and not rather "given away"? Or is it perhaps a usage of the Scriptures that someone who is given away can also be called sold? But the best sense of the words "You were sold for nothing" and "You sold your people for no price" is this: those to whom you handed over your people were ungodly, and they did not earn the handing over of that people to them by worshiping God, in such a way that their worship might be seen as a kind of price. And when it is said, "nor will you be redeemed with silver," he does not say "nor with a price," but "nor with silver," so that we may understand the price of redemption of which the apostle Peter speaks: "For you were not redeemed with silver and gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish." For by "silver" the prophet signified all money when he said, "you will not be redeemed with silver," since they were indeed to be redeemed at the price of the blood of Christ, but not at a price paid in money.

In what the Lord says — "And I will not again remove a man from before them out of the nations that Joshua son of Nun left; and he let them remain in order to test Israel by them, whether they would keep the way of the Lord and walk in it as their fathers kept it, or not. And the Lord let these nations remain, so as not to remove them quickly, and he did not hand them over into the hand of Joshua" — the reason is shown clearly enough why Joshua did not destroy all those nations in war: if this had happened, there would have been none by whom these people could be tested. And those nations could have served their benefit, if, tested by them, they were not found reprobate; and once they were found to be such as the Lord had commanded them to be, those nations would then have been removed from before them, if they lived in that way, and there would be no need for them to be exercised by wars. For the words of the Lord are to be taken as extending up to this point: "Because this nation has so forsaken my covenant, which I commanded their fathers, and they have not obeyed my voice, I too will not again remove a man from before them" — that is, an adversary. The remaining words, however, are those of the writer, explaining why the Lord said he would not remove a man from the nations that Joshua son of Nun left. Then, adding the reason why he left them, he says: "and he let them remain in order to test Israel by them, whether they would keep the way of the Lord and walk in it as their fathers kept it, or not," meaning us to understand that the fathers who kept the way of the Lord were those who were with Joshua, that is, at the time when he was alive. For above he reported that another generation rose up after those who lived with Joshua, and that with them began the transgressions that offended the Lord; and to test them, that is, to prove them, the nations had been left and not exterminated by Joshua.

Then, lest it be thought that Joshua had acted on his own counsel, as a merely human decision, in leaving those nations, Scripture adds: "And the Lord let these nations remain, so as not to remove them quickly; and he did not hand them over into the hand of Joshua." Then it goes on: "And these are the nations which Joshua left, in order to test Israel by them, all who had not known all the wars of Canaan, but for the sake of the generations of the children of Israel, to teach them war." This, then, was the reason in their testing: that they should learn to wage war, that is, to wage war with as much godliness and obedience to the law of God as their fathers, who pleased the Lord God even in waging war — not because war is something to be desired, but because godliness is praiseworthy even in war. As for what follows, "but those before them did not know them," what does he mean us to understand but the nations which those who lived before these people did not know through war — the nations left for these people's testing, that is, their proving? Then, listing what they were, he says: "five satrapies of the foreigners," which he sets out more plainly in the books of Kingdoms. Satrapies are, as it were, small kingdoms over which satraps presided: a name that is, or was, a title of a certain rank in those parts. "And all the Canaanites," he says, "and the Sidonians and the Hivites who dwelt in Lebanon, from Mount Hermon as far as Lebo-hamath. And it came about that Israel was tested by them." As if to say: this was done so that Israel might be tested by them, "to know whether they would listen to the commandments of the Lord" — not so that God, who knows all things, even those to come, might know, but so that they themselves might know, and by their own conscience either glory or stand convicted, whether they listened to the commandments of the Lord "which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses." Since, then, it was made plain to them that they had not obeyed God in the matter of these nations, which had been left for their testing, that is, for their exercise and proving, God therefore spoke either those words in which the angel was openly sent and spoke more explicitly, or those a little earlier, where he says: "Because this nation has so forsaken my covenant, which I commanded their fathers, and they have not obeyed my voice, I too will not again remove a man from before them."

Now in Deuteronomy it is said in the person of God, speaking about these hostile nations: "I will not drive them out in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you; little by little I will drive them out, until you multiply and grow and inherit the land." The Lord could have kept this promise of his toward the obedient, so that the extermination of those nations would take place as the territory of the Israelites grew, since their great numbers would not let the lands from which the adversaries were driven out lie desolate. But as for his saying, "lest the wild beasts multiply against you," it would be surprising if he did not mean us to understand, in a way, the bestial desires and lusts that tend to arise from a sudden success in earthly prosperity. For God could hardly have been able to exterminate men and yet unable to destroy the beasts, or rather to prevent them from being born at all.

"And the Lord raised up a savior for Israel, and he saved them." Then, as if someone asked which savior, it says, "Othniel the son of Kenaz." Here we must take the name in the accusative case, as if it said "Othnielem." We should note that Scripture also calls a man a savior when God saves people through him. For "the children of Israel cried to the Lord; and the Lord raised up a savior for Israel, and he saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb, and he heard them." Among the figures called hyperbata, this kind is rare, because it also contains what the Greeks call hysterologia. If the later words "and he heard them" were put first, the passage would be clearer. The order is: "And the children of Israel cried to the Lord, and he heard them, and the Lord raised up a savior for Israel." Then there are the words inserted here, "and he saved them," followed by "Othniel" (that is, "Othnielem") "the son of Kenaz." It would be plainer if it read: "And the Lord raised up as a savior for Israel Othniel the son of Kenaz, and he saved them."

Scripture testifies that under the judge Othniel the land of promise rested from wars for forty years, which is as much peace as the beginnings of the Roman Empire managed to enjoy, and then only under King Numa Pompilius.

It may be asked whether the judge Ehud lied when he killed Eglon, king of Moab. While he was lying in wait to strike him, alone with the king, he said to him, "I have a secret word for you, O king," so that the king would send away everyone who was with him. When this had been done, Ehud said again, "I have a word of God for you, O king." But this need not be a lie, since Scripture often uses "word" for a deed as well, and that is in fact what it was. As for his saying "a word of God," we should understand that God had commanded him to do this. God had raised him up as a savior for his people, and in those times such things had to be done at God's command.

It is fair to ask how King Eglon could have been "very thin" when "the fat closed over the wound" when he was struck. We should understand that this was said in the kind of expression that is meant to be taken in the opposite sense. In the same way a grove is called lucus because it has very little light [lux], and people answer "there's plenty" when there is none, and "he blessed the king" is said for "he cursed the king," as is written about Naboth in the book of Kings. In fact, in the translation made not from the Septuagint but from the Hebrew, we find: "Now Eglon was very fat."

"And Ehud went out and passed the guards, and he shut the doors of the upper room on him and locked them." This is said by way of recapitulation, to supply what had been left out. We must understand that he did this first, and only then came down from the upper rooms and passed the guards.

One might be puzzled how King Eglon's servants opened with a key what Ehud had not locked with a key; or, if he had locked it with a key, why he did not take the key with him so that they could not open it with a key. So either another key was brought, or the lock was of a kind that could be shut without a key but not opened without one. There are such locks, like those called ueruclata [?].
Under the judge Ehud, Israel had peace in the land of promise for eighty years, twice as long, that is, as the memorable peace the Romans had under King Numa Pompilius.

"And after him arose Shamgar the son of Anath, and he struck down six hundred men of the foreigners, besides the calves of the oxen, and he saved Israel." It may be asked how this man fought for Israel after Ehud, and how he is said to have saved Israel, since they had not again been taken captive or bound under the yoke of slavery. But "he saved" should be understood to mean not that the enemy had done any harm, but that the enemy was not allowed to do harm. We should believe that the enemy had begun to try war and was driven off by this man's victory. What is meant by the added phrase "besides the calves of the oxen" is obscure. Perhaps he also slaughtered oxen in the fighting, and so it says that he killed six hundred men, besides what he did in killing oxen? But why "calves"? Perhaps it is a Greek idiom to call even full-grown cattle calves. People in Egypt are said to speak this way commonly, just as among us hens of any age are called chicks. The translation from the Hebrew does not have "besides the calves of the oxen," as this one based on the Septuagint does. Instead, the one from the Hebrew says that six hundred men were killed with a ploughshare, which this one does not have.

What does Barak mean when he answers Deborah, "If you will go, I will go; and if you will not go with me, I will not go, for I do not know the day on which the Lord prospers the angel with me"? Was it as though he could not hear the day from a prophetess? And she did not tell him the day but went with him. And what does "the Lord prospers the angel with me" mean? Does it show that the actions of angels too are prospered, that is, helped by the Lord so that they turn out well? Or is "prospers the angel with me" an idiom meaning "gives me success through an angel"?

"And the Lord struck Sisera and all his chariots with terror." See how Scripture teaches that God works in people's hearts in order to bring about the outcome he has determined. He certainly struck Sisera with terror, or with confusion, in order to hand him over.

Where Jael, the woman who killed Sisera, had spoken to Barak, who was looking for him, Scripture says of Barak that "he went in to her." We should note that when Scripture says a man went in to some woman, it does not necessarily follow that he lay with her. Scripture does often say "he went in to her" meaning only that he had intercourse with her. But here "he went in to her" is meant literally: he went into her house. These words do not refer to intercourse.

In the song of Deborah it says: "The inhabitants of Israel failed, they failed, until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel. They chose new gods like barley bread; then they overthrew the cities of the princes." Here the jumbled word order makes the passage obscure and raises a question. How are we to understand "They chose new gods like barley bread; then they overthrew the cities of the princes"? It sounds as though God favored them in overthrowing the cities of the princes at the very time they chose new gods like barley bread. But we have often learned from other passages of Scripture how hyperbata arise, and when they are straightened out and the words return to their proper order, the sense becomes clear. This, then, is the order: "The inhabitants of Israel failed, they failed; they chose new gods like barley bread, until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel; then they overthrew the cities of the princes."

It may be asked how it can be said, "They chose new gods like barley bread." Barley bread, though it is to be rejected in comparison with wheat bread, still nourishes and is food that sustains life. But the new gods, which those who fell away from the living God are said to have chosen, cannot be counted as food for the soul, but rather as poison. Perhaps the comparison should be taken only as far as it holds. Then it would be understood as said for this one reason: just as it often happens through a jaded appetite that people reject what they ought to choose and enjoy what they ought to despise, so through the fault of a perverse will, as if through the sickness of a jaded appetite, they scorned the truth. Though they had the true God as their God, what they chose in the false gods was nothing but novelty. And so they chose deadly food as if it were barley bread, thinking not that they would perish by it, but that they would even get life from it, as from food that was harmless, though cheaper. So the comparison is made according to their opinion and their sickness of mind, not according to the truth, for those new gods cannot be compared to any life-giving food.

"And it happened when the children of Israel cried to the Lord because of Midian, that the Lord sent a man, a prophet, to the children of Israel, and he said to them." Why this prophet's name is not given, which is very unusual in Scripture, is a hidden matter, though I do not think there is no reason for it. After the words in which he reproached the people for their disobedience, Scripture goes on to say, "And the angel of the Lord came and sat under the oak that was in Ophrah." So it is not absurd to understand that this angel is meant by the word "man," and that after speaking these words he came to the oak mentioned and sat there. It is well known that angels are often called men. Still, it is not easy to find a clear case where one who was an angel is called a prophet, though we do read of one who was a prophet being called an angel. But if angels are known to have spoken prophetically, that is, to have foretold things to come, why could an angel not be called by the name of prophet? Yet, as I have said, no explicit and clear testimony on this point comes to mind.

When the angel says to Gideon, "The Lord is with you, mighty in strength," the phrase is in the nominative case, not the vocative. That is, it means "The Lord, the mighty one, is with you," not "you mighty one."

We should note that when the angel was speaking to Gideon, he said, as if on the Lord's own authority, "Have I not sent you?" For who sent him, if not the one who sent the angel to him? Deborah, by contrast, did not say to Barak, "Have I not commanded you?" but "Has not the Lord God of Israel commanded you?" Here, however, it does not say, "Has not the Lord sent you?" but "Have I not sent you?"

Gideon answers the angel, "In me, lord" (that is, "Look at me"), "by what means shall I save Israel? Look, my thousand is the weakest in Manasseh." This is taken to mean that he was in command of a thousand men, such commanders being called chiliarchs in the Greek of Scripture. Or does it mean something else?

We should note that Gideon does not say to the angel, "I will offer a sacrifice to you," but "I will offer my sacrifice and set it before you." From this we should understand that he wanted to offer the sacrifice not to the angel but through the angel. The angel himself shows this clearly. He did not take the sacrifice from him as if it were for himself, but said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened bread and put them on that rock, and pour out the broth." And when Gideon had done this, "the angel of the Lord stretched out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread, and fire flared up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread." So the angel himself performed the office of a minister in the sacrifice that Gideon offered. A human minister, being human, would have lit the fire without a miracle; this angel, being an angel, lit it miraculously. Only then did Gideon realize that he was an angel of the Lord, for Scripture immediately adds, "And Gideon saw that he was an angel of the Lord." Before this, then, he spoke to him as to a man, though he believed him to be a man of God, so that he wanted to offer the sacrifice in his presence, as if he would be helped by the presence of his holiness.

It may be asked why Gideon dared to offer sacrifice to God somewhere other than the place God had commanded. For God had forbidden sacrifice to be offered to him anywhere except at his tabernacle, which was later succeeded by the temple. In Gideon's time the tabernacle of God was at Shiloh, so sacrifice could lawfully be offered only there. But we should understand that Gideon had at first taken that angel for a prophet and consulted him as he would consult God about offering the sacrifice. If the angel had forbidden it, it certainly would not have been done. But since he approved and agreed that it should be done, Gideon followed God's authority in doing it. For God established those legal ordinances to give laws to human beings, not to himself. So whatever God himself commands outside those ordinances should be understood as carried out not by transgressors but rather by the devout and obedient, like Abraham with the sacrifice of his son. In the same way Elijah sacrificed outside the Lord's tabernacle in order to refute the priests of the idols. We must understand that he did so by command of the Lord, who told him to do it through revelation and inspiration, as he would a prophet. Yet the custom of sacrificing outside the tabernacle had become so common that even Solomon is found to have sacrificed on the high places, and his sacrifice was not rejected. Still, the kings who, along with their praiseworthy deeds, did not destroy the high places, where the people had grown used to sacrificing against God's law, are censured, and the king who did destroy them is praised all the more. So God tolerated rather than forbade the custom of his people, by which they made offerings outside his tabernacle, yet not to foreign gods but to the Lord their God, and even so he heard those who offered. But as for what Gideon did, who does not see that the angel arranged it so that it would happen prophetically, and that in this prophecy that rock was being commended to us? Sacrifice was not offered to the rock, of course, but fire is recorded as coming out of it to consume the sacrifice. The gift of the Holy Spirit, which Christ the Lord has poured out on us so abundantly, is signified both by the water that the rock poured out when it was struck in the wilderness and by fire. In the gospel this gift is signified by water, where the Lord himself says, "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." There the evangelist added, "Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive." It is also signified by fire, where we read that when the Spirit came upon those gathered together, "there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it rested on each one of them." And the Lord himself says, "I came to cast fire upon the earth."

"And the number of those who lapped with their hand, with their tongue, was three hundred men." Most Latin manuscripts do not have "with their hand," but only "with their tongue," because that is how they understood what was said above, "like dogs." The Greek, however, has both, "with their hand, with their tongue," so that we understand that they scooped up water with their hand and tossed it into their mouth. This was like dogs drinking. Dogs do not put their mouths to the water and draw in what they drink, as oxen do, but snatch it into their mouths with their tongues. These men are understood to have done the same, except that they tossed the water into their mouths with their hand and caught it with their tongue. The translation from the Hebrew puts it more plainly in these words: "So the number of those who had lapped, tossing the water into their mouth with their hand, was three hundred men." People do not usually drink by scooping up water with their tongue like dogs without using their hands, nor had these men been commanded to do so. But when they had gone down to the water to drink, many knelt down and drank, since that was easier and less effort. A few did not bend the knee but stooped, and drank like dogs, but with water tossed into their mouths by hand. Their number, three hundred, suggests the sign of the cross because of the Greek letter T, which stands for this number. The fact that it is a Greek letter also foreshadows that the Gentiles were more likely to believe in the Crucified. That is why the apostle uses the name "Greeks" for all the Gentiles when he says "to the Jew first and to the Greek" and "to Jews and Greeks," often mentioning circumcision and uncircumcision in this way, since Greek stands out so among the languages of the Gentiles that they can all fittingly be signified by it. This number should also be noted in the servants born in Abraham's house, with whom he freed his kinsman from the enemy, when Melchizedek blessed him in a great mystery. There were eighteen more than three hundred, for they are said to have been three hundred and eighteen. The extra eighteen seem to me to signify the time in which this would happen, namely the third, which was to be the time under grace. For the first time is before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace. Each of these times is signified by the number six because of its perfection, and three sixes make eighteen. That is also why the woman whom the Savior found bent over had been ill for eighteen years, and he straightened her up and freed her from the devil's bond, as the gospel tells. As for the fact that the men through whom Gideon was to win were chosen in such a way that they were said to drink like dogs, this signifies that the Lord chose what is contemptible and lowly, for the dog is held in contempt. Hence he says, "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs." And David, to cast himself down as someone contemptible, called himself a dog when speaking to Saul.

What is meant by what is written of Gideon, "He went down, he and Purah his servant, to the part of the fifty who were in the camp"? Some Latin manuscripts have "to the part where there were fifty guards each in the camp," while others have "to the fiftieth part, into the camp." The obscure phrasing has given rise to several different renderings by the translators. Either it was the part of the camp guarded by fifty men, or, if we are to understand that there were fifty guards at each post all around, they went down to one part where there were fifty.

The man whom Gideon overheard telling his neighbor a dream, so that Gideon would be assured of the coming victory, said he had seen a cake of barley bread rolling through the camp, striking the tent of Midian and overturning it. I think this should be understood in the same way as the dogs: through what the world despises, which is what the cake of barley bread signifies, the Savior was going to put the proud to shame.
Gideon ordered his three hundred to shout, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon," that is, for this Gideon. This signifies that the sword would accomplish what pleased the Lord and Gideon.

People often ask what an ephud, or ephod, is. If it is a priestly garment, as most say, or rather an overgarment, called in Greek ependyma or epomis, which might better be rendered in Latin as superhumerale, a garment worn over the shoulders, then it is fair to be puzzled how Gideon made it out of so much gold. For it is written: "And the weight of the gold earrings that he had asked for was one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold, besides the bracelets and the necklaces and the purple coverings that were on the kings of Midian, besides the collars that were on the necks of their camels. And Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel went whoring after it there, and it became a stumbling block to Gideon and his house." How, then, could this garment have been made from so much gold? For Samuel's mother also made for her son, as we read, an "ephud bar," which some have translated "linen ephod," when she gave him to the Lord to be brought up in the temple. There it appears more clearly that this was a kind of garment. Or was it said that "he set it up in his city" so that we would understand from this that it was made of gold? For it does not say "he put it" but "he set it up," because it was so solid and strong that it could be set up, that is, stand where it was placed.

So when Gideon had done this unlawful thing, all Israel went whoring after it, that is, by following it against the law of God. It is fair to ask here how Scripture can call it fornication on the part of the people who followed and revered it, since it was not an idol, that is, the image of some false and foreign god, but an ephod, one of the sacred objects of the tabernacle, belonging to the priestly vestments. The reason, of course, is that it was not lawful to make anything of the kind outside God's tabernacle, where the things were kept that God had commanded to be made there. That is why Scripture goes on to say: "And it became a stumbling block to Gideon and to his house," that is, it led him to fall away from God, whom he had offended. For this too was in a way a kind of idol: something made by hand and worshipped as God outside God's tabernacle. Yet the very things that God commanded to be made in the tabernacle were meant to serve the worship of God; none of them was to be worshipped as God or as an image of God.

And yet by "ephud" or "ephod", through the figure of speech in which the part stands for the whole, we may understand everything that Gideon set up in his city as if for the worship of God, in imitation of God's tabernacle. The ephod would be named because it is the mark of priestly honor, as Scripture often notes. Gideon's sin, then, would be that he made something like the tabernacle outside God's tabernacle, as a place where God would be worshipped. It was not that he set up an ephod of solid gold as an object of adoration, but that from the gold taken as plunder he made the things belonging to the furnishings and equipment of a sanctuary, all of which are signified by "ephod" because, as I said, of the preeminence of the priestly vestment. For the ephod itself, if it is the shoulder-piece of the priestly vestment, was not ordered to be made of gold alone, though it does contain some gold: God commanded that it be made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen. But since the Seventy translators put it this way, first listing everything that Gideon had received from the spoils and then adding, "And Gideon made it into an ephod," it seems to say that the ephod was made out of the whole of what had been listed. Yet here too we can understand the figure of speech in which the whole stands for the part, so that "he made it into an ephod" means "he made an ephod from it" or "he made an ephod out of it", not using up the whole of it on the ephod, but spending as much of it as was needed. Indeed, the translation made from the Hebrew reads: "And Gideon made an ephod from it." For what the Septuagint writes as "ephud" is said to be "ephod" in the Hebrew. But not all the priests wore a shoulder-piece of this kind, made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen; only the high priest did. So the ephod we mentioned that Samuel's mother made for him was certainly not of this kind, since when he was handed over to be brought up he was of course a boy, not the high priest. That is why, as was said, it is called "ephud bar", or rather "ephud bat", as those who know Hebrew assert, which means a linen ephod. But I think Gideon made the vestment that was the chief garment and ornament of the high priest, and that through it the other furnishings of the sanctuary that he had set up in his city, apart from God's tabernacle, are signified. And because of this sin it became a stumbling block to him and to his house, so that his great number of sons perished, as Scripture later relates.

A question arises that should not be passed over: how could the land have had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon, when after the victory by which he freed the Hebrews he made an abomination from the gold of the spoils, and all Israel went whoring after it, and it became a stumbling block to him and to his house? How, then, after so great a wickedness, committed by both Gideon and the people, did the land rest for forty years, when Scripture usually shows that whenever the people went whoring away from the Lord God, they lost peace rather than gained it, and were subjected to their enemies rather than protected from their attacks? But we must understand that Scripture, as it often does, spoke by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, when it said that Gideon made an ephod against the law of God from the gold that had been taken from the defeated and overthrown enemy, because it wanted to say in one place both where the gold came from and what was done with it. This sin, however, was committed later, at the end of Gideon's days, when the evils also followed that Scripture then went on to relate, after it had mentioned how many years the land was at rest in Gideon's days. It mentioned those years by way of recapitulation, that is, returning to the order of events that it had departed from when it spoke first of that stumbling block, which actually came last.

"And it came to pass, when Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned away and went whoring after the Baals, and they made Baal-berith a covenant for themselves, that he should be their god." Both the Baals and Baal-berith are to be understood as idols. So the people committed a greater transgression and fornication after Gideon's death than they did in his lifetime on account of the ephod. For the ephod, though made unlawfully, was nevertheless one of the sacred objects of the tabernacle, whereas this fornication after idols cannot claim even a false defense on the grounds of ancestral religion. Hence, even if that ephod was made not at the end of Gideon's time but earlier, God bore it patiently enough for peace to continue in the land, because, although something he had forbidden had been done, there had not been a great departure from him who had commanded that something of the kind be made in his tabernacle and in his honor. But now he would not leave unpunished the graver offenses committed and the people's utterly open fornication after idols.

A buckthorn, which is a kind of thornbush, is brought in as a figure, saying to all the trees that came together to it so that it might reign over them: "If in truth you anoint me to reign over you, come, trust in my protection; and if not, let fire come out of the buckthorn and devour the cedars of Lebanon." The meaning is obscure, but once the right punctuation is found it becomes plain. It should not be read as "and if fire does not come out of the buckthorn"; rather, there should be a pause after "and if not", and then "let fire come out of the buckthorn" should follow. That is: "And if you do not trust in my protection", or "And if you do not in truth anoint me to reign over you, let fire come out of the buckthorn and devour the cedars of Lebanon." These are the words of one threatening what it could do if they refused to have it reign over them. But because it does not say, "fire will come out of the buckthorn and will devour the cedars of Lebanon," but "let it come out and devour," the passage has become more obscure than if only the punctuation were hidden. Yet it is a more forceful threat, and in a way one of more immediate effect, if someone says, "If you will not do what I want, let my anger rage against you," meaning "let it rage now; why should I hold it back?", than if he says, "it will rage," threatening future punishment in the manner of a promise.

"And God sent forth an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem." It is not easy to determine whether this word signifies God commanding or God permitting. Where "sent forth" (emisit) is used here, the Greek has ἐξαπέστειλεν, which is also found in the Psalms, where we read: "Send forth your light." In some places, however, our translators have rendered ἐξαπέστειλεν in the Greek as "sent" (misit), not "sent forth" (emisit) [?]. So it can also be understood to mean that God sent forth the evil spirit as one already wanting to go between them, that is, he gave the evil spirit power to disturb their peace. Yet it has not seemed absurd that an evil spirit should even be sent by the Lord to carry out just punishment, so much so that some have rendered ἐξαπέστειλεν as "sent in" (immisit) [?].

The words that Zebul, ruler of the city of Shechem, sent by messengers to Abimelech include this: "And now rise up by night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush in the field. And in the morning, as soon as the sun rises, you will make haste and advance against the city." Where some Latin versions have "maturabis" (you will make haste) and others "manicabis", the Greek has a word that could not be rendered by one word: "you will rise at dawn". Perhaps "maturabis" was used here from the morning hour (matutinum), although it is also commonly used at other times for hastening something. But "manicabis" does not strike me as a Latin word. What is puzzling, though, is that after saying "as soon as the sun rises", he added "you will rise at dawn", although dawn itself, called ὄρθρος in Greek, means the time before the sun, which is now very commonly described as when the sky has begun to grow light. So it must be understood that the word "morning" refers to dawn itself. "As soon as the sun rises" was added to make clear that it was to be done not when the sun had already risen, but as soon as the brightness of the rising sun appeared. For dawn grows light from no other source than when the light of the sun returning to that part of the sky we see in the east begins to reach it. That is why in the Gospel too one evangelist says that one and the same event happened at dawn, while it was still dark, and another says that it happened at sunrise: the light of dawn, however faint, certainly came from the sun as it was rising, that is, coming up to its rising and casting its brightness from the nearness of its presence. Some unlearned people have thought this light is not the sun's, but the light that was created in the beginning, before God created the sun on the fourth day.

"And after Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, the son of his father's brother, a man of Issachar." He said "the son of his father's brother" (filium patris fratris eius), meaning his paternal uncle's son, when it would have been more orderly, more usual and clearer to say filium fratris patris eius, "the son of the brother of his father". For he was the son of his paternal uncle, as is found more plainly in the translation made from the Hebrew. So the phrase patris fratris here is not declined from the nominative pater fratris ("father of a brother") but from patris frater ("brother of a father"), which is what a paternal uncle is. For whether you put the nominative hic pater fratris or hic patris frater, the genitive is huius patris fratris. But another question arises: how could Abimelech's paternal uncle be a man of Issachar, that is, a man of the tribe of Issachar, when Abimelech's father was Gideon, and Gideon was of the tribe of Manasseh? How, then, were Puah and Gideon brothers, so that Puah could be the paternal uncle of Abimelech, and this uncle's son Tola could succeed Abimelech himself, as this narrative says? Well, Gideon and Puah could have had the same mother, born to her by different fathers, and so have been brothers as sons of one mother, not of one father. For women commonly married from one tribe into another. Thus Saul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, gave his daughter to David, a man of the tribe of Judah; and Jehoiada the priest, who was certainly a man of the tribe of Levi, married the daughter of King Joram, a man of the tribe of Judah. This is how we come to read in the Gospel that Elizabeth and Mary were kinswomen, although Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron. From this we understand that some woman of the tribe of Levi, of the daughters of Aaron, had married into the tribe of Judah, and that this is how the kinship between the two came about, so that the Lord's flesh might descend not only from a royal line but also from a priestly one.

Among the other things that Jephthah sends by messengers to the king of the Ammonites, he also says this: "Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god has inherited for you, and shall we not inherit all that the Lord our God has inherited from before you?" Some Latin translators thought this should be rendered: "Will you not possess whatever Chemosh your god has given you as an inheritance?" Here Jephthah might seem to have affirmed that this god called Chemosh was able to give something as an inheritance to his worshippers. Others, however, have: "Will you not possess whatever Chemosh your god has possessed?" And this sounds as though he was able to possess something. Or perhaps it was said in accordance with the fact that the nations have been placed under angels, according to the song of Moses the servant of God? Was the angel under whom the Ammonites were placed, then, called Chemosh? Who would dare to assert this, when it can be understood as said according to the king's own opinion, since he believed that his god possessed this, or had given it to him as a possession? This sense comes out more clearly in the words the Greek has: "Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god has inherited for you?" The words "for you" should be understood as if it said "as it seems to you". He inherited it "for you", who think so, not because he could inherit anything. Finally, in what follows, "and all that the Lord our God has inherited," he did not say "has inherited for us", as if to say "as it seems to us", but that he truly inherited it "from before you", since he took it from them and gave it to these: "these," he says, "we shall inherit."

Concerning Jephthah's daughter, whom her father offered to God as a burnt offering: in the war he had vowed that, if he won, he would offer as a burnt offering whoever came out of his house to meet him; having made this vow, he won, and when his daughter came to meet him, he fulfilled what he had vowed. This tends to be a great question and one very hard to settle, both for some who piously seek and long to know what it means, and for others who oppose these holy Scriptures with ignorant impiety and make this their chief accusation, that the God of the Law and the Prophets even took delight in human sacrifices. To their slanders we reply first of all as follows. The God of the Law and the Prophets, or to put it more explicitly, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, did not delight even in those sacrifices in which burnt offerings of cattle were offered. Rather, because they were symbolic and were shadows of things to come, he wished through them to commend to us the very realities that these sacrifices signified. And there was also this useful reason why they were changed, and are now not only no longer commanded but actually forbidden to be offered: so that we should not think that God truly delights in such things according to some carnal desire.

But it is fair to ask whether future things ought to have been signified even by human sacrifices. This is not because we should shudder at and dread, in this matter, the deaths of people who would die at some time anyway, if those who gladly accepted having this done to them were commended to God for an eternal reward. But if that were so, this kind of sacrifice would not displease God, and yet the same Scripture testifies plainly enough that it does displease him. For although he willed and commanded that all the firstborn be dedicated to him and belong to him, he nevertheless willed that the firstborn of human beings be redeemed from him, so that people would not believe that the sons they had first received at birth were to be sacrificed to God. Then he speaks of this more openly, for God so disapproves of human burnt offerings that he forbids them, detesting them in other nations and commanding his own people not to dare to imitate them. "But if," he says, "the Lord your God destroys before you the nations whose land you are entering to inherit, and you inherit them and dwell in their land, take heed to yourself that you do not seek to follow them after they have been destroyed from before you, and that you do not inquire after their gods, saying, 'As the nations do to their gods, so will I do too.' You shall not do so to the Lord your God; for they have done to their gods abominations that the Lord hates, since they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods."

To pass over other passages of this kind, what could show more plainly than these testimonies of holy Scripture that God, by whom this Scripture was given to the human race, not only does not love but actually hates such sacrifices, in which human beings are slaughtered? What he plainly loves and crowns is this: when some righteous person, suffering injustice, contends for the truth even unto death, or is killed by enemies whom he has offended for the sake of righteousness, repaying them good for evil, that is, love for hatred. Such is the blood the Lord speaks of as righteous blood, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah. Above all, he himself shed his blood for us and offered himself as a sacrifice to God; and he offered himself precisely by being killed by enemies for the sake of righteousness. In imitation of him thousands of martyrs contended for the truth even unto death and were sacrificed by raging enemies. Of them Scripture says: "Like gold in the furnace he tried them, and like a burnt offering he accepted them as a victim." Hence the apostle too says: "For I am already being sacrificed."

But Jephthah did not make his daughter a burnt offering to the Lord in that way; he did it rather in the manner in which cattle had been commanded to be offered, whereas human beings had been forbidden to be sacrificed. It seems more like what Abraham did. Yet the Lord commanded that act specifically; he never ordered by a general law that such sacrifices should ever be made to him, and indeed he forbade them altogether. So what Jephthah did differs from what Abraham did, since Abraham offered his son because he was commanded to, while Jephthah did something that was both forbidden by the law and commanded by no special order. Moreover, God showed how little he delights in such sacrifices not only later in his law but already then, in the case of Abraham's son himself, when he stopped the father, whose faith he had tested by his command, from killing his son, and provided a ram by which the sacrifice could be lawfully completed according to the custom of the ancients, suited to those times.

If, however, someone is troubled by the question how Abraham could piously have believed that God delights in such sacrifices, if they are unlawfully offered to God, and therefore thinks that Jephthah too rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God, let him first consider that vowing something of one's own accord is one thing, and obeying someone who commands it is another. If a servant is ordered by his master to do something contrary to the established custom of the household, and does it with praiseworthy obedience, it does not follow that he should not be punished if he presumes to do it of his own accord. Then again, Abraham had grounds for believing that he should not spare his son because of the divine command: not believing that God gladly accepts such victims, but that he had commanded this so that he might raise the slain son to life and thereby, as a wise God, reveal something. For this is said of him in the letter entitled to the Hebrews, where his faith is praised because he believed that God was able to raise his son. Jephthah, on the other hand, vowed a human sacrifice of his own accord, without God commanding or demanding it, and against God's lawful precept. For it is written thus: "And Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord and said: If you will indeed deliver the sons of Ammon into my hand, then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the sons of Ammon shall be the Lord's, and I will offer him as a burnt offering."

Certainly with these words he did not vow some beast that he could offer as a burnt offering according to the law; for it is not and never was the custom for cattle to come out to meet leaders returning victorious from war. As far as dumb animals are concerned, dogs are wont to run out to meet their masters, frisking about them in fond service; but he could not have had them in mind in his vow, lest he seem to have vowed, to the insult of God, something not only unlawful but also contemptible and unclean according to the law. Nor did he say, "Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, I will offer it as a burnt offering," but, "Whoever comes out, I will offer him." There, beyond any doubt, he had nothing but a human being in mind, though perhaps not his only daughter. And yet, at so great a moment of glory for her father, who could have been ahead of her, unless perhaps his wife? As for his saying not quaecumque ("whatever woman") but quicumque ("whatever man") "comes out of the doors of my house," Scripture commonly uses the masculine gender for either sex; as it is said of Abraham, "rising up from the dead one" (in the masculine), when it was his wife who had died.

Scripture seems to have passed no judgment on this vow and deed, as it judged most plainly concerning Abraham when, at God's command, he offered his son; it has merely left it written for readers to judge. So too with the deed of Judah son of Jacob, when he went in to his own daughter-in-law unknowingly, yet, as far as it lay with him, committed fornication, because he thought she was a prostitute: Scripture neither approved nor condemned this, but left it to be weighed and assessed by consulting justice and the law of God. Since, then, God's Scripture has pronounced no verdict either way on this deed of Jephthah, so that our understanding might be exercised in judging it, we might now say that such a vow displeased God and was brought to this punishment, that his only daughter, of all people, came out to meet her father (for if he had expected this and not wanted it, he would not, as soon as he saw her, have torn his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become a stumbling block in my eyes"); and then, though so long a delay of sixty days was granted to his daughter, the Lord did not stop him from killing his only and dearest child, as he stopped Abraham, until, by fulfilling his vow, he struck himself with the heaviest bereavement while in no way appeasing God by the sacrifice of a human being. And so, we might say, this kind of punishment was repaid to the father so that the example of such a vow would not be left unpunished, lest people either think they were vowing something great to God when they vowed human victims, and, more horrible still, their own children; or else make such vows not in earnest but in pretence, hoping, as if on the example of Abraham, that God would prevent the fulfilment of such vows. We might say this, I say, were it not that two testimonies of the divine Scriptures in particular hold us back from that opinion, so that we should examine this event, committed to memory in books of such great authority, more carefully and more cautiously, as far as the Lord helps us, lest we pronounce a rash judgment in either direction. The first is that in the letter to the Hebrews this Jephthah is mentioned among such men that we would be afraid to blame him; for it is written there: "And what more shall I say? For time fails me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah, and David and Samuel and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises." The second is that where these things are narrated about him, that he vowed such a vow and fulfilled it, Scripture says beforehand: "And the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah; and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over the watchtower of Gilead, and from the watchtower of Gilead to the far side, to the sons of Ammon. And Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord," and the rest concerning this very vow; so that everything that was done thereafter seems meant to be understood as the work of the spirit of the Lord that came upon him. These testimonies compel us to ask why it was done rather than readily condemn what was done.

But first, regarding what I cited from the letter to the Hebrews: among the praiseworthy men commemorated there is not only Jephthah but also Gideon, of whom Scripture likewise says, "And the spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon." And yet his deed, when he made an ephod out of the gold of the spoil, and all Israel went whoring after it, and it became a snare to the house of Gideon, not only can we not praise, but, since Scripture has judged it most plainly, we have no hesitation in condemning; yet no injury is done by this to the spirit of the Lord, who strengthened him so that he overcame the enemies of his people with such ease. Why, then, is he mentioned among those who through faith conquered kingdoms and wrought righteousness, unless because holy Scripture, while truthfully praising people's faith and righteousness, is not thereby prevented from truthfully noting their sins as well, where it knows of any and judges it fitting? For in the fact that this same Gideon, asking for a sign, made a test with the fleece, as he himself put it, I do not know whether he did not transgress the commandment where it is written, "You shall not test the Lord your God." Nevertheless, even in his testing the Lord showed what he wished to foretell: namely, by the fleece soaked with rain while the whole threshing floor round about was dry, he prefigured first the people of Israel, among whom were the saints with heavenly grace, like a spiritual rain; and afterwards, by the threshing floor soaked with rain while the fleece was dry, he prefigured the Church spread throughout the whole world, possessing heavenly grace not in a fleece, as under a covering, but in the open, while that former people was, as it were, cut off from the dew of that same grace and left dry. Nor was it in vain that, because of the good and faithful life in which we must believe he died, he earned such testimony in the letter to the Hebrews among the faithful and those who wrought righteousness.

But whether, since it was after the words "the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah" that the events followed in which he vowed that vow, conquered the enemy, and paid what he had vowed, all of it is to be attributed to the spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice too should be regarded as if the Lord had commanded it to be done, as he did with Abraham, I would not readily say. For in the case of Gideon this difference can certainly be pointed out: after the sin he committed when he made the ephod, after which the whole people went whoring, no success of his is recorded; whereas after Jephthah vowed his vow, his notable victory followed, to obtain which he had made the vow, and having obtained it he paid what he had vowed. Yet on the other hand we must consider that Gideon, though not after he made the ephod, nevertheless after he tested the Lord, which is certainly a sin, won deliverance for the people with a great slaughter and defeat of the enemy. For it is written thus: "And Gideon said to the Lord: Let not your indignation be kindled against me, and I will speak once more and test once more with the fleece." He feared God's anger, of course, because he knew he was sinning by testing him, which God most plainly forbids in his law. Yet this sin of his was followed both by the clear evidence of a wonderful sign and by the great success of victory and the deliverance of the people. For God had already resolved to come to the aid of his afflicted people, and he made use of the mind of this leader, whom he had taken up for this work, not only when it was faithful and pious but also when it was faltering and sinning, both to foretell what he wished and to fulfil what he had spoken.

For not only through these men, who, even if they sinned, are nevertheless counted among the righteous, but even through Saul himself, who was rejected in every way, God bestowed many things on his people; and the spirit of God even leapt upon him and he prophesied, not when he was acting justly but when he was raging against the holy and innocent man David. For the spirit of the Lord accomplishes what he knows and has determined must be accomplished, through the good and through the wicked, through those who know and those who do not. He even brought forth a remarkable prophecy through Caiaphas, the fiercest persecutor of the Lord, who did not know what he was saying: that Christ had to die for the nation. Who, then, was at work, if not the spirit of the Lord, concerned to foretell things to come, so that when the judge Gideon wanted to test the Lord and did not believe what the Lord had already told him about saving the people by his hand, it should come into his mind to ask precisely this: that the fleece be first soaked with rain and afterwards dry, and the threshing floor first dry and afterwards watered? Thus his lapse in faith is to be put down to his weakness and fault, while the fact that God used even such a state of his mind for what needed to be signified to the human race is to be understood as belonging to God's mercy and wonderful providence.

If, however, someone says that Gideon did and said everything knowingly, by prophetic revelation, so that such signs might be shown through him; that he did not lapse in faith but believed what the Lord had already promised him, and chose to make the test with the fleece as a prophetic action, so that his testing was as blameless as Jacob's deceit; and that when he said to the Lord, "Let not your indignation be kindled against me," he did not say it because he feared God's anger but because he was confident that God was not angry, since he was doing what he perceived as a prophet must be done at the dictation of his spirit: let him say so, as he sees fit, provided only that he does not dare to excuse from sin the making of the ephod, which Scripture itself blamed, whatever it may signify. For the fact that three hundred men, whose very number points to the sign of the cross, took earthenware jars and shut burning torches inside them, and when the jars were broken the lights suddenly flashing forth in great numbers terrified so vast a multitude of the enemy, seems to be something Gideon did on his own judgment; for Scripture does not say that the Lord instructed him to do it. And yet who but the Lord inspired his mind and counsel to perform so great a sign? By it he prefigured that his saints would hold the treasure of the gospel light in earthen vessels, as the apostle says: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels." When these little vessels, as it were, were broken in the suffering of martyrdom, a greater splendour of their glory flashed forth, which overcame the impious enemies of the gospel preaching by the brightness of Christ, unexpected by them.

Whether, then, it was through those who knew or through those who did not know that the spirit of the Lord, in the prophetic times, brought about the prefiguring and foretelling of things to come, we must not on that account say that their sins were not sins, simply because God, who knows how to make good use even of our evils, used even their sins to signify what he wished. Accordingly, if vowing or paying a sacrifice, whether of any human death or even of one's own child, was no sin because it signified something great and spiritual, then God forbade such things and declared that he hated them in vain; for the things he commanded to be done also, of course, point to some signification of great spiritual realities. Why, then, would he forbid those things, since they could equally have been done lawfully for the sake of the same signification of the same realities for which these were lawfully done? Only because human sacrifices did not please God, even when they signified something that it is profitable to believe, when it is not a matter of someone being killed by enemies for righteousness' sake, because he wished to live rightly or refused to sin, but of a human being slaughtered by a human being like a beast, as a chosen victim.

What then if someone says: since the sacrifices of cattle, simply because they had become customary, made people less intent on seeking the great sacrament of Christ and the Church, even though those who understood rightly referred them too to the signifying of spiritual things, God therefore, wishing to rouse the sleeping minds of men by a striking and unexpected event, all the more so because he had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to him, saw to it that something of this kind should be offered to him, so that the very astonishment might give rise to a great question, and the great question might stir up the zeal of a pious mind to search out a great mystery, and the mind of a person searching piously into the depth of prophecy might draw up the Lord Christ from the depths of the Scriptures, like a fish on a hook? We do not oppose this reasoning and reflection. But the question of the mind of the one who vows is one thing; the question of the providence of God, who makes the best use of his mind whatever its state, is another. Therefore, if the spirit of the Lord, which came upon Jephthah, actually commanded him to make this vow, which Scripture indeed has not revealed, yet if he commanded it, whose orders it is not permitted to disregard, then Jephthah is not to be blamed for folly but rather praised for obedience. For even if a man kills himself, which it is certainly wicked to do by human will and decision, it must surely be understood as done in obedience rather than in wickedness if it was commanded by God; we have discussed this question sufficiently in the first book of The City of God. But if Jephthah, following a human error, thought he should vow a human sacrifice, then his sin was justly punished through his only daughter (which he himself seems to show clearly enough by his own words when he says, "Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become a stumbling block in my eyes," tearing his clothes as well). Yet even here his error has some praise of faith, in that he feared God so as to pay what he had vowed, and did not evade the sentence of divine judgment upon himself, whether hoping that God would stop him, as he did Abraham, or resolving to do God's will, understood even when he did not intervene, rather than to disregard it.

Yet here too one may rightly ask whether it is more correctly understood that God did not want this done, and that he would rather have been obeyed if it were not done, since he had shown that he did not want it both in the case of Abraham's son and in the prohibition of the law. Yet if Jephthah had refrained for that reason, he would have seemed to be sparing himself in his only daughter rather than following God's will. He rather understood, then, in the fact that his daughter came out to meet him, that God was punishing him, and he faithfully submitted to the just penalty, fearing a harsher punishment for evasion, as it were. For he believed that the soul of his daughter, a good woman and a virgin, would be well received, because she had not vowed herself to be sacrificed, but had not resisted her father's vow and will and had followed the judgment of God. For just as death is not to be inflicted willingly on oneself by anyone, nor willingly on anyone else, so it is not to be refused when God commands it, by whose ordinance it must be undergone at one time or another; and no one who shrinks from suffering it is striving to avoid it altogether, but only to put it off.

Now let us inquire, as far as God helps us, and briefly set out what the spirit of the Lord prefigured in this event, whether through Jephthah unknowing or knowing, through his imprudence or his obedience, through his offence or his faith. For this passage of the holy Scriptures prompts us and in a way urges us to think of a certain man mighty in valour. For Jephthah is described as such, and his name means "Opening"; and the Lord Christ, as the Gospel indicates, opened the minds of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. This Jephthah his brothers rejected and drove out of their father's house, taunting him with being the son of a harlot, as if they themselves had been born of a lawful wife. The chief priests and the scribes and the Pharisees, who seemed to glory in their observance of the law, did the same against the Lord, as though he were destroying the law and therefore were not, so to speak, a legitimate son. And although he took his body from the holy Virgin, as the faithful know, yet, as far as the nation is concerned, his mother can also be called the Jewish synagogue. Let anyone who wishes turn over the books of the prophets and see how often and with what severity of language and indignation from the Lord that nation is rebuked for its fornications like an unchaste woman. Hence also the very recent instance in this book, whether when after the ephod that Gideon made all Israel is said to have gone whoring, or when they went after the gods of the nations that surrounded them, for which the divine wrath was stirred against them, so that they were crushed for eighteen years by the sons of Ammon. But were not those priests and scribes and Pharisees, whom we have said were prefigured in them, also born of that same nation of Israel, they who persecuted and drove out Jephthah as if he were not a legitimate son, just as these did to the Lord Christ? But the likeness is sketched in this respect: that these men, as I said, being observers of the law, so to speak, seemed to themselves to have rightly cast out, as legitimate sons, one who was not legitimate, since he appeared to act against the precepts of the law. For it is in this sense that that people is said to have committed fornication: by not keeping the precepts of the law, it was not keeping faith, as it were, with its husband.

This is what is written of Jephthah: And the sons of the wife grew up and drove Jephthah out. The word used here, "grew up", means figuratively "prevailed". This was fulfilled in the Jews, who prevailed over Christ's weakness because he willed it so, in order to endure at their hands the sufferings he had to bear. In the same way Jacob, signifying this very thing, prevailed over the angel, and he wrestled with him to foreshadow it. So they said to Jephthah: You shall not inherit in our father's house, because you are the son of a harlot. It is as if they were saying what we read in the Gospel: This man is not from God, since he breaks the sabbath in this way. Of themselves, boasting as it were that they were legitimate sons, they said to the Lord: We were not born of fornication; we have one father, God. And Jephthah fled from the face of his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. He fled because he hid how great he was. He fled because he was hidden from them in their rage, for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. He fled because they saw the weakness of the one who was dying but did not see the power of the one who was rising again. He lived in a good land, or, to put it more exactly, "the best" land. For what in Greek is [?] is called "best" in Latin, and that is what "Tob" means. Here, it seems to me, we should understand his resurrection from the dead. For what land is better than an earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?

Then there is what is said of Jephthah: after he fled from the face of his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, robbers gathered to him and went about with him. Even before the passion the Lord was reproached for eating with tax collectors and sinners, when he answered that it is not the healthy who need a physician but the sick. He was also counted among the wicked when he was crucified among robbers and carried one of them from the cross into paradise. Yet it was after he rose again, and began to be in the land of Tob in the sense explained above, that wicked men gathered to him for the forgiveness of sins. They walked with him because they lived according to his commands. Nor does this cease to happen, now and from now on, as long as the wicked take refuge in him, so that he may justify the ungodly who turn to him, and the unrighteous may learn his ways.

Next, those who had cast Jephthah out (he too was a Gileadite) turned to him and sought him, so that through him they might be delivered from their enemies. How clearly this foreshadows that those who cast Christ out turn back to him again and find salvation in him! We may take these to be the people whom the apostle Peter reproached for that very crime, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. He urged them to turn to the one they had persecuted, and they were cut to the heart and sought salvation from him whom they had estranged from themselves. And what is it to be delivered from enemies but to be delivered from sins? For he says to them: Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you. Or rather, what is signified may be the calling of the nation of Israel that is hoped for at the end. This indeed seems more apparent in the words: And it came to pass after some days. This certainly means "after a time", and so it suggests that we should understand not what happened soon after the Lord's passion but what is to come later. The fact that it was the elders of Gilead who came to Jephthah also seems to point the same way, so that their old age stands for later and final times. Gilead means "Casting away" or "Revelation". Both fit the matter quite aptly, since they first cast away the Lord Christ, and later he will be revealed to them.

Jephthah was sought as leader against the Ammonites, so that by their defeat those who wished to fight against them under his leadership might be delivered. Since Ammon means "Son of my people" or "People of grief", what is signified is surely either those enemies from that very nation who were foretold to persist in unbelief, or else all without exception who are predestined to Gehenna, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth for them, as for a people of grief. The devil and his angels may also, not unfittingly, be understood as the people of grief, either because they bring eternal misery on those they deceive or because they themselves are consigned to eternal misery.

It is a fine touch, setting out the prophecy far more plainly, that Jephthah answered the elders of Gilead: Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house and send me away from you? And why have you come now that you are in distress? Something like this was prefigured in Joseph, whom his brothers cast off by selling him, and who, when they were in distress from famine, turned to him for help and mercy. But here the meaning of things to come shines out much more fully, because it was not the very brothers who drove Jephthah out who came to him, but the elders of Gilead, pleading with him on behalf of that whole people. In the same way the one nation is called Israel, both in those who lived then and rejected Christ and in those who later turned back to him for help. For these words are spoken to a hostile people that keeps up and nurses long hatreds, whether in its ancestors or in its descendants, and that is at last converted in those who are to be converted at that time: Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? For it seemed to those who persecuted him that they had driven Christ out of the house of David, in which there will be no end to his kingdom.

And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah: Not so; now we have come to you. It is as if the Jews converted to Christ were saying: Then we came to persecute; now we come to follow. They also declare that he will be their head against their enemies. He replies that if he conquers their enemies, he will be their prince. Gideon refused this, although the Israelites had [?] wanted it, for he answered them: The Lord will be your prince. The word "prince" signifies a king, something that nation did not yet have in the time of the judges. They began to have one in Saul, and after him in his other successors, about whom we read in the books of Kingdoms. For in Deuteronomy, where they are told what kind of king they should have if they want one, he is called not king but prince. But because this Jephthah prefigured the one who is the true king (as was also written in the title fixed to his cross, which Pilate did not dare to erase or alter), we must believe that this is why he said: I will be your prince. They, for their part, had said: You shall be our head, since the head of man is Christ, and he is the head of the body, the church. Indeed, after Jephthah delivered them from all their enemies he did not become their king. This lets us understand that what was said concerned the prophecy about Christ rather than Jephthah himself in the strict sense. Scripture ends its account of him like this: And Jephthah judged Israel six years; and Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city of Gilead. So he judged Israel like the other judges; he did not reign there as a prince, as did those described in the volumes of Kingdoms.

After this same Jephthah was appointed their leader, he first sent messengers to the enemy carrying words of peace. This shows what the apostle says, the apostle in whom Christ was speaking: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all men. It would take too long to go through all the words that Jephthah sent, since we are in haste. Yet as far as the meaning of things to come is concerned, it seems to me that they should be understood in this way: in them we see the teaching of Christ, instructing us how we should walk, that is, how we should live, among those who are not called according to his purpose; for the Lord knows those who are his. And when he was about to fight [?] the enemies, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him. This signifies the Holy Spirit imparted to the members of Christ.
