He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over the watchtower of Gilead, and went from the watchtower of Gilead across to the Ammonites. This signifies the members of Christ advancing toward winning victory over the enemies. For Gilead means "Casting away" and Manasseh "Necessity". So those who are advancing must pass beyond those who cast away, that is, those who despise them. Necessity too must be passed beyond, in case someone who is advancing gets past those who despise him only to give way to those who terrify him. The watchtower of Gilead must also be passed, since Gilead also means "Revelation". A watchtower is a height for looking out or looking down, that is, viewing from above. So the watchtower of Gilead seems to me fittingly to signify pride in revelation. This is why the apostle says: And lest I be exalted by the greatness of the revelations. Therefore this too must be passed beyond; that is, one must not stay in it, because of the danger of falling. Once these have been passed, the enemies are easily overcome. This is what is meant by the words: and from the watchtower of Gilead across to the Ammonites. We have already spoken about these enemies above.

And Jephthah vowed a vow and said: If you will indeed deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the Lord's, and I will offer him as a burnt offering. Whomever Jephthah had in mind here, by human reckoning, he does not seem to have had in mind his only daughter. Otherwise, when he saw that she had come out to meet him, he would not have said: Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become a stumbling block in my eyes. "You have hindered me" was said as though he meant that he had been hindered from carrying out what he had intended. But whom could he have expected to meet him first, when he had no other children? Did he have his wife in mind? And did God will that this should not happen, and also that he should not leave the vow unpunished, so that no one would dare such a thing again, and also that by his great providence this very event should prefigure the mystery of the church? The prophecy, then, has been fitted from both sides: from what he had in mind when he vowed, and from what happened against his will. For if he had his wife in mind, the bride of Christ is the church: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. This is a great mystery, says the apostle, but I speak of Christ and the church. But this Jephthah's wife could not be a virgin. So in the fact that it was his daughter who met him instead, the audacity of a man vowing a forbidden sacrifice did not go unpunished, and the virginity of the church was prefigured. Nor is it far from the truth that the same church is signified by the word "daughter". For of whom else was that woman a type to whom, when she had been healed after touching the fringe of his garment, the Lord said: Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace? And certainly, as no one doubts, he called his disciples the sons of the bridegroom, which plainly shows that he himself is the bridegroom: Can the sons of the bridegroom fast, he says, while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast. The church, then, which the blessed apostle calls a chaste virgin, will be a burnt offering when, in the resurrection of the dead, what is written is fulfilled in full: Death is swallowed up in victory. Then he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father (and that kingdom is the church itself), he whose figure the man who made the vow bore. But since this will happen when the sixth age of the world has been completed, a respite of sixty days was requested for her virginity. For the church is gathered from all the ages. The first is from Adam to the flood; the second from the flood, that is, from Noah, to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from that deportation to the Virgin's giving birth; the sixth from then to the end of this world. Through these six ages, as through sixty days, the holy virgin church has wept over her virginity. Though she was a virgin, there were still sins to be wept over, and because of them this same virgin, spread through the whole world, says every day: And forgive us our debts. He preferred, however, to call these sixty days two months, I think because of the two men: the one through whom came death, and the other through whom came the resurrection of the dead. It is because of these two that we also speak of two testaments.

It became a statute in Israel that from year to year they gathered to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days in the year. I do not think this signifies anything after the burnt offering has been completed, which will be unto eternal life. Rather, it signifies the past times of the church, in which those who mourn were blessed. The four days figure the church's universality, because of the four parts of the world through which it is spread far and wide. As for the history in its literal sense, I think the Israelites decreed this only because they understood that God's judgment in this matter had been brought forth chiefly to strike the father, so that no one would ever dare to vow such a sacrifice again. For why would mourning and lamentation be decreed if that vow had been a cause of joy?

Later the people of Ephraim were defeated by this same Jephthah. If this too is to be referred to the judgment of God that will take place at the end, as the Lord himself says: Bring here those who did not want me to reign over them and slay them before me, then the forty-two thousand who fell there are not recorded as an empty number either. Just as the two months, made up of sixty days, signify the number six of the six ages, so there too seven taken six times figures the same thing, as regards the six ages of the world; for six times seven is forty-two. And it is not without reason that Jephthah himself judged the people for six years.

One may ask why the angel, when he announced to Samson's mother that she would have a son, since she was barren, said to her: "Now take care: do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean." What, after all, is meant by "unclean"? Perhaps the breakdown of discipline that had begun in Israel had made them slip even into eating the kinds of animals that God had forbidden. And why should we not believe that people who were going over even to the worship of idols could have done this far more readily?

When Samson's mother told her husband how the angel had announced to her that she would have a son, she said: "And I asked him where he came from and his name. He did not tell me." One may ask whether she spoke the truth, since we do not read this where the angel speaks to her. But we should understand that Scripture said nothing about it there and mentions here what it left out there. There is another difficulty. She does not say: "I asked him what he was called, and he did not tell me his name." She says: "I asked him where he came from." So what she adds, "and he did not tell me his name," seems not to follow. When she asked where he came from, she was not asking his name but his place or city, since she took him for a man. For she called him a man of God, though she said he was like an angel in appearance or bearing, because what she saw was so glorious, as she herself related. But suppose the sentence is divided like this: "And I asked him where he came from, and his name," so that "I asked him" is understood with both, and then comes "He did not tell me." Then there is no problem, for "He did not tell me" can refer to both: he told her neither where he came from nor his name.

Again, the same woman says that the angel told her, "The boy will be a Nazirite of God from the womb to the day of his death," but we do not read that the angel said this. And what we do read that he said, "He will begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines," the woman does not mention. So she left out something she had heard. Yet we should not believe that she said anything she had not heard. Rather, when Scripture brought the angel into the narrative speaking to the woman, it did not set down all of his words. The phrase "from the womb to the day of his death" is used because under the Law those who had taken a vow for a set time were called Nazirites, according to what Scripture had commanded through Moses. That is why Samson was ordered never to let a razor come upon his head and never to drink wine or strong drink. Samson kept all his life what those called Nazirites kept for a fixed number of days, when they made a vow and then fulfilled it.

Scripture says: "For Manoah did not know that he was an angel of God." Clearly his wife, too, believed he was a man. So when Manoah said to him, "Let us press you now to stay, and let us prepare a kid of the goats before you," he was inviting him as one would invite a man, intending that he should feast with him on what he had offered in sacrifice. For "to prepare a kid of the goats" is normally said only when a sacrifice is made. And indeed the angel replied in a way that shows he had been invited to a meal: "Even if you press me, I will not eat of your bread." Then he added: "And if you make a burnt offering, you shall offer it to the Lord." He said "if you make a burnt offering" precisely because Manoah had said "let us prepare a kid of the goats before you." Not every sacrifice was a burnt offering. Nothing of a burnt offering was eaten, because the whole of it was burned, and that is why it was called a holocaust. But since the angel was not going to eat, he urged that a burnt offering be made instead, yet not to himself but to the Lord. He did so chiefly because at that time the nation of Israel had grown used to sacrificing to all sorts of false gods. That was how they had offended God then, so that they were handed over to their enemies for forty years.

What does it mean that once the angel who was speaking with Manoah and his wife had revealed himself, Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God"? Clearly he was thinking of the statement in the Law where it is written: "No one can see my face and live." So, being human, they believed they had seen God, particularly after so great a miracle: the one who had earlier spoken with them as though he were a man stood in the fire of the sacrifice. But were they calling it God in the angel, or calling the angel himself God? For this is what is written: "And Manoah took the kid of the goats and the grain offering and offered them on the rock to the Lord who works wonders; and Manoah and his wife were watching. And it came to pass that as the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord also went up in the flame. And Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground. And the angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord. And Manoah said to his wife: We shall surely die, for we have seen God." In these words he does not say, "We shall surely die, for we have seen the angel of the Lord," but "we have seen God." So the question arises whether they understood God to be in the angel or were calling the angel himself God. A third possibility, that they had taken the angel for God, cannot be maintained, since Scripture says quite plainly: "Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord." But why were they afraid of death? Scripture in Exodus had not said, "No one sees the face of an angel and lives." It said "my face" when God was speaking. Or was Manoah so shaken by the very fact that he had recognized God in the angel's presence that he feared death? Then his wife answered him: "If the Lord had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a sacrifice from our hand, nor would he have shown us all these things, nor would he have let us hear such things." Did they believe that the angel himself had accepted the sacrifice, because they saw him standing in the flame of the altar? Or did they understand from this that the Lord had accepted it, because the angel had done this to show that he was an angel? Whichever it was, the angel had already said: "But if you make a burnt offering, you shall offer it to the Lord," that is, not to me but to the Lord. So we should understand that the angel's standing in the flame of the altar rather signified the Angel of Great Counsel: in the form of a servant, that is, in the human nature he was to take on, he would not receive sacrifice but would himself become the sacrifice.

What does it mean that Samson struck the foreigners "leg upon thigh"? Who has a leg upon his thigh, since the leg runs downward only from the knee to the ankle? Then again, if it meant the part of the body where he wounded them, were all the men he struck really wounded in one and the same part of the body? If that were credible, we might perhaps suppose that he fought with the leg-bone of some animal, as with a club, and struck them on the thigh with it, just as it is written of him that he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. But, as I said, it is not credible that while fighting he kept to a single place on which to strike them. Besides, Scripture does not say, "He struck them with a leg upon the thigh," but "leg upon thigh." Clearly, then, the obscurity comes from an unusual idiom. It is as if it said: he struck them in a truly astonishing way, so that in their astonishment and dismay they put leg upon thigh, that is, the leg of one foot upon the thigh of the other, the way people sit when they are stunned with amazement. It is as if one said: he struck them "hand to jaw," that is, with such slaughter that they put their hands to their jaws in sorrowful amazement. The translation made from the Hebrew shows clearly enough that this is the sense, for it reads: "And he struck them with a great blow, so that in their dismay they laid calf upon thigh." That amounts to saying they laid leg upon thigh, since the calf is of course the back of the leg.

What does Samson mean when he says to the men of Judah: "Swear to me that you yourselves will not kill me, and hand me over to them, so that you yourselves do not fall upon me"? Some have interpreted this expression as "so that you yourselves do not come against me." But a passage in the book of Kings shows that he said this so as not to be killed by them. There, when Solomon orders a man to be put to death, he says: "Go, fall upon him." This is not understood because it is not our custom to speak this way. In the same way, when military officers say, "Go, lift him up," meaning "Kill him," who would understand it except someone familiar with that way of speaking? Among us, too, people commonly say "he cut him short," meaning "he killed him," and no one understands this unless he is used to hearing it. For this is the general nature of all idioms: like languages themselves, they are not understood unless they are learned by hearing or reading. Amen.
